title: ChatGPT Atlas Review 2026: What It Was, Now Discontinued
excerpt: ChatGPT Atlas review: what OpenAI's AI browser and agent mode offered, its security issues, and why it was discontinued in August 2026.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is ChatGPT Atlas worth using in 2026?

ChatGPT Atlas was OpenAI's Chromium-based browser that put ChatGPT directly into the browsing experience via a sidebar and an "agent mode" that could act on webpages for you. It's no longer the right question to ask whether it's "worth it" — OpenAI discontinued Atlas on August 9, 2026, folding it into a unified OpenAI desktop app alongside the ChatGPT app and Codex, so this review covers what it was, why it mattered, and what replaced it.

**At a glance**

| | ChatGPT Atlas |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free to install; agent mode required Plus ($20/month) or Pro ($200/month) |
| Free tier | Yes — browsing, sidebar chat, and summarization; agent mode was gated |
| Best for | macOS users who wanted ChatGPT baked into everyday browsing |
| Standout feature | Agent mode — letting ChatGPT click, fill forms, and complete tasks inside real websites |
| Current status | Discontinued August 9, 2026; merged into OpenAI's unified desktop app |

Atlas launched on October 21, 2025 as a standalone macOS app, built on Chromium (the same open-source engine behind Chrome and Edge). Rather than being a chatbot you visit in a tab, it was a full browser with ChatGPT wired into a persistent sidebar, so you could ask questions about whatever page you were looking at without switching windows. Windows, iOS, and Android versions were promised at launch but never shipped before OpenAI pulled the plug roughly ten months later.

If you're looking for OpenAI's actual chatbot rather than the browser it briefly shipped, our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review) covers the assistant itself — pricing tiers, model access, and day-to-day features — which is now the product to use since Atlas's browsing features were absorbed back into that app and the unified desktop experience.

## What ChatGPT Atlas actually was

Atlas wasn't a new AI model — it ran on the same underlying ChatGPT models available through the regular chatgpt.com and app experience, wrapped inside a full web browser shell. The pitch: most people spend their day in a browser anyway, so putting the assistant there directly, with visibility into the page you're on, should beat switching between a browser tab and a separate ChatGPT tab.

The browser had three main pieces: a Chromium-based engine (existing bookmarks, extensions, and browsing habits mostly carried over), a persistent sidebar for chatting about the current page, and "agent mode," which let ChatGPT take control of the browser itself — clicking, filling in forms, and navigating pages to complete multi-step tasks like booking a hotel room, largely unsupervised within a session.

Pricing for Atlas itself was never separate from a regular ChatGPT subscription — there was no "Atlas Plus" SKU. Anyone with a free ChatGPT account could browse with the sidebar; agent mode and higher usage limits required Plus or Pro, the same tiers covered in our [ChatGPT pricing breakdown](/blog/chatgpt-review). Treat figures here as historical: Atlas no longer exists as a download, so the feature/plan gating below reflects its last known state before the August 2026 shutdown, not a live product.

## Features that actually differentiated it

**Agent mode.** The headline feature, generating both the most attention and the most anxiety. Instead of describing a task and copying the AI's output somewhere yourself, you could hand Atlas a goal — comparing prices across travel sites, filling out a repetitive form, booking something — and watch the browser highlight in blue while it clicked and typed for you. It was gated to Plus and Pro accounts, reflecting how compute-heavy this kind of "actually operate a browser" agent work is versus a normal chat reply.

**Browser memories.** Atlas could retain facts pulled from pages you visited to use as context later — remembering a product you compared last week when you asked a related question today. OpenAI said summaries of visited content were stored on its servers for a limited window (reporting varied between roughly seven and thirty days) before deletion, with original page content deleted immediately after summarization. Whether browsing data trained OpenAI's models was a separate, off-by-default toggle, with Business/Enterprise accounts excluded entirely.

**Sidebar chat about the current page.** The simplest but most-used feature: a persistent panel that could summarize an article, compare products across open tabs, or answer questions about an open document, without copy-pasting into a separate chat window.

**"Auto" search mode.** Added in January 2026, letting a single search box decide whether to show a ChatGPT-generated answer or standard web results — a hedge against criticism that AI summaries were quietly replacing links to source sites.

**Vertical tabs and tab groups.** Later updates (November 2025 and January 2026) added a resizable tab sidebar and tab grouping — standard modern-browser conveniences Atlas was slow to ship relative to Chrome or Edge.

## Who it was actually for

- **macOS power users comfortable trying new browsers.** Atlas only ever shipped on macOS, so anyone on Windows, iOS, or Android never got an official release to evaluate.
- **People already paying for ChatGPT Plus or Pro.** Free users got the sidebar; agent mode, the genuinely differentiated feature, sat behind a paid plan — so the browser worked better as a bonus for existing subscribers than a reason to subscribe on its own.
- **Early adopters willing to accept security trade-offs.** Letting an AI agent click around inside your logged-in sessions (email, shopping, banking-adjacent sites) is a different risk profile than a chatbot that can only talk.
- **Teams evaluating it for work** were told Business/Enterprise data wouldn't train models by default, which mattered for organizations considering it during its short lifespan.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely novel agent mode — AI that could operate a real browser, not just describe steps | Only ever launched on macOS; Windows/iOS/Android were promised but never shipped |
| Chromium base meant extensions and bookmarks mostly carried over | Discontinued after ~10 months, so setup and workflow habits were a dead end |
| Sidebar chat removed copy-paste friction of a separate ChatGPT tab | Agent mode required a paid Plus/Pro subscription |
| "Auto" search mode addressed "AI replacing links to sites" criticism | Real memory-injection vulnerability ("Tainted Memories") found within its first year |
| No separate cost beyond an existing ChatGPT subscription | Slower than mature browsers on basics like tab groups |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Because Atlas was built on Chromium, it inherited broad compatibility with existing Chrome-style extensions rather than requiring a new plugin ecosystem — a real advantage over building a browser from scratch. It never exposed its own developer API; agent-mode behavior ran through the same backend as regular ChatGPT, and the standalone [OpenAI API](https://platform.openai.com) developers use to build ChatGPT-style features was never Atlas-specific. There was no dedicated Atlas Zapier or Slack integration — those connect to ChatGPT or the API layer generally, not the browser shell.

## Security and privacy concerns worth knowing about

This is the part of Atlas's short life most worth understanding even now, because "an AI agent that clicks around inside your logged-in browser sessions" is a security model other AI browsers are still working through. In October 2025, security firm LayerX disclosed a vulnerability nicknamed "ChatGPT Tainted Memories," combining social engineering with a cross-site request forgery technique to inject hidden instructions into Atlas's memory feature without a user's knowledge — instructions researchers said could persist across sessions and devices once planted. OpenAI disputed the severity, saying it couldn't reproduce the CSRF portion and had seen no evidence of real-world exploitation. Neither claim should be taken as final, but the episode is a reminder that agentic browsing carries real prompt-injection risk regardless of the product.

## Where it was a strong fit

Atlas made the most sense for people who wanted to test-drive genuinely agentic AI browsing — an assistant completing real multi-step tasks on live websites, not just answering questions — and who were comfortable being early adopters. If you were already a Plus or Pro subscriber on a Mac curious about agent mode specifically, there was no extra cost to trying it.

## Where to think twice (and what to use instead now)

There's nothing left to buy, since Atlas isn't purchasable anymore — but a few things matter if you're researching it after the fact:

- For **the actual ChatGPT experience today**, use the standard app, chatgpt.com, or the unified desktop app that absorbed Atlas's browsing features; see our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review).
- For an **agentic AI browser today**, Perplexity's Comet (launched shortly before Atlas) occupies a comparable category, alongside AI features in Chrome and Edge.
- For **regulated environments**, Atlas's short lifespan and documented memory-injection vulnerability are a useful caution about how new this whole category still is.
- If you needed **Windows, iOS, or Android support**, Atlas never delivered on that promise.

## The bottom line

ChatGPT Atlas was a genuinely interesting first attempt at putting an agentic AI directly inside a browser rather than bolting a chatbot onto the side of one — agent mode's ability to actually operate websites, not just describe how, was a real step beyond a standard chat assistant. But it launched on one platform, took nearly a year to add basic conveniences competitors already had, drew a credible security disclosure about its memory feature, and was discontinued after roughly ten months when OpenAI folded browsing into a unified desktop app instead of maintaining Atlas separately. What Atlas was trying to do now lives in the ChatGPT product and its successor desktop app, not a standalone download — because there isn't one anymore.

For OpenAI's current flagship product, read our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review), and browse more [AI & software deals](/category/software) for other tools in this space.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is ChatGPT Atlas still available to download?**
No. OpenAI discontinued Atlas on August 9, 2026, after announcing in March 2026 that it would combine Atlas, the ChatGPT desktop app, and Codex into one unified desktop application.

**What happened to ChatGPT Atlas?**
It was folded into a single OpenAI desktop app that also absorbed the standard ChatGPT app and the Codex coding tool, rather than continuing as a separate browser product.

**Was ChatGPT Atlas free?**
Installing and browsing with the sidebar was free with any ChatGPT account. Agent mode required a Plus ($20/month) or Pro ($200/month) subscription, the same tiers used for regular ChatGPT.

**Was ChatGPT Atlas safe to use?**
It carried the same general risks as any AI agent acting inside your logged-in browser sessions. A security firm disclosed a memory-injection vulnerability ("Tainted Memories") in October 2025 that OpenAI disputed the severity of; either way, agentic browsing carries real prompt-injection risk as a category, not just as a one-off Atlas bug.

**Did ChatGPT Atlas ever come to Windows?**
No. It launched exclusively on macOS in October 2025; announced Windows, iOS, and Android versions never shipped before discontinuation.

**How was Atlas different from using ChatGPT in a regular browser tab?**
Atlas put the assistant into a persistent sidebar with visibility into your open page, plus agent mode, which could click and navigate on your behalf — something a chatbot in a normal tab can't do to the page around it.

**What's a good alternative to ChatGPT Atlas now?**
Perplexity's Comet browser occupies a similar agentic-browsing niche. For the core ChatGPT experience without the discontinued browser wrapper, see our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review).

**Did Atlas use a different AI model than regular ChatGPT?**
No — it ran on the same underlying models available through the standard app; Atlas was a browser shell around the assistant, not a separate model.

title: Voilà AI Assistant Review 2026: Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: Voilà AI Assistant is a browser extension that summarizes, writes, and chats with any webpage. Here's what it costs and who it's actually for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Voilà AI Assistant worth installing as your browser's AI copilot?

Voilà AI Assistant is a browser extension (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari, plus desktop and mobile apps) from getvoila.ai that layers a GPT-powered sidebar over any webpage for writing, summarizing, and chatting with pages, PDFs, and YouTube videos. It's a solid pick if you want one assistant that follows you across tabs, though the free tier's 250 requests run out fast and heavier users will end up on a paid plan.

### At a glance

| | Voilà AI Assistant |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | $10/month (Premium, billed monthly) or $8/month billed annually |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — 250 free requests, no credit card required |
| Best for | People who want one AI helper available on every website, not a separate app to switch to |
| Standout feature | Right-click/select-text activation that lets you summarize, rewrite, or ask questions about whatever is on screen without copy-pasting into a chat window |

## What Voilà actually is

Voilà is built by getvoila.ai as a "personal AI that saves your time," and its core idea is placement rather than a new model. Instead of opening a separate tab for ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, it installs as an extension that sits in a sidebar, floating icon, or right-click menu on every page. Highlight a paragraph, right-click, and you can summarize, translate, or ask a follow-up without leaving the page. That's the whole pitch: less tab-switching, more "ask right where you're reading."

Under the hood, Voilà doesn't train its own foundation model. According to its own marketing, it routes requests to GPT-5 and a lighter GPT-5 mini model depending on your plan, with an "auto model selection" feature on paid tiers. Worth flagging plainly: this is a wrapper product, not an independent AI lab, and output quality is ultimately bounded by whatever OpenAI model it's calling in the background. If OpenAI changes model availability or pricing, Voilà's own plans and limits are likely to shift too.

The extension covers Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari, plus desktop apps for macOS/Windows and mobile apps for iOS/Android, so the same assistant and history can, in principle, follow you off the browser too.

## Voilà AI Assistant pricing

Voilà uses a three-tier consumer pricing structure (plus a separate team plan), gated primarily by monthly request count and which models you can access.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | 250 requests total, page summarization, chat with webpages, no credit card required |
| Premium | $10/mo monthly, $8/mo billed annually | 3,000 requests/month, automatic model selection, web access, page/YouTube chat, image generation |
| Ultimate | $20/mo monthly, $16/mo billed annually | Unlimited requests, access to GPT-5.6 / GPT-5 mini, web access, document and image chat, early feature access |
| Teams | From $16/seat/month | Shared workflows, collaboration tools, unlimited requests, added privacy controls |

There's a catch worth calling out on the top tier: Voilà states its "fair usage policy" for GPT-5.6 caps heavy users at roughly 500,000 words a month — about seven average-length books, in the company's own framing — after which requests fall back to the smaller GPT-5 mini model. So "unlimited requests" on Ultimate doesn't mean unlimited access to the strongest model; it means unlimited requests to whichever model you're currently allowed. That's a vendor claim, not an independently verified figure.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — AI browser-extension pricing moves often as underlying model costs shift, so double-check current numbers on Voilà's own pricing page before buying.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**In-page activation.** The biggest practical difference from a standalone chatbot is that Voilà works via highlight-and-right-click or a floating button on the page you're already on. You select content and act on it in place instead of retyping or copy-pasting into a separate window — for anyone doing a lot of reading-and-reacting (research, support tickets, long email threads), that shaves off real friction compared to tab-switching to ChatGPT.

**Page, PDF, and video chat.** Beyond one-shot summarization, Voilà lets you have an ongoing conversation about the document or page you're on — ask a PDF contract what a clause means, or ask a YouTube video what its main argument was without watching it. Like any AI summarizer it can miss nuance in dense material, so treat its answer as a first pass, not a final read.

**Email and writing shortcuts.** Voilà includes templated writing helpers aimed at inbox work — an "Instant Reply" feature with preset response styles, plus rewriting, grammar correction, paraphrasing, and translation that apply to any text field on the web.

**Image generation on paid tiers.** Premium and Ultimate add image generation from the same sidebar, so you can go from "summarize this" to "make me a graphic based on this" without switching tools.

**Cross-device continuity.** Since Voilà also ships desktop and mobile apps, chat history and preferences can carry across a laptop, a phone, and a browser.

## Who it's actually for

- **Casual researchers and students** wanting quick summaries of articles, PDFs, and videos will be fine on the free tier for occasional use, but will hit the 250-request ceiling within days of daily use.
- **Content creators and customer-facing staff** who write email and page summaries constantly are the clearest fit for Premium — 3,000 requests a month covers a busy habit, and built-in image generation removes a separate tool.
- **Power users** who lean on AI for long documents or near-constant use are the audience for Ultimate, mainly for the higher (if fair-use-capped) ceiling and stronger model.
- **Distributed teams** wanting shared workflows and centralized billing are pointed at the Teams plan, priced per seat for small groups.
- **Anyone already paying for ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro** should weigh whether a $10–$20/month add-on is worth it versus pinning a browser tab to the assistant they already have — Voilà's value is convenience, not a smarter model.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Works on any website via right-click or highlight, no copy-pasting | Free tier's 250 requests is a fixed allotment, not a recurring amount, and disappears quickly |
| Chat with PDFs, webpages, and YouTube videos in one tool | A wrapper around GPT models it doesn't control — future OpenAI pricing/availability shifts could affect Voilà's own plans |
| Cross-platform: browser extensions plus desktop and mobile apps | "Unlimited" on the top tier is fair-use capped by word volume, not obvious until you read the fine print |
| Built-in image generation and writing templates reduce tool-switching | Extension permissions mean it can read page content, which some workplaces are cautious about granting |
| Annual billing brings a real discount (roughly 20% off monthly rates) | No published enterprise compliance certifications (e.g. SOC 2) visible publicly — confirm directly if that matters |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Voilà's main "integration" is structural rather than a list of third-party app connectors: it works inside the browser you're already using, not by plugging into Slack, Notion, or Zapier by name. There's no publicly documented open API, and no mention of a Zapier app or native Slack/Notion integration on its marketing pages as of this review — confirm directly with Voilà's support team if that matters for your workflow. Where it does integrate well is with content types: webpages, PDFs, images, and YouTube videos are all first-class inputs inside the sidebar.

## Where it's a strong fit

Voilà earns its keep for people whose work is fundamentally about reading and reacting to what's already on screen — research, customer support, content moderation, or anyone skimming articles, PDFs, and video transcripts who needs a fast summary or rewrite without breaking their browsing flow. Bundling writing, translation, and summarization into one sidebar covers a lot of daily browser tasks without needing three separate extensions.

## Where to think twice

If you need a completely free tool for ongoing daily use, Voilà isn't it — 250 total free requests is a light trial, not a sustainable no-cost habit. If your organization requires documented compliance certifications like SOC 2 or HIPAA before installing browser extensions with page-reading permissions, get written confirmation from Voilà directly, since none is advertised publicly. If you need guaranteed access to the most capable model regardless of volume, the fair-use cap on Ultimate's GPT-5.6 access means heavy users get quietly downgraded mid-month. And if you already have a ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini subscription and are comfortable pinning a browser tab to it, the marginal convenience here may not justify a second AI subscription.

## Bottom line

Voilà doesn't try to out-think ChatGPT or Claude — it tries to be more convenient by living inside every page you're already on. For people whose day is spent skimming, summarizing, and rewriting content across dozens of tabs, that convenience is real and the $10/month Premium tier is reasonably priced. For anyone fine opening a separate tab, or needing guaranteed top-tier model access without a fair-use asterisk, it's a harder sell. Try the free 250 requests first to see if the workflow actually changes how you work before paying.

## FAQ

**Is Voilà AI Assistant free?**
There's a free tier with 250 total requests and no credit card required, covering basic summarization and webpage chat. Regular daily use exhausts that allotment within days to a couple of weeks, at which point you'd need Premium ($10/month) or Ultimate ($20/month) to continue.

**What AI model does Voilà use?**
Voilà states it routes requests to GPT-5 and GPT-5 mini, with paid tiers offering "auto model selection" and Ultimate advertising access to a GPT-5.6 model subject to a monthly fair-use word cap. It doesn't build its own foundation model — it's a wrapper interface over existing models.

**Is Voilà safe to install as a browser extension?**
Like any extension that reads page content to work, Voilà needs permission to access pages you visit — inherent to how highlight-and-summarize features function. If page-reading permissions or compliance certifications (SOC 2, GDPR) matter for your organization, review Voilà's current privacy policy directly rather than assuming.

**What's the difference between Premium and Ultimate?**
Premium ($10/month, $8/month annual) gives 3,000 requests a month with auto model selection and image generation. Ultimate ($20/month, $16/month annual) removes the fixed cap (subject to fair-use limits on the top model), adds the stronger GPT-5.6 model, and includes document/image chat plus early feature access.

**Does Voilà work on mobile?**
Yes — alongside browser extensions for Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari, Voilà offers desktop and mobile apps, with account history intended to carry across devices.

**Can Voilà summarize PDFs and YouTube videos, not just webpages?**
Yes, chatting with PDFs and YouTube videos is a core feature across paid tiers, letting you ask questions about a document's or video's content without reading or watching the whole thing.

**How does Voilà compare to just using ChatGPT directly?**
ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini require opening a separate tab and typically copy-pasting content in. Voilà's differentiator is working in place, via right-click or highlight — the tradeoff is paying an extra monthly fee for that convenience layer on top of models you might already access elsewhere. See our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review) for the underlying model family directly.

**Does Voilà offer a business or team plan?**
Yes, a Teams plan starts at $16 per seat per month with shared workflows, collaboration tools, unlimited requests, and added privacy controls, aimed at small distributed teams.

title: Resoomer Review 2026: Free AI Text Summarizer, Verdict
excerpt: Resoomer offers a free, unlimited AI text summarizer with no sign-up. Here's how it compares to paid tools and who it's actually built for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Resoomer worth using in 2026?

Yes, if you want a fast, free way to condense articles, PDFs and essays without creating an account. Resoomer's summarizer, translator and text-to-speech tools cost nothing and have no character cap, but the output is a straightforward extractive summary rather than a polished AI rewrite, so it fits research and study tasks better than professional content work.

**At a glance**

| | Resoomer |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (no paid tier found on the official site as of publication) |
| Free tier | Yes — full summarizer, no character limit, no account needed |
| Best for | Students, researchers and readers condensing articles, PDFs and essays |
| Standout feature | No sign-up, no word cap, and one-click browser extensions for Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Brave and Vivaldi |

## What Resoomer actually is

Resoomer is a French-built web app that calls itself a "cognitive studio" for processing text. It's not a chatbot and it's not built around a named large language model the way ChatGPT or Claude are — the company doesn't publish which underlying technology powers its summarizer, and there's no public model card to point to. Instead, Resoomer works more like a dedicated text-processing pipeline: paste or upload a document, and it extracts and condenses the key sentences and ideas into a shorter version, alongside separate tools for translation, paraphrasing, spell-checking, synonym lookup, word counting, text-to-speech reading, and side-by-side text comparison.

That distinction matters for expectations. Tools like ChatPDF or a general chatbot will read a PDF and then converse with you about it, generating new sentences in response to your questions — you can read our [ChatPDF review](/blog/chatpdf-review) for that approach. Resoomer instead outputs a compressed version of the original text itself, closer to a highlighter that also rewrites the highlighted parts into flowing sentences. For pulling the gist out of a dense article, textbook chapter, or research paper fast, that's often exactly what you want — and you don't need to explain anything or write a prompt to get it.

The site accepts document uploads in PDF, EPUB, DOCX, ODT and TXT formats, and it supports text in 66 languages according to Resoomer's own site copy. There's no account requirement to use the core summarizer, which is unusual among AI writing tools in 2026 — most competitors gate meaningful usage behind at least an email signup.

## Pricing: what you actually get

Resoomer's own marketing pages describe the tool as free, and at the time of this review the publicly accessible site showed no visible pricing page, paid tier, or subscription flow — every core feature (summarizer, translator, paraphraser, text-to-speech, word counter, comparison tool) was available without payment or account creation.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free (the only tier found) | $0 | Full summarizer with no character limit, translation, paraphrasing, spell-check, synonym finder, word counter, text-to-speech, text comparison, browser extensions, no account required |

This is worth flagging clearly: unlike most of the AI tools we cover, Resoomer doesn't appear to monetize through a premium subscription at all right now. That's good news for anyone who wants a no-cost tool, but it also means there's no paid tier to point to for higher usage limits, priority processing, or extra languages if you ever hit friction with the free version. Pricing and feature availability here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change without notice, so confirm current terms directly on [resoomer.com](https://resoomer.com) before relying on any specific detail.

## Features walkthrough

**Extractive summarization.** Paste text or upload a document and Resoomer returns a condensed version built from the source material's own key sentences and phrasing, adjustable by summary length. This is the tool's core function and the reason most people land on it.

**No character or length cap.** Resoomer's site explicitly advertises no limit on input length, which stands out — many free summarizers (including some browser-extension competitors) cap you at a few thousand words or force a paid upgrade for long documents.

**Document format support.** Beyond pasted text, Resoomer imports PDF, EPUB, DOCX, ODT and TXT files directly, so you can drop in a whole ebook chapter or a scanned research paper's PDF version rather than copy-pasting manually.

**Multi-language coverage.** Resoomer states support for 66 languages for both summarization and translation, which makes it usable well beyond English-language content — useful for students or researchers working across sources in multiple languages.

**Browser extensions.** Dedicated extensions exist for Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Brave and Vivaldi, letting you right-click any webpage or highlighted passage and summarize it in place without switching tabs to the main site.

**Auxiliary text tools.** Beyond summarizing, Resoomer bundles a paraphraser, synonym finder, spell-checker, word counter, text-to-speech reader and a text comparison tool — useful add-ons if you're studying or editing, though none of them are the primary reason to choose Resoomer over a general-purpose AI assistant.

## Who it's actually for

**Students and researchers** get the most direct value: dropping in a long PDF or journal article and getting a shorter version back, with no account friction and no per-document limit, is a genuinely useful study shortcut, especially combined with the text-to-speech reader for reviewing material on the go.

**Teachers and librarians** working with reading-difficulty accommodations (Resoomer explicitly calls out dyslexia and ADHD as use cases) may find the combination of summarization and audio reading useful for adapting long texts for students who need shorter or read-aloud versions.

**Journalists and writers** doing background research on a topic can use it to quickly triage a stack of source articles before deciding which ones deserve a full read, though they shouldn't expect Resoomer's output to read like an original, stylistically polished piece — it's a compression of the source, not a fresh take on it.

**Content marketers and professional writers** who need publish-ready copy, a specific tone, or original analysis will likely find Resoomer's extractive approach too limited on its own — pairing it with a generative tool (or using a general AI writing assistant from the start) will get closer to a finished draft.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely free with no account required | No named underlying model or published methodology to evaluate accuracy against |
| No character/length limit on the free tier | Extractive summaries can read choppy compared to a generative rewrite |
| Supports 66 languages and five document formats | No paid tier means no path to extra features if you outgrow the free version |
| Browser extensions across six major browsers | Not built for conversational Q&A about a document the way chat-based tools are |
| Useful bundle of auxiliary tools (paraphraser, TTS, word counter) | Ad-supported free web tools of this kind can carry more on-page ads than a subscription product |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Resoomer's ecosystem is deliberately narrow: browser extensions for Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Brave and Vivaldi are the main integration point, letting you summarize a highlighted passage or a full webpage directly from the browser toolbar. There's no public API, no Zapier or Slack integration, and no mobile app referenced on the official site — this is a browser-first, single-purpose tool rather than a platform meant to plug into a broader workflow. If you need summarization inside a larger automation pipeline or a team's existing app stack, a general AI API (from an assistant like Claude or ChatGPT) will be a better fit than Resoomer.

## Where it's a strong fit

Resoomer is a strong fit any time you have a long piece of text — an article, a PDF, an ebook chapter — and just need the gist quickly, without wanting to sign up for anything or worry about hitting a word limit. Its free-and-unlimited positioning also makes it a reasonable pick for students on a budget, or anyone who wants to try text summarization without committing to a subscription tool first.

## Where to think twice

Skip Resoomer if you need the summary to read as original, natural prose rather than a compression of the source's own sentences — a generative AI assistant will rewrite more fluidly. Skip it too if you want to ask follow-up questions about the document rather than just get a shorter version of it; that's a chat-based tool's job, not an extractive summarizer's. Teams that need enterprise features like SSO, audit logs, or a documented data-handling policy for sensitive documents should also look elsewhere, since Resoomer doesn't publish enterprise compliance details the way larger AI vendors do. And if accuracy on highly technical or numerical content (legal contracts, financial reports) matters, treat any extractive summarizer's output as a starting point to verify against the original, not a final answer.

## Bottom line

Resoomer does one thing well and charges nothing for it: turning long text into a shorter version, with no account, no word cap, and support for a wide range of document formats and languages. It won't replace a conversational AI assistant if you need back-and-forth analysis of a document, and its extractive style won't feel as smooth as a generative rewrite — but as a free, frictionless first pass for condensing reading material, it earns its place in a student's or researcher's toolkit. For lighter research browsing, the browser extension alone is worth installing.

## FAQ

**Is Resoomer really free?**
Yes — at the time of this review, every core feature (summarizer, translator, paraphraser, spell-checker, text-to-speech, word counter, text comparison) was available without payment or an account. Confirm current terms on the official site, since free tools occasionally add paid tiers over time.

**Do I need to create an account to use Resoomer?**
No. The core summarization tool works without sign-up, which is uncommon among AI writing tools in 2026.

**Is there a limit on how much text I can summarize?**
Resoomer's own site states there's no character limit, unlike many competing free summarizers that cap input length or file size.

**What file types does Resoomer accept?**
PDF, EPUB, DOCX, ODT and TXT, in addition to pasted text.

**Does Resoomer use ChatGPT or another named AI model?**
Resoomer doesn't publish which underlying technology powers its summarizer. It's best understood as a dedicated extractive text-processing tool rather than a wrapper around a specific named large language model.

**How accurate is Resoomer's summarization?**
Because Resoomer doesn't publish benchmark data or a model card, there's no independently verifiable accuracy figure to cite. Extractive summarizers generally preserve factual accuracy well (since they reuse the source's own sentences) but can miss nuance that a generative rewrite would capture — treat any summary as a starting point and check it against the original for anything important.

**What's a good alternative if I need to chat with a document instead of just summarizing it?**
Try a document-chat tool like ChatPDF — see our [ChatPDF review](/blog/chatpdf-review) — or a general AI assistant such as ChatGPT or Claude, both of which can summarize and then answer follow-up questions about the same document.

**Is Resoomer good for beginners?**
Yes. There's no learning curve — paste text or upload a file, choose a summary length, and read the result. It's arguably simpler to pick up than most AI writing tools precisely because it does one job.

For more AI and software coverage, see our [AI & software deals](/category/software) hub.

title: PDFgear Review 2026: Free AI PDF Reader and Editor
excerpt: PDFgear review 2026: is this free AI-powered PDF reader and editor worth using? Pricing, Copilot AI chat features, and honest pros and cons.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## PDFgear Review 2026: Is This Free AI PDF Reader Worth It?

PDFgear is a free desktop, web, and mobile PDF toolkit that bundles a GPT-3.5-powered "Copilot" for chatting with, summarizing, and editing documents through plain-language commands. It's a genuinely capable all-in-one reader for anyone who doesn't want to pay for Acrobat, though the AI layer is a bonus feature bolted onto a PDF editor rather than a standalone chat product.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $0 — every core tool, including the AI Copilot, is free with no paywalled tier as of this review |
| **Free tier/trial** | Full feature set free; no account required for most desktop functions |
| **Best for** | Anyone who wants a free PDF reader/editor with AI summarization built in, without subscribing to Acrobat or a chat-only tool |
| **Standout feature** | Type instructions like "delete page 10" or "summarize this contract" directly into a sidebar chat, and the AI both answers and executes the edit |

PDFgear is easy to confuse with narrower "AI PDF" products. This site already covers [ChatPDF](/blog/chatpdf-review), a browser-only chat-with-your-document tool, and separately tracks an AI PDF Summarizer built by PDF Guru. PDFgear is a different animal: a full desktop-first PDF editor (think a free Acrobat alternative) that happens to have chat-based AI features layered on top, rather than a tool built around chat as its only interface.

## What PDFgear actually is

PDFgear is made by a company of the same name and ships as a Windows and Mac desktop application, a set of browser-based online tools, and iOS/Android apps. Unlike most "free" PDF tools that gate editing, converting, or merging behind a paywall or a watermark, PDFgear's marketing positions the entire toolkit — reading, editing, converting, merging, splitting, compressing, and e-signing — as free with no account required for the desktop app's core functions.

The AI layer, branded **PDFgear Copilot** (also referenced on the site as an AI/chat feature inside the reader), is what the vendor calls "the first AI-powered PDF software." The vendor states Copilot runs on GPT-3.5. That's worth flagging plainly: GPT-3.5 is a few generations behind the frontier models powering paid competitors' summarization in 2026, so treat its reasoning on dense technical or legal documents as a helpful first pass, not a substitute for careful reading — the model choice affects how much you should trust nuanced answers on complex contracts or research papers.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described here reflect PDFgear's public site as of this review's publish date and can change without notice — always confirm current terms on the official site before relying on a specific limit.

## Pricing

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app (Windows/Mac) | Free | Full editor, converter, merge/split/compress, e-sign, OCR, and Copilot AI chat — no watermarks or paywalled tools disclosed on the official site |
| Online tools (browser) | Free | Individual web-based tools (edit, convert, merge, sign) usable without installing the app |
| Mobile apps (iOS/Android) | Free | Reader and basic editing on the go |
| eSignGear (companion e-sign platform) | Separate product | Runs under its own branding at esigngear.com; not bundled pricing with PDFgear itself |

There is no published paid tier for PDFgear's core desktop, web, or mobile tools at the time of writing — the company's revenue model isn't fully transparent from the marketing pages, and the site doesn't disclose one. That's unusual enough that it's worth treating the "completely free" claim as the vendor's own framing rather than an independently audited fact, since free-forever consumer software occasionally introduces monetization later (ads, an enterprise tier, or usage caps) without much notice. Nothing on the current site suggests that's imminent, but it's a reasonable thing to watch if you build a workflow around it.

## Features walkthrough

**AI Copilot chat sidebar.** Instead of hunting through ribbon menus, you type what you want in plain English — "compress this file," "delete pages 3 to 5," "translate page 1 to Spanish" — and Copilot both interprets the request and carries it out inside the open document. For document Q&A, you can ask it to summarize a manual, pull key clauses from a contract, or answer a specific question about the file's contents, similar in spirit to what ChatPDF does but without leaving the desktop editor.

**Full PDF editing, not just annotation.** Many "free" PDF tools only let you highlight or comment for free and charge for actual edits. PDFgear's free tier includes editing text and images directly in the PDF, adding or deleting pages, rotating and reordering, and applying page numbers — the kind of editing that competitors commonly reserve for paid plans.

**Format conversion in both directions.** PDF to Word, PDF to JPG, Word to PDF, JPG to PDF, and a general PDF converter are all free tools on the site, useful for anyone who needs to pull tables or paragraphs out of a scanned document into an editable format.

**OCR for scanned documents.** PDFgear includes OCR to make scanned or image-based PDFs searchable and selectable, which matters if you're trying to run the AI chat feature against a document that started life as a photo or scan rather than a native digital PDF — AI summarization on unrecognized image text won't work well without this step.

**E-signing via a companion product.** Signing is handled through PDFgear's own sign-PDF-online tool for lightweight use, with a more full-featured e-signature workflow spun out under the separate eSignGear brand for anyone needing legally binding signature audit trails.

## Who it's actually for

- **Students and researchers** who want to summarize a long reading assignment or paper without paying for a subscription chat tool — the free Copilot chat covers the core "explain this document to me" use case adequately for lighter reading.
- **Freelancers and small business owners** who need to edit, convert, merge, and sign contracts or invoices regularly and don't want to pay for Acrobat's subscription just to edit text in a PDF.
- **Anyone replacing Acrobat Reader** as a daily driver — if your main complaint about Adobe's tools is the price or the constant upsell prompts, PDFgear's desktop app covers the same ground for most everyday tasks at no cost.
- **Less ideal for teams needing enterprise controls.** There's no visible admin console, team seat management, SSO, or compliance certification (SOC 2, HIPAA) disclosed on the public site, so businesses with formal data-governance requirements should look elsewhere or verify directly with PDFgear's team before adopting it for regulated documents.
- **Less ideal if you need frontier-model accuracy** on complex documents — since Copilot is built on GPT-3.5, treat AI-generated summaries of dense legal or technical PDFs as a starting point to verify, not a final answer.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Full editing, converting, merging, and OCR are free — not just a limited trial | AI Copilot runs on GPT-3.5, an older model, so nuanced summarization can be less reliable than newer AI-PDF tools |
| No account required for most desktop functionality | No published enterprise/team plan, admin console, or compliance certifications |
| Available across Windows, Mac, web, iOS, and Android | Business model behind "always free" isn't clearly disclosed, so long-term pricing stability isn't guaranteed |
| Chat-based commands can execute real edits (delete pages, compress, translate), not just answer questions | Desktop-first design means the online/web tools are less full-featured than the installed app |
| Vendor states user data isn't stored, with encrypted transmission | No independent third-party audit of that privacy claim is publicly available |

## Integrations and ecosystem

PDFgear doesn't advertise a developer API, Zapier connector, or Slack integration on its public marketing pages — it's built as a consumer-facing standalone app rather than a workflow-automation building block. Its ecosystem is mostly its own suite: the desktop app, the online tools directory, mobile apps, and the separate eSignGear product for more formal e-signature workflows. If your use case depends on piping PDF processing into another automated pipeline (for example, auto-summarizing incoming email attachments), PDFgear isn't built for that; a chat-tool API like ChatPDF's or a dedicated document-automation platform would fit better.

## Where it's a strong fit

PDFgear earns its keep as a genuinely free replacement for Acrobat Reader plus a lightweight AI assistant, especially for people who occasionally need real editing (not just viewing) and don't want a subscription. The chat-command interface for actions like "delete this page" or "merge these two files" is a nice touch that saves menu-hunting, and having OCR, conversion, and e-signing all under one free roof is unusual. For students, freelancers, and casual home users handling contracts, forms, and reports, it covers the vast majority of day-to-day PDF tasks without a credit card.

## Where to think twice

If you need airtight accuracy on legal or technical document analysis, the GPT-3.5 backbone is a real limitation — pair it with your own read-through rather than trusting a Copilot summary as the final word on a contract's terms. If your organization needs formal compliance documentation (SOC 2, HIPAA, data residency guarantees) or centralized team administration, skip PDFgear for that use case; none of that is disclosed on its public site. And if you want a chat-first tool that lives in a browser tab without installing anything, PDFgear's desktop-first design will feel like more setup than the ChatPDF-style experience.

## Bottom line

PDFgear delivers more free functionality than most competitors bundle into a paid tier, and its AI Copilot is a useful bonus rather than the whole product — which is exactly why it's worth choosing over a chat-only tool if you also need real PDF editing. It won't out-reason a frontier-model AI assistant on a dense filing, and it lacks the enterprise trimmings some teams require, but as a free, cross-platform PDF reader and editor with AI chat built in, it's one of the more complete free options available right now.

## FAQ

**Is PDFgear actually free, or is there a hidden paid tier?**
Based on the vendor's public site, the desktop app, online tools, and mobile apps are all free with no disclosed paid tier for core PDF editing, converting, or AI chat features. No pricing page or upgrade prompt is documented publicly, though this could change, so it's worth confirming current terms directly on pdfgear.com before building a critical workflow around it.

**What AI model powers PDFgear's Copilot chat feature?**
The vendor states Copilot is powered by GPT-3.5. That's an older model generation than what many 2026-era paid AI-PDF tools use, so expect solid performance on straightforward summarization and page-editing commands, but verify anything nuanced yourself.

**Does PDFgear require an account or sign-up?**
No account is required for most of the desktop app's core functions, according to the vendor's site. Some online tools or mobile features may prompt for sign-in depending on the specific task; PDFgear's site doesn't fully clarify which ones.

**Is my document data private when I use the AI chat feature?**
PDFgear states it does not store user data and uses encrypted transmission for files processed through its tools. That's the vendor's own claim; there's no independently published third-party audit confirming it, so sensitive or regulated documents should be handled with that caveat in mind.

**How does PDFgear compare to ChatPDF?**
ChatPDF is a browser-only chat interface built specifically around asking questions of a single uploaded document, with a free tier capped at a small number of documents per day. PDFgear is a full desktop/web/mobile PDF editor with chat-based AI as one feature among many — better if you also need to edit, convert, or sign PDFs; more setup than necessary if all you want is quick document Q&A in a browser tab. See our [ChatPDF review](/blog/chatpdf-review) for more detail on that tool specifically.

**Can PDFgear handle scanned PDFs or photos of documents?**
Yes — PDFgear includes an OCR tool to convert scanned or image-based PDFs into searchable, selectable text. Running OCR first is important if you want the AI chat feature to accurately summarize or answer questions about a document that started as a scan rather than a native digital PDF.

**Is PDFgear good for beginners?**
The chat-command interface is arguably easier for non-technical users than a traditional PDF editor's menu system, since you can type what you want in plain language instead of locating the right toolbar icon. The trade-off is that, like any AI feature, results are only as good as the request you type and the model behind it.

**What are the main alternatives to PDFgear?**
For chat-first document Q&A without installing software, [ChatPDF](/blog/chatpdf-review) is a common alternative. For users who need enterprise compliance certifications or team administration, paid tools like Adobe Acrobat with its AI Assistant, or dedicated enterprise document platforms, are worth comparing against PDFgear's free but less formally governed offering.

For more free and discounted software picks, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Abhyas AI Review 2026: JEE/NEET Prep Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: Abhyas AI is Aditya Educational Institutions' adaptive JEE/NEET/EAPCET prep platform. Here's how its features, pricing, and access model actually work.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Abhyas AI Worth It for JEE and NEET Prep?

Abhyas AI (ABHYAS.AI) is an adaptive learning platform built by Aditya Educational Institutions for JEE, NEET, and AP EAPCET aspirants in India. It uses machine learning to sequence video lessons and practice questions around a student's weak topics, backed by a large question bank and tutor support. It's genuinely useful, but access is tied to enrolling with Aditya's coaching programs rather than an open, self-serve subscription.

| Quick fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Made by | Aditya Educational Institutions (est. 1984) |
| Best for | JEE Main/Advanced, NEET, and AP EAPCET students, mostly in Andhra Pradesh/Telangana |
| Standout feature | Machine-learning study sequencing that skips content a student has already mastered |
| Free tier / trial | No public free tier — access is bundled with Aditya coaching enrollment |
| Starting price | Not published; tied to institute enrollment fees, not a standalone subscription |

## What Abhyas AI Actually Is

Abhyas AI isn't a general-purpose AI chatbot or writing tool — it's a subject-specific exam-prep engine built for Indian competitive exams. Aditya Educational Institutions, a coaching chain that's run junior colleges and IIT/NEET coaching centers since 1984, built the platform to sit alongside its classroom teaching, not replace it. Students who enroll at an Aditya campus (or an affiliated partner institution — the site lists 127 partner institutions) get access to the Abhyas AI portal and its companion mobile app, published on the Play Store as "Aditya Abhyas."

The pitch is straightforward: instead of working through a textbook chapter by chapter, the platform tracks what a student gets right and wrong across a large question bank, then resequences what to study next. Aditya's own marketing claims the platform has supported more than 15,000 admissions since 2020, including to AIIMS Delhi, IIT Bombay, and IIT Guwahati, with a question bank covering over 300,000 questions across 860+ topics. These are vendor-published numbers, not independently audited, so treat them as directional rather than verified.

## Pricing: There's No Public Price List

This is the biggest practical difference between Abhyas AI and most tools reviewed on this site. There's no pricing page, no monthly-plan comparison, and no self-serve checkout. The homepage's only calls to action are "Login" and "New User" registration — access is granted once a student enrolls in an Aditya Educational Institutions program (or a partner institution that licenses the platform), and the platform's cost is effectively folded into that coaching fee rather than sold as a standalone SaaS subscription.

That means there's no "Pro" or "Team" tier to compare, and no way to buy just the software without enrolling in the physical coaching program it's attached to. If you want a JEE/NEET prep tool you can subscribe to directly, from outside India or without joining a specific coaching center, Abhyas AI likely isn't reachable that way — you'd need to contact the institute (info@abhyas.ai) to ask about enrollment and access.

Pricing, feature availability, and enrollment terms for Abhyas AI were not published anywhere we could verify as of this post's date and should be confirmed directly with Aditya Educational Institutions before assuming any figure, since coaching-fee structures like this change by campus, batch, and academic year.

## Features Walkthrough

**Adaptive study sequencing.** The platform's core claim is that it uses machine learning to figure out which topics a student has actually mastered and which need more work, then reorders the study plan so time isn't spent re-covering material a student already knows. This is the same underlying idea behind spaced-repetition and mastery-based learning tools used elsewhere, just applied to the JEE/NEET/EAPCET syllabus specifically.

**Large, exam-specific question bank.** Aditya states the platform draws from more than 300,000 categorized practice questions and 600+ previous years' exam papers across 860+ topics. For exams like JEE Advanced and NEET, where question patterns repeat across years, having a deep, tagged bank matters more than raw video-lecture hours.

**Mistake-pattern analytics.** Beyond simple right/wrong scoring, the platform is marketed as identifying "common traps" — the specific wrong-answer patterns that show up repeatedly for a topic — and flagging them back to the student, rather than just reporting an aggregate score.

**Ask-a-Tutor access.** Students route specific doubts to subject experts rather than relying only on AI-driven sequencing. Aditya lists 200+ subject experts behind the platform, making this a hybrid of software and human tutoring rather than a pure self-serve AI product.

**5,000+ hours of video content.** The video library goes from fundamentals to advanced problem-solving per topic, and it's this library the adaptive engine resequences for each learner.

## Who It's Actually For

- **Students already enrolled at an Aditya campus or a partner coaching institute** get the most value, since the platform is designed to run alongside classroom teaching at those institutions rather than as an independent product.
- **JEE Advanced, JEE Main, NEET, and AP EAPCET aspirants** specifically — this isn't a general study tool for board exams, competitive coding, or exams outside this narrow set of Indian entrance tests.
- **Students in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana** are the natural fit, given Aditya's regional footprint and the 127 partner institutions the platform lists, though the app itself is available to anyone who can get enrollment access.
- **Not a fit for** students outside India, students preparing for exams outside JEE/NEET/EAPCET, or anyone looking for a self-serve online subscription they can buy without going through a coaching enrollment.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Deep, exam-specific question bank (300,000+ questions, 600+ past papers) | No public pricing or self-serve signup — access requires institute enrollment |
| Adaptive sequencing aims to cut time spent on already-mastered topics | Tightly scoped to JEE/NEET/AP EAPCET — no use outside these exams |
| Backed by human subject-expert tutors, not just AI output | Admissions/track-record numbers are vendor-reported, not third-party audited |
| Companion mobile app ("Aditya Abhyas") with 50K+ downloads and a 3.5-star rating on the Play Store | 3.5 stars across 354 reviews suggests a meaningful share of mixed feedback |
| Backed by an institution with a multi-decade coaching track record (since 1984) | Not usable by students outside Aditya's institute network in any documented way |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Abhyas AI's ecosystem is intentionally narrow rather than broad. There's a companion Android app ("Aditya Abhyas") for on-the-go access to lessons and practice questions. There's no public API, no Zapier or Slack integration, and no browser extension — this isn't built to plug into a wider software stack the way a productivity AI tool would be. The real "integration" is with Aditya's own classroom teaching: it extends what happens in a physical coaching batch, with Ask-a-Tutor bridging the software and the institute's teaching staff.

## Where It's a Strong Fit

If a student is already committed to an Aditya coaching program for JEE, NEET, or AP EAPCET, Abhyas AI is a reasonable value-add rather than an extra cost decision — it comes as part of what the institute already offers. For that audience, a large exam-tagged question bank plus adaptive resequencing plus tutor backup is a sensible way to structure revision time ahead of a high-stakes exam, where every hour spent re-covering a mastered topic is an hour not spent on a weak one.

It's also worth asking about when evaluating which coaching institute to join in Andhra Pradesh or Telangana, where the software layer might be a genuine differentiator — though it shouldn't be the only factor in that decision.

## Where to Think Twice

Skip this one if you're outside India and want a general SAT/GRE/GMAT-style AI prep tool — Abhyas AI is scoped entirely to Indian JEE/NEET/EAPCET syllabi and won't transfer. Skip it if you want a tool you can subscribe to directly without enrolling in a physical coaching program, since there's no documented standalone signup. Skip it if you need a fully free tool to self-study without institutional backing — cost here is tied to coaching fees, not an independent software subscription. And weigh the Play Store rating with some caution: 3.5 stars across 354 reviews is respectable but not exceptional, so read a sample of recent reviews for your specific exam track — coaching quality, teachers, and a student's own study discipline still matter more than any single software layer.

## The Bottom Line

Abhyas AI is a credible, purpose-built adaptive learning platform for a narrow but high-stakes audience — JEE, NEET, and AP EAPCET aspirants going through Aditya Educational Institutions' coaching network. The question-bank depth, mistake-pattern analytics, and tutor backup are features that actually move the needle for entrance-exam prep, and the institute's multi-decade track record gives it more credibility than a brand-new edtech startup. What holds it back from a broader recommendation is structural, not technical: no public pricing, no self-serve signup, no way to use it independent of enrolling in Aditya's programs. If you're already in that ecosystem, it's worth using fully; if you're shopping for a JEE/NEET AI tool on your own terms, confirm enrollment and access directly with the institute first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Abhyas AI free to use?**
There's no publicly documented free tier. Access is provided as part of enrollment with Aditya Educational Institutions or a partner coaching institute, so the effective cost is tied to that institute's fees rather than a standalone software price.

**Can I sign up for Abhyas AI without joining an Aditya coaching program?**
Based on what's published on the platform's own site, no — the "New User" registration flow is built for students entering through institute enrollment. Contact Aditya Educational Institutions directly (info@abhyas.ai) to confirm current access options.

**What exams does Abhyas AI cover?**
JEE Main, JEE Advanced, NEET, and AP EAPCET are the exams Aditya explicitly lists results and question-bank coverage for. It is not built for board exams, exams outside India, or general academic subjects unrelated to these entrance tests.

**Does Abhyas AI replace classroom coaching?**
No. It's positioned as a companion to Aditya's classroom teaching, combining AI-driven practice sequencing with human tutor access (the "Ask-a-Tutor" feature) rather than as a fully self-directed replacement for a teacher.

**Is there a mobile app?**
Yes. "Aditya Abhyas," published by Aditya Educational Institutions, is available on the Google Play Store with 50,000+ downloads and a 3.5-star rating from 354 reviews as of this review.

**How accurate are the admissions numbers Abhyas AI advertises?**
The 15,000+ admissions and specific rank claims (like AIR 4 in JEE Advanced) come from Aditya's own marketing materials. They aren't independently audited, so treat them as the vendor's stated track record rather than a verified third-party statistic.

**Are there alternatives to Abhyas AI?**
For India-focused competitive exam prep with AI-driven study plans, other platforms in this space include Physics Wallah, Unacademy, and Allen Digital, though each has a different coaching-versus-software balance and its own pricing model worth comparing separately. For general AI-powered study and note-taking tools that aren't exam-specific, see our [TurboLearn AI review](/blog/turbolearn-ai-review) and [YouLearn AI review](/blog/youlearn-ai-review).

**Is my data safe on Abhyas AI?**
The platform doesn't publish a standalone, detailed privacy policy breakdown on its marketing pages beyond standard institute enrollment terms. If data handling is a concern, ask Aditya Educational Institutions directly for their privacy policy and data-retention terms before enrolling.
