We couldn't pull a fully rendered price table from wan.video's own pricing page (it loads client-side), so if you're evaluating the official app's subscription tiers, confirm current credit costs and free-generation limits directly on create.wan.video before committing — that, along with fal.ai's and Replicate's rate cards, is more reliable than any third-party summary. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can shift quickly, so treat every number above as a snapshot.

Compared to Runway (roughly $12–$76/month for bundled credits) or Hailuo's credit-based plans, Wan's pay-per-second API pricing tends to work out cheaper per clip for high-volume users, especially at 480p/720p, but you're assembling the workflow yourself rather than getting one polished app.

## Core features walkthrough

**Open weights you can actually run yourself.** This is Wan's biggest structural difference from the rest of the field. Apache 2.0 licensing means no attribution requirement and no restriction on commercial use of the output, which matters if your legal team is nervous about training-data or output-ownership terms buried in a SaaS ToS.

**A tiered model lineup instead of one-size-fits-all.** The 1.3B text-to-video model is deliberately lightweight so it runs on consumer GPUs, while the 14B and MoE-based 27B models trade compute cost for quality. That range lets technical teams pick a model matching their hardware budget rather than being locked into whatever a hosted app defaults to.

**Multi-task coverage beyond plain text-to-video.** The family includes image-to-video, first-last-frame-to-video (supply the opening and closing frame and the model interpolates motion between them), video editing/VACE variants, and — in later releases — speech-to-video and character-animation models. Few competitors ship this many purpose-built variants rather than one general model with prompt tricks.

**Native audio in newer releases.** Wan 2.5 and 2.7, as distributed through hosted APIs, generate synced audio alongside video rather than requiring a separate pass, which is still not universal among competing video models.

**Bilingual text rendering.** Alibaba's documentation for Wan 2.1 highlights reliable text generation inside video in both Chinese and English, a detail that matters for on-screen graphics or captions and that many Western-built models still handle inconsistently.

## Who it's actually for

- **ML engineers and technical creators comfortable with ComfyUI or Python** get the most out of Wan — self-hosting or calling the API directly gives full control over resolution, frame count, and cost, with no vendor markup beyond raw compute.
- **Startups and agencies building a video feature on an API** benefit from Wan's per-second pricing on fal.ai/Replicate, which can undercut bundled-credit SaaS pricing at volume.
- **Casual creators who just want a simple app** are better served trying wan.video first, but should expect a less mature UI than Runway, Hailuo, or Higgsfield.
- **Enterprises needing indemnification or dedicated support** should look at Alibaba Cloud's DashScope/Model Studio enterprise offering and confirm compliance terms with Alibaba Cloud sales directly.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Apache 2.0 open weights — free to self-host, unrestricted commercial use | Consumer app is less refined than Runway/Hailuo for non-technical users |
| Very competitive per-second pricing through fal.ai/Replicate at volume | Official pricing page loads dynamically and is harder to verify at a glance |
| Wide range of purpose-built model variants (T2V, I2V, FLF2V, VACE, audio) | Fast version churn (2.1 → 2.2 → 2.5 → 2.7) makes it easy to compare the wrong two |
| Strong bilingual on-screen text rendering | Self-hosting the larger 14B/MoE models needs serious GPU VRAM |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Wan's biggest ecosystem advantage is that it isn't tied to one platform. The open-weight releases integrate directly into **ComfyUI** (dedicated Wan node packs exist in the community), and model files are distributed through Hugging Face and the official GitHub repos under Apache 2.0. For teams that don't want to manage GPUs themselves, hosted API access is available through **fal.ai**, **Replicate**, and **Alibaba Cloud's DashScope/Model Studio**, each with its own SDK — useful for building video generation into a product rather than using it interactively. There's no official Zapier or Slack integration; that would need to be built on the API.

## Where it's a strong fit

- You want to self-host a video model and control cost, latency, and data residency yourself.
- You're building a product feature and need predictable, usage-based pricing over a bundled monthly plan.
- You want a specific task variant — image-to-video, first-last-frame interpolation, speech-to-video — rather than a general prompt box.

## Where to think twice

- If you want one polished app with a simple subscription and don't want to touch an API or ComfyUI, Hailuo or Runway will likely feel more finished today.
- If you need enterprise SLAs, indemnification, or SOC 2-style compliance documentation, go directly to Alibaba Cloud's enterprise offering rather than the free consumer app or a third-party reseller, and get those terms in writing first.
- If you lack a capable GPU and don't want per-second API fees, the consumer app's free tier may be too limited for regular use — check current quotas on create.wan.video before assuming otherwise.
- If you need long-form video in one generation, Wan's clip lengths — even in the newer 2.7 releases — top out at roughly 15 seconds per Replicate's listings, so longer content means stitching multiple clips together.

## Bottom line

Wan AI is less a single app to review and more an increasingly important open model family that other products and pipelines run underneath the hood. If you're a developer, technical creator, or team building a video feature, its open weights and per-second API pricing make it one of the more cost-effective, flexible options in AI video today. If you just want to type a prompt and get a good clip with zero setup, wan.video's consumer app is usable but not as smooth as some closed competitors, so try the free tier before paying for credits or moving to a hosted API.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Wan AI free to use?**
The model weights (Wan 2.1, 2.2, and later) are released under Apache 2.0, so self-hosting is free beyond your own compute cost. The wan.video consumer app has a free tier with limited generations; paid credits or a subscription unlock more usage. Confirm current free-tier limits on the official site, since they change.

**What's the difference between Wan 2.1, 2.2, and newer versions?**
Wan 2.1 introduced the original open-weight text-to-video, image-to-video, and editing models. Wan 2.2 added a Mixture-of-Experts architecture and far more training data for better motion and detail. Later versions distributed through hosted APIs (2.5, 2.7) added native audio, 1080p resolution, and longer clips.

**Can I use Wan-generated video commercially?**
For the open-weight releases under Apache 2.0, yes — there's no restriction on commercial use, though the license prohibits clearly harmful uses like misinformation or privacy violations. If you're using Alibaba Cloud's hosted service instead, check that service's own terms, since they can differ from the open-weight license.

**Do I need a powerful GPU to run Wan myself?**
Only if you're self-hosting. The lightweight 1.3B text-to-video model runs on roughly 8GB of VRAM, but the larger 14B and MoE-based models need substantially more. Without that hardware, use the hosted app or an API provider like fal.ai or Replicate instead.

**How does Wan compare to Runway, Hailuo, or Higgsfield?**
Those are closed, hosted-only products with more mature consumer apps. Wan's advantage is being open-weight and available across multiple hosting platforms at competitive per-second pricing, which suits developers and high-volume use more than casual one-off creators. See our [Hailuo AI review](/blog/hailuo-ai-review) and [Higgsfield AI review](/blog/higgsfield-ai-review) for those alternatives.

**Does Wan generate audio with video?**
Not in the original Wan 2.1 release, but newer versions (Wan 2.5 and 2.7, as distributed through hosted APIs like Replicate) generate synced audio alongside the video in the same pass.

**Where can I find more AI video tool options?**
Browse our full [AI & software deals](/category/software) hub for other AI video, image, and productivity tool reviews and coupons.

title: Google Nano Banana Review 2026: Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: Google Nano Banana (Gemini image generation) excels at text-in-image rendering and multi-image edits. Here is what it costs and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Google Nano Banana actually good at AI image generation?

Nano Banana is Google's nickname for its Gemini image generation and editing models, spanning Nano Banana 2 Lite, Nano Banana 2, and the flagship Nano Banana Pro. It's genuinely strong at prompt-following, legible text-in-image rendering, and multi-image editing, and free to try inside the Gemini app, though top quality (4K, Pro reasoning) is gated behind Google AI subscriptions or metered API billing.

### At a glance

| | Google Nano Banana |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free in the Gemini app (limited daily generations); API billed per image/token |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — Gemini app free tier plus a free quota in Google AI Studio/API |
| Best for | Anyone who wants photo edits, product mockups, or text-heavy graphics without opening Photoshop |
| Standout feature | Multi-image composition — blending up to 14 reference images while keeping characters and style consistent |

## What Nano Banana actually is

"Nano Banana" started as an internal codename that leaked onto AI image-generation leaderboards in mid-2025, and Google eventually leaned into the meme rather than fight it — official product pages now use the name alongside the real model names. Under the hood, it's Google DeepMind's Gemini image family, not a separate architecture: the same Gemini large language model given the ability to output pixels instead of (or alongside) text, which is why it reasons about a prompt before drawing rather than just pattern-matching to training images.

The current lineup:

- **Nano Banana 2 Lite** (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image) — cheapest, fastest, capped at 1K resolution, meant for high-volume or latency-sensitive use.
- **Nano Banana 2** (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image) — the general-purpose workhorse, up to 4K output, most editing features below.
- **Nano Banana Pro** (Gemini 3 Pro Image) — the top tier for complex, multi-step visual reasoning (dense infographics, precise text layout, tricky composites), billed noticeably higher per image.
- The original **Nano Banana** (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) still exists but Google has flagged it for deprecation, with Nano Banana 2 Lite as the recommended replacement.

You'll meet these models in three places: the consumer Gemini app/website (the image tool, marked with the 🍌 emoji in the UI), Google AI Studio for prompt testing, and the Gemini API for building it into your own product.

## Pricing — what it actually costs

Google runs this as two separate pricing systems depending on where you use it, and they don't map cleanly onto each other.

**In the Gemini app**, image generation is bundled into the same free/paid tiers as Gemini's chat features — no separate "image plan." Free accounts get a limited number of generations per day; Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers get progressively higher usage multipliers (roughly 2x, 4x, and up to 20x the free allowance, per Google) plus access to higher-end models and the ability to "regenerate with Pro" on lower tiers. Check exact current pricing on Google's [AI plans page](https://one.google.com/about/google-ai-plans/), since names and prices have changed more than once and vary by region.

**Through the Gemini API / AI Studio**, you pay per token, with image output billed at a flat per-image token cost baked into the response:

| Model | Input | Output | Approx. cost/image |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nano Banana 2 Lite | $0.25/1M tokens | $1.50 per 1K image | Cheapest, 1K only |
| Nano Banana 2 | $0.50/1M tokens | $60/1M tokens | ~$0.045–$0.15 by resolution |
| Nano Banana Pro | $2.00/1M tokens | $120/1M tokens | ~$0.13–$0.24 by resolution |
| Legacy (2.5 Flash Image) | — | — | ~$0.039/image, half on batch |

Batch API requests (queued, non-real-time) run at roughly half the standard price across the lineup — useful if you're generating large volumes of product images or thumbnails and don't need them instantly.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly — Google has revised model names, prices, and quotas multiple times in the past year, so confirm current numbers on [Google's Gemini API pricing page](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing).

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**Multi-image composition.** Nano Banana can take up to 14 reference images in a single request — Google's docs describe roles like up to 10 general objects, 4 character references, and 3 style references (caps vary by model tier). You can hand it a photo of a person, a product shot, and a style reference, and ask it to combine them into one coherent scene — something most competing image models handle far more clumsily.

**Character and style consistency.** Because the model references prior images in the same conversation, you can generate a character once and then ask for that same character in a different pose, outfit, or setting without it drifting into a different-looking person — a common failure mode for diffusion-only models without conversational context.

**Legible text rendering.** Text-in-image has historically been the weak point of AI image generators (garbled letters, backwards words). Nano Banana is noticeably better at rendering clean, readable text for infographics, menus, posters, and diagrams — Google markets this specifically as a differentiator over older Imagen-based tools.

**Conversational editing.** Instead of rewriting a full prompt from scratch, you describe the change in plain language ("make the background darker," "remove the logo," "change her jacket to red") and the model edits in place while keeping the rest of the composition intact.

**Google Search grounding (select models).** Some tiers pull real-time information from Google Search when generating imagery tied to current data — Google's examples include weather visuals or stock charts — a genuinely unusual capability among image generators that normally have no sense of "right now."

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and marketers** get the most value from the free Gemini app tier or a low-cost AI Plus subscription — the free daily quota covers casual, occasional use.
- **Small teams and agencies** doing volume work (batch product photo edits, ad variants) are better served by the API with batch pricing, since costs on Nano Banana 2 stay low even at scale.
- **Developers building image features into an app** should go straight to the API/AI Studio for programmatic control over resolution, aspect ratio, and reference images, and the choice between Lite (speed) and Pro (quality) per request.
- **Design professionals needing precise, print-ready output** will likely reach for Nano Banana Pro, but should budget for its higher per-image cost.
- **Anyone needing a fully offline or on-prem image model** should look elsewhere — this is cloud-only, with no local/self-hosted option.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Strong at rendering legible text inside images | Free-tier daily limits run out quickly with heavy use |
| Multi-image blending (up to 14 references) beats most rivals | Naming (Nano Banana vs. Gemini 3.x Flash/Pro Image) is confusing across Google's own pages |
| Conversational, in-place editing avoids full prompt rewrites | Every image carries a SynthID watermark, unwanted by some commercial users |
| Competitive per-image API pricing, especially Lite and batch | Pro-tier "thinking" mode adds billed tokens and latency |
| Search grounding for real-time visual data is a rare extra | 4K output and top quality require a paid plan or metered spend |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Nano Banana isn't a standalone app — it's woven into Google's existing surfaces: the Gemini app and website, Google AI Studio for prompt testing, and the Gemini API for third-party integrations. Google has also rolled the same underlying models into other products, including an experimental "Google Pics" photo surface. There's no dedicated Zapier or Slack app for Nano Banana specifically, but since it's exposed via a standard API, it can be wired into any workflow tool that supports a generic HTTP call.

## Where it's a strong fit

Nano Banana is at its best for fast, iterative edits described in plain language rather than precise prompt-engineering, and for use cases where legible in-image text matters — social graphics, marketing collateral, infographics, and product mockups mixing a real photo with a generated background or style. Developers bolting image generation onto an existing product will also find the pricing tiers practical, routing high-volume requests to Lite and reserving Pro for images that need it.

## Where to think twice

Skip it, or test carefully first, if any of these apply:

- **You need a fully free, unlimited tool** — the free Gemini app tier has real daily caps, with no free unlimited path for high-volume use.
- **You require images with no visible watermark or embedded provenance marker** — every output includes a SynthID watermark by design, with no option to turn it off.
- **You need offline, on-device, or self-hosted generation** — this is cloud-only; there's no local weights or offline mode.
- **You're doing extremely fine-grained, pixel-level control** (exact object placement, precise masking) — like most general-purpose AI image models, it's better at holistic composition than surgical, Photoshop-level editing.
- **Your workflow depends on a specific commercial license guarantee** — check Google's current terms for exact usage rights before paid commercial work at scale.

## The bottom line

Nano Banana earned its reputation fast because it's simply better than most competing image models at two unglamorous but high-value things: keeping text legible and keeping a character consistent across edits. If you're already inside Google's ecosystem, the free Gemini app tier is a reasonable way to try it, and the API pricing is competitive enough that developers should give it a serious look alongside Midjourney and other generators. The catch is less about quality and more about Google's own presentation — a marketing meme layered over a shifting lineup of "real" model names and quietly changing prices — so double-check the current tier and price before budgeting for it.

## FAQ

**Is Nano Banana free to use?**
Yes, with limits. The Gemini app includes a free daily quota for image generation, and the API/AI Studio also offer a limited free tier for testing. Heavy or commercial use runs into those caps and typically needs a paid Google AI plan or metered API billing.

**What's the difference between Nano Banana, Nano Banana 2, and Nano Banana Pro?**
They're different Gemini image model tiers, not different products. Nano Banana 2 Lite is cheapest and fastest (1K cap); Nano Banana 2 supports up to 4K; Nano Banana Pro is the priciest, highest-quality tier for complex compositions and dense text. The original Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) is being phased out.

**Does Nano Banana watermark its images?**
Yes. Every image carries a SynthID watermark, a machine-detectable marker Google uses across its generative media to flag AI origin, with no option to disable it.

**Can I use Nano Banana images commercially?**
Generally yes under Google's terms, but rights and restrictions can vary by plan and use case (real people, trademarks, likenesses). Confirm current terms on Google's official Gemini/AI Studio terms pages before commercial use.

**How does it compare to Midjourney?**
Nano Banana's edge is text rendering and multi-image/character consistency, where diffusion-focused tools like Midjourney have historically struggled; Midjourney still leads for many on raw aesthetic variety. Our [Midjourney review](/blog/midjourney-review) covers that side in more depth.

**Is Nano Banana a separate product from the Gemini chatbot?**
No — it's a feature inside the same Gemini app and API. Our [Google Gemini review](/blog/google-gemini-review) covers the assistant's chat and Workspace side; this article focuses on image generation specifically.

**Do I need coding skills to use it?**
No, not for the Gemini app or AI Studio's playground, which are point-and-click. You only need API familiarity to integrate it into your own software.

**What resolutions does it support?**
Up to 4K on the higher-tier models (512px/1K on Lite), with aspect ratios including 1:1, 16:9, 3:2, 4:3, and 9:16 — check the current [Gemini API image docs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/image-generation) for the full list.

For more AI coverage, see our [Google Gemini review](/blog/google-gemini-review), [Midjourney review](/blog/midjourney-review), and [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Leonardo AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Leonardo AI gives you Phoenix, FLUX, Ideogram and more in one pay-as-you-go platform. Here's how it stacks up and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Leonardo AI worth using in 2026?

Yes, if you want one platform that gives you a whole toolbox of image and video models — FLUX, its own Phoenix models, Ideogram, GPT Image and more — plus editing and upscaling tools, all under a single pay-as-you-go balance. It's less about one signature aesthetic and more about flexibility, which suits people who need control and variety over a single "house style."

**At a glance**

| | Leonardo AI |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Pay-as-you-go — buy a dollar credit balance, no forced monthly plan |
| Free tier/trial | Web app has historically included a modest daily free-token allowance; confirm current amount on the official site, as this has shifted with the PAYG rollout |
| Best for | Creators, marketers and small teams who want access to multiple image/video models plus a canvas-style editor in one place |
| Standout feature | Multi-model access (Phoenix, FLUX, Ideogram, GPT Image, Nano Banana and more) plus Blueprints — 50+ pre-built generation workflows |

## What Leonardo AI actually is

Leonardo AI launched in 2022 as an independent generative-image startup and quickly built a following among game artists and concept designers for its fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models and its own **Phoenix** image models trained in-house. In mid-2024, design giant Canva acquired Leonardo AI, keeping it running as its own product and API at leonardo.ai. That acquisition matters upfront: Leonardo now has design-company backing rather than operating as a scrappy standalone the way it did at launch.

Unlike Midjourney, which is built entirely on its own proprietary diffusion models, Leonardo takes a multi-model marketplace approach. Alongside its own Phoenix models, the platform gives users direct access to third-party models including FLUX (Dev, Schnell, and the Kontext Pro/Max and 2.0 Pro variants), Ideogram 3.0, GPT Image (1.5 through 2.5 "Sunburst"), Google's Nano Banana models, ByteDance's Seedream models, and Lucid Origin/Realism. On the video side, it plugs into Kling (2.1 through 3.0, plus O1/O3), Seedance, FLUX 3 Video, and its own Motion 2.0 tool. In practice, Leonardo functions less like a single-model image generator and more like a hub — you pick the underlying model per job depending on whether you need photorealism, illustration, product shots, or motion.

## Pricing: how Leonardo AI's model actually works now

Leonardo AI's pricing changed meaningfully in 2025–2026: it moved away from its older named subscription tiers (commonly referenced elsewhere as Basic, Standard and Pro) toward a **pay-as-you-go (PAYG)** balance system. Per Leonardo's own documentation, "no monthly commitments, transparent dollar based costs, and automatic top-ups" now define the pricing model — you fund an account balance in US dollars, spend it on generations at per-model rates, and top it up manually or automatically when it runs low. Leonardo states its standardized PAYG rate matches what former Pro-tier subscribers paid, with migrating Basic and Standard subscribers seeing notable savings (Leonardo cites up to 42% and 24% respectively) on future top-ups.

This is a genuinely different structure from Midjourney's flat monthly tiers, and it's a detail older "best AI image generator" roundups often get wrong by quoting legacy $10/$24/$48-style subscription numbers Leonardo has since moved away from. Treat any specific dollar figure you see elsewhere with some skepticism unless it's dated recently.

| Cost driver | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Account balance | Prepaid in US dollars; doesn't expire |
| Per-generation cost | Varies by model and settings (resolution, batch size, upscaling); an in-app calculator estimates cost before generating |
| Top-ups | Manual, or automatic once balance drops below a set threshold |
| API access | Billed separately from web-app usage as a distinct credit purchase |
| Free usage | Historically a modest renewing daily token allowance; confirm current allowance on the official site since PAYG rollout details are still settling |

Pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly — check Leonardo's pricing calculator before budgeting for a project, especially for video, which costs more per output than still images.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

- **Multi-model access from one interface.** Switch between Leonardo's own Phoenix models and third-party models (FLUX, Ideogram, GPT Image, Nano Banana, Seedream) depending on the job — the single biggest practical difference from single-model tools like Midjourney.
- **Blueprints.** A library of 50+ pre-built generation workflows for specific outcomes (product photography, character design, style transfer) so you don't hand-engineer a prompt and settings from scratch each time. Leonardo has said it plans to let users build custom Blueprints in the future.
- **Video and motion tools.** Leonardo integrates third-party video models (Kling, Seedance, FLUX 3 Video) plus its own Motion 2.0 tool for animating stills — a category most pure image generators still handle less directly.
- **Pro Upscaler (Precise and Creative modes).** Two upscaling paths — one for keeping an image faithful while increasing resolution, another for adding creative detail — which matters for anyone shipping final assets rather than just concepting.
- **Developer-friendly API.** A documented REST API with webhooks for async status, separate credit billing, and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server so AI coding assistants can call Leonardo directly.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and freelancers** who need flexibility across styles/models for different client briefs get more mileage from Leonardo's multi-model approach than from a single-aesthetic tool, especially since PAYG billing avoids paying for a fixed monthly quota that goes unused.
- **Small marketing and content teams** producing varied assets (product shots, social graphics, ad creative) benefit from Blueprints cutting down prompt-engineering time.
- **Developers and agencies** building generation into their own product get a real API, webhook support, and now MCP integration — a stronger developer story than Midjourney offers, since Midjourney has no first-party public API.
- **Enterprise design teams already on Canva** may see deeper integration value over time given the acquisition, though Leonardo still operates as its own standalone app and API rather than being fully merged into Canva.
- **Pure aesthetic purists** who want one distinctive look out of the box with minimal tinkering may still prefer Midjourney's more opinionated default style.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Many current-generation image and video models in one account | Learning curve — deciding which model fits a job isn't always obvious |
| PAYG pricing avoids paying for an unused fixed monthly quota | Per-generation costs vary by model, making budgeting less predictable |
| Blueprints speed up common tasks without manual prompt engineering | Video generation costs add up quickly relative to still images |
| Documented API, webhooks and MCP server support for developers | API credits billed separately from web-app balance, adding friction |
| Backed by Canva, adding stability and integration potential | Free tier appears more limited than before; confirm current allowance |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Leonardo's clearest ecosystem strength is its **API**: a documented REST interface with in-app key management, webhook callbacks for real-time status instead of polling, and a pricing calculator to estimate credit usage before running a job. It now also offers an **MCP server**, letting AI coding assistants call Leonardo's generation capabilities directly. Given the Canva acquisition, expect tighter Canva integration over time, though Leonardo is still a separate app and API today. There's no public mention of Zapier or Slack-style no-code integrations at the time of writing — confirm current support directly with Leonardo if you need that.

## Where it's a strong fit

Leonardo AI is a strong fit if you regularly need more than one visual style or medium — say, photorealistic product renders one day and stylized character art the next — and don't want to juggle separate subscriptions to get there. It's also a solid pick for developers who want to build generation into their own product, since the API and webhook setup are more mature and better documented than most image-generation competitors offer publicly. Teams budgeting per-project rather than per-seat will appreciate PAYG, since it scales cost with actual usage instead of a flat recurring fee.

## Where to think twice

Leonardo AI is a weaker fit if you want the simplest possible flat-fee plan with no per-generation math — the PAYG shift, while fairer for light users, makes cost harder to predict up front than a flat tier, especially once video enters the mix. It's also not the right pick if you need a single, highly consistent visual signature with minimal setup: the breadth of model choice that makes Leonardo flexible also means more decisions per project. Skip it, or test thoroughly first, if your team needs formal enterprise compliance documentation (SOC 2, HIPAA) — Leonardo's public materials don't foreground this, so confirm directly with its sales team before signing anything. And if you want a fully free tool for ongoing heavy use, expect to pay for any serious volume of generations here.

## Bottom line

Leonardo AI earns its place by being the AI image platform that doesn't force you to bet on one model's aesthetic. Between its own Phoenix models, third-party heavyweights like FLUX and Ideogram, a genuine video/motion suite, and a real developer API, it covers more ground than most single-model competitors — and Canva's backing gives it staying power. The tradeoff is that PAYG pricing, while more flexible, asks for a bit more cost math than a flat subscription would. If you value model variety and API access over one default look and a fully predictable bill, Leonardo is worth setting up an account for; if you want one distinctive style with zero pricing calculation, a single-model tool may suit you better.

## FAQ

**Is Leonardo AI free to use?**
The web app has historically offered a renewing daily allowance of free generation tokens, but the platform has shifted toward a pay-as-you-go balance model for real usage. Check the current free allowance on Leonardo's official site, since it has changed with the PAYG rollout.

**How does Leonardo AI's pricing work now?**
You fund an account balance in US dollars and spend it per generation at rates that vary by model, resolution and features like upscaling. There's no forced monthly tier anymore — Leonardo says its PAYG rate matches what former Pro-tier subscribers paid, with savings for users migrating from older Basic/Standard tiers.

**Does Leonardo AI have an API?**
Yes. It offers a documented REST API with webhook support for async status updates, plus an MCP server for connecting AI coding assistants directly. API credits are purchased and billed separately from web-app usage.

**What models does Leonardo AI support?**
Its own in-house Phoenix models, plus FLUX (Dev, Schnell, Kontext Pro/Max, 2.0 Pro), Ideogram 3.0, GPT Image (1.5–2.5), Nano Banana, Seedream and Lucid Origin/Realism, along with video models like Kling, Seedance and FLUX 3 Video.

**Is Leonardo AI owned by Canva?**
Yes — Canva acquired Leonardo AI in 2024. It continues to operate as its own product and API rather than being merged directly into Canva's editor, though deeper integration over time is a reasonable expectation.

**How does Leonardo AI compare to Midjourney?**
Midjourney focuses on one polished, proprietary aesthetic via a flat monthly subscription. Leonardo offers many underlying models plus a public API and video tools, priced through a pay-as-you-go balance. See our [Midjourney review](/blog/midjourney-review) for more.

**Is Leonardo AI good for beginners?**
It's approachable for basic prompt-to-image work, but the number of available models can overwhelm newcomers at first. Blueprints help by giving beginners pre-built workflows instead of requiring manual prompt engineering.

**Does Leonardo AI store or train on my images?**
Data handling and usage-rights terms vary by plan and have shifted as Leonardo's ownership and pricing model changed; review its current terms of service and privacy policy before uploading sensitive or client-owned material.

Looking for other AI creative tools? Browse the latest [AI & software deals](/category/software) for more coverage.

title: Dreamina AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Dreamina AI packs ByteDance's Seedream/Seedance models plus Sora 2 and Veo 3.1 access into one app. Here's what it costs and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Dreamina AI worth using for AI image and video generation?

Dreamina AI, built by ByteDance's CapCut division, is a browser-based creative platform that turns text prompts, photos, and sketches into images and short AI videos using a mix of ByteDance's own Seedream/Seedance models plus licensed access to Sora 2 and Veo 3.1. It's a strong pick if you want one dashboard for multiple video models, but the credit system makes serious video work expensive fast.

### At a glance

| | Dreamina AI |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free tier with daily bonus credits; paid plans start around $18/month (billed monthly) |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — daily free credits for image and limited video generation, no credit card required to start |
| Best for | Creators and small teams who want text-to-image, image-to-video, and talking-avatar tools in one place, without juggling separate subscriptions to Midjourney, Runway, and a lip-sync app |
| Standout feature | In-app access to multiple third-party and in-house video models (Seedance 2.5, Sora 2, Veo 3.1) from one credit pool, so you can compare outputs without separate accounts |

## What Dreamina actually is

Dreamina lives at dreamina.capcut.com and is part of ByteDance's CapCut family of creative tools — the same company behind TikTok. That parentage matters: Dreamina isn't a scrappy independent startup betting everything on one model. It's a distribution play by a company that already owns one of the world's largest short-video audiences, bundling AI generation into the same ecosystem that already handles editing and publishing.

On the image side, Dreamina offers its own Seedream models (Seedream 5.0 Pro, Seedream 5.0 Lite, and Seedream 4.5 at the time of writing) alongside Google's Nano Banana and Nano Banana Pro models. On video, it runs its own Seedance line (Dreamina says Seedance 2.5 is its newest, supporting up to 50 reference images for character consistency) plus in-app access to OpenAI's Sora 2 and Google's Veo 3.1. That's the core differentiator versus most single-model AI tools: Dreamina works more like a model marketplace with one shared credit balance, letting you pick whichever engine handles a prompt best rather than committing to one vendor's strengths and blind spots. Model lineups like this shift often, so treat the names above as a snapshot and check the generation screen for what's currently on offer before planning a project around a specific model.

## Dreamina AI pricing

Dreamina's marketing site keeps most plan pricing behind a "sign in to see final pricing" wall — unusual for a consumer AI tool and harder to verify than most. Based on third-party pricing trackers (Futurepedia) rather than the primary source, the structure looks like this:

| Plan | Price | Credits | What it unlocks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0/month | Daily bonus credits (limited) | Basic text-to-image and short video generation, with usage limits and watermarks |
| Basic | ~$18/month | ~1,010 credits/month (roughly 505 images or ~42 videos) | Watermark removal, longer video length, higher resolution, smoother video up to 60fps |
| Standard | ~$42/month | ~4,040 credits/month | Everything in Basic, higher usage ceilings |
| Advanced | ~$84/month | ~13,110 credits/month | Everything in Standard, described as the best per-credit value for heavy users |

Because Dreamina's own pricing page doesn't expose these numbers without an account, and because credit costs for video can be adjusted per model (Sora 2 or Veo 3.1 generations typically burn more credits than a Seedream image or a lightweight Seedance clip), confirm current plan names, prices, and per-model credit costs on Dreamina's pricing screen before subscribing. Pricing and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date per the best available third-party sources, and can change quickly in this category.

## Core features that actually differentiate Dreamina

**Multi-model routing from one credit pool.** Instead of forcing you into one house style, Dreamina lets you switch between Seedream/Seedance and licensed Sora 2 or Veo 3.1 outputs inside the same project, paying from the same balance. If Sora 2 nails a camera move that Seedance fumbles, you can try both without a second subscription.

**Character consistency across up to 50 references.** Dreamina says its newest Seedance model accepts up to 50 reference images to help keep a character's face, outfit, and proportions consistent across a longer sequence — a common failure point in AI video. This is a vendor claim rather than something independently benchmarked here, so test it on your own footage before committing to a full production.

**Photo editing beyond generation.** Dreamina includes AI photo editing tools like background replacement, scene/canvas expansion (outpainting), and style transfer presets (anime, caricature, painterly looks) — closer to a lightweight Photoshop-plus-generator combo than a pure prompt-to-image tool.

**Talking avatars with lip sync.** Upload a photo and audio clip, and Dreamina generates a talking-avatar video with lip-sync matched to the track — useful for explainer clips or localized dubbing mockups without hiring a presenter.

**Sketch-to-video and cartoon generation.** Beyond photorealistic output, Dreamina supports sketch-to-video and stylized cartoon generation, aimed more at storyboard artists and social creators than photoreal VFX work.

## Who Dreamina is actually for

- **Solo content creators and TikTok/Reels creators** — the CapCut-adjacent branding and short-form focus (30-second clips, talking avatars, cartoon styles) map onto social workflows, and free daily credits let you test the waters first.
- **Small teams that want to A/B test video models** — the Basic or Standard tier suits a team making a steady trickle of short marketing clips who wants to compare Sora 2 against Seedance without three separate subscriptions.
- **Heavy video producers** — the Advanced tier's larger allotment targets volume, but do your own math on cost-per-finished-clip first, since licensed models burn credits faster.
- **Pure image generators on a budget** — a dedicated image tool may give more control per dollar; Dreamina's shared pool also funds video, so image-only users may pay for headroom they don't use.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Multiple video models (Seedance, Sora 2, Veo 3.1) from one account and credit pool | Pricing page hides plan details behind a sign-in wall |
| Free daily credits to test image and video generation without a card | Video credit consumption, especially on licensed models, burns through allotments fast |
| Covers image generation, photo editing, video, and talking avatars in one tool | Backed by ByteDance/CapCut — some orgs may have data-residency or trust concerns |
| Character-reference support (up to 50 images, per vendor claims) for video consistency | Consistency claims aren't independently benchmarked; results vary by prompt |
| Built-in style transfer and outpainting reduce the need for a separate photo editor | No confirmed API/developer access at review time |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Dreamina is a standalone web app rather than a plug-in-heavy platform. There's no confirmed public API, Zapier connector, or Slack integration on its marketing pages — confirm directly with support if programmatic access matters to you. Its practical "integration" story is ecosystem proximity: outputs are a natural fit for further editing in CapCut and eventual publishing to TikTok, even though the tools aren't deeply wired together as of this review.

## Where Dreamina is a strong fit

- You want to experiment with several different AI video models (in-house and licensed) without maintaining three or four separate subscriptions.
- Your output is mostly short-form (social, marketing snippets, talking-avatar explainers) rather than long-form cinematic production.
- You value having image editing (background swap, outpainting, style transfer) alongside generation in the same tab.
- You're comfortable starting on the free tier to judge output quality before paying for credits.

## Where to think twice

- **If you need transparent, comparison-ready pricing up front** — the sign-in wall on Dreamina's pricing page is a real friction point; third-party trackers get closer than the vendor site, but numbers can lag reality.
- **If your organization has strict data-sovereignty or vendor-trust requirements** — as a ByteDance product, some enterprise teams may face policy restrictions a Western-owned alternative wouldn't trigger; check your vendor policy first.
- **If you need guaranteed API/developer access** — Dreamina reads as a finished consumer app, not an extensible platform; confirm whether any API exists before building automation around it.
- **If you're on a tight, predictable video budget** — credit costs vary by model, and licensed models like Sora 2 or Veo 3.1 cost more per clip than in-house Seedance.
- **If you need a fully free, unlimited tool** — the free tier is a trial mechanism (limited, likely watermarked), not a permanent free plan.

## The bottom line

Dreamina's real pitch isn't that its own Seedream and Seedance models beat every specialist outright — it's that you get several strong video and image models from one interface and one credit pool, backed by a company with genuine distribution muscle in short-form video. That's useful if you want to compare Sora 2 against Seedance on the same brief without separate accounts, or want image generation, photo editing, and talking avatars without juggling four tools. The trade-offs are real: pricing transparency lags a mature SaaS product, credit costs for premium video can eat a plan fast, and ByteDance ownership will be a non-starter for some organizations regardless of quality. If your use case is short-form social video and you're fine testing the free tier first, Dreamina is worth a look. If you need predictable enterprise pricing, API access, or want to avoid ByteDance-owned software, look elsewhere.

## Dreamina AI FAQ

**Is Dreamina AI free to use?**
There's a free tier with daily bonus credits for image and limited video generation, but it has usage caps and likely watermarks. Regular or high-volume use requires a paid plan.

**Who owns Dreamina AI?**
Dreamina is built by CapCut, ByteDance's video-editing division — the same parent company behind TikTok.

**What AI models does Dreamina use?**
For images: its own Seedream models (5.0 Pro/Lite, 4.5) plus Google's Nano Banana and Nano Banana Pro. For video: its own Seedance models plus licensed access to OpenAI's Sora 2 and Google's Veo 3.1. Availability can change, so check the generation screen for the current lineup.

**How much does Dreamina AI cost?**
Third-party trackers put paid plans starting around $18/month for roughly 1,010 credits, scaling to around $84/month for larger allotments, but Dreamina's own site requires sign-in to show final pricing — confirm current numbers there before subscribing.

**Does Dreamina AI have a watermark on free outputs?**
Watermark removal is listed as a paid-plan feature, which strongly implies free-tier outputs carry a watermark. Confirm current behavior in-app since free-tier terms can change.

**Is Dreamina good for talking-avatar or lip-sync videos?**
Yes — talking-avatar generation with audio-driven lip sync is one of its named features, aimed at quick explainer or presenter-style clips without filming a real person.

**Does Dreamina AI offer an API for developers?**
No public API or developer documentation was found on Dreamina's marketing pages at review time; it reads as a consumer web app rather than a build-on-top platform. Confirm directly with support if you need programmatic access.

**What are the best alternatives to Dreamina AI?**
For pure image generation, [Midjourney](/blog/midjourney-review) remains a strong specialist option. For AI video specifically, [Runway](/blog/runway-review) is a comparable multi-tool platform worth comparing on pricing and output style before you commit to either.

For more AI and software tool coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Prezi AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Prezi AI drafts zooming presentations and runs live polls. Here's what its pricing tiers, features, and analytics mean before you subscribe.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Prezi AI Review 2026: Is the Zooming Presentation Tool Worth It?

Prezi AI is worth trying if you want a non-linear, zoomable presentation with built-in live audience polls and Q&A, not just another slide-deck generator. It drafts a full Prezi from a prompt and can restyle an imported PowerPoint. It's a weaker fit if all you want is a fast, flat slide deck for export.

## At a glance

| | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free (Basic plan, no credit card required) |
| Free tier/trial | Free plan covers core zooming presentations and viewing; AI generation limits, offline access, and analytics are gated behind paid tiers |
| Best for | Presenters and trainers who want a zoomable, non-linear canvas plus live polls/Q&A rather than a flat slide export |
| Standout feature | AI drafts a full zooming presentation from a prompt or restyles an imported deck, and every Prezi can run live audience polls, quizzes, and Q&A via a QR code |

## What Prezi AI actually is

Prezi isn't a new AI startup bolting a chatbot onto a blank canvas — it's a 2009-founded presentation company, headquartered jointly in Budapest and San Francisco, known for "zooming presentations": instead of a linear stack of slides, you work on one large canvas and Prezi's viewer pans and zooms between sections, making it easier to show how ideas relate rather than just what order they come in. Co-founders Adam Somlai-Fischer, Peter Halacsy, and Peter Arvai built the original zoom-and-pan engine; the company now reportedly serves well over 100 million users worldwide.

Prezi AI is the generative layer added on top of that existing product, introduced in 2024. Describe what you want in a prompt and Prezi drafts a canvas with sections, layout, and copy already placed; you can also drop in an existing PowerPoint, Google Slides deck, Canva file, PDF, or Word document and have Prezi restyle it rather than starting blank. Prezi doesn't publish which underlying language or image models power this drafting step, so treat "AI-generated" here as Prezi's own framing, not a verified technical spec.

Where Prezi AI meaningfully diverges from tools like [Gamma](/blog/gamma-review) or [PPT AI](/blog/ppt-ai-review) is that generation is only half the product. Prezi layers live-session features on top of whatever you generate: audience members join by scanning a QR code (no app, no login) and can answer polls, submit questions, or take a quiz while you're presenting, and Prezi turns the results into analytics showing which parts of the content people understood and where they got stuck. A deck generator alone doesn't solve "did my audience actually follow this" — Prezi is built around that use case specifically.

## Pricing

Prezi's plan structure resembles most SaaS presentation tools: free to start, then paid individual tiers adding capacity and AI generation, plus team/business plans with admin controls. Prezi's pricing page renders dynamically and doesn't expose static prices, and figures have changed before without notice, so rather than guessing dollar amounts, here's what each tier generally includes — **confirm the current price for your region on [Prezi's pricing page](https://prezi.com/pricing/) before subscribing.**

| Plan tier | Who it's for | What's generally included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free / Basic | First-time users | Zooming canvas editor, capped AI generation, public sharing, basic templates |
| Plus (individual) | Regular solo presenters | Higher AI limits, private presentations, more storage, desktop offline access |
| Premium (individual) | Consultants, trainers | Highest individual AI limits, branding removal, priority support, live-session analytics |
| Teams / Business | Small-to-mid teams | Shared brand templates, centralized billing, team analytics, admin/user management |
| Enterprise | Large orgs, compliance needs | SSO, dedicated account management, custom contracts, security guarantees |

Worth flagging: like most AI-generation products, Prezi meters AI drafting/restyling separately from plain editing, so a paid seat usually means a higher cap, not unlimited AI. This detail, and exact prices/free-tier caps, was last checked as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change.

## Core features walkthrough

**Prompt-to-canvas AI drafting.** Describe your topic and Prezi generates a structured, zoomable presentation with sections and imagery placed already, rather than a flat sequence of slides. Same "skip the blank page" pitch as Gamma or PPT AI, but the output is Prezi's own canvas, not exportable slides-first content.

**Import and restyle.** Bring in an existing PowerPoint, Google Slides deck, Canva design, PDF, or Word doc and have Prezi AI reformat it into a zooming presentation — useful if your organization has a library of static decks to modernize without rebuilding from scratch.

**Live polls, quizzes, and Q&A.** Every Prezi can run interactive audience features during a live or hybrid session. Viewers join via QR code, no app or account required, removing the friction that kills most audience-response tools.

**Post-session content repurposing.** Prezi says it can turn a finished presentation into a narrated video, podcast-style audio, transcript, or standalone quiz after the session — useful for training content that needs to live on past the meeting.

**Comprehension analytics.** Because polls and quizzes are built in, Prezi can show which sections audiences got wrong most often, turning a one-way presentation into a feedback loop — a feature with no real equivalent in a pure slide-generation tool.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo presenters and freelancers** giving the same pitch or training repeatedly get the most from Plus/Premium AI limits and offline access, iterating on one canvas instead of rebuilding slides each time.
- **Corporate trainers and educators** are the clearest fit for the whole product — the live quiz and comprehension-analytics loop is built for anyone who needs to prove a session landed, not just deliver it.
- **Small teams and agencies** co-authoring decks get more from the Teams plan's shared templates and centralized billing than from AI drafting alone.
- **Enterprises with compliance requirements** (SSO, dedicated support, contractual terms) are pushed toward the Enterprise tier, where pricing is quote-based.
- **Anyone who just needs a fast, flat slide deck to export as PPTX and never touch again** is better served by a straightforward generator — see the trade-offs below.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Zooming, non-linear canvas is genuinely different from slide-based competitors | Real learning curve for teams used to linear slides; can feel gimmicky for a simple update deck |
| Built-in live polls, Q&A, and quizzes via QR code, no separate app needed | Free tier's AI generation cap is tight; heavier use pushes you into paid tiers fast |
| Import and restyle of existing PowerPoint/Slides/Canva files preserves prior work | Pricing isn't posted as static numbers — check the live pricing page or sales for team/enterprise quotes |
| Comprehension analytics from live sessions has no real equivalent among competitors | Exported flat PPTX loses what makes the zooming canvas distinct, and can look plainer than the live version |
| Long track record (founded 2009), large existing user base | AI drafting still needs manual cleanup on layout, imagery, and copy tone, like most AI presentation tools |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Prezi imports directly from PowerPoint, Google Slides, Canva, PDF, and Word, covering most existing content libraries without a manual re-typing step. It exports presentations and supports embedding for sharing elsewhere. It doesn't market a public API or a large third-party app marketplace the way some newer AI tools do — the ecosystem play is "bring your existing files in, present with the audience layer on top," not plugging into a broader Zapier/Slack-style stack. Confirm current API/integration availability directly with Prezi if that matters to your workflow.

## Where it's a strong fit

Prezi AI earns its place when the presentation is part of a live, interactive session — sales pitches with audience Q&A, corporate training where you want to check comprehension, or a recurring talk where the zooming format shows how ideas connect rather than just listing them. QR-code polling with no app requirement gets real-time feedback most slide tools don't offer.

It's also solid for teams with existing decks who want to refresh them without rebuilding from a blank canvas — import-and-restyle starts from your actual content, not a generic AI-invented outline.

## Where to think twice

If you need a fully free, unlimited tool with no plan to ever upgrade, Prezi's free-tier AI cap will feel restrictive fast — you'll hit the ceiling and need Plus or Premium to keep generating.

If your team is attached to a linear, slide-by-slide workflow and mainly needs a polished PPTX to email around, the zooming canvas is a format shift some find awkward, and exporting flattens away what makes Prezi different — [Gamma](/blog/gamma-review) or [PPT AI](/blog/ppt-ai-review) get you to a familiar-looking deck faster.

If your organization needs enterprise compliance guarantees (SOC 2, DPAs, SSO) confirmed upfront, that sits behind a sales conversation, not a self-serve page.

If you need offline, on-prem, or fully self-hosted use, Prezi is cloud-based SaaS — offline access on some plans means a cached desktop copy, not running the platform outside Prezi's own infrastructure.

## Bottom line

Prezi AI is genuinely different from the wave of "type a prompt, get a deck" tools, because the AI drafting step is bolted onto a mature zooming-canvas platform with live audience engagement and comprehension analytics built in, not the other way around. If your presentations are one-way exports that live in an email attachment, that extra machinery is overhead you don't need, and a leaner generator serves you better. If your presentations are live sessions where you want to know whether the room understood you, Prezi AI's combination of prompt-to-canvas drafting, no-app polling, and post-session analytics is hard to find bundled anywhere else. Start on the free plan and judge the zooming format on your own content before paying.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Prezi AI free to use?**
Prezi offers a free Basic plan with no credit card required, including the zooming canvas editor and a capped amount of AI generation. Heavier drafting, offline access, and advanced analytics require Plus, Premium, Teams, or Enterprise — confirm current caps on [Prezi's pricing page](https://prezi.com/pricing/), since free-tier limits change over time.

**How is Prezi AI different from Gamma or PPT AI?**
Gamma and PPT AI generate flat, exportable slide decks quickly from a prompt or document. Prezi AI generates onto its own non-linear zooming canvas and bundles in live polls, Q&A, quizzes, and post-session comprehension analytics — features neither offers natively. See our [Gamma review](/blog/gamma-review) and [PPT AI review](/blog/ppt-ai-review) if a flat slide export is closer to what you need.

**Can I import an existing PowerPoint into Prezi?**
Yes. Prezi imports PowerPoint, Google Slides, Canva files, PDFs, and Word documents, and its AI can restyle imported content into Prezi's zooming format instead of rebuilding from a blank prompt.

**What AI model does Prezi AI use?**
Prezi doesn't publish the underlying model(s) powering its generation features, so treat capability claims as Prezi's own marketing framing, not a verified technical spec.

**Does Prezi work well for live audience engagement without a separate app?**
Yes — one of its clearer differentiators. Audience members scan a QR code to join polls, quizzes, and Q&A in their phone browser, with no app download or account creation required.

**Is Prezi AI good for beginners?**
The prompt-to-canvas step is beginner-friendly like most AI generators — a usable first draft, fast. The canvas editor itself has a steeper learning curve than a flat slide editor if you want to fine-tune the pan-and-zoom path, since you're editing spatial relationships, not a simple slide order.

**What are the best alternatives to Prezi AI?**
For fast, flat slide-deck generation without the zooming-canvas learning curve, see our [Gamma review](/blog/gamma-review) and [PPT AI review](/blog/ppt-ai-review). For general software savings, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Sora 2 Review 2026: Features, Shutdown and Alternatives
excerpt: Sora 2 review 2026: OpenAI's video-and-audio model was discontinued this year — what it offered, why it was shut down, and what to use now.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Sora 2 worth using in 2026?

Sora 2 was OpenAI's text-to-video-and-audio model and companion app, and it was genuinely capable — strong physics, synced sound, a consent-based "cameo" feature. But it's largely moot now: OpenAI announced on March 24, 2026 it was discontinuing Sora, shut the app down April 26, 2026, and retires the API September 24, 2026. This review covers what it offered and what to use instead.

## At a glance

| | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Current status | Discontinued — app shut down April 26, 2026; API shuts down September 24, 2026 |
| Starting price (while live) | Free tier via ChatGPT (compute-limited); full access from ChatGPT Plus, $20/month |
| Free tier/trial | Yes, generous but capacity-limited generations; no permanent free plan survived |
| Best for | Was best for social-style short clips with dialogue/sound and cameo-based content |
| Standout feature | Synchronized audio (speech, sound effects, ambient soundscapes) generated with the video, not layered on after |

## What Sora 2 actually was

Sora 2 was OpenAI's second-generation video-generation model, launched September 30, 2025 alongside a standalone iOS app (Android followed roughly two months later). It succeeded the original Sora model OpenAI first previewed in February 2024, built to fix the two things reviewers criticized most about that first version: audio and physical realism.

Two things separated Sora 2 from most of the field at launch. First, it generated audio in the same pass as the video — dialogue, footsteps, ambient background noise, sound effects — rather than requiring a separate voice or sound tool bolted on afterward, which is still how many competing text-to-video tools work. Second, OpenAI put real effort into physical plausibility: a missed basketball shot rebounds off the rim instead of the model "teleporting" it into the hoop to satisfy the prompt, a common failure mode in earlier-generation video models (including Sora's own first version). OpenAI's own materials described this as the model no longer "hallucinating" its way around physics it doesn't understand — worth reading as OpenAI's characterization of its own model rather than an independently verified benchmark, since standardized physics-accuracy scoring for video models isn't a settled practice.

The other defining piece of Sora 2 wasn't the model at all, it was the app. OpenAI shipped a TikTok-style vertical feed alongside the model, with algorithmic recommendations, a "cameo" feature that let a user record a short video/audio sample and then appear (with revocable consent) in other people's AI-generated clips, and social features like remixing and sharing. That app-first framing is a meaningful difference from [Runway](/blog/runway-review) or [Hailuo AI](/blog/hailuo-ai-review), both built as creation tools first, with no built-in public feed or social discovery layer.

## Pricing while it was live

Pricing below reflects Sora 2 as it existed before OpenAI's discontinuation announcement on March 24, 2026, and shouldn't be taken as current — the product no longer accepts new sign-ups and is being wound down entirely by September 24, 2026.

| Access tier | Price | What it included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free (ChatGPT Free) | $0 | Limited Sora generations, subject to OpenAI's compute availability at any given time |
| ChatGPT Plus | $20/month | Sora 2 access with higher generation limits than free |
| ChatGPT Pro | $200/month | Sora 2 Pro — OpenAI's higher-quality video tier, plus priority access during high-demand periods |
| Sora 2 API (standard) | $0.10/second (720p) | Programmatic access for developers; $0.05/second on the batch API |
| Sora 2 Pro API | $0.30–$0.70/second depending on resolution (720p/1024p/1080p) | Higher-resolution output; $0.15–$0.35/second on the batch API |

There was never a dedicated "Sora-only" subscription — access rode on top of existing ChatGPT Plus/Pro plans, part of why the shutdown affects ChatGPT subscribers rather than a standalone customer base the way it would for Runway or Hailuo.

## Features walkthrough

- **Synchronized audio generation.** Sora 2 produced speech, sound effects and ambient soundscapes in the same generation pass as the visuals, rather than as a separate step — arguably its biggest differentiator versus most competing video models at the time.
- **Improved physics and multi-shot consistency.** The model respected cause and effect (objects bounce, fall or fail realistically instead of morphing to fit the prompt) and kept a consistent "world state" — character appearance, setting, lighting — across multiple shots in one generation.
- **Cameo.** Users recorded a short verification video and voice sample, after which their likeness could appear in Sora-generated videos — their own or, with permission, other users' — with the ability to revoke access at any time. OpenAI positioned this as a consent-first alternative to the uncontrolled deepfake risk already dogging other video tools.
- **A built-in social feed.** Sora 2's app had a vertical, algorithmically-ranked feed for discovering and remixing other people's generations — the part of the product that drew the most comparisons to TikTok, and reportedly the part OpenAI leadership grew least comfortable subsidizing.
- **Rights-holder and moderation controls.** Sora 2 initially defaulted to allowing recognizable copyrighted characters and public figures unless the rights holder opted out — a stance OpenAI walked back under pressure, adding granular opt-in/opt-out controls, restrictions on certain public figures (it specifically restricted depictions of Martin Luther King Jr. after complaints from his estate), and teen-specific limits with parental controls tied to a ChatGPT account.

## Who it was actually for

- **Social-first short-form creators** who wanted dialogue and sound baked into a single generation rather than stitching a silent clip to a separate voice tool — Sora 2's clearest edge over competitors.
- **ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscribers** already inside OpenAI's ecosystem who wanted video generation without signing up for a separate vendor.
- **Developers prototyping video features** via the API, at $0.10–$0.70 per second depending on model tier and resolution.
- A weaker fit for **professional production and VFX work**: Artificial Analysis ranked Sora 2 Pro behind competitors like Runway's Gen-4.5 and ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 on several benchmarks even before the shutdown.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Synchronized audio generation was ahead of most competitors at launch | Discontinued — API shuts down entirely on September 24, 2026 |
| Genuinely improved physics/causality vs. the original Sora model | Ranked behind some rivals on independent leaderboards despite the audio edge |
| Cameo offered real consent and revocation controls, not just an opt-out disclaimer | Watermark-removal tools appeared within about a week of launch |
| Access rode on existing ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscriptions — no separate signup | Rights-holder controls were reactive, added after backlash |
| API pricing was transparent and usage-based | User base fell from roughly one million to under 500,000 before shutdown |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Sora 2's main integration point was ChatGPT itself — Plus and Pro subscribers got access inside the same account and billing relationship, plus a standalone Sora app for the social feed and cameo features. For developers, OpenAI shipped a Sora 2 preview in its API in October 2025 (announced at DevDay), with per-second, resolution-tiered pricing and a cheaper batch option for non-real-time jobs. There was no dedicated Zapier, Slack or third-party plugin ecosystem around Sora — it lived inside OpenAI's own surfaces only.

## Where it was a strong fit

Sora 2 made the most sense for short-form, sound-inclusive social content — a single generation with matching dialogue or ambient audio saved a real editing step compared to most competing generators, which still hand you a silent clip. The cameo system was also a more thoughtful approach to consent than most "upload a face" features elsewhere in AI video, even though it arrived alongside a rocky rollout of copyright and likeness controls.

## Where to think twice (and why it doesn't matter now)

The honest answer here is that "should I use Sora 2" is now the wrong question, it's discontinued. If you're researching it because you saw old reviews or screenshots, know that:

- The consumer app stopped working on April 26, 2026, and no new accounts have been onboarded since OpenAI's March 24, 2026 announcement.
- The developer API is scheduled to be shut off completely on September 24, 2026, so any project still calling it needs a migration plan now, not later.
- If you need offline/on-prem generation or a vendor that won't sunset the product mid-project, Sora 2 was never a good fit even while it was live — OpenAI reportedly cited compute costs of roughly $1 million a day and declining engagement as factors.
- For production-grade editing control, [Runway](/blog/runway-review) remains the more mature choice, with its Gen-4.5 model and Aleph editing tools built for filmmakers and agencies rather than a social feed.
- For fast, low-cost clips for marketing or social content, [Hailuo AI](/blog/hailuo-ai-review) is a closer like-for-like replacement for the casual generation Sora 2 was used for, at a lower price point and without a ChatGPT-subscription dependency.

## The bottom line

Sora 2 was a legitimately strong video model wrapped in a product bet — a TikTok-style social app — that OpenAI wasn't willing to keep subsidizing. Its audio-and-video-in-one-pass approach and cameo consent system were ahead of a lot of the competition on paper, and reviewers generally agreed the model itself was solid, if not always the outright leader. But solid model quality couldn't offset a reported $1-million-a-day compute bill against a user base that had roughly halved from its peak, and OpenAI pulled the plug less than six months after launch. For anyone comparing AI video tools today, Sora 2 is as much a cautionary example of platform risk as a case study in model design — budget for migration risk with any single-vendor AI video tool. For active options, see [Runway](/blog/runway-review), [Hailuo AI](/blog/hailuo-ai-review), or browse [AI & software deals](/category/software) for tools still actively supported.

## FAQ

**Is Sora 2 still available?**
No. OpenAI announced on March 24, 2026 that it was discontinuing Sora, shut down the consumer app on April 26, 2026, and is retiring API access on September 24, 2026. No new sign-ups have been accepted since the announcement.

**Why did OpenAI shut down Sora?**
No single official reason was given, but reporting pointed to compute costs (reportedly around $1 million a day), a decline in active users (from roughly one million at peak to fewer than 500,000), and a broader strategic shift toward enterprise products over consumer social apps.

**What happens to videos I already made in Sora 2?**
Check your ChatGPT/OpenAI account settings directly for current data-retention and export guidance before the September 24, 2026 API cutoff — OpenAI hasn't published stable, citable export mechanics this review can confirm, and details are likely to shift as the shutdown date approaches.

**Was Sora 2 free to use?**
It had a free tier through ChatGPT's free plan with compute-limited generations, but full access required ChatGPT Plus ($20/month) or ChatGPT Pro ($200/month) for the higher-quality Sora 2 Pro tier.

**How was Sora 2 different from the original Sora?**
The original Sora (previewed February 2024) generated silent video only and had more visible physics errors, objects and scenes would shift or "teleport" to satisfy a prompt. Sora 2 added synchronized audio generation and meaningfully improved physical consistency and multi-shot continuity.

**Is there a replacement for Sora 2's cameo feature elsewhere?**
Not with an identical consent-and-revocation model as far as this review can confirm. Several competing tools offer likeness-based avatar or face-swap features, but check each tool's specific consent and rights-management terms rather than assume parity with what Sora 2 offered.

**What should I use instead of Sora 2 now?**
For production-grade editing and camera control, [Runway](/blog/runway-review) is the closer comparison. For fast, low-cost social-style clips, [Hailuo AI](/blog/hailuo-ai-review) is a reasonable substitute for what a lot of people used Sora 2 for casually.

title: Submagic Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Submagic auto-captions and edits short-form video fast, but its credit-based pricing needs a closer look. Full pricing and feature breakdown.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Submagic Review 2026: Is It Worth It for Short-Form Video?

Submagic is a browser-based AI editor built specifically for short-form video creators, adding auto-generated captions, B-roll, sound effects, and viral-style subtitle animations to raw footage in minutes. It's genuinely fast for TikTok/Reels/Shorts editing, though its per-video credit system and 2-minute cap on the entry plan make it pricier than it first looks for high-volume creators.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $19/month (Starter, billed monthly) |
| Free tier/trial | No credit card required to try; no permanent free plan |
| Best for | Solo creators and small teams editing short-form vertical video |
| Standout feature | Auto-captioning in 123 languages with viral-style subtitle presets |

## What Submagic actually is

Submagic is a France-based AI video editing platform aimed squarely at people who publish short-form vertical video for a living — podcast clippers, TikTok creators, UGC agencies, and social media teams. Instead of positioning itself as a full timeline editor like Premiere or CapCut, it leans into one job: take a raw clip, run it through automated captioning, B-roll insertion, and pacing cleanup, and hand back something close to publish-ready.

The company states it serves more than 4 million users spanning solo creators, media companies, and business teams. Submagic doesn't publicly disclose which underlying speech-to-text or generative models power its captioning and B-roll matching — like most tools in this category, it treats that as proprietary, so take any specific accuracy figure as a vendor claim rather than an independently verified benchmark.

## Pricing

| Plan | Monthly price | Annual price (per month) | Credits / videos | Max video length | Export quality |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $19 | $12 | 45 credits (~15 videos) | 2 minutes | 1080p, 30 FPS |
| Pro | $39 | $23 | 120 credits (~40 videos) | 5 minutes | 1080p, 30 FPS |
| Business | $69 | $41 | 300 credits (~100 videos) | 30 minutes | 4K, 60 FPS |
| Custom (Enterprise) | Contact sales | Contact sales | Negotiated | Negotiated | 4K, 60 FPS |

Submagic doesn't run on a flat per-seat subscription the way many SaaS tools do — it runs on a credit system, where each processed video consumes credits depending on length and the features used (auto-zoom, premium B-roll, and Storyblocks audio all draw more credits on higher tiers). Annual billing knocks the effective monthly price down by roughly 35–41% across all three tiers, which matters here more than usual because the credit allotments, not just feature lists, change between plans.

There's also a separate API credit add-on, priced from roughly $57 to $1,000 a month for blocks of processing minutes (about $0.10–$0.23 per minute depending on volume), aimed at teams building Submagic's captioning into their own pipeline rather than using the web app directly.

Pricing, credit allotments, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — AI video tools iterate fast on both pricing tiers and what's gated behind them, so confirm current numbers on [Submagic's pricing page](https://submagic.co/pricing) before subscribing.

There is no permanent free plan — Submagic offers a no-credit-card trial to test the editor, then requires a paid plan to keep exporting.

## Features walkthrough

**Auto-captioning with viral-style presets.** This is the core of the product. Submagic transcribes spoken audio and generates burned-in captions styled after the bold, high-contrast, word-by-word animated look popularized by top-performing TikTok and Reels content. Submagic states its captioning supports 123 languages and claims roughly 99% transcription accuracy — a figure that, like most speech-to-text accuracy claims, will vary by audio quality, accent, and background noise, so treat it as a ceiling rather than a guarantee.

**AI B-roll and stock footage insertion.** Rather than manually hunting for cutaway footage, Submagic can automatically detect moments in a script that would benefit from supplementary visuals and drop in matched B-roll from its library — Storyblocks-sourced clips and audio on the Pro and Business tiers, a smaller "free" library on Starter.

**Silence removal and pacing cleanup.** The editor automatically trims dead air and awkward pauses, which is the single most tedious manual task in short-form editing and the one most creators cite as the reason they'd pay for automation in the first place.

**Magic Clips and highlight detection.** For creators repurposing long-form content (podcasts, webinars, livestreams) into shorts, Submagic can scan a longer recording and surface the segments most likely to work as standalone clips, saving the scrubbing-through-hours-of-footage step.

**AI avatars and scriptless generation.** Newer additions let users generate a talking AI avatar video from a script alone, without filming anything — a feature aimed more at faceless-channel operators than at creators clipping their own footage.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and podcast clippers**: The Starter plan's 2-minute cap fits typical TikTok/Reels/Shorts lengths, and 45 credits a month is enough for a few posts a week without needing the Pro tier's extra length or premium B-roll.
- **Agencies and UGC teams managing multiple accounts**: Pro's 5-minute cap and premium B-roll/audio library cover most branded short-form work, and the higher credit pool supports posting daily across a handful of client accounts.
- **Media companies and high-volume publishers**: Business unlocks 30-minute clips, 4K/60fps export, unlimited custom templates, and priority support — useful for teams repurposing full podcast episodes or long interviews into dozens of clips a week.
- **Developers building captioning into their own product**: The API add-on lets teams pipe Submagic's transcription and styling into an existing app or workflow rather than using the hosted editor at all.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Fast turnaround from raw clip to captioned, styled short | Credit-based system makes real monthly cost harder to predict than a flat subscription |
| Wide language support (123 languages) for captions and translation | No permanent free plan — only a no-card trial |
| Automated B-roll, silence removal, and highlight detection cut real manual editing time | Starter plan's 2-minute cap and standard export quality feel restrictive for the price |
| Scales up to 4K/60fps and 30-minute clips on the Business plan | Underlying transcription/AI models aren't publicly disclosed, so accuracy claims can't be independently verified |
| API access available for teams wanting to embed captioning in their own workflow | Premium B-roll, audio, and auto-zoom are locked behind Pro and Business, not Starter |

## Integrations and ecosystem
