title: Math AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Math AI (Farabi Math AI) scans homework problems and gives step-by-step solutions. Here's what it costs, what it does well, and its real limits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Math AI worth downloading?

Math AI (marketed as Farabi Math AI, listed on the App Store as "Math AI Homework Helper, Solver") is a solid pick if you need fast, camera-scanned step-by-step help with algebra, calculus, or basic arithmetic. It's free to try, but full step-by-step breakdowns sit behind a subscription, and it's iOS-only as of this writing.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free to download; step-by-step solutions unlock with a paid plan from roughly $4.99/week |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — free download with limited solves, plus a short trial on some subscription tiers |
| **Best for** | Students who want quick photo-based answers to homework problems |
| **Standout feature** | Camera scanning that reads handwritten or printed math and returns multiple solving methods |

Math AI isn't a productivity suite or a general chatbot wearing a math costume — it's a narrow, purpose-built utility. Point your phone camera at a problem, and it tries to recognize the expression, work through it, and hand back an explanation. That narrowness is both its appeal and its limit.

## What Math AI actually is

Math AI is developed under the "Farabi Math AI" brand by a mobile app studio (App Store listings show the publisher as Must Have Apps / Lunapark Medya Internet Teknolojileri, a Turkey-based mobile app company), and it's distributed through its own site at mathhero.co. The app has been live on Apple's App Store since 2021, updated regularly since, and shows more than 30,000 ratings averaging 4.7 out of 5 stars in Apple's own listing data as of this writing.

The company doesn't publish exactly which underlying AI model or OCR engine powers its recognition and solving pipeline — typical for smaller math-solver apps, which usually combine computer-vision OCR for reading the problem with either a rules-based solving engine or a third-party language model for the explanation layer, rather than a custom-trained foundation model. If the exact model matters for your use case, ask the app's support team directly rather than trusting the marketing copy.

Functionally, Math AI sits in the same lane as Photomath, Microsoft Math Solver, Mathway, and newer entrants like MathGPT and Gauth — all built around the same core loop: scan, recognize, solve, explain. What differentiates them comes down to accuracy on messy handwriting, depth of explanations, subject coverage, and price.

## Pricing

Math AI is free to download, but full step-by-step explanations and unlimited scans sit behind an auto-renewing subscription. Based on the in-app purchase tiers listed on Math AI's App Store page:

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| **Free download** | $0 | Camera scanning, a limited number of free solves, basic history |
| **Weekly (with trial)** | Around $4.99–$5.99/week, often with a short (roughly 3-day) free trial | Unlimited step-by-step solutions, graphing calculator, multiple solving methods |
| **Weekly (no trial)** | Around $5.99–$6.99/week | Same as above, billed immediately with no trial period |
| **Annual (Math AI Pro)** | Around $19.99–$39.99/year depending on promotion | Full feature access at a lower effective monthly cost than the weekly plans |
| **Lifetime / one-time (listed as "Math Hero")** | Seen ranging roughly $9.99–$59.99 depending on promotional pricing | One-time unlock, no recurring billing |

These figures come from pricing strings published in the app's own App Store listing rather than a dedicated pricing page, and app stores frequently A/B test price points and promos for the same tier — so what you're quoted in-app may not match any single row above exactly. Like most subscription utility apps, the weekly plan is the most expensive way to pay by a wide margin; using it beyond a single session, go annual or one-time instead. Pricing, free-tier limits, and features were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change without notice — check the current in-app pricing screen before subscribing.

## Features walkthrough

**Camera-based problem scanning.** This is the app's core mechanic. Point your camera at a printed textbook page or a handwritten worksheet, and the app attempts to isolate the expression, recognize the characters, and convert it into something it can compute against. Handwriting recognition is inherently the weaker link — clean, printed math scans far more reliably than sloppy handwriting or crowded pages with multiple problems.

**Step-by-step explanations, not just answers.** Rather than a single final number, Math AI walks through intermediate steps — the point for a student trying to learn the method, not just fill in a blank. It also advertises scrolling through multiple solving methods for the same problem, useful when a teacher wants a specific technique (e.g., completing the square vs. the quadratic formula).

**Built-in graphing calculator.** For algebra and pre-calculus work involving functions, having a graphing tool inside the same app avoids switching to a separate calculator mid-problem.

**Subject breadth.** The app's own listing claims coverage from basic arithmetic and pre-algebra through algebra, calculus (limits, derivatives, integrals, curve sketching), and statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, permutations, combinations). That's a wide net for a mobile scanning app, though coverage claims and real-world reliability on edge cases — word problems, multi-step proofs, unusual notation — can diverge, so treat unfamiliar or high-stakes problem types with some skepticism until tested.

**Solve history.** Previously solved problems save to a history tab, a small but genuinely convenient feature for reviewing a batch of homework later rather than rescanning.

## Who it's actually for

- **Middle and high school students** doing algebra, geometry, or early calculus homework are the clearest fit — the scan-and-explain workflow maps directly onto "I'm stuck on problem 7."
- **College students** in intro calculus or statistics may find it useful for arithmetic-heavy steps, but should expect it to struggle more as problems move further from standard textbook phrasing.
- **Parents helping with homework** get a low-effort way to check a step-by-step method before helping their kid.
- **Advanced math, research, or proof-heavy work** is a poor fit — this is a homework-scan utility, not a computer algebra system like Wolfram Mathematica, and isn't built for symbolic proof verification.
- **Anyone who needs Android** should confirm availability directly — at the time of writing its confirmed presence is on Apple's App Store, and a live Google Play listing could not be verified.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Fast camera scanning for printed and handwritten problems | Full step-by-step access requires a paid subscription |
| Genuine step-by-step explanations, not just final answers | Weekly plan pricing is expensive if you forget to cancel |
| Multiple solving methods shown per problem | No published information on the underlying AI/OCR model |
| Broad subject coverage from arithmetic through calculus and stats | Handwriting recognition accuracy varies with messy input |
| Solve history for reviewing past problems | Android availability unclear at time of writing |
| High App Store rating (4.7★ from 30,000+ ratings per Apple's listing) | No web app — mobile only |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Math AI is a standalone consumer mobile app, not a platform with an API, browser extension, or third-party integrations. It supports sharing solved step-by-step explanations directly to WhatsApp, Snapchat, and iMessage — useful for sending a solution to a classmate — but there's no Zapier connector, LMS plugin, or developer API. If you need programmatic access to a math-solving engine for a classroom tool, a dedicated computation API like Wolfram Alpha's is the better fit.

## Where it's a strong fit

Math AI earns its keep the moment a student is stuck on a specific homework problem and needs a fast, visual walk-through of the method. The camera-first workflow removes the friction of typing equations by hand, the multiple-solving-methods view is a nice touch for matching a teacher's preferred approach, and the subject range spans most of what a K-12 or early-college student would encounter.

## Where to think twice

Skip Math AI, or at least don't pay for the subscription yet, if you fall into any of these:

- **You need a fully free tool.** The free download only gets limited solves — if budget is the priority, compare free alternatives like Microsoft Math Solver or the free tiers of Photomath and Mathway first.
- **You're working on anything beyond standard textbook problems.** Multi-step proofs, unusual notation, or research-level math are outside this app's realistic scope.
- **You're on Android and need a confirmed, currently listed app.** Verify availability directly in the Play Store first.
- **You want transparency about the AI model powering the app.** The lack of published technical detail here is a real gap if that matters to you.
- **You're prone to forgetting to cancel trials.** The weekly plans auto-renew at a much higher rate than the annual option, and short trial windows are easy to let lapse into a paid week.

## Bottom line

Math AI does what it says on the label: scan a math problem, get a step-by-step explanation, move on with your homework. It's not trying to be a general AI tutor or a research-grade computer algebra system, and judged against that narrower goal, its 4.7-star App Store rating from tens of thousands of users suggests it holds up reasonably well for the everyday case of "I'm stuck on this one problem." The subscription pricing is the main friction point — the weekly plan is expensive relative to what you get, so anyone using it beyond a single assignment should go straight to the annual or one-time option instead of the weekly trial. If you want a fast camera-based homework helper, it's a reasonable choice; if you want a broader AI tutor, deeper subject coverage, or a free option, compare it against Photomath, Microsoft Math Solver, Mathway, or Gauth first.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Math AI actually free?**
It's free to download and includes a limited number of free solves, but unlimited step-by-step solutions require a paid subscription or one-time-purchase tier.

**How accurate is Math AI on handwritten problems?**
The company doesn't publish accuracy benchmarks, and like every camera-based math scanner, recognition quality drops with messy handwriting, cluttered pages, or unusual notation. Printed problems scan more reliably than handwriting.

**What subjects does Math AI cover?**
Per its own listing: basic arithmetic, pre-algebra, algebra (quadratics, systems of equations, inequalities), calculus (limits, derivatives, integrals), and statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, permutations, combinations).

**Is Math AI available on Android?**
At the time of writing, its confirmed presence is on Apple's App Store; a corresponding Google Play listing could not be confirmed, so Android users should check the Play Store directly.

**Does Math AI store my solved problems?**
Yes, in an in-app history tab for your own reference. Check the developer's published privacy policy, linked from the app's store listing, for specifics on data handling.

**What's the cheapest way to use Math AI long-term?**
Based on the published in-app pricing tiers, the annual "Math AI Pro" plan or the one-time "Math Hero" unlock work out far cheaper per month than the weekly subscription, which is priced for short-term use.

**How does Math AI compare to Photomath or Mathway?**
All three follow the same scan-and-solve model. Photomath and Mathway are more established with longer track records and their own free tiers; compare current pricing and subject needs across all three before choosing.

**Is Math AI good for beginners who've never used a math-solver app?**
Yes — the camera-scan-to-explanation flow needs no setup beyond pointing your phone at a problem.

title: Dora AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Dora AI builds 3D-animated, no-code websites from a prompt or Figma file. Here's the pricing, features, and who it actually suits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Dora AI worth using to build a website in 2026?

Dora AI is a no-code, AI-assisted website builder best known for generating 3D-animated, visually striking sites from a text prompt or a Figma import. It's a strong pick for designers, agencies, and indie makers who want a portfolio or landing page with real visual flair — it's a weaker choice if you need enterprise CMS, blogging, or e-commerce depth.

## At a glance

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free plan available; paid plans add custom domains and code export (exact current pricing should be confirmed on Dora's official pricing page, as it changes) |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — free plan plus a free trial on paid tiers |
| Best for | Designers, agencies, and indie makers who want an animated, visually distinctive site without writing code |
| Standout feature | Text-to-website generation combined with a full 3D/animation canvas and native Figma import |

## What Dora AI actually is

Dora AI (dora.run) is a no-code web design platform built around one core promise: you describe a site in a prompt, or drop in a Figma file, and Dora generates a working, animated website you can then edit visually. The company's own positioning leans hard into "3D animated websites without writing a line of code" — aimed less at a simple five-page brochure site and more at an Awwwards-style interactive portfolio or product launch page.

Under the hood, Dora combines a generative AI layer (used for the initial text-to-website step and some in-editor suggestions) with a visual canvas editor that behaves more like a design tool — think Figma or Spline — than a traditional CMS block editor. Dora doesn't publicly disclose which specific AI model powers its generation step, so treat output-quality claims as the vendor's own framing rather than an independently benchmarked fact.

Third-party traffic analytics show Dora's user base skewing global and indie-heavy — meaningful traffic from India, the US, Brazil, Vietnam, and Germany — consistent with a tool popular among solo designers and small agencies rather than large enterprise marketing teams.

## Pricing

Dora runs on a freemium model: there's a free plan for trying the editor and publishing on a Dora subdomain, and paid plans that unlock things typically gated on website builders — custom domains, higher publish/traffic limits, code export, and removal of Dora branding. Paid tiers commonly come with a free trial period as well.

Because pricing pages on AI website builders change frequently, this article won't state specific dollar figures for each plan. Check Dora's own pricing page directly before you commit, since free-tier limits and what's gated behind each paid tier can shift without notice. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability referenced here were last checked around this post's publish date and can change.

| Plan tier (typical structure) | What it generally includes |
| --- | --- |
| Free | Editor access, AI site generation, publish to a Dora subdomain, limited features |
| Paid (entry) | Custom domain support, expanded publishing limits, more AI generation credits |
| Paid (higher tier) | Code export, team/collaboration features, priority support, higher usage ceilings |

## Features walkthrough

**Text-to-website generation.** You type a prompt describing the site you want — industry, vibe, sections — and Dora generates a starting layout with copy placeholders, imagery, and animation already applied. It's meant as a fast first draft, not a finished site; expect to spend real time in the editor afterward.

**Figma import.** If you or your team already designs in Figma, Dora can import that design and turn it into an editable, publishable site rather than making you start from a prompt. This is arguably Dora's most practical feature for professional designers, since it slots into an existing workflow instead of replacing it.

**3D and motion-first canvas editor.** Unlike drag-and-drop builders built around static blocks, Dora's editor treats animation, scroll effects, and 3D elements as first-class citizens. This is the main reason people choose Dora over something like Wix or Squarespace — the tradeoff is a steeper learning curve if you've never used a spatial/canvas-style design tool before.

**One-click publishing and hosting.** Sites publish directly from the editor, with Dora handling hosting — no separate deploy step. That convenience comes with the usual builder tradeoff: you're tied to Dora's infrastructure and export options rather than owning a portable codebase by default.

**Responsive and interaction controls.** Dora gives designers control over breakpoints and interaction triggers (hover, scroll, click) in the same canvas, closer to how a tool like Framer or Webflow's designer handles it than how a simple template builder would.

## Who Dora AI is actually for

- **Solo designers and freelancers** building portfolio sites, personal brand sites, or one-off client landing pages will get the most out of Dora's animation and 3D capabilities — this is squarely the use case it's built for.
- **Small agencies and studios** pitching visually ambitious microsites (product launches, event pages, campaign landers) can move fast with the Figma import + AI-generation combo, especially on paid tiers with code export.
- **Startups needing a fast, distinctive landing page** before a launch can use the free or entry paid tier to get something live quickly, then decide whether to invest further.
- **Teams needing a content-managed marketing site** — blogging, structured collections, or e-commerce — are better served by Webflow, Framer, or WordPress; Dora isn't built around long-form content management.
- **Non-designers wanting a simple, guided setup** (a small local business owner, say) may find Dora's canvas-first approach more complex than a template-driven builder like Wix or Squarespace.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Genuinely distinctive visual output — 3D/animated sites most template builders can't produce | Steeper learning curve than block-based builders if you're new to canvas-style editors |
| Figma import fits into existing professional design workflows | Not built for blogging, large content libraries, or e-commerce |
| Fast first draft via text-to-website generation | Underlying AI model isn't publicly disclosed, so output quality claims are the vendor's own |
| Free plan lets you test the editor before paying | Free tier publishes to a Dora subdomain with limited features |
| One-click hosting removes deployment complexity | Being tied to Dora's hosting/export model means less portability than a fully custom build |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Dora's main "integration" story is design-tool interoperability rather than a broad app marketplace: Figma import is the standout, letting design teams bring existing work straight into the builder instead of rebuilding from scratch. Beyond that, expect the usual website-builder basics — custom domain connection and standard publishing/hosting handled in-platform.

Dora is not positioned as an extensible platform with a large plugin ecosystem, public API, or native Zapier/Slack-style integrations the way established builders like Webflow or Framer have built out over years. If your workflow depends on connecting a site builder to a CRM or email tool via native integrations, verify that specific integration exists before committing — Dora's ecosystem is comparatively young and design-tool-centric rather than automation-centric.

## Where Dora AI is a strong fit

Dora earns its keep when the goal is a visually memorable, animation-forward site and you're comfortable working in a design-canvas environment rather than a block editor. Portfolio sites, product launch pages, event microsites, and personal brand sites are the sweet spot — anywhere the "wow factor" of scroll-triggered 3D and motion actually matters to the outcome, and where you don't need deep content management underneath it.

It's also a reasonable fit if your team already lives in Figma: using Dora primarily as a "Figma to live, hosted site" pipeline is arguably more reliable than leaning entirely on prompt-based generation.

## Where to think twice

Skip Dora, or at least test thoroughly on the free tier first, if any of the following apply to you:

- **You need a fully free, permanently hosted site with no branding or domain limitations** — the free tier is a trial surface, not a long-term free hosting solution, in line with how most website builders structure their free plans.
- **You need blogging, a CMS, or e-commerce** — Dora's strength is visual/motion design, not structured content management or online stores; a CMS-native builder will serve you better.
- **You need a portable, framework-agnostic codebase you fully own** — you're building on Dora's platform and export model, not standing up your own independent stack from day one.
- **You're not comfortable with a canvas/spatial editor** — if block-based, form-fill website builders feel more intuitive to you, a template-first tool will get you to a finished site faster with less friction.
- **Your team needs enterprise compliance guarantees (SOC 2, dedicated SLAs, etc.)** — verify this directly with Dora before assuming it's in place; it isn't part of the tool's public positioning the way it is for larger, longer-established SaaS platforms.

## The bottom line

Dora AI is a genuinely differentiated pick in a crowded AI-website-builder field, not because its AI generation step is flawless, but because the underlying canvas is actually built for the kind of 3D, scroll-driven design most competitors treat as an afterthought. If you're a designer or small studio who wants a site that looks and moves differently from the templated majority — and you're willing to spend time refining what the AI drafts — it's worth trying on the free plan first. If your priority is a content-heavy marketing site, a blog, or an online store, look elsewhere.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Dora AI free to use?**
Dora offers a free plan that lets you use the editor and publish on a Dora subdomain with limited features. Paid plans add things like custom domains and code export. Confirm current free-tier limits on Dora's own pricing page, since they can change.

**What AI model does Dora AI use?**
Dora doesn't publicly disclose which specific AI model or models power its text-to-website generation, so there's no independently verifiable model name to report here.

**Can I import a Figma design into Dora?**
Yes — Figma import is one of Dora's core features, letting you turn an existing design file into an editable, publishable website rather than starting purely from a text prompt.

**Does Dora AI support e-commerce or blogging?**
Not as a primary strength. Dora is built around visual, animated site design rather than structured content management, so a dedicated CMS or e-commerce platform will typically serve those needs better.

**How does Dora compare to Framer or Webflow?**
Framer and Webflow both offer more mature CMS and integration ecosystems built up over years. Dora differentiates on its 3D/animation-first canvas and Figma import, but is comparatively younger with a narrower feature set outside of visual design.

**Is Dora AI good for beginners with no design experience?**
It's more approachable than hand-coding, but its canvas-style editor has a steeper learning curve than template-driven builders like Wix or Squarespace. Beginners wanting the simplest possible setup may prefer a more guided, block-based tool.

**Can I export the code from a site built in Dora?**
Code export is generally positioned as a higher-tier paid feature rather than something available on the free plan. Confirm current export capabilities and any format limitations directly on Dora's site before relying on it.

**Does Dora AI have an API or third-party integrations?**
Dora isn't currently positioned as a platform with a broad public API or extensive third-party integration marketplace. Its main interoperability strength is Figma import rather than automation-style integrations like Zapier or Slack.

title: StoryCraftr Review 2026: Free Open-Source AI Novel Tool
excerpt: StoryCraftr is a free, open-source CLI tool for AI-assisted novel writing. Here is how its worldbuilding, outline, and chapter features actually work.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is StoryCraftr worth using for writing a novel?

StoryCraftr is a free, open-source CLI tool that uses OpenAI, OpenRouter, or local Ollama models to help novelists outline, world-build, and draft chapters. It's genuinely useful for writers comfortable with a terminal, but there's no polished web app, no built-in editor, and you supply and pay for your own AI provider.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (MIT-licensed, open source) |
| **Free tier / trial** | Entire tool is free; you pay only for your own OpenAI/OpenRouter API usage (or run Ollama locally for $0) |
| **Best for** | Writers comfortable with a terminal who want AI-assisted outlining and drafting without a subscription |
| **Standout feature** | Full book-project structure (worldbuilding, outline, chapters) generated and iterated through a chat-style CLI |

## What StoryCraftr actually is

StoryCraftr is an open-source project built by developer Rodrigo Estrada ([raestrada on GitHub](https://github.com/raestrada/storycraftr)) and maintained under the broader "AI Craftr" suite, which also includes PaperCraftr for academic writing. It's distributed as a Python package installed via `pipx` or run on-demand with `uvx`, and it works from your computer's command line rather than a browser.

Under the hood, StoryCraftr uses [LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/) to talk to whichever model provider you configure: OpenAI's GPT-4o and other GPT models, OpenRouter (access to models like Llama 3.1 70B and dozens of others), or a locally-run Ollama instance for anyone who wants to keep everything offline and free. Embeddings — used to keep long book projects consistent as they grow — default to `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5`, with lighter alternatives available for weaker hardware.

The GitHub repository has around 170 stars, an MIT license, and commits as recently as March 2026, so it's actively maintained rather than an abandoned side project — though it's clearly a smaller, community-run tool next to venture-backed writing platforms like Sudowrite or NovelAI. There's no store entry for StoryCraftr in our catalog because it isn't a paid SaaS product with a checkout page — there's nothing to buy, so no coupon link applies here.

## Pricing: there isn't any (mostly)

This is the detail that separates StoryCraftr from most other "AI writing tool" reviews: the software itself costs nothing, ever. You install it, point it at a model provider, and start generating outlines and chapters — no subscription tier, no waitlist, no upsell screen.

What you do pay for is the underlying AI model, if you choose a hosted one:

| Provider option | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| StoryCraftr itself | $0 | Open source, MIT license, install via pipx/uvx |
| OpenAI (e.g. GPT-4o) | Pay-per-token, billed by OpenAI | Supply your own `OPENAI_API_KEY`; cost scales with usage |
| OpenRouter | Pay-per-token, billed by OpenRouter | One key, many third-party models (Llama, Mistral, etc.) |
| Ollama (local) | $0 | Runs open models on your own machine; needs decent RAM/GPU |

For a full-length novel draft with several rounds of outline iteration and chapter regeneration, a writer using GPT-4o could plausibly spend anywhere from a few dollars to a few tens of dollars, depending on how many drafts they run — there's no official estimate from the project, and spend depends on your own usage and OpenAI's current rates. Running everything through Ollama trades model quality and speed for zero API cost.

Pricing and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly, since model providers set their own rates independently of the StoryCraftr project — check OpenAI's and OpenRouter's current pricing pages before relying on cost estimates for a long project.

## Core features walkthrough

**Project-based book structure.** Running `storycraftr init` creates a self-contained project with its own `storycraftr.json` config — language, author, genre, and a "behavior" file shaping how the AI writes for that book. You can run multiple projects side by side with different providers or tones.

**Worldbuilding generation.** A `worldbuilding` command set generates geography, history, culture, and technology/magic-system details on request — for example, describing a magic system "based on advanced technology" — meant to keep a fictional world consistent as a book grows past a first draft.

**Outline and chapter generation.** `outline` commands produce a plot outline, character summaries, and chapter synopses; `chapters` commands turn those into drafted chapter text, cover copy, and epilogues. Later chapter generations can reference earlier established details instead of starting from a blank context each time.

**Interactive chat with iteration commands.** `storycraftr chat` opens a REPL-style session for running commands conversationally, plus an `iterate` family for surgical edits — the docs give the example of inserting a new chapter with one instruction (`!iterate insert-chapter 3 "Add a flashback between chapters 2 and 3."`), rather than regenerating the whole manuscript.

**Multi-provider and offline flexibility.** Because model access runs through LangChain, switching from OpenAI to OpenRouter to a local Ollama setup is a config change, not a rewrite.

**VSCode extension.** A companion [extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=StoryCraftr.storycraftr) auto-detects a `storycraftr.json` project and lets you launch chat sessions from inside the editor.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo genre writers comfortable with a command line** get the most out of StoryCraftr — the workflow assumes you're fine typing commands instead of clicking through a dashboard.
- **Developers who also write fiction** are the ideal audience: the VSCode extension, LangChain backend, and pipx/uvx install path speak to a technical user who already lives in an editor and terminal.
- **Budget-conscious writers with an OpenAI/OpenRouter key** can use it as a near-free alternative to a $20–30/month subscription tool, or go fully offline with Ollama.
- **Non-technical writers wanting a clean interface** are the group it's not built for — no rich text editor, no outline board, no support line.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Completely free and open source (MIT license) | No graphical interface — CLI only, plus an optional VSCode extension |
| Choice of OpenAI, OpenRouter, or fully local/offline Ollama models | Requires comfort with terminal commands and JSON config |
| Structured project format links worldbuilding, outline, and chapters | No official support team — help via GitHub issues only |
| Iteration commands allow targeted edits, not full regenerations | Output quality depends entirely on which model you plug in |
| No subscription lock-in; costs (if any) come only from the model provider | Small project (~170 GitHub stars), single primary maintainer |

## Integrations and ecosystem

StoryCraftr's main integration point is its own multi-provider design: OpenAI's API, OpenRouter's API (proxying dozens of third-party models), and Ollama for local inference. It doesn't offer a Zapier connector, Slack app, or public REST API — the "integration" is a config change, not a plugin marketplace. The VSCode extension is the one first-party integration outside the CLI. Being MIT-licensed, the project also accepts community contributions and forks on GitHub.

Readers who want a deeper look at running models locally with Ollama specifically — one of StoryCraftr's supported backends — can see our [Ollama review](/blog/ollama-review) for the setup and hardware tradeoffs involved.

## Where it's a strong fit

StoryCraftr earns its keep when you want AI-assisted novel drafting without a monthly SaaS fee and don't mind bringing your own API key or running models locally. It fits naturally if you're already working in a code editor or terminal daily, or if you specifically value being able to inspect, fork, or modify the tool's source rather than trusting a closed vendor with your manuscript pipeline. It's also a good match if you want the flexibility to swap AI providers per project — cheap local models for early drafts, a stronger hosted model for polish passes.

## Where to think twice

StoryCraftr is not the right pick if you need a polished, beginner-friendly app with a visual interface — there's no rich text editor, drag-and-drop outline board, or export tooling; you're generating and editing plain text through a terminal. It's also not for anyone who wants guaranteed support: as a small project maintained largely by one developer, help comes from GitHub issues, not a ticket system with SLAs.

Skip it if you need enterprise features like SSO, audit logs, or a signed data processing agreement — there's no company behind it selling a hosted service. And if you want a tool that's fully free with zero setup, note the "free" path still requires either installing Ollama and downloading model weights, or paying a model provider for API access — it isn't one-click free like some browser-based assistants. Output quality also depends entirely on whichever model you connect, so there's no fixed accuracy rate to quote.

## The bottom line

StoryCraftr suits a specific type of writer: technically comfortable, cost-conscious, and happy working from a terminal or VSCode instead of a dedicated writing app. It handles the unglamorous scaffolding of a book project — consistent worldbuilding, a structured outline, and chapter drafts that reference earlier decisions — better than retyping the same prompts into a generic chatbot, without asking for a credit card. It's not a replacement for commercial, GUI-driven fiction tools if what you want is a friendly editor or a support team to fall back on. If you already have an OpenAI/OpenRouter key, or you're willing to run models locally through Ollama, it's worth the half hour it takes to install and try before deciding if the CLI workflow sticks.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is StoryCraftr actually free?**
Yes, the tool is open source under the MIT license with no subscription or paywall. The only cost you might incur is from the AI model provider you connect — OpenAI or OpenRouter charge per token, while local Ollama models cost nothing per use.

**Do I need to know how to code to use StoryCraftr?**
Not exactly, but you need to be comfortable installing CLI tools, editing a JSON config file, and running terminal commands — the setup friction is higher than a web-based app.

**What AI models does StoryCraftr support?**
OpenAI models (like GPT-4o), a wide range of third-party models through OpenRouter, and locally-hosted open models through Ollama. Model choice is set per project in `storycraftr.json`.

**Does StoryCraftr store or see my manuscript?**
It runs locally and doesn't operate its own cloud service, so project files stay on your computer. If you use a hosted provider (OpenAI or OpenRouter), prompts pass through that provider's API under their own data policies. Running entirely through Ollama keeps everything on your own hardware.

**Is there a StoryCraftr app or web version?**
No. It's a command-line tool with an optional VSCode extension. There's no standalone desktop app or hosted web version as of this writing.

**How is StoryCraftr different from tools like Sudowrite or NovelAI?**
Sudowrite and NovelAI are hosted, subscription browser tools with built-in editors aimed at non-technical writers. StoryCraftr is free, open source, and CLI-based, aimed at writers who want to control which AI model they're paying for, if any.

**Can I use StoryCraftr completely offline?**
Yes — with Ollama and a local model, it can generate outlines, worldbuilding, and chapters with no internet-connected API calls or per-use cost, though local models are generally less capable than the largest hosted ones.

**Is StoryCraftr actively maintained?**
The GitHub repository shows commits within the last several months and an active release history, including recent Windows support, so it appears actively maintained, though it remains small relative to funded commercial writing tools.

Because StoryCraftr has no commercial storefront, there's no coupon page to link to here — but you can browse more AI tool coverage, including tools that do run promotions, on our [AI & software deals](/category/software) page.

title: AI SEO by Leap AI Review 2026: Discontinued, Here's Why
excerpt: Leap AI's SEO tool ("Leap Rank") is gone — the page now returns a 410 error. Here's what it offered, its old pricing, and what to use instead.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is AI SEO by Leap AI still worth using in 2026?

No — as of this review, the "AI SEO" product (branded "Leap Rank") that Leap AI marketed as a way to "replace your SEO agency with AI" has been discontinued. The tryleap.ai domain now runs an unrelated AI text-detection and humanization service, and the old SEO workflow-automation landing page returns a 410 Gone response. This review covers what the tool offered, why it disappeared, and what to use instead.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Product name | Leap AI / "Leap Rank" (AI SEO workflow automation) |
| Status | Discontinued — page returns HTTP 410 as of September 2026 |
| Former starting price | Free plan ($0), Pro at $99/month, custom Business plan |
| Former free tier | Limited workflow runs/month, 1 concurrent run |
| Best for | Historical reference only — not usable today |
| Current tryleap.ai product | AI content detector + AI humanizer (unrelated to SEO) |

## What "AI SEO by Leap AI" actually was

Before it became an AI-text-humanizing site, tryleap.ai belonged to Leap Labs Inc., a company building a no-code AI workflow-automation platform called "Leap." Leap wasn't a dedicated SEO writing tool the way Surfer SEO or Jasper are — it was a general-purpose automation builder (drag-and-drop workflows connecting AI models to other business tools), and "AI SEO" was one of several marketed use cases, sold under the name **Leap Rank**.

The Leap Rank landing page pitched itself as a way to "automate your entire SEO content workflow with Leap Rank," combining AI-powered keyword research, competitive data gathering, and SEO-optimized content generation into a repeatable, no-code workflow rather than a single "type in a keyword, get an article" box. Other marketed use cases on the same platform included sales outreach automation, social content generation, customer-feedback analysis, and recruitment screening — SEO content was a niche template among many, not the company's core identity.

Leap didn't run its own proprietary language model. Per its (now-archived) integrations page, workflows were built on a "bring your own API key" model, orchestrating calls to OpenAI and Anthropic models plus connectors like Slack, Notion, Gmail, Salesforce, Zendesk, GitHub, Perplexity, and the AI search tool Exa. In other words: Leap was the workflow glue, and you supplied (and paid for) the actual LLM calls through your own API credentials on the paid tiers, or shared usage on the free tier.

We could not verify, via the company's own current channels, exactly when or why the product was retired — the tryleap.ai homepage, pricing page, and blog have all been fully replaced, with no shutdown notice or redirect explaining the transition. What we can verify directly: the `/ai-seo` URL that hosted the Leap Rank page was live and indexed as recently as mid-January 2026, and now returns an HTTP 410 Gone status — a deliberate "this is permanently gone" signal, not a temporary outage. The Wayback Machine has snapshots through early 2026 if you want to see the historical page yourself.

## Pricing (as it existed before discontinuation)

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described below reflect the last archived state of the product (accessed via the Wayback Machine, snapshot dated March 2026) and are provided for historical reference only — none of this is purchasable today.

| Plan | Price | What was included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | Limited workflow runs per month, community support, bring-your-own API keys, 1 concurrent run |
| Pro | $99/month | Unlimited workflow runs, priority support, bring-your-own API keys, team invites, up to 5 concurrent runs |
| Business | Custom | Everything in Pro, custom integrations, dedicated account manager, unlimited team invites, 30+ concurrent runs, SLA and premium support |

There was no plan priced specifically for the SEO use case — Leap Rank was a marketing angle on top of the same three-tier workflow platform, not a separate SKU.

## Features walkthrough (historical)

Based on the archived product pages, the SEO-specific capabilities Leap Rank advertised were:

- **AI-driven keyword and topic research** folded into a broader workflow, rather than a standalone keyword tool.
- **Automated data gathering** — pulling competitive or on-page data into the workflow before content generation, similar in spirit to how tools like Surfer or Frase brief a draft, though Leap's version ran through its no-code builder rather than a purpose-built SEO editor.
- **SEO-optimized content drafting**, generated via connected LLM calls (OpenAI/Anthropic) rather than a fine-tuned in-house model.
- **Content repurposing across formats** — the same underlying workflow engine was marketed for turning one piece of content into social posts, video-derived content, or multiple output formats, which is a workflow-automation strength more than an SEO-specific one.
- **300+ third-party integrations** (the company's own stated figure — we could not independently verify the exact count) for pushing generated content into CMSs, Slack, email tools, and CRMs once it was drafted.

None of this amounted to a dedicated SEO content editor with on-page scoring, SERP analysis, or content-brief generation the way tools purpose-built for SEO (Surfer SEO, Frase, Clearscope) work. Leap Rank was closer to "SEO content creation as one Zapier-style automation template" than a standalone SEO writing suite.

## Who it was actually for

Going by the archived marketing, Leap positioned itself for:

- **Marketing teams at startups** wanting to automate repetitive content and outreach tasks without hiring engineers, using SEO content generation as one of several templates.
- **Agencies or in-house teams already using OpenAI/Anthropic API keys** who wanted a no-code layer connecting those models to tools like Slack, Notion, and their CMS.
- **Businesses with existing workflow-automation budgets** (the $99/month Pro tier and custom Business tier suggest a small-team-to-mid-market price point, not a solo blogger's SEO tool).

It was a poor fit for anyone specifically shopping for a dedicated SEO writing assistant with keyword-difficulty scoring, SERP-based content briefs, or an editor tuned for on-page optimization — that was never really Leap's core product, just one of its marketed use cases.

## Pros and cons (as it existed)

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| No-code workflow builder could automate more than just SEO content (sales, ops, recruiting) | SEO features were shallow compared to dedicated SEO content tools |
| Wide integration list (Slack, Notion, Salesforce, Zendesk, GitHub, and more) | Required your own OpenAI/Anthropic API keys and their associated costs on top of the subscription |
| Free tier existed for testing workflows | Free tier capped at very limited runs and one concurrent workflow |
| Transparent three-tier pricing | Now fully discontinued — no migration path or successor product was announced |

## Integrations and ecosystem (historical)

The archived integrations directory listed connectors across marketing, sales, operations, and development, including Slack, OpenAI, Anthropic, Notion, Gmail, Mailchimp, Salesforce, Zendesk, GitHub, Trello, Loom, Ghost, Typefully, Perplexity, Exa, Fal.ai, and Ragie (a RAG-as-a-service platform). The company also advertised a public API reference and a stated willingness to build "typically within 24 hours" any integration a paying customer requested — the vendor's own claim, unverifiable now that the page is gone.

## Where it was a strong fit

If you were a small team comfortable stitching together AI workflows and just needed SEO content as one node in a larger automation (research → draft → publish → repurpose → distribute), Leap's integration breadth made it a reasonable fit over building the same pipeline manually with Zapier plus a separate AI writer.

## Where to think twice — and why it matters now

Everything here is now moot for one simple reason: **the product doesn't exist anymore.** If you're reading vendor comparison lists, old roundup posts, or cached search results that still recommend "AI SEO by Leap AI" or "Leap Rank," treat that information as stale. Specifically skip acting on it if:

- You need a tool you can sign up for and use today — the SEO product is gone, full stop.
- You want a dedicated SEO content editor with SERP-based briefs, keyword-difficulty data, or on-page scoring — Leap Rank never had those anyway; look at [LinkDR](/blog/linkdr-review) for backlink-side SEO work or dedicated SEO content platforms instead.
- You're comparing AI agent/workflow platforms broadly rather than SEO tools specifically — [Dynamiq](/blog/dynamiq-review) is a more current AI agent orchestration platform worth evaluating instead.
- You want your content strategy to account for how AI answer engines now surface content, not just classic SEO — our [Answer Engine Optimization guide](/blog/answer-engine-optimization-guide) covers that shift in more depth than any single tool review can.

## Bottom line

"AI SEO by Leap AI" is a cautionary example of how quickly AI-tool branding can vanish: a workflow-automation company marketed an SEO use case under the name Leap Rank as recently as January 2026, and by the time of this review the entire domain had been repurposed for an unrelated AI-detection and humanization product, with the SEO page returning a permanent 410 Gone. There's no indication of a successor product, migration path, or refund process specific to the old SEO offering. If you landed here because you saw "Leap AI" mentioned as an SEO tool somewhere, the safest move is to treat that reference as outdated and look at currently-maintained SEO content platforms instead.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Leap AI's AI SEO tool still available?**
No. The dedicated SEO landing page (previously called "Leap Rank") returns an HTTP 410 Gone status as of this review, meaning the page has been intentionally and permanently removed rather than just temporarily down.

**What does tryleap.ai offer now instead?**
The domain currently hosts an AI content detector and AI humanizer product, unrelated to SEO or workflow automation. It has its own separate pricing (a free detection tier plus paid humanization word limits starting around $9.99/month), which is a completely different product from the one this review covers.

**Was Leap AI's SEO tool ever a dedicated SEO writing platform?**
Not exactly. It was a no-code AI workflow-automation platform (built by Leap Labs Inc.) that marketed SEO content generation as one of several use cases — alongside sales outreach, social content, and recruitment automation — rather than a purpose-built SEO editor like Surfer SEO or Frase.

**How much did it cost before it was discontinued?**
Based on the last archived pricing page (dated March 2026), plans were Free ($0, limited runs), Pro ($99/month, unlimited workflow runs), and a custom-priced Business tier. There was no SEO-specific pricing tier.

**Did Leap AI's workflow platform use its own AI model?**
No. It operated on a "bring your own API key" basis, routing workflow steps through OpenAI and Anthropic models that customers connected themselves, rather than a proprietary in-house model.

**What should I use instead for AI-assisted SEO content in 2026?**
Since this specific product is gone, look at currently-maintained SEO content tools and, if backlinks rather than content are your focus, see our [LinkDR review](/blog/linkdr-review). For broader AI workflow/agent automation (the category Leap actually competed in), see our [Dynamiq review](/blog/dynamiq-review). For a content strategy angle that accounts for AI-driven search, read our [Answer Engine Optimization guide](/blog/answer-engine-optimization-guide).

**Is there a coupon or discount for Leap AI's SEO tool?**
No — since the product is discontinued, there's nothing to redeem a coupon against. Browse current, active [AI & software deals](/category/software) instead.

**Can I still access my old Leap Rank workflows if I was a customer?**
This review can't confirm that, since the company hasn't published anything about account access, data export, or sunset timing for the SEO product. If you had an active account, contacting the current site's support channel directly is the only way to get a definitive answer.

title: AIEasyPic Review 2026: AI Headshots, Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: AIEasyPic trains a personal AI model from your photos for headshots and stylized art. Here's real pricing, features, and who it fits best.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is AIEasyPic worth using for AI headshots and image generation?

AIEasyPic is a browser-based AI image generator built around personal model training, AI headshots, face swaps, and text-to-image/video tools using Stable Diffusion-family models. It's a reasonable pick if you want a single place to train a custom AI model of your own face and generate stylized images from it, but the free tier is capped at 20 watermark-free images a month and paid plans require an annual commitment to get the advertised discount.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $6.60/month (Basic, billed yearly) or $12/month billed monthly |
| Free tier | 20 watermark-free images/month with a free account |
| Best for | Solo creators who want custom AI headshots or personal AI model training |
| Standout feature | Train a personal AI model from your own photos, then generate in dozens of styles |

## What AIEasyPic actually is

AIEasyPic is a web app for generating and editing images with AI, aimed less at professional designers and more at everyday users who want AI-generated headshots, avatars, face swaps, or stylized art without touching a prompt-engineering-heavy tool like Midjourney. According to the company's own site, the platform is "built upon recent advances made with Stable Diffusion, ControlNet, and LoRAs" — the same open-source model family that powers a large share of the consumer AI-image market. AIEasyPic doesn't disclose the exact checkpoint or version numbers it runs, so treat "Stable Diffusion-based" as the company's own description rather than a fully documented technical spec.

The core workflow is model training: you upload a batch of your own photos, the platform trains a small custom model (a LoRA, in Stable-Diffusion terms) on your face, and you then generate new images of "you" in whatever style or scenario you pick — from corporate headshots to fantasy art to cartoon styles. Beyond that personal-model flow, AIEasyPic also offers standalone text-to-image generation, text-to-video, face swapping, background removal, and upscaling, all bundled into the same credit-based account.

The company reports on its homepage that its users have generated several million images across tens of thousands of accounts — a vendor-marketing figure, not independently audited, so treat it as directional.

## AIEasyPic pricing

AIEasyPic runs on a credit system: every plan grants a monthly credit allowance, and each generation (image, upscale, video frame, etc.) consumes credits at a rate that varies by tool. There's no store coupon-page entry for AIEasyPic on this site at the time of writing, so the figures below come directly from the vendor's own pricing page.

| Plan | Price (billed yearly) | Price (billed monthly) | Monthly credits | Model training |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | $0 | Up to 20 watermark-free images/month | Not included |
| Basic | $6.60/mo | $12/mo | 2,000 | Train 1 model |
| Starter (most popular) | $17.40/mo | $29/mo | 5,000 | Train 2 models |
| Hobby | $29.40/mo | $49/mo | 10,000 | Train 5 models |

All paid plans unlock the full tool set (every style preset, text-to-video, face swap, background removal), a faster generation queue, higher-resolution output, and "pro upscale," with the queue depth and number of trainable models scaling up by tier. The yearly discount shown above (40–45% off the monthly rate) only applies if you commit to annual billing; paying month-to-month means paying the higher listed rate with no discount.

If you burn through your monthly allotment, AIEasyPic also sells one-off credit packs — starting around $9.99 for 1,000 credits and dropping to roughly $0.007 per credit at the largest 14,000-credit pack — so heavy users aren't forced into the next subscription tier just to finish a project. Per AIEasyPic's own site, plan credits do not roll over between months, while purchased top-up credits don't expire.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm current numbers on AIEasyPic's own pricing page before subscribing.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

- **Custom model training from your own photos.** This is the feature the rest of the product is built around: upload a set of reference photos, train a personal model, and reuse it across sessions instead of re-uploading photos every time you want a new image of yourself.
- **AI headshot generation.** Once a model is trained, one of the most common use cases is professional-looking headshots for LinkedIn, resumes, or team pages — generated in business-appropriate styles without a photographer.
- **Face swapping.** Users can swap a face into an existing image or template, useful for quick memes, mockups, or visualizing a style on your own face before committing to a full generation batch.
- **Broad style-preset library.** The platform covers photography styles (HDR, portrait, macro), digital-art styles (pixel art, 3D render, isometric), cartoon/animation-inspired looks, and classic art movements (cubism, minimalism) — useful if you want variety without writing detailed prompts yourself.
- **Text-to-video and upscaling add-ons.** Beyond stills, paid plans add text-to-video generation and a "pro upscale" option for higher-resolution output, keeping most of a small creator's image workflow inside one tool rather than juggling separate apps.

## Who AIEasyPic is actually for

- **Solo creators and job seekers** who want a handful of polished AI headshots without booking a photographer — the Basic plan's single trainable model and 2,000 monthly credits are enough for a one-off headshot project.
- **Content creators and small marketing teams** who need a steady stream of stylized visuals (thumbnails, social graphics, avatars) and want to train a couple of recurring subject models — this is where the Starter plan's 2 trained models and larger credit pool fit better.
- **Hobbyists experimenting with AI art styles** on a budget, using the free tier's 20 images a month to test styles before deciding whether to subscribe.
- **Agencies or teams needing multiple client models** will likely outgrow even the Hobby tier's 5 trained models quickly and should budget for recurring credit top-ups.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier lets you test the tool before paying (20 images/month) | No free tier for model training — that requires a paid plan |
| Annual billing cuts the price by 40–45% versus monthly | Monthly billing carries a real premium if you don't want a yearly commitment |
| Wide range of style presets covers photography, art, and cartoon looks in one place | Exact model versions (which Stable Diffusion checkpoint, whether Flux/SDXL variants are used) aren't clearly documented by the vendor |
| Credit top-ups don't expire, so unused purchased credits aren't wasted | Plan credits don't roll over month to month, so unused monthly credits are lost |
| Text-to-video, face swap, and upscaling are bundled into the same account | No published API or third-party integrations for developers to build on |

## Integrations and ecosystem

AIEasyPic is a self-contained web app rather than a platform with a documented public API, Zapier connector, or Slack/plugin ecosystem. There's no evidence on the vendor's site of developer-facing integrations at the time of writing — everything happens inside the AIEasyPic dashboard, and generated images are downloaded directly rather than pushed into a connected app or CMS. If your workflow depends on programmatic image generation or piping outputs into another tool automatically, that's a real gap here relative to API-first image platforms.

## Where AIEasyPic is a strong fit

- You want AI-generated headshots or personal avatars without hiring a photographer or learning prompt engineering from scratch.
- You're comfortable committing to an annual plan to get the lower per-month price, and you know roughly how many images you'll need each month.
- You want one tool that covers stills, face swaps, and light video generation instead of stitching together three separate apps.
- You're a hobbyist who just wants to try a few dozen free, watermark-free images a month without paying anything.

## Where to think twice

- **If you need a fully free tool long-term** — 20 images a month with no model training is a trial cap, not a sustainable free plan for regular use.
- **If your team needs enterprise compliance features** (SOC 2, SSO, audit logs, dedicated data-processing agreements) — AIEasyPic's site gives no indication it offers enterprise-tier compliance documentation, so larger organizations with procurement requirements should look elsewhere or confirm directly with support first.
- **If you need API access or automation** — there's no public developer API to integrate AIEasyPic into an existing pipeline or app.
- **If you're highly price-sensitive on a month-to-month basis** — the advertised low prices only apply with annual billing; paying monthly costs noticeably more per month.
- **If accuracy and consistency across generations matters a lot** — like any Stable-Diffusion-family tool, output quality and likeness accuracy from a trained personal model can vary between batches, and AIEasyPic doesn't publish benchmark data on consistency or accuracy to set expectations against.

## Bottom line

AIEasyPic is a solid, low-friction option if your main goal is AI headshots, personal avatars, or exploring a wide range of art styles using your own face as the subject, and you're fine training a model and committing to an annual plan to keep costs down. It's less compelling if you want a genuinely free ongoing tool, need developer-facing API access, or require documented enterprise compliance. For most solo users and small creators, the Basic or Starter plan covers a real project's worth of headshots or content without much friction — just budget for the credit system's "no rollover" rule and confirm current pricing before subscribing, since AI image-tool pricing shifts often.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is AIEasyPic free to use?**
There's a free tier that allows up to 20 watermark-free image generations per month with a registered account, but custom model training and the full style library require a paid plan.

**How much does AIEasyPic cost?**
Paid plans start at $6.60/month (Basic) when billed yearly, or $12/month if billed monthly, scaling up to the Hobby plan at $29.40/month yearly ($49/month monthly) for more credits and trainable models.

**What AI models does AIEasyPic use?**
The company describes its technology as built on Stable Diffusion, ControlNet, and LoRAs — it doesn't publicly specify exact checkpoint versions, so treat this as the vendor's own general description rather than a full technical spec.

**Do unused credits roll over?**
No. According to AIEasyPic, monthly plan credits do not carry over to the next billing cycle, while separately purchased credit packs don't expire.

**Can I use AIEasyPic to train a model of myself?**
Yes — training a personal model from your own uploaded photos is the core feature behind AIEasyPic's headshot and avatar generation, though it requires at least the Basic paid plan.

**Does AIEasyPic have an API for developers?**
There's no publicly documented API or third-party integration (Zapier, Slack, etc.) listed on AIEasyPic's site as of this review — it's designed as a standalone web app, not a developer platform.

**Is AIEasyPic good for beginners?**
Yes — the style-preset library means you don't need to write detailed prompts to get usable results, which makes it more approachable than prompt-heavy generators for someone new to AI image tools.

**What are the alternatives to AIEasyPic?**
For AI headshots specifically, tools like HeadshotPro focus on a narrower, headshot-only workflow. For broader AI art without model training, general-purpose text-to-image tools are worth comparing on price and style range first.

title: Remaker AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Remaker AI face swap and photo tools tested: credit pricing, batch swapping, privacy policy, and who should (and shouldn't) use it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Remaker AI Worth Using for Face Swaps and Photo Edits?

Remaker AI is a credit-based online toolkit built around face swapping, AI photo editing, upscaling, and background removal. It's genuinely useful for quick, casual face-swap or photo-cleanup jobs and works without an account for basic swaps, but it isn't a professional retouching suite and its pricing is credit-metered rather than a flat subscription, so heavy users can burn through credits fast.

### At a glance

| | Details |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Credit packs from $5.99 (200 credits); no fixed monthly plan advertised |
| **Free tier/trial** | Free credits on signup; some tools (like basic face swap) usable without an account |
| **Best for** | Casual face swaps, quick photo edits, background removal, simple AI portraits |
| **Standout feature** | One-click multi-face and batch face swapping, including video/GIF swaps |

Remaker AI markets itself as "the easiest way to recreate any image." The company doesn't publicly name the underlying generative models it uses, so treat any "quality" claims here as Remaker's own framing rather than an independently verified benchmark.

## What Remaker AI Actually Is

Remaker AI runs entirely in the browser (with mobile apps for iOS and Android) and bundles a handful of separate AI utilities under one account: face swap, an AI photo editor that edits images from text prompts, an image upscaler, a background remover, a magic eraser for removing objects, an AI image generator, an AI portrait generator, a tattoo generator, and photo effect filters. It's aimed at casual creators, meme-makers, and small businesses that need quick image fixes, not at studios that need pixel-level control.

## Pricing: How Remaker AI's Credits Work

Remaker AI doesn't sell a traditional monthly subscription tier structure the way most SaaS tools do. Instead, it runs on a **one-time credit purchase model**: you buy a pack of credits, and each tool (face swap, upscale, background removal, generation) consumes a set number of credits per use. According to Remaker's own site, credit packs currently range from **$5.99 for 200 credits up to $299 for 20,000 credits**, new users get a batch of free credits just for signing up, and purchased credits carry no expiration date.

| Plan type | What you get |
|---|---|
| Free (no account) | Basic single face swap, watermark-free, limited daily use |
| Free (signed-up) | Starter credit balance to try premium tools |
| Credit pack — entry | $5.99 for 200 credits |
| Credit pack — top tier | $299 for 20,000 credits |

Because this is a pay-as-you-go model rather than tiered subscriptions, there's no "Pro" vs "Team" feature gating — what changes is how many credits you have to spend. The exact credit cost per action isn't broken out in a public table, so confirm the per-feature credit cost on Remaker's pricing page before buying a large pack.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AI image tools adjust credit costs and free allowances frequently, so double-check current numbers on Remaker's site before committing to a large credit purchase.

## Features Walkthrough

**Face swap (single, multi-face, and video).** This is Remaker's flagship tool: upload a source image and a target face, and it swaps faces in photos, group shots, GIFs, or short video clips. It handles single-face and multi-face group photos differently — Remaker recommends its dedicated Multi-Face Swap mode for group shots rather than the basic swapper, since accuracy on multiple faces in one frame is harder for any face-swap model to get right.

**Batch processing.** Rather than swapping one image at a time, Remaker lets users queue multiple images for the same face swap, which matters if you're processing a photo set (event photos, a meme series, product mockups with a consistent face) rather than a single one-off image.

**AI photo editor and magic eraser.** Beyond face swapping, Remaker includes prompt-based photo editing (draw over an area and describe what should replace it) and a magic eraser for removing unwanted objects, people, or watermarks from the background of a shot. These are the tools most likely to overlap with what you'd otherwise do in Photoshop's generative fill or a dedicated background-removal app.

**Upscaling and background removal.** Straightforward utility tools — enlarge low-resolution images without excessive blur, or strip a background out entirely for product photos, profile pictures, or compositing. These are commodity features across the AI photo-tool space, but having them bundled with face swap in one credit pool is convenient if you're doing several small edits on the same image.

**AI portrait, tattoo, and effects generators.** Turn a selfie into a stylized AI portrait, generate a tattoo design from a prompt, or apply filter-style photo effects. These lean more novelty/creative than professional, but they're the kind of features that make Remaker feel like a broader creative playground rather than a single-purpose face-swap app.

## Who Remaker AI Is Actually For

**Casual users and meme-makers** get the most out of Remaker as-is — the no-signup, watermark-free basic face swap covers most one-off needs, and the free credits on signup are enough to test the rest of the suite before paying.

**Small creators and social media managers** doing recurring batch work (swapping a consistent face across a set of images, or cleaning up multiple product photos) benefit from the batch processing and larger credit packs, since the per-image cost drops as you buy bigger packs.

**Businesses needing high-volume image production** are a weaker fit — there's no team seat management or API tier advertised, so anyone needing to integrate face swap or upscaling into an internal pipeline should confirm directly with Remaker whether that's possible.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| No signup required for basic face swap | No flat monthly subscription — costs scale per action via credits |
| Credits never expire once purchased | Per-feature credit cost isn't clearly published |
| Broad bundle of tools (swap, upscale, erase, generate) in one account | Multi-face accuracy is inconsistent; dedicated mode needed for groups |
| Works on web, iOS, and Android | No visible API or team/enterprise tier |
| States uploaded images are deleted within 48 hours | Underlying AI models aren't publicly disclosed |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Remaker AI is primarily a standalone web and mobile experience — there's no publicly documented API, Zapier connector, or Slack/Discord integration for automating face swaps or edits at the time of writing. If a workflow integration matters to you (e.g., triggering an upscale automatically when a file lands in a folder), you'd need to confirm directly with Remaker's support whether any developer access exists, since none is advertised on the marketing site.

## Where Remaker AI Is a Strong Fit

- You need a quick, free, no-account face swap for a one-off meme, group photo, or joke, and don't mind a watermark-free but rate-limited free experience.
- You want several lightweight photo tools (background removal, upscaling, object erasing) without juggling five different single-purpose apps.
- You're comfortable with a pay-per-use credit model instead of a recurring subscription, and your usage is occasional rather than daily.

## Where to Think Twice

- **If you need predictable monthly costs** for heavy, regular use — a credit-metered model can get more expensive than a flat subscription once you're running dozens of swaps or edits a week, and Remaker doesn't publish a clear per-action credit cost table to help you estimate spend upfront.
- **If you need programmatic/API access** to build face swap or upscaling into your own app or pipeline — no public API tier is advertised.
- **If accuracy and consistency on group/multi-face photos matter for professional use** (event photography, marketing composites) — Remaker itself flags that the standard swapper works best on single-face images, and results on crowded shots are less reliable even with the dedicated multi-face mode.
- **If you require enterprise data handling guarantees (SOC 2, formal DPAs, on-prem/offline processing)** — Remaker states images are deleted within 48 hours and not used to train models, but there's no published compliance certification for regulated industries.

## Bottom Line

Remaker AI is a solid pick if you want a fast, low-commitment way to face-swap a photo, clean up a background, or upscale an image without installing anything or paying for a subscription you'll barely use. The free, no-signup basic face swap is a genuinely useful entry point, and the credit-based pricing means you're not locked into a recurring charge. Where it falls short is transparency — the per-action credit costs aren't spelled out clearly, there's no API for builders, and multi-face accuracy needs its own dedicated mode to work reliably. For occasional, personal, or small-creator use it's a reasonable, low-risk tool; for regular commercial or high-volume production work, budget carefully or look for a tool with published API pricing and a flat subscription instead.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Remaker AI free?**
Basic single face swaps can be used without creating an account, and Remaker AI states this core swap is watermark-free. Most other tools (upscaling, batch processing, the photo editor, generators) draw down from a credit balance, and new sign-ups receive some free credits to try them.

**How does Remaker AI's pricing work?**
Instead of a monthly subscription, Remaker sells one-time credit packs — according to the company's site, starting around $5.99 for 200 credits and going up to $299 for 20,000 credits. Purchased credits don't expire, but each tool action (a swap, an upscale, a generation) consumes credits from your balance.

**Does Remaker AI store my uploaded photos?**
Remaker states on its site that uploaded images are deleted within 48 hours and that it does not store, save, or use uploaded photos to train its models. If data handling is a hard requirement for your use case, confirm current policy details directly on Remaker's privacy page before uploading sensitive images.

**Can Remaker AI swap faces in group photos?**
Yes, but the standard face swap tool is optimized for single-face images. For group shots with multiple people, Remaker recommends its dedicated Multi-Face Swap feature, and even then accuracy on crowded photos can be less consistent than single-face swaps.

**Does Remaker AI have an API?**
No public API or developer access is advertised on Remaker's marketing site at the time of writing. If you need to automate face swapping or image editing programmatically, you'd need to confirm directly with Remaker's support whether any developer tier exists, or look at an alternative tool built for API access.

**What are the best alternatives to Remaker AI?**
Depending on what you need, alternatives worth comparing include dedicated background-removal tools, standalone AI upscalers, or broader AI image-editing suites bundled into design tools like [Pixlr](/blog/pixlr-review). None of these are a perfect one-to-one swap for Remaker's specific face-swap focus, so compare feature sets directly against your use case.

**Is Remaker AI beginner-friendly?**
Yes — the workflow for face swapping is a simple three-step upload-and-click process with no technical setup, and the web app requires no downloads. The mobile apps follow the same simplified flow.

**Does Remaker AI work on mobile?**
Yes, Remaker AI is available as apps for both iOS and Android in addition to the browser-based web tool, so face swaps and edits can be done directly from a phone.
