title: Grok 2 Review: What xAI's Model Was, and What Happened
excerpt: Grok 2 was xAI's 2024 chatbot with FLUX.1 image generation. Here's what it offered, and why Grok 3 and Grok 4 replaced it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Grok 2 still worth using in 2026?

No — Grok 2 is a retired xAI model, not something you can sign up for today. xAI announced it on August 13, 2024, rolled it out to X Premium+ subscribers that month, and it's been fully superseded since: Grok 3 replaced it as xAI's flagship in February 2025, and Grok 4 followed in July 2025. Grok 2 no longer appears in xAI's current model docs.

**What happened, at a glance**

| | Grok 2 |
|---|---|
| Announced | August 13, 2024 (xAI blog post) |
| Rolled out | Grok-2 mini on X, August 14, 2024; full Grok-2, August 20, 2024 |
| Original access | X Premium and Premium+ subscribers; enterprise API "later that month" |
| Standout feature at launch | FLUX.1-based image generation (with Black Forest Labs), plus chat/coding/reasoning gains over Grok 1.5 |
| Superseded by | Grok 3 (February 17, 2025), then Grok 4 (July 9, 2025) |
| Current status | Discontinued as a frontier model; a source-available "Grok 2.5" release followed in August 2025 as its final chapter |

If you're looking for what's actually live right now, xAI's current lineup runs on the Grok 4 generation and later point releases — check [docs.x.ai/docs/models](https://docs.x.ai/docs/models) for the exact current model names and API pricing, since xAI ships updates faster than most review content can track.

## What Grok 2 actually was

Grok 2 was xAI's second-generation large language model, positioned as a meaningful jump over Grok 1.5, the model that had shipped a few months earlier. xAI's own announcement described it as a "frontier" assistant with upgraded performance in three areas it called out specifically: general chat, coding, and reasoning. Alongside the full Grok-2 model, xAI shipped Grok-2 mini, a smaller, faster sibling meant to trade some capability for speed — the same "full model plus a lighter mini variant" pattern most model labs use to cover both quality-sensitive and latency-sensitive use cases.

xAI said an early version of Grok-2, tested on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena leaderboard, outperformed Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4-Turbo on that benchmark at the time. That's a vendor-reported, point-in-time leaderboard result rather than an independent, durable benchmark — Arena rankings shift constantly as newer models are added, and Grok 2's placement there reflects a competitive landscape from mid-2024, not today's.

The other headline feature was image generation. xAI partnered with Black Forest Labs to bring FLUX.1 — an independently developed image model, not something xAI built in-house — into the Grok product on X, marking the first time Grok users could generate images directly from the chat interface rather than just text and vision understanding. This generated some controversy: FLUX.1's integration into Grok had comparatively light content filtering versus rivals like DALL-E or Midjourney, and users quickly demonstrated it generating images of copyrighted characters and public figures with minimal restriction — a dynamic that drew media scrutiny in the weeks after launch.

## How it was accessed and priced (historical)

Grok 2 was never sold as a standalone product with its own pricing page — access ran through existing xAI/X subscriptions and API billing, both of which have changed materially since. Treat everything below as historical context, not a current price list.

- **On X:** Grok-2 and Grok-2 mini launched exclusively for X Premium and Premium+ subscribers in August 2024. In December 2024, xAI expanded access to free X accounts as well, though with usage limits that scaled up for paid tiers.
- **Via API:** xAI opened enterprise API access "later that month" per its original announcement, pricing it separately from the consumer X subscription. Specific Grok-2 API rates aren't something worth reproducing here since the model isn't purchasable through the API anymore — if you need current xAI API pricing, that's now published against Grok 4-generation models on [docs.x.ai](https://docs.x.ai).
- **Later life:** In August 2025, xAI released "Grok 2.5" under a source-available license — a final iteration of the Grok 2 line, by which point it had already been sitting behind Grok 3 and Grok 4 as xAI's actual frontier offering for months.

Pricing, availability, and model line-ups in this space change fast; the figures above reflect Grok 2's documented rollout between August 2024 and August 2025 and shouldn't be read as anything currently purchasable.

## Features that actually differentiated it at the time

**Chat, coding, and reasoning gains over Grok 1.5.** xAI's own framing centered on these three areas as Grok 2's core improvement, without publishing granular task-by-task comparisons alongside the announcement — general users experienced it as a noticeably sharper assistant than the version it replaced, per xAI's characterization.

**Real-time X integration.** Like earlier Grok versions, Grok-2 pulled in live information from the X platform itself — a differentiator against chatbots with a fixed training cutoff and no connection to a live social feed, and arguably Grok's most persistent identity trait across every generation since.

**FLUX.1 image generation.** The single most talked-about addition. It made Grok one of the first major chat assistants to bundle a capable third-party image model directly into the same interface, at a moment when most competitors kept image generation as a separate product or a more heavily filtered feature.

**Vision understanding.** xAI described Grok-2 as capable in "both text and vision understanding" — accepting image input as context, not just generating images as output.

**Grok-2 mini as a speed/cost tradeoff.** For anyone building on the API, having a lighter mini variant alongside the full model meant an actual choice between latency and depth, rather than one-size-fits-all pricing.

## Who it was actually for (at the time)

- **X Premium/Premium+ subscribers curious about xAI's assistant.** Since Grok-2 access rode on the existing X subscription, it cost nothing extra for anyone already paying for Premium or Premium+ — making it low-risk to try.
- **Developers wanting an alternative frontier API to OpenAI/Anthropic.** The August 2024 enterprise API rollout gave builders a third major lab to evaluate against, at a moment when the frontier-model market was still consolidating around a handful of names.
- **Users interested in less-restricted AI image generation.** The FLUX.1 integration's lighter content filtering was, for better or worse, a genuine differentiator versus more conservative image tools at the time.

None of this maps cleanly onto "who should use it today," because Grok 2 access itself has been superseded — anyone in any of these groups is now using Grok 3, Grok 4, or whatever xAI's current release is, whether they realize the model changed or not.

## Pros and cons (as it stood historically)

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Meaningful step up from Grok 1.5 in chat, coding, and reasoning per xAI | Vendor-reported Arena result, not an independent or durable benchmark |
| Bundled FLUX.1 image generation directly into chat, early among major assistants | Light content filtering on image generation drew real controversy over copyrighted/public-figure outputs |
| No extra cost for existing X Premium/Premium+ subscribers | Full capability gated behind a paid X tier until the December 2024 free-tier expansion |
| Gave developers a third major frontier-API option via enterprise access | Specific Grok-2 API pricing was never widely durable public information |
| Grok-2 mini offered a genuine speed/cost tradeoff for builders | Superseded within about six months by Grok 3, and again by Grok 4 five months after that |

## Integrations and ecosystem (historical)

Grok-2's main "integration" was the X platform itself — it lived inside the Grok tab of the X app rather than as a separate app or browser extension, with real-time data access coming from X's own content, not third-party plugins. The API rollout gave developers programmatic access via the standard API-key pattern, rather than anything like a Zapier or Slack app. None of that ecosystem is specific to Grok 2 anymore — the same API surface today routes to xAI's current models instead.

## Where Grok 2 was a strong fit, historically

Grok 2 made the most sense for people already embedded in the X ecosystem who wanted an assistant tied to real-time platform data, and for early adopters curious about a less-filtered image generator bundled into a chat product rather than sold separately. Developers evaluating a third frontier lab beyond OpenAI and Anthropic also had a reasonable case for testing the API when it launched.

## Where to think twice (and what to use instead now)

There's nothing to sign up for anymore, since Grok 2 isn't a current product — but a few things matter if you're researching it after the fact:

- For **xAI's actual current chatbot**, use Grok through the X app or grok.com, and check [docs.x.ai/docs/models](https://docs.x.ai/docs/models) for whichever Grok 4-generation model is current — model names and capabilities there change more often than most review content can keep up with.
- If you need **current, comparable API pricing**, don't reuse any Grok-2-era figures you find elsewhere online; xAI's published rates have changed materially since 2024.
- If **image generation with minimal content filtering** was the appeal, know that content-moderation policies across AI image tools — including current Grok models — shift over time and should be checked against xAI's current terms rather than assumed to match 2024 behavior.
- If you need a **stable, long-supported model for production use**, building against a model generation that's already been fully retired (as Grok 2 has) is a reminder to track a vendor's deprecation policy before committing, not just its launch announcement.

## The bottom line

Grok 2 mattered in August 2024 as proof that xAI could ship a competitive frontier model just months after Grok 1.5, and its FLUX.1 image generator was a genuinely early, notable move to bundle capable image generation directly into a chat assistant. But it was never designed to last as xAI's flagship — Grok 3 replaced it within about six months, Grok 4 replaced that five months later, and by August 2025 even its final "Grok 2.5" iteration was arriving as a legacy release rather than a competitive one. If you're evaluating xAI's Grok today, you're evaluating a model two full generations past this one; Grok 2 belongs to AI's fast-moving history, not its current shopping list.

Browse more [AI & software deals](/category/software) for tools you can actually use today.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Grok 2 still available to use?**
Not as a current, actively supported xAI offering. It's been superseded by Grok 3 and Grok 4, and doesn't appear in xAI's current model documentation. A source-available "Grok 2.5" was released in August 2025 as a final legacy iteration, but it isn't xAI's frontier model.

**What replaced Grok 2?**
Grok 3, released February 17, 2025, replaced Grok 2 as xAI's flagship model. Grok 3 was itself replaced by Grok 4 on July 9, 2025. xAI has continued shipping updates since, so check [docs.x.ai/docs/models](https://docs.x.ai/docs/models) for whichever model is current when you're reading this.

**Was Grok 2 free to use?**
At launch in August 2024, it required an X Premium or Premium+ subscription. xAI expanded access to free X accounts, with usage limits, starting in December 2024.

**What was Grok 2's image generation feature?**
An experimental integration with FLUX.1, an image model built by Black Forest Labs (not xAI itself), that let X users generate images directly from the Grok chat interface. It drew scrutiny for comparatively light content filtering compared to rivals.

**Did Grok 2 have an API?**
Yes — xAI opened enterprise API access shortly after the August 2024 consumer launch. That API surface still exists today, but it now serves xAI's current models rather than Grok 2.

**How was Grok 2 different from Grok-2 mini?**
Grok-2 mini was a smaller, faster variant of the same generation, trading some capability for lower latency and cost — a common pattern where a "mini" sibling ships alongside a flagship model for use cases that prioritize speed.

**Is it worth researching Grok 2 for a project today?**
Only for historical context. If you're deciding what to build on or subscribe to now, look at xAI's current Grok models rather than Grok 2's 2024 specs, which no longer reflect what you'd actually get.

**Where can I find xAI's current pricing and models?**
xAI publishes its live model list and API pricing at [docs.x.ai/docs/models](https://docs.x.ai/docs/models) — treat that page, not older articles (including this one's historical pricing notes), as the source of truth for what's current.

title: Be My Eyes Review 2026: Be My AI Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: Be My Eyes pairs free live volunteer video calls with GPT-4-powered Be My AI. Here's what it costs, what it does, and who it's really for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Be My Eyes worth using for visually impaired users?

Yes. If you're blind or low vision, Be My Eyes is worth installing because it's free and does two things well: connect you to a real human volunteer on video within seconds, and — via its Be My AI feature built on OpenAI's GPT-4 — describe photos and answer follow-up questions instantly, no volunteer required.

| At a glance | Details |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free for blind/low-vision users |
| Free tier / trial | Full app is free; no paid consumer tier |
| Best for | Blind and low-vision individuals needing visual assistance |
| Standout feature | Be My AI — GPT-4-powered photo description and chat |

Be My Eyes doesn't have a matching store entry on this site, so there's no coupon page to link to here — everything below is sourced from the company's own site and public documentation rather than a listing we maintain.

## What Be My Eyes actually is

Be My Eyes is a Danish-founded accessibility app that's been around since 2015, built around one simple idea: point a blind or low-vision user's phone camera at something, and a sighted volunteer on a live video call tells them what they're looking at. Over the years the company expanded that idea into a broader platform — volunteer calling, business support lines for companies like NatWest and Barilla, workplace accessibility tools, and smartglasses integration.

The bigger shift came in 2023 with the launch of **Be My AI**, built in partnership with OpenAI on top of GPT-4's image-understanding capabilities. Instead of waiting for a volunteer to pick up, users can snap a photo and get an instant, detailed description, then ask follow-up questions — "what does the label say," "is this shirt still wearable," "read me the ingredients list." It rolled out as an open beta starting September 25, 2023 on iOS, with Android following that December, and has since become the feature most new users associate with the app.

It's worth being precise about what Be My Eyes is not. It's not a general-purpose AI chatbot wearing an accessibility skin, and it's not trying to replace orientation-and-mobility training. The company itself states plainly that Be My AI "does not and should not replace a white cane, guide dog, or other mobility aid" — a caveat that matters more here than in most AI tool reviews, because over-trusting an AI description in this context risks physical safety, not just wasted time.

## Pricing: what it actually costs

Pricing information below reflects the publicly stated terms as of this review's publish date and can change — always confirm current details on Be My Eyes' own site before relying on them.

| Plan | Who it's for | Cost | What's included |
|---|---|---|---|
| Be My Eyes (consumer app) | Blind and low-vision individuals | Free | Volunteer video calling, Be My AI, 180+ language support for calls, smartglasses pairing |
| Specialized Help / Business lines | Blind and low-vision individuals contacting partner companies | Free to the user | Direct video support from trained company reps (banks, retailers, tech support) |
| Be My Eyes for Business | Companies (e.g., NatWest, Microsoft, Google, Barilla) | Custom/enterprise pricing, not publicly listed | Accessible customer support integration, staff training, brand visibility in the app |

There is no separate "premium" consumer subscription tier as of this writing — the core promise of the product is that it's "free, easy to use and always there for you" for the people who actually need visual assistance. The revenue model instead runs through the business side: companies pay to be listed as a Specialized Help partner or to license the underlying technology, while individual blind and low-vision users pay nothing. That's a meaningfully different structure than most AI tools in this category, where the free tier is a funnel toward a paid one.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**Be My AI photo description and chat.** This is the headline feature. Take or upload a photo, and GPT-4's vision capability generates a detailed written description — then ask follow-up questions about specific details ("what color is the packaging," "is there an expiration date visible") in the same thread. Responses are delivered in written form across 29 languages, which specifically matters for deaf-blind users relying on braille displays, since it skips the audio-based interaction video calling requires.

**Live volunteer video calling.** The original feature is still the backbone of the app for situations where AI description isn't precise enough or where a live human is genuinely faster — matching socks, navigating an unfamiliar space, reading handwriting an AI might misparse. Calls are anonymous by design: volunteers see only what's shared through the camera and hear the caller's voice, nothing else.

**Specialized Help business lines.** Beyond ordinary volunteers, partner companies staff dedicated support lines inside the app, so a blind user can video-call a trained representative at their bank or a tech company directly rather than routing through a phone tree that assumes sight.

**Smartglasses and hands-free use.** The app extends to compatible smartglasses hardware, letting users get visual assistance without holding a phone up — relevant for anyone doing something else with their hands, like carrying groceries or holding a cane.

**Global volunteer network.** Be My Eyes reports operating in 150+ countries with 180+ supported languages on the volunteer side, a meaningfully large scale for a free, crowd-powered service — most competing volunteer-calling tools operate at a fraction of that footprint.

## Who it's actually for

- **Blind and low-vision individuals, day to day.** The core use case: reading mail, checking expiration dates, matching outfits, navigating unfamiliar spaces, getting a second opinion on something a screen reader can't parse. Both the free AI and free volunteer features cover this without any plan decision to make.
- **Deaf-blind users.** The written, chat-based nature of Be My AI (versus voice-only video calls) is specifically useful here, since responses can be read via braille display.
- **Companies building accessible customer support.** The Specialized Help / Be My Eyes for Business track targets brands wanting a genuinely accessible support channel instead of an inaccessible IVR or chat widget — and it's the part of the business that generates revenue.
- **Occasional sighted volunteers.** Anyone with a smartphone and a few spare minutes can sign up as a volunteer, a low-friction way to contribute to accessibility work.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Completely free for blind and low-vision users, no paid tier to upsell into | Be My AI can still misread or hallucinate details in a photo, same as any GPT-4-based vision tool |
| Combines instant AI description with real human backup when AI isn't enough | Live volunteer availability isn't guaranteed 24/7 in every language at every hour, despite broad coverage |
| Written, multi-language AI responses work well for deaf-blind users on braille displays | Not a substitute for mobility training, a cane, or a guide dog — and the company says so directly |
| Large global volunteer base (150+ countries) reduces call wait times in major languages | Business-side pricing for Be My Eyes for Business isn't publicly listed, so companies have to contact sales |
| No paywalls or feature gating for the core assistance features | Depends on decent camera quality and lighting for accuracy |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Be My Eyes isn't built around third-party integrations the way a productivity SaaS tool would be — its "ecosystem" is closer to a partner network. It pairs with compatible smartglasses hardware for hands-free use, and on the business side integrates with corporate support workflows through Specialized Help, with documented partnerships including Microsoft, Google, NatWest, TracFone, and Barilla. There's no public consumer-facing API or Zapier-style automation — the product is an app-based assistance service, not a developer platform.

## Where it's a strong fit

Be My Eyes is a strong fit for anyone who wants a zero-cost, always-available way to get visual information translated into something usable — an instant AI description of a can label, or a live volunteer helping navigate a hotel room for the first time. Pairing AI-first speed with human-backup accuracy is sensible: ask Be My AI first for anything low-stakes, and fall back to a volunteer call when precision matters (medication dosages, safety-critical labels, unfamiliar environments). It's also a fit for organizations wanting a real accessible support channel rather than a generic chatbot bolted onto their site.

## Where to think twice

Skip relying on Be My AI alone if the situation is safety-critical — reading a medication label correctly, crossing an unfamiliar intersection, verifying something that could cause harm if misdescribed. The company's own guidance is explicit that AI descriptions shouldn't replace a cane, guide dog, or other mobility aid, and GPT-4-class vision models can misread fine print, get colors or counts wrong, or miss details entirely — hedge accordingly rather than treating any single AI description as ground truth. If you need guaranteed real-time human support in a less common language at 3 a.m., volunteer availability, while broad, isn't contractually guaranteed. And if you're a business evaluating Specialized Help, expect a direct sales conversation rather than self-serve, transparent pricing online.

## Bottom line

Be My Eyes earns its place among accessibility tools by doing something rare for an AI-adjacent product: staying completely free for the people who need it most while being honest about its own limits. Be My AI is a genuinely useful layer on the original volunteer-calling idea — fast, private, available in 29 written languages — but works best as a first-pass tool backed up with a live volunteer or your own judgment when accuracy matters. For blind and low-vision users, there's essentially no downside to installing it; for businesses, the accessibility upside is real, but pricing requires a direct conversation with the company.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Be My Eyes actually free?**
Yes. The consumer app, including both live volunteer video calling and the Be My AI photo-description feature, is free for blind and low-vision users. There is no premium consumer subscription tier as of this writing.

**What AI model powers Be My AI?**
Be My AI is built on OpenAI's GPT-4 vision capabilities, developed in partnership between Be My Eyes and OpenAI. It launched in open beta on iOS in September 2023, with Android following in December 2023.

**Does Be My AI replace a guide dog or white cane?**
No, and Be My Eyes says so directly in its own materials. Be My AI is described as a supplementary tool, not a substitute for mobility aids or orientation-and-mobility training.

**How many languages does Be My Eyes support?**
Volunteer video calling supports 180+ languages through its global volunteer network. Be My AI's written chat responses are available in 29 languages.

**Is my data private when I use Be My Eyes?**
Volunteer calls are designed to be anonymous — volunteers see only what's shared through the camera and hear the caller's voice, with no other identifying information exchanged. For how photo data submitted to Be My AI is stored or used by the underlying AI provider, check Be My Eyes' current privacy policy, since data-handling details for AI features can change as the technology partnership evolves.

**Are there alternatives to Be My Eyes?**
Yes — Microsoft's Seeing AI and Envision are other well-known apps in the same visual-assistance category, each with a different feature mix (Seeing AI leans toward on-device, task-specific recognition like currency and document reading; Envision offers both a phone app and dedicated smartglasses hardware). Which one fits best depends on your mix of AI description, live human support, and hardware needs.

For more free and paid AI tools worth trying, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: LobeChat Review 2026: Open-Source AI Chat UI, Verdict
excerpt: LobeChat lets you self-host a multi-model AI chat interface for free, or use LobeHub Cloud. Here's the license, pricing, and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is LobeChat worth using?

LobeChat (now developed under the LobeHub brand) is an open-source AI chat interface you can self-host for free or run through LobeHub's paid cloud service. It's a strong pick if you want one interface for multiple AI models and full control over your data — less so if you just want a polished app with zero setup.

| At a glance | |
|---|---|
| Cost | Free (self-hosted, source-available) or LobeHub Cloud from $0/mo (500,000 credits) |
| License | LobeHub Community License (Apache 2.0-based, commercial-derivative restrictions apply) |
| Self-hosting | Yes — Docker, Docker Compose, Vercel, Zeabur, Sealos, Alibaba Cloud |
| Best for | Developers, privacy-conscious users, teams wanting a unified multi-model chat UI |
| Standout feature | Bring-your-own-API-key access to dozens of model providers in one interface |

## What LobeChat actually is

LobeChat is an open-source front end for large language models — a self-hostable alternative to the individual ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini web apps, except it lets you plug in API keys from many providers at once and switch between them in the same conversation window. The project is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, and Drizzle ORM, and it's distributed on GitHub under the `lobehub/lobe-chat` repository, where it has accumulated over 80,000 stars.

The team behind it has been expanding the product beyond a single chat window into what it now calls LobeHub — an "agent platform" built around persistent AI agents, agent groups that collaborate on tasks, scheduling, and shared workspaces. Anyone evaluating LobeChat today is really evaluating two overlapping things: the open-source chat framework you can run yourself, and the hosted LobeHub Cloud product that layers a subscription and managed infrastructure on top.

Unlike a typical SaaS AI tool, LobeChat doesn't have a single "pricing page" that tells the whole story. Running it yourself is free software, but you still pay whoever's model API you connect it to (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and so on), unless you point it at a local model. LobeHub Cloud is a separate, optional layer for people who'd rather not manage servers or API keys.

## License and cost — what "open source" actually means here

The repository is released under the **LobeHub Community License**, an Apache 2.0-based license with an added condition: you're free to run it, modify it, and use it as your own frontend or backend service, but if you want to build and distribute a derivative product based on LobeChat's code, you need a commercial license from the LobeHub team. Self-hosting for personal or internal team use is unrestricted; repackaging LobeChat as your own competing product is not. Because it's source-available rather than a plain MIT/Apache project with no strings attached, teams with strict open-source procurement policies should read the license text directly.

## LobeHub Cloud pricing

If you don't want to self-host, LobeHub sells a managed cloud version with a credits-based subscription. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability below were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly for AI products, so confirm current numbers on LobeHub's own pricing page before committing.

| Plan | Price | Monthly credits | Storage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/mo | 500,000 | 10 MB files | Access to a base model, community support |
| Starter | $9.90/mo (~$118.80/yr annual) | 5,000,000 | 1 GB files | 5,000 vector storage entries, agent memory |
| Premium | $19.90/mo (~$238.80/yr annual) | 15,000,000 | 2 GB files | 10,000 vector entries, priority email support |
| Ultimate | $39.90/mo (~$478.80/yr annual) | 35,000,000 | 4 GB files | 20,000 vector entries, priority chat + email support |

There's also an Enterprise tier for teams that want private deployment or white-labeled branding, priced on request. The free plan's 500,000 monthly credits translate to roughly a few hundred messages on the included base model — fine for testing, tight for daily use.

The self-hosted route sidesteps this subscription entirely: you run the software for free and pay only for whichever model API calls you make, or nothing at all if you connect a local model server. For a developer already paying for an OpenAI or Anthropic API key, self-hosting is usually cheaper long-term; for a non-technical user who wants a working chat app today, LobeHub Cloud's free or Starter tier removes the setup step.

## Core features that differentiate it

**Multi-provider model access.** Instead of locking you into one vendor, LobeChat lets you register API keys for a long list of providers — OpenAI, Anthropic's Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, Zhipu's GLM, and others — and switch between them per conversation. This is the biggest reason people choose it over a vendor's own web app: one interface, one chat history, many models.

**Plugin and MCP support.** LobeChat supports function-calling plugins and is compatible with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the emerging standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources. The project describes access to "10,000+ skills" through this plugin ecosystem, a figure that comes from LobeHub's own marketing rather than an independently verified count.

**Agent Builder and agent groups.** Beyond single-turn chat, the platform lets you configure persistent "agents" with their own instructions, memory, and tool access, and — in the newer LobeHub layer — group multiple agents together to collaborate on a task. This pushes LobeChat closer to an agent-orchestration tool than a plain chatbot UI.

**Knowledge base and vector storage.** Paid LobeHub Cloud tiers include a set number of vector storage entries, which back retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — uploading documents and having the model reference them in conversation. Self-hosted deployments can wire up their own vector database, but that takes extra configuration LobeHub Cloud handles for you.

**Voice interaction.** The project ships with text-to-speech and speech-to-text support via its own `@lobehub/tts` library, letting you talk to and hear responses from whichever model you've connected.

## Who it's actually for

- **Developers and self-hosters** comfortable with Docker or Vercel get the most value — free software, full data control, and the ability to swap model providers without switching apps.
- **Privacy-conscious individuals or small teams** can self-host on their own infrastructure and point it at any model API, including local models.
- **Teams wanting a single AI workspace** without managing infrastructure are better served by LobeHub Cloud's Starter or Premium tier, which adds agent memory and managed vector storage.
- **Non-technical users who just want "a ChatGPT-like app"** may find the setup friction higher than simply using ChatGPT or Claude directly — see our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review) or [Claude AI review](/blog/claude-ai-review).
- **Businesses needing a branded, white-labeled deployment** should look at LobeHub's Enterprise tier rather than the open-source edition, given the license's redistribution restriction.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free and open-source to self-host | License restricts building/distributing derivative commercial products |
| Connect many model providers in one interface | Self-hosting requires comfort with Docker/env vars/API keys |
| Active project — 80,000+ GitHub stars, frequent updates | Pivot toward "agent platform" features can feel like scope creep for chat-only users |
| Plugin/MCP ecosystem for extending capability | Free LobeHub Cloud tier's message allowance is thin for daily use |
| Voice, knowledge base, and multi-agent features built in | Some claims ("10,000+ skills") come from vendor marketing, not an independent count |
| No vendor lock-in — swap model providers anytime | Still pay model-provider API costs on top of self-hosting, unless using local models |

## Integrations and ecosystem

LobeChat's biggest ecosystem strength is provider-agnosticism: rather than a fixed set of integrations, it's built to plug into whichever model APIs you supply keys for. It supports MCP-compatible plugins for tool use, and its cloud deployment options extend to Vercel, Zeabur, Sealos, Alibaba Cloud, and RepoCloud for one-click hosting, in addition to a standard Docker Compose setup for anyone running their own server. There's no official mention of a dedicated desktop application in the current documentation, so if an offline-installable desktop client matters to your decision, verify current availability directly on LobeHub's site.

## Where it's a strong fit

LobeChat earns its following among developers who want to experiment with multiple LLMs side by side without paying for separate subscriptions to each vendor's app, and among anyone who values owning their chat data outright. The plugin/MCP support also makes it a reasonable base for people building their own AI-assisted workflows.

## Where to think twice

If you need a tool that works out of the box with zero configuration, LobeChat's self-hosted path will frustrate you — you're setting up a database, environment variables, and API keys, not clicking "sign up." If your team needs a fully vetted, enterprise-compliance-ready product with formal SLAs, the open-source edition alone won't get you there; evaluate the paid Enterprise tier and confirm its compliance posture with LobeHub directly. And if you need a fully free tool with zero downstream provider costs, remember self-hosting still requires paying a model API (or running a local model) — LobeChat itself being free doesn't make usage free.

## Bottom line

LobeChat is one of the more capable open-source options for anyone who wants a single, self-hostable interface across multiple AI model providers, backed by a genuinely active project and a growing plugin ecosystem. It's not plug-and-play, though — the real audience is developers and technically comfortable users willing to trade setup time for data control and vendor flexibility. If you'd rather skip the infrastructure work, LobeHub Cloud's free or Starter tier gets you most of the same interface without server management, at the cost of a subscription and usage credits.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is LobeChat free?**
The self-hosted software is free under the LobeHub Community License. You'll still need your own API keys for whichever AI model providers you connect, which have their own usage costs — or connect a local model to avoid API fees. LobeHub Cloud, the managed hosted version, has a free tier plus paid plans starting at $9.90/month.

**Do I need to know how to code to self-host LobeChat?**
Not necessarily, but you need basic comfort with command-line tools, Docker, or a platform like Vercel, plus the ability to manage API keys. If that sounds daunting, LobeHub Cloud removes the setup step entirely.

**What AI models does LobeChat support?**
Many providers rather than one — including OpenAI, Anthropic's Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, and Zhipu's GLM models, as long as you supply an API key for that provider.

**Is my data private if I self-host LobeChat?**
Self-hosting keeps your chat data on infrastructure you control, a meaningful privacy improvement over a third-party app — though prompts still leave your server whenever sent to an external model API, unless you run a fully local model. LobeHub Cloud handles data under its own hosted terms, which you should review directly.

**How is LobeChat different from just using ChatGPT or Claude directly?**
ChatGPT and Claude are single-vendor apps tied to one company's models. LobeChat is a neutral interface connecting to several vendors' models in one app, plus self-hosting and plugin/agent features neither of those apps offers. See our [ChatGPT review](/blog/chatgpt-review), [Claude AI review](/blog/claude-ai-review), and [Google Gemini review](/blog/google-gemini-review) for how the underlying models compare.

**Can I use LobeChat commercially, and how is it different from LobeHub?**
You can run it internally or for customers under the Community License, but distributing your own product based on LobeChat's code requires a commercial license from LobeHub. LobeChat is the original open-source chat framework; LobeHub is the broader brand and hosted platform layering agent orchestration and a subscription cloud service on top of it. The GitHub repository is still named `lobe-chat`.

title: Supermemory Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Supermemory review: how the AI memory API for agents works, its 2026 pricing tiers, MCP support, and who should actually use it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Supermemory worth using to give your AI agent long-term memory?

Supermemory is a memory API for AI apps and agents — it stores conversation history, documents, and user context in a vector-graph database, then retrieves the relevant slices back into a model's prompt so ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, or a custom agent can "remember" things across sessions. It's a strong fit for developers building agents that need persistent, per-user memory; it's overkill if you just want a single chatbot to recall your last message.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free plan ($0/month, $5 in monthly credits); paid plans from $19/month |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — free plan with $5/month in usage credits, no credit card details published as required |
| **Best for** | Developers and teams building AI agents, copilots, or chatbots that need memory to persist across sessions |
| **Standout feature** | Model- and harness-agnostic memory layer usable via API, SDKs, or MCP, so it plugs into Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and custom agents without lock-in |

## What Supermemory actually is

Supermemory positions itself as infrastructure, not an end-user product. Instead of being a chatbot you open and type into, it's a backend service that other AI products and agents call over an API to store and recall memories — a database purpose-built for one job: remembering things about a specific user, task, or tenant, and surfacing the right fragment of that history back into an LLM's context window at the right moment.

The company describes its approach as extracting and "dreaming on" the context of every user, task, and tenant — reprocessing stored memories in the background so retrieval gets smarter over time, rather than doing simple keyword or vector lookups on raw logs. It runs on a vector-graph database, combining semantic similarity search with relationship mapping so it can connect related facts, not just retrieve isolated snippets.

Supermemory is explicitly model-agnostic — it doesn't care whether the calling application is powered by GPT, Claude, Gemini, or an open-weight model, it just stores and returns memory. That's different from memory features built into a single vendor's product (like ChatGPT's built-in memory), which only work inside that one app.

## Pricing

Supermemory uses a subscription-plus-usage model: every paid plan comes with a monthly credit balance, and actual API calls (storage, search, retrieval-augmented operations) draw down against that balance at the same per-operation rates regardless of tier. Only unique content gets billed, and purchased top-up credits don't expire, though subscription credits reset every month.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | $5 in monthly credits |
| Pro | $19/month | $20 in monthly credits, auto top-up, 3 team seats, priority support |
| Max | $100/month | $130 in monthly credits (6.5x the credits of Pro), Gmail connector |
| Scale | $399/month | $600 in monthly credits, S3 and web-crawler connectors, unlimited team seats, dedicated support, SOC 2/HIPAA/self-hosted options |

On top of the plan tiers, Supermemory publishes a flat usage rate card that applies no matter which subscription you're on:

- **Memory storage**: $5 per million SM tokens for plain text, $10 per million for rich content (images, structured data, etc.)
- **SuperRAG retrieval**: $1 per million tokens for text, $2 per million for rich media
- **Search & traversal**: $5 per million queries
- **Operations** (general API calls): $100 per million operations

Qualifying early-stage startups and academic researchers can apply for the Scale plan free for three months — worth checking if you're prototyping and don't yet have revenue to justify $399/month.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AI infrastructure pricing moves fast, so confirm current numbers on Supermemory's own [pricing page](https://supermemory.ai/pricing) before committing a production budget.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**Vector-graph memory, not just vector search.** Most "AI memory" tools are a vector database with a marketing wrapper — embed text, store it, run nearest-neighbor lookups. Supermemory layers a graph structure on top so memories connect by relationship, which matters for agents doing multi-step reasoning rather than single-turn chat.

**Model- and harness-agnostic access.** Supermemory says it works with any model and harness — ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Grok, and custom agents alike — via API, SDK, plugin, or MCP, without locking your memory layer to one vendor's ecosystem.

**MCP (Model Context Protocol) support.** Supermemory can be dropped directly into MCP-compatible tools like Claude Desktop and coding agents such as Cursor — a lower-friction path than wiring a custom API integration if you just want persistent memory inside an existing AI coding workflow.

**Connectors for real data sources.** Higher tiers add native connectors — Gmail on Max, S3 and a web crawler on Scale — so memory can ingest email threads, cloud files, or crawled web content, not just chat input.

**Self-hosting and compliance posture.** Supermemory says it's SOC 2 certified, HIPAA compliant, and GDPR aligned, with deployment options in a customer's own data center, VPC, or fully local/self-hosted runs on Scale and Enterprise — relevant for teams handling regulated data that can't rely purely on a shared multi-tenant cloud.

## Who it's actually for

**Solo developers and indie hackers** prototyping an agent or copilot can start on the free plan or Pro at $19/month and get persistent memory without building a retrieval pipeline from scratch.

**Small teams shipping an AI product** are the target for Pro or Max — three team seats, the jump to $130 in monthly credits, and the Gmail connector make sense once memory needs scale past a single builder's side project.

**Companies with compliance requirements** (healthcare, finance, regulated user data) are pushed toward Scale, where SOC 2/HIPAA-aligned handling, self-hosting, unlimited seats, and dedicated support live.

**Enterprises** needing custom SLAs or volume pricing beyond the published rate card should contact sales, since enterprise terms aren't published.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Model-agnostic — works across ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and custom agents | No published Enterprise pricing — requires a sales conversation |
| Free tier for testing before committing to a paid plan | Usage-based billing adds complexity versus a flat fee |
| MCP support makes Claude Desktop/coding-agent integration low-friction | Non-technical users get no direct benefit — it's developer infrastructure |
| SOC 2/HIPAA-aligned handling and self-hosting for compliance-sensitive teams | Self-hosting and some connectors gated behind the $399/month Scale plan |
| Top-up credits don't expire, giving some budget flexibility | Retrieval quality depends on how the calling app structures stored memories |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Supermemory exposes a REST API and SDKs for direct programmatic integration, alongside plugins and MCP support for dropping memory into tools like Claude and coding agents (Cursor is explicitly named). Connector support scales with plan tier: Gmail unlocks on Max, and S3 plus a web crawler unlock on Scale. There's no public mention of a native Zapier or Slack app on the marketing pages reviewed for this piece — verify current connector coverage on Supermemory's [docs site](https://supermemory.ai/docs) if that matters for your workflow.

## Where it's a strong fit

Supermemory earns its keep in agent-heavy workflows: a coding assistant that needs to remember a codebase's conventions across sessions, a support agent that should recall a user's prior tickets without re-reading the whole history, or a personal assistant accumulating knowledge about its user over months. Because it's model-agnostic, it's also a reasonable hedge for teams that might switch LLM providers later — the memory layer doesn't need rebuilding if the model underneath changes. The MCP path is a particular strength for developers already inside Claude Desktop or MCP-enabled coding tools.

## Where to think twice

Supermemory says it handles over 1 trillion tokens a month across 100,000+ organizations — treat that as a vendor statement rather than an independently audited figure, since no third-party benchmark was available to verify it.

Skip Supermemory if you need a single, fully free memory solution with no usage-based component — the free tier's $5/month credit allowance gets consumed quickly by real traffic, and every paid tier bills usage on top of the subscription. Skip it too if your product is a simple single-session chatbot with no need for cross-conversation memory, or if you need a fully self-hosted, on-prem deployment without paid tiers — that's gated to Scale ($399/month) and Enterprise, not Free or Pro. Teams without in-house engineering resources should also be cautious: this is API-first infrastructure for developers, not a drag-and-drop tool.

## Bottom line

Supermemory is a credible, purpose-built answer to a real problem in AI application development: giving agents memory that persists, connects related facts through a graph structure, and works regardless of which model sits on top. The free tier and $19/month Pro plan make it accessible to try before committing, while Scale's compliance features and self-hosting give it a real path into regulated industries. The tradeoffs are typical of usage-based developer infrastructure — costs grow with traffic, and some capability is reserved for the highest tier. If you're building anything that needs an AI agent to remember users or tasks over time, it's worth testing on the free plan first.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Supermemory free to use?**

There's a free plan that includes $5 in monthly usage credits, which is enough to test integration and light usage but will likely need a paid plan once an application sees real traffic.

**What models and tools does Supermemory work with?**

Supermemory is designed to be model-agnostic, working with ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Grok, and other AI harnesses via its API, SDKs, plugins, or MCP support.

**How is Supermemory priced beyond the base subscription?**

Every plan includes a monthly credit balance, and actual usage (memory storage, search, retrieval, and general operations) draws down against those credits at published per-operation rates that are the same across all tiers.

**Can Supermemory be self-hosted?**

Yes, self-hosting is available, but it's limited to the Scale plan ($399/month) and Enterprise agreements — it isn't included on the Free or Pro tiers.

**Is Supermemory compliant for healthcare or regulated data?**

The company states it is SOC 2 certified, HIPAA compliant, and GDPR aligned, with data center, VPC, or local deployment options — worth independently confirming against your specific compliance requirements before storing regulated data.

**Does Supermemory replace a vector database I'd otherwise build myself?**

It's designed to, combining vector search with graph relationships and a retrieval pipeline out of the box, so most teams won't need to separately stand up and maintain their own vector database for agent memory.

**What are the alternatives to Supermemory?**

Alternatives include building directly on a vector database (like Pinecone or Weaviate) plus custom retrieval logic, or using memory features built into specific model providers' own products, though those are typically locked to that one vendor's ecosystem.

**Is Supermemory beginner-friendly for non-developers?**

No — it's API-first developer infrastructure. Non-technical users won't interact with it directly; it's meant to be integrated into another product or agent by a developer.

title: Monica AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Monica AI Review 2026: an honest look at the multi-model browser assistant's pricing, features, credit system, and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Monica AI worth installing as your browser assistant?

Monica is a browser extension and app that puts GPT, Claude, Gemini, and other models behind one sidebar, so you can chat, summarize a page, translate text, or generate images without switching tabs. It's a genuinely convenient way to access multiple frontier models in one place, but the credit-based pricing and a rough record on cancellation complaints mean it's worth reading the fine print before you subscribe.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free plan available; paid plans start at Monica Pro, with Unlimited and Team tiers above it |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — limited daily queries and a small pool of "advanced" model credits per month |
| **Best for** | Browser-first users who want GPT, Claude, and Gemini access plus page summarization/translation without juggling separate subscriptions |
| **Standout feature** | Sidebar access to multiple frontier models plus built-in web-page summarization, translation, and ChatPDF in one extension |

### What Monica actually is

Monica (useMonica.ai, also styled Monica.im) is an all-in-one AI assistant shipping as a Chrome/Edge extension, a Windows/Mac desktop app, and iOS/Android mobile apps. Its pitch: instead of paying for and switching between ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini separately, you open one sidebar (Cmd+M or Ctrl+M) and pick the model for the task at hand.

Under the hood, Monica doesn't train its own foundation model — it's a wrapper and productivity layer over third-party models. Its Chrome Web Store listing and marketing pages reference access to OpenAI's GPT line (including reasoning models like o1/o3-mini), Anthropic's Claude family, Google's Gemini, and image/video generation tools including Sora. Which models are available on which plan shifts as vendors ship new versions — treat any specific model list as a snapshot, not a permanent feature set, and check the extension's model picker for what's live today.

The company built its business by layering browser-native features on top of that model access: highlight text on any page and Monica can rewrite, translate, or explain it; open a YouTube video or long article and it can summarize it; drop in a PDF and it becomes a queryable document via a built-in ChatPDF-style tool. That's the actual differentiator versus just having a ChatGPT tab open — Monica lives inside the page you're already on.

### Pricing

Monica runs on a tiered subscription model layered with a credits system: standard chat usage on cheaper/older models is generally unmetered on paid plans, while "advanced" usage — reasoning models, higher-end image/video generation, and premium features — draws from a monthly pool of advanced credits that resets each billing cycle. Monica's own help documentation describes credits as being "based on your user type and subscription," and add-on credit packs can be purchased once your monthly allowance runs out.

| Plan | Who it's for | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| **Free** | Casual, occasional use | Limited daily queries, a small trial allowance of advanced/image/video credits, browser sidebar access |
| **Monica Pro** | Individuals who use AI chat and writing regularly | Expanded advanced-credit allowance, access to premium models, writing/translation tools, priority processing |
| **Monica Unlimited** | Power users and heavy daily use | The largest personal-plan credit pool, marketed as the top individual tier (note: "Unlimited" refers to the plan name — actual advanced-model usage still draws from a monthly credit allowance, not literally unlimited premium generations) |
| **Monica Team** | Small teams and businesses | Seat-based pricing, shared team workspace, centralized billing, and admin controls, per Monica's Team Edition FAQ |

Monica's pricing page loads exact dollar figures dynamically rather than as static text, and third-party sources don't agree closely enough on current numbers to reprint responsibly here — **confirm current monthly and annual prices for Pro, Unlimited, and Team directly on [Monica's pricing page](https://monica.im/pricing)** before subscribing. As of this post's date, the general tier structure above was accurate, but Monica has changed tier names and credit allowances before, so re-verify the exact numbers at checkout rather than assuming.

### Core features that actually differentiate it

- **Multi-model sidebar chat.** Instead of one model, you get a picker — useful if you've noticed one model handles code better and another handles tone/writing better, since you're not locked into a single vendor's output style.
- **Page and video summarization.** Monica can condense a long article or a YouTube video's transcript into a short summary without leaving the tab, which is a real time-saver for research-heavy browsing.
- **Built-in translation.** A "bilingual reading" mode overlays translations on web pages, plus standalone text and PDF translation — handy if you regularly read non-English sources.
- **ChatPDF-style document Q&A.** Upload or open a PDF and ask questions against it, rather than manually copy-pasting chunks into a chat window.
- **Image and video generation.** Text-to-image and text-to-video tools sit in the same sidebar, including newer generation models as Monica adds them — useful for quick visual drafts without opening a separate app.
- **Agent/automation tools.** Monica has added agent-style features (branded "Monica Agent" and "Browser Operator" in its extension listing) aimed at multi-step tasks and browser automation, though these are newer additions worth testing against your own workflow before relying on them.

### Who it's actually for

- **Solo users who want one subscription instead of three.** If you're currently paying separately for ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and a translation tool, consolidating into Monica Pro can be cheaper — but only if your usage fits inside its advanced-credit allowance; heavy daily use of premium models can burn through credits faster than expected.
- **Researchers and students who read a lot online.** The page-summarization, YouTube-summary, and PDF Q&A tools are built for exactly this workflow and are arguably Monica's strongest differentiator over a plain chatbot tab.
- **Non-English-first users.** The built-in bilingual reading and translation tools are a genuine convenience generic chatbots don't offer out of the box.
- **Small teams needing shared AI access.** Monica Team adds seat management and centralized billing, useful if you want to avoid handing out individual model-vendor logins to every employee.
- **Not ideal for developers** who need raw API access and predictable per-token billing — Monica's credit system adds an abstraction layer that makes cost prediction harder than going directly to OpenAI's or Anthropic's own API pricing.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| One subscription for multiple frontier models instead of three separate ones | Credit system makes real usage limits harder to predict than flat per-model pricing |
| Deep browser integration — summarize, translate, and query PDFs without leaving the page | "Unlimited" plan name doesn't mean unlimited advanced-model usage; it's still credit-metered |
| Available across Chrome/Edge, desktop, and mobile with a consistent sidebar | Multiple Trustpilot reviews describe billing and cancellation problems (see below) |
| High Chrome Web Store rating (4.9/5 across tens of thousands of reviews) | You're dependent on Monica's pass-through access rather than a direct vendor relationship |
| Built-in agent/automation tools for multi-step browser tasks | Newer agent features are less battle-tested than the core chat/summarize tools |

### Integrations and ecosystem

Monica is primarily a browser-extension-first product rather than an API-and-integrations platform. It works as a Chrome and Edge extension, a Windows and Mac desktop app, and iOS/Android mobile apps, all syncing through the same account. It doesn't position itself as a Zapier- or Slack-style integration hub — its "integration" story is really about sitting on top of the browser and other AI models rather than connecting out to third-party business tools. If your workflow depends on Slack bots, Zapier automations, or a documented public API, check Monica's current developer documentation before assuming support exists.

### Where it's a strong fit

Monica earns its keep for people whose daily AI usage is spread across "chat with a model," "summarize this page," and "translate this text" — the kind of scattered, browser-native tasks that normally mean several different tabs and tools. If you spend a lot of time reading and researching online and want one tool that follows you across pages instead of a chatbot you have to manually copy content into, the sidebar model works well.

### Where to think twice

- **If you need predictable, flat-rate pricing** — the advanced-credit system means your effective cost per premium query can vary, which is a worse fit than a flat per-seat plan if your team needs to forecast AI spend precisely.
- **If billing reliability and easy cancellation are a dealbreaker** — independent reviews on Trustpilot (Monica's page sits around a 1.6/5 TrustScore from a small sample of reviews) include repeated complaints about being charged after cancellation and disputes over what "unlimited" plans include. Read Monica's current cancellation policy carefully and watch your renewal date if you're unsure.
- **If you need a fully free tool** — the free tier is limited enough that any regular use of premium models will push you toward a paid plan.
- **If your organization needs enterprise-grade compliance guarantees (SOC 2, HIPAA, etc.)** — verify Monica's current certifications directly with their sales team rather than assuming parity with the underlying model vendors' own enterprise offerings.
- **If you want a direct vendor relationship** — because Monica passes through third-party models, you're subject to its own rate limits and model-access decisions on top of the underlying vendors', an extra layer of dependency some users would rather avoid.

### The bottom line

Monica is a legitimately useful browser-native AI assistant if what you actually want is quick multi-model chat plus summarization, translation, and PDF Q&A without leaving your current tab — that combination is hard to replicate by stitching together separate tools. Where it gets shakier is the business side: credit-metered pricing makes cost harder to predict than a flat subscription, and a cluster of independent complaints about billing and cancellation means anyone subscribing should read the current terms carefully and watch renewal dates. If you're a heavy single-model power user who mostly wants raw chat, going direct to that model's own app may be simpler; if your days involve a lot of scattered browser research, Monica's sidebar approach earns its place.

### FAQ

**Is Monica AI free to use?**
Monica has a free tier with limited daily queries and a small trial allowance of advanced-model credits. Regular use of premium models generally requires a paid plan.

**What AI models does Monica give you access to?**
Monica acts as a front end to multiple third-party models, historically including OpenAI's GPT line, Anthropic's Claude family, and Google's Gemini, along with image and video generation tools. The lineup changes as Monica adds newer versions, so check the in-app model picker for what's currently available.

**Does Monica train its own AI model?**
No — Monica is a productivity and browser-integration layer over third-party foundation models, not a model developer itself.

**How does Monica's credit system work?**
Basic chat is generally unmetered on paid plans, while "advanced" features (premium/reasoning models, image and video generation) draw from a monthly pool of credits tied to your subscription tier. Credits reset each billing cycle, and add-on packs can be purchased if you run out.

**Is Monica available outside of Chrome?**
Yes. Beyond the Chrome/Edge extension, Monica offers Windows and Mac desktop apps and iOS/Android mobile apps, all syncing to the same account.

**Are there complaints about Monica's billing or cancellation process?**
Yes — independent Trustpilot reviews include multiple reports of being charged after cancellation and disagreements over what "unlimited" plans include. If you subscribe, review the cancellation policy and monitor your renewal date closely.

**What's a good alternative to Monica if I only need one AI model?**
Going directly to that vendor's own app (ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini) gives you a direct billing relationship and typically clearer usage limits, at the cost of losing Monica's browser-native summarization and translation tools.

**Is Monica good for teams?**
Monica Team adds seat-based access and centralized billing, per Monica's own Team Edition FAQ, but teams with strict compliance requirements should confirm current certifications directly with Monica before committing.

For more AI and software tool coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Luma AI Review 2026: Dream Machine Pricing & Features
excerpt: Luma AI (Dream Machine) review covering Ray 3.2 video pricing, credits, key features, and how it differs from the unrelated Luma AI by Serviceaide.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Luma AI (Dream Machine) worth using for AI video generation?

Luma AI — the video-generation company behind Dream Machine and the Ray model family — is one of the stronger text-to-video and image-to-video tools available, with genuinely cinematic motion and camera control that few competitors match. It's best for creators, agencies and marketers who need short AI video clips fast, though the credit-based pricing gets expensive once you're generating at scale.

Note: this review covers **Luma AI (Luma Labs, lumalabs.ai)**, the video-generation company behind Dream Machine and the Ray models — not the unrelated enterprise IT chatbot "Luma AI by Serviceaide," which [TheSmartFares has reviewed separately](/blog/luma-ai-serviceaide-review). Different companies, different products, same name.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $30/month (Plus plan, 10,000 credits) |
| Free tier/trial | "Try for free" access to the web app; no published free credit amount |
| Best for | Solo creators, marketing teams and agencies producing short AI video/image content |
| Standout feature | Ray 3.2 model's frame-level camera and motion control, plus multi-model orchestration in one canvas |

## What Luma AI actually is

Luma Labs started out building neural radiance field (NeRF) capture tools before pivoting into generative video with Dream Machine's 2024 launch. Dream Machine made Luma's name as one of the first widely accessible text-to-video and image-to-video generators, producing short clips with notably more coherent motion than most tools available at the time.

Since then, the product has evolved into a broader creative workspace the company calls Luma Agents — an "infinite canvas" combining Luma's own models with a growing list of third-party ones, coordinated by an orchestration layer called the Luma Agent. Dream Machine's video capability remains the core; it's just wrapped in a more ambitious multimodal platform than at launch.

Luma's own models include Ray 3.2 (video, built around "directing every frame" through keyframe and camera control) and Uni-1 / Uni-1.1 (image generation and editing, described by Luma as a "brand intelligence" model tuned to stay consistent with reference assets like logos and characters). The platform also plugs in third-party generators — Google's Veo, Kuaishou's Kling, ByteDance's Seedream/Seedance, ElevenLabs' audio models and Nano Banana image models — all selectable in the same canvas. That multi-model access is arguably Luma's biggest differentiator: you're not stuck with one house style if a shot calls for something else.

## Pricing

Luma sells access through the web app on a monthly credit subscription, plus a separate pay-per-generation API for developers who want the models in their own product rather than Luma's canvas.

| Plan | Price | Credits/month | What's included |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plus | $30/mo ($25/mo billed yearly) | 10,000 | Luma + third-party image/video models, guest collaborator access, commercial use rights |
| Pro | $90/mo ($75/mo billed yearly) | 40,000 | Everything in Plus, plus a 4x usage multiplier on Luma Agent workflows |
| Ultra | $300/mo ($250/mo billed yearly) | 150,000 | Everything in Pro, plus a 15x usage multiplier |
| Team / Enterprise | Custom (contact sales) | Shared team pool | Team management, project organization, usage analytics, SSO (Team); custom fine-tuning and dedicated training (Enterprise) |

Developers pay per generation instead of a flat subscription: vendor-published rates put Ray 3.2 video at roughly $0.15–$1.20 for a 5-second clip (scaling with resolution), with HDR/EXR export costing 2–3x base price; Uni-1.1 image generation runs about $0.04–$0.06 per image, roughly double for the "Max" variant. A separate "Scale" tier offers dedicated capacity for high-volume API users.

Credits reset each billing cycle and don't roll over, and failed generations are automatically refunded — worth knowing since a five-second clip at higher resolutions can burn through a meaningful chunk of a Plus allotment in a handful of attempts. Luma doesn't publish a specific free-credit number for new sign-ups; confirm the current trial allowance on Luma's own site.

Pricing, free-tier limits and available models were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AI video tooling and its pricing structures move fast, so double-check current numbers on [Luma's pricing page](https://lumalabs.ai/dream-machine/pricing) before committing to a plan.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

- **Frame-level directorial control.** Ray 3.2 supports multi-keyframe input (Luma states up to 16 keyframes), letting you specify how a shot starts, moves and ends rather than hoping a single prompt produces the right camera pan or subject motion — the feature that separates Luma from prompt-only video generators.
- **Multi-model orchestration.** Instead of forcing every job through one house model, the Luma Agent can route a request to whichever integrated model — Luma's own or a third-party one like Veo or Kling — best fits the brief, inside a single canvas.
- **Master Reference Assets for consistency.** Lock in a character, logo or brand style as a reference the system reuses across generations, which matters for ad and brand work where visual consistency across clips is non-negotiable.
- **Video-to-video and reframing.** Ray 3.2 can restyle or edit existing footage and reframe aspect ratios (useful for repurposing one video across vertical, square and widescreen placements) without a full re-render.
- **Built-in localization.** The platform can translate and dub video audio into other languages with synced visuals — aimed at teams repurposing content for multiple markets rather than one-off clips.

## Who Luma AI is actually for

- **Solo creators and freelancers** testing AI video for social content will likely start on Plus; 10,000 monthly credits stretch further for image-heavy work than long or high-resolution video runs.
- **Marketing teams and agencies** producing recurring branded video are the clearest fit for Pro or Ultra — higher credit pools and usage multipliers matter when iterating multiple takes, and Master Reference Assets keep brand style consistent across a campaign.
- **Developers building video generation into their own product** should skip the app subscriptions and use the pay-per-generation API instead, avoiding payment for canvas features they won't use.
- **Enterprises with compliance or scale needs** — SSO, dedicated capacity, custom fine-tuning — need the Team/Enterprise tier and a sales conversation; none of that is self-serve.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Frame-level camera/motion control, more precise than most competitors | No published free-tier credit amount |
| Multiple third-party models (Veo, Kling, Seedream) inside one canvas | Cost per clip hard to predict, especially at higher resolutions |
| Master Reference Assets keep characters/brand elements consistent | Credits reset monthly, don't roll over |
| Pay-per-generation API for developers who skip the canvas app | Entry-level Plus plan runs out fast for heavier use |
| Built-in localization/dubbing for repurposing video across languages | No on-premise or offline option |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Luma's primary integration path is its own API (documented at platform.lumalabs.ai, with an in-browser API Playground) which developers can call directly without touching the consumer app. The company doesn't publicly list native Zapier, Slack or similar no-code integrations the way some SaaS tools do — its ecosystem play is more about which AI models it plugs into its own canvas than about connecting to outside business software. If your workflow depends on no-code automation, you'd need to build that bridge yourself through the API.

## Where it's a strong fit

Luma AI is a strong pick if you need short, high-motion-quality AI video clips and care about directing the shot rather than accepting whatever a single prompt produces. The keyframe control and video-to-video editing put it ahead of tools that only do one-shot text-to-video generation, and several third-party models in one workspace saves maintaining separate subscriptions to compare outputs. Agencies, in-house marketing teams, and developers who want a capable video API without training their own model get the most value here.

## Where to think twice

Skip Luma, or budget carefully, if you need a fully free ongoing tool — there's no lasting free tier, only a limited trial, and every serious generation draws down paid credits. The credit-based pricing makes exact cost-per-video hard to predict in advance; higher resolutions and HDR/EXR exports multiply the cost per clip, so a handful of high-end renders can eat a Plus plan's monthly allowance quickly. Long-form video isn't the target use case either — this is built around short clips (typically 5–10 second blocks). And if your organization needs on-premise or offline deployment for data-residency reasons, that's not offered; Luma is cloud-hosted only, with enterprise controls like SSO reserved for the custom Team/Enterprise tier.

## The bottom line

Luma AI earns its reputation on Ray 3.2's motion quality and the directorial control it gives you over camera movement and framing — a real edge over prompt-and-pray video generators, and the multi-model canvas means you're rarely stuck with one look. The trade-off is a credit system that's harder to budget against than a flat per-seat SaaS price, and a free tier that's more of a taste test than a workflow you can build on. For anyone producing recurring short-form AI video, it's worth the Plus or Pro subscription; for occasional, one-off use, the API's pay-per-generation model is likely cheaper.

## FAQ

**Is Luma AI free to use?**
There's a "Try for free" entry point, but Luma doesn't publish an exact free-credit allowance, and there's no lasting free tier — sustained use requires a paid Plus, Pro or Ultra subscription, or pay-per-generation API credits.

**What's the difference between Luma AI and Dream Machine?**
Dream Machine was Luma's original video-generation product, launched in 2024. The company has since broadened the platform into a multimodal creative workspace (Luma Agents) built around the Ray and Uni model families, but the video generation that made Dream Machine's name is still the core.

**How much does Luma AI cost?**
Plans start at $30/month (Plus, 10,000 credits) and go up to $300/month (Ultra, 150,000 credits), with annual billing offering a modest discount. Developers using the API instead pay per generation, roughly $0.15–$1.20 for a 5-second Ray 3.2 video clip depending on resolution.

**Does Luma AI have an API for developers?**
Yes. A separate pay-per-use API (with a higher-throughput "Scale" tier) through a developer console at platform.lumalabs.ai, independent of the consumer app subscriptions.

**Is this the same Luma AI used for IT service desks?**
No. This review covers Luma Labs, the video-generation company. "Luma AI" is also the name Serviceaide uses for its own, unrelated IT-service-desk virtual agent — see [our review of that product](/blog/luma-ai-serviceaide-review) if that's what you're looking for.

**How does Luma AI handle data and content ownership?**
Paid plans (Plus and above) include commercial use rights for generated content. Check Luma's current terms of service and privacy policy directly for specifics on data retention and training use, since these details can change.

**What are the best alternatives to Luma AI?**
Depending on your needs, alternatives include Runway, Pika, OpenAI's Sora, and Google's Veo (also selectable inside Luma's own canvas as a third-party model) — worth comparing on cost-per-clip and motion quality.

**Is Luma AI beginner-friendly?**
The web canvas is approachable for anyone comfortable with prompt-based tools, and the Luma Agent is designed to reduce the need for prompt-engineering expertise. The credit-based cost structure takes some getting used to if you're new to usage-based AI pricing rather than flat subscriptions.
