title: Framer AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Framer AI turns prompts into editable sites inside Framer's design canvas. Here's what it costs, what it does well, and who should use it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Framer AI worth using to build a website in 2026?

Framer AI is the AI agent built into the Framer website builder, not a separate product — it turns a text prompt into an editable site, then helps write copy, manage CMS content, build code components, and audit pages before launch. It's a strong fit for Framer's design-grade builder with AI as a first-draft accelerant; less useful if you just want a bare text-to-site tool.

## At a glance

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free (limited AI credits); paid site plans start at $10/month (Basic), $30/month (Pro) |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — free plan includes 500 AI credits, a Framer subdomain, and core editor access |
| Best for | Designers, agencies, and marketing teams who want a real design-canvas builder with AI as an accelerant, not a replacement |
| Standout feature | AI agent works inside the same canvas as manual design — generate, then refine visually, rather than being locked into whatever the prompt produced |

## What Framer AI actually is

Framer AI isn't a standalone app — it's the AI layer inside Framer, the no-code website builder long known for its design-tool-grade canvas (closer to Figma than a typical drag-and-drop site builder). The AI agent sits on top of that canvas: you describe a page or update in plain language, and it generates editable sections, copy, and visuals directly in your project, which you can then adjust manually.

That distinction matters. A lot of "AI website builder" tools generate a site and hand you a fairly rigid result to tweak inside a narrow editor. Framer's pitch is closer to "AI as one more input into a design tool you can otherwise fully control" — prompt for a hero section, then manually adjust typography, breakpoints, spacing, and component behavior.

Framer's own AI product pages describe letting users choose between different underlying AI models for certain tasks, though Framer doesn't consistently commit to one disclosed model powering every agent feature. Treat specific model-version claims as Framer's marketing language rather than an independently verified spec, and check Framer's current AI page if the exact model matters to you.

## Pricing

Framer prices around the website builder itself, with AI capability gated by a credits system layered on top of the regular plan tiers. Every plan includes a monthly allotment of AI credits consumed by agent actions (generating pages, localization, code components) — heavier AI use means staying within your allotment or upgrading.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability below were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — confirm current numbers on Framer's own pricing page before committing, since AI-credit systems tend to get adjusted as usage patterns shift.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | 500 AI credits, Framer subdomain, up to 10 CMS collections, 1,000 pages, 1 GB bandwidth, one free translation locale, up to 3 collaborators |
| Basic | $10/month | Free custom domain, 2 CMS collections, 50 GB bandwidth, built-in SEO tools, up to 30 custom pages, password protection |
| Pro | $30/month | Free custom domain, 10 CMS collections, 100 GB bandwidth, staging environment, branching with previews, site redirects, up to 150 custom pages |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom limits and AI-credit volume discounts, unlimited editors, SSO/SCIM, uptime guarantee, enterprise security review |

Worth knowing: extra design editors run roughly $20/month per seat and content editors around $10/month (viewers are free), extra locales are a paid add-on, and advanced hosting/A-B testing sit behind further add-ons on Pro. The plan's sticker price isn't necessarily your total monthly cost for a team or multilingual site.

## Features walkthrough

**Prompt-to-site generation.** You describe the site, page, or specific update you want, and the AI agent creates editable pages, sections, copy, and visuals inside your actual Framer project — not a preview you have to accept or reject wholesale. That's the meaningful difference from builders where AI output and manual editing live in separate modes.

**Iterative, conversational refinement.** Beyond the first draft, keep prompting the agent to adjust what it built, or switch to manual canvas editing at any point — layout, typography, components, breakpoints, spacing, and effects stay directly editable.

**CMS and content agent tasks.** The agent can create CMS collections and populate them with content, useful for standing up a blog or structured content section faster than manually defining fields one at a time — a step beyond most AI site builders, which stop at layout and copy generation.

**Custom code components on request.** Framer has always supported custom code components for interactions a no-code editor can't otherwise produce; the AI agent extends that by letting you describe an interaction and have it attempt to build the component.

**Pre-publish audits and traffic analysis.** The agent can review a site before publishing and flag contrast problems, missing alt text, typos, and basic SEO gaps, plus analyze traffic and suggest next steps. It's not a substitute for a real accessibility audit, but it catches things easy to miss on a fast-moving project.

## Who Framer AI is actually for

- **Designers and design-literate marketers** who want AI for a fast first draft they'll finesse by hand get the most value — the canvas rewards direct manipulation, not just prompting.
- **Small agencies and freelancers** can use the AI agent to compress the first-draft phase, then rely on Framer's CMS, staging, and branching (Pro plan) for client handoff.
- **Startups and small teams** needing a marketing site with a blog can lean on the free or Basic tier plus CMS population.
- **Enterprise teams** with compliance/SSO needs have a path via the Enterprise plan, though it requires talking to sales.
- **People wanting a purely prompt-driven, zero-manual-editing experience** may find the canvas-first approach has more of a learning curve than a template-locked builder.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| AI output lands directly in a fully editable, professional-grade canvas rather than a locked preview | AI credits are a separate consumable resource on top of the plan price — heavy AI users may need to budget for upgrades |
| CMS population and code-component generation go beyond basic layout/copy AI | Additional editor seats, extra locales, and advanced hosting are all separate add-on costs |
| Pre-publish audit catches basic accessibility/SEO issues before launch | Framer doesn't clearly commit to a single disclosed AI model powering every agent feature |
| Free plan includes a meaningful AI credit allotment to test the workflow | Canvas-based editing has a steeper learning curve than block/template builders for non-designers |
| Staging, branching, and redirects on Pro suit real production workflows | Custom domain and higher CMS limits are locked behind paid plans, same as most builders |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Framer's integration story centers on its own platform features rather than a large third-party plugin marketplace: built-in SEO tools, a CMS with API-style content modeling, custom code components, and staging/branching on the Pro plan. It also supports embedding external code and common analytics/marketing scripts, covering much of the "integration" need for a marketing site.

Framer doesn't market a Zapier-style automation ecosystem or a large public app directory. If your workflow depends on a native integration with a specific CRM or email platform, verify it directly (often via embedded code or webhook) before assuming it works out of the box.

## Where Framer AI is a strong fit

Framer AI earns its place when you want AI to accelerate a real design workflow rather than replace it. If you're comfortable in a canvas-style editor and want the agent to generate a first draft, populate a CMS, or write a one-off code component — then finish the job by hand — this is one of the more capable combinations of "AI generation" and "actual design control" on the market.

It's also a solid fit for teams already invested in Framer who want the AI layer as a productivity boost, not their primary selection criterion for an AI builder.

## Where to think twice

Skip Framer AI, or test the free plan thoroughly first, if any of the following apply:

- **You want a fully free, ad-hoc site with no eventual custom-domain or CMS ceiling** — the free plan caps out at a Framer subdomain and limited CMS collections.
- **You need a large-scale content library or complex data relationships** — Framer's CMS suits a marketing site or blog, not a headless CMS replacement.
- **You want zero manual editing** — Framer's canvas-first model rewards hands-on refinement; a locked-down AI builder may suit you better.
- **Your team needs enterprise compliance on a small budget** — SSO, SCIM, and uptime guarantees sit on the custom-priced, sales-driven Enterprise plan.
- **You're tracking AI usage costs closely** — credits sit on top of plan pricing, so heavy agent use can push costs past the base price.

## The bottom line

Framer AI is best understood as a well-integrated AI layer on top of an already strong design tool, not a standalone AI website generator competing purely on prompt quality. The generation step gets you a usable first draft; the real value is that everything it produces lands in the same editable canvas you'd use manually, plus CMS population and code-component generation that go further than most competitors. If you want AI to save time on the first draft and then take over creatively, it's one of the stronger options available. If you want a fully hands-off, prompt-only experience instead, weigh that against simpler alternatives before committing.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Framer AI free to use?**
Yes, in a limited way — the free plan includes 500 AI credits plus core editor access, a Framer subdomain, and CMS access, so you can test the agent before paying. A real production site typically needs at least the Basic paid plan for a custom domain.

**How much does Framer AI cost on paid plans?**
Site plans start at $10/month (Basic) and $30/month (Pro), with AI credits included at each tier and Enterprise offering custom pricing with volume discounts. Confirm current figures on Framer's pricing page.

**What happens when I run out of AI credits?**
Framer allots a monthly amount of AI credits per plan, consumed by generation and localization actions; once used up, you'd generally wait for the next cycle or upgrade. Confirm exact mechanics on Framer's site, since credit systems are prone to adjustment.

**What AI model powers Framer AI?**
Framer's own marketing references choosing between different AI models for certain agent tasks, but doesn't consistently disclose a single model powering every feature. Treat specific model-version claims as Framer's own language rather than an independently confirmed spec.

**Can Framer AI build a blog or CMS-driven site?**
Yes — the agent can create CMS collections and populate content, and Framer's CMS supports multiple collections even on the free plan (higher limits on paid tiers), making it reasonable for a marketing site with a blog.

**Is Framer AI good for beginners with no design experience?**
It's more approachable than hand-coding, but Framer's canvas-based editor has more of a learning curve than a simple, block-based builder aimed at non-designers.

**Does Framer AI have an API or third-party integrations?**
Framer supports embedding custom code and common scripts, plus a capable native CMS, but doesn't market a broad Zapier-style automation marketplace. Verify any specific CRM or email integration directly rather than assuming native support.

**How does Framer AI compare to other AI website builders?**
Compared with prompt-first builders like [Dora AI](/blog/dora-ai-review), Framer AI leans more on integrating generation into a full, manually editable design canvas plus CMS and code-component tools — better for ongoing hands-on control, while prompt-first tools may reach a finished-looking result faster with less editing.

For more AI tool coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: WriteText.ai for WooCommerce Review 2026: Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: WriteText.ai's WooCommerce plugin auto-generates product descriptions, meta tags and alt text. Here's what it costs and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is WriteText.ai good for WooCommerce stores?

WriteText.ai's WooCommerce plugin generates product descriptions, meta tags, Open Graph text, and image alt text directly inside your catalog, then publishes them without copy-pasting. It's a solid fit for stores with dozens to thousands of SKUs needing consistent, SEO-aware copy fast — less so for a five-product shop that can write descriptions by hand in an afternoon.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $90 flexible plan (pay-as-you-go credits) or $149/month Pro plan |
| **Free tier/trial** | Free trial with full Pro-feature access, no credit card required |
| **Best for** | WooCommerce stores with a large or fast-growing product catalog |
| **Standout feature** | Native WooCommerce field mapping — descriptions, meta tags, OG text, and alt text generated and pushed directly to product/category pages |

WriteText.ai isn't a general-purpose writing assistant like Jasper or Copy.ai bolted onto WooCommerce as an afterthought — it's built around a narrower job: reading your product data and turning it into on-brand, SEO-formatted content at catalog scale. That focus is both its strength and its limitation.

## What WriteText.ai for WooCommerce actually is

WriteText.ai is a content-generation platform aimed specifically at ecommerce catalogs, with separate plugin/app integrations for WooCommerce, Shopify, and Magento, plus an API for custom platforms, PIM systems, and ERP setups. The company states it's "an independent tool developed to work with WordPress/WooCommerce, Magento, and Shopify" and isn't affiliated with or endorsed by any of those platforms.

The WooCommerce integration ships as a plugin listed on the WordPress.org plugin directory (installs shown as 60+ at the time of this review), installs like a standard WordPress plugin, and connects to WriteText.ai's cloud service to pull product data, generate copy, and push it back into your store's product and category fields. There's no separate API key to manage — generation happens on WriteText.ai's backend, which is what the pricing below is paying for.

This is a different category of tool than a general AI chatbot you'd paste a product name into. It's built to run across a catalog of hundreds or thousands of SKUs, with automation, bulk generation, and new-product detection baked in.

## Pricing

WriteText.ai runs on a credit-based system across three published plans. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — confirm current numbers on WriteText.ai's own pricing page before buying, since AI tool pricing moves fast.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| **Starter (flexible)** | From $90, no monthly commitment | Pay-as-you-go credits (tiers from 1,000 up to 20,000 credits at roughly $0.09/credit); core text generation, custom templates, brand voice, product research, basic SEO |
| **Pro** | $149/month (yearly option available) | 2,000 credits/month at roughly $0.075/credit; everything in Starter plus full automation workflows, advanced SEO and AEO tools, keyword analysis and tracking, negative keyword exclusion, People Also Ask content generation, custom prompts and image blocks, API access |
| **Managed Setup** | $999 | 6,000 credits, everything in Pro plus guided onboarding, tailored template configuration, a dedicated account manager, and 1:1 training sessions |

WriteText.ai's public documentation doesn't spell out exactly how many words or products a single credit covers — that likely depends on content length and which fields you're generating (a full description plus meta tags and alt text will use more credits than a short description alone). Confirm the current credit-to-content ratio with WriteText.ai directly before buying a larger block.

A free trial is available with full access to Pro-tier features, and WriteText.ai states no credit card is required to start it.

## Core features that differentiate it

**Native WooCommerce field mapping.** Rather than generating a block of text you then paste in, the plugin writes directly into product descriptions, meta tags, Open Graph fields, and image alt text tied to your actual WooCommerce fields — including category pages, not just individual products.

**Product-type awareness.** WooCommerce supports several product structures (simple, variable, grouped, bundled, virtual, downloadable), and WriteText.ai says it adjusts generated descriptions and meta fields to reflect the specific format rather than treating every listing the same.

**Bulk generation and automation.** The Pro plan's "full automation workflows" run keyword analysis, content generation, and publishing as one sequence based on rules you configure, rather than a manual click per product. The plugin can also detect newly added products automatically and send email notifications so new SKUs don't sit undescribed.

**SEO, AEO, and GEO framing.** WriteText.ai markets its output as optimized not just for traditional search engines but for answer engines (AEO) and generative engines (GEO), with keyword tracking and People Also Ask content generation on the Pro tier.

**Multilingual catalogs.** The company states support for 25+ languages, for stores selling into multiple markets that need consistent SEO-formatted copy without hiring separate copywriters per language — though native-speaker spot checks are still worth budgeting for before publishing non-English output at scale.

## Who it's actually for

**A small WooCommerce shop with under 50 products** will likely find the $90+ Starter credit pack more cost-effective than the $149/month Pro plan, especially if automation and keyword tracking aren't priorities yet.

**A growing catalog store (hundreds of SKUs, regular new-product additions)** is the clearest fit for Pro — automated new-product detection and the full automation workflow directly address a catalog that's outgrown manual copywriting, and the SEO/AEO tooling helps that content surface in search and AI-answer results.

**A larger merchant or agency managing multiple WooCommerce stores** with complex product structures (bundles, variable products, multi-market catalogs) is the target for Managed Setup, where paying for onboarding beats self-serving a first complex rollout.

**Anyone using a non-WooCommerce platform** should check WriteText.ai's Magento or Shopify integration, or its API, instead — the generation engine is shared, but field mapping and installation differ by platform.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Writes directly into WooCommerce product, category, meta, and alt-text fields | Credit-to-word ratio isn't publicly documented; needs a test run to budget |
| Handles varied WooCommerce product types (variable, bundled, virtual, downloadable) | Starter plan lacks automation and advanced SEO tools available on Pro |
| Bulk/automated generation suits large or fast-growing catalogs | Modest install base (60+) on WordPress.org vs. more established plugins |
| Free trial with full Pro-tier access, no card required | Managed Setup's $999 entry is a meaningful commitment for small merchants |
| Multilingual support (25+ languages) for cross-market catalogs | Cloud-based only — no offline/on-prem generation option |

## Integrations and ecosystem

The WooCommerce plugin installs as a standard WordPress plugin and needs no separate developer setup for core functionality — WriteText.ai states it "works out of the box for most stores," with optional front-end developer help only for custom theme styling. Beyond WooCommerce, the same platform connects to Shopify and Magento through dedicated integrations, and to custom ecommerce platforms, PIM systems, and ERP solutions via API access (Pro plan and above). There's no mention of native Zapier or Slack connectors in WriteText.ai's public documentation — automation runs inside the platform's own workflow engine rather than through third-party automation tools, so teams that lean on Zapier-style cross-app automation should confirm this fits their stack first.

## Where it's a strong fit

WriteText.ai earns its keep on WooCommerce stores that are either launching a large catalog at once or continuously adding new products and can't keep pace with manual copywriting. The direct field-level integration removes a genuinely tedious step, and the product-type-aware generation is a detail generic AI writing tools don't handle.

Multi-market sellers who need the same catalog described consistently across 25+ languages, without briefing separate freelance copywriters per language, are another clear use case — provided they budget time for spot-checking non-English output before it goes live.

## Where to think twice

If your catalog is small enough to write by hand in a day or two, the Pro plan's $149/month is hard to justify — Starter credits or a general-purpose AI writing tool will likely cost less for occasional use. If your team needs a fully free tool with no eventual paywall, this isn't it; the trial is generous but time-limited.

If your workflow depends heavily on Zapier, Slack, or other third-party automation tools, check WriteText.ai's current integration list first — its automation appears self-contained. And if you need offline or on-premise content generation for compliance reasons, a cloud SaaS tool won't fit.

Because the WordPress.org listing shows a modest install count, buyers relying on public reviews for validation will find less crowd-sourced feedback than a longer-established plugin — worth weighing against the vendor's own trial period.

## Bottom line

WriteText.ai for WooCommerce is a narrowly-scoped, purpose-built tool rather than a general AI writing assistant repurposed for ecommerce. For stores with real catalog scale — new products added regularly, multiple product types, or multi-language listings — the native field mapping and automation genuinely save time that would otherwise go into manual copywriting. For a small, static catalog, the ongoing subscription cost is harder to justify, and the free trial is the right way to find out which camp your store falls into before paying anything.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is WriteText.ai free for WooCommerce?**
No, but it offers a free trial with full Pro-tier feature access (including automation and advanced SEO tools) and states no credit card is required to start. After the trial, plans run on paid credits from roughly $90 (Starter) or $149/month (Pro).

**How much does WriteText.ai cost for WooCommerce specifically?**
The same platform-wide pricing applies: a flexible Starter credit pack from $90, a $149/month Pro plan with 2,000 monthly credits, and a $999 Managed Setup plan with guided onboarding. Exact credit consumption per product isn't publicly documented, so test with a small batch first.

**Does WriteText.ai work with all WooCommerce product types?**
Yes — WriteText.ai states it handles simple, variable, grouped, bundled, virtual, and downloadable product types, adjusting generated descriptions and meta fields to match each format.

**Do I need to know how to code to install it?**
No. The plugin installs like a standard WordPress plugin and works "out of the box for most stores" without developer involvement, though custom theme styling may benefit from optional front-end help.

**What languages does WriteText.ai support?**
The company states support for 25+ languages, for merchants selling the same catalog across multiple international markets.

**Is WriteText.ai's generated content actually good for SEO?**
It's built around SEO, AEO, and GEO, with keyword analysis, tracking, and People Also Ask content generation on Pro. As with any AI copy, results depend on your product data quality and should be reviewed before publishing — no tool guarantees rankings.

**How is this different from just using ChatGPT or Jasper for product descriptions?**
General AI tools require manually feeding each product's details in and copying output back into WooCommerce. WriteText.ai reads product data directly and pushes generated content into the correct fields automatically, and accounts for WooCommerce-specific product types.

**Is there a separate WriteText.ai plugin for Magento or Shopify?**
Yes. WriteText.ai maintains dedicated integrations for WooCommerce, Shopify, and Magento, each with platform-specific installation and field mapping, plus an API for custom platforms.

For more AI and software deals, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Miro AI Review 2026: Intelligent Canvas, Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: Miro AI review covering Intelligent Canvas, Sidekicks, Flows, AI credit limits, and how it fits into Miro's Free through Enterprise plans.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Miro AI worth it, or is it just a feature bolted onto a whiteboard tool?

Miro AI is genuinely useful for teams already living on Miro's canvas — it can turn sticky notes into structured diagrams, summarize a messy brainstorm, and run multi-step "Flows" that pull in outside tools. But it's not a standalone AI product: you're paying for Miro's collaboration platform first, and AI is a metered add-on layered on top with monthly credit caps that get restrictive on lower tiers.

## What Miro AI actually is

Miro is a visual collaboration platform — an infinite online whiteboard used for brainstorming, diagramming, product planning, and workshop facilitation. Miro AI is not a separate product; it's an AI layer built into the same canvas, marketed as the "Intelligent Canvas." The idea is that Miro AI can read everything already on a board — sticky notes, diagrams, comments, uploaded documents — and use that as context, rather than working from a blank prompt box like a typical AI chat tool.

The AI layer is made up of a few distinct pieces: **AI Sidekicks** (pre-built or custom agents that operate on a board and build on existing team work), **Flows** (visual, multi-step automated workflows that chain AI actions together — say, pull tickets from Jira, cluster them, generate a summary, drop it onto a board as a diagram), **AI Playbooks** (ready-made workflow templates for jobs like strategic planning, competitor analysis, research synthesis, and technical architecture), and **generative content tools** that turn a prompt or a cluster of sticky notes into a diagram, flowchart, mind map, wireframe, or dashboard.

Miro doesn't publicly name which underlying large language model(s) power these features, and it doesn't publish independent benchmark numbers for output accuracy — treat any claims about output quality as Miro's own positioning rather than a verified fact.

## Pricing — AI is a credit-metered layer on top of Miro's regular plans

This is the part that trips people up: you don't buy "Miro AI" separately. You subscribe to a regular Miro plan (Free, Starter, Business, or Enterprise), each with a monthly allotment of AI credits consumed by generation, summarization, and Flow actions.

Pricing and AI credit allowances below were accurate as of this post's date (September 2026) per Miro's official pricing page — credit systems shift as vendors iterate, so confirm current numbers on [Miro's pricing page](https://miro.com/pricing/) before subscribing.

| Plan | Price | AI credits | MCP calls/day | AI Flows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Limited trial allotment | 100 | Limited trial |
| Starter | $8/member/month (billed yearly) | 25/member/month | 500 | Limited trial |
| Business | $20/member/month (billed yearly) | 50/member/month | 2,000 | Included |
| Enterprise | Custom (from 30 members) | Custom, 2,500+ org-wide | 10,000 | Included |

A few things worth knowing about that table: the Free plan caps you at 3 editable boards total, regardless of AI usage — for most real teams that's a bigger limitation than the AI credit trial. Starter unlocks unlimited private boards but keeps AI Flows in a "limited trial" state, meaning the multi-step automation piece isn't fully available until Business. Business is really where Miro AI becomes a working tool rather than a taste test — full Flows access, 2,000 daily MCP calls (Miro's connector protocol for linking AI agents to external tools like Claude, GitHub Copilot, or Cursor), and double the per-member credit allowance of Starter. Enterprise pricing isn't published; you talk to sales, and it comes with security controls (regional data hosting, centralized user management) that smaller teams don't need.

One credit-economy detail to flag: 25–50 credits per member per month sounds generous until you're running Flows that chain several AI actions together, at which point one workflow can burn multiple credits in a single run. If your team plans to lean on AI Flows regularly, budget for Business at minimum.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (limited); paid plans from $8/member/month (Starter) |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — 3 editable boards, limited AI credit trial, no credit card required |
| Best for | Teams already using Miro for brainstorming, planning, or diagramming who want AI layered into that existing workflow |
| Standout feature | Intelligent Canvas — AI that reads and acts on the full board context, not just a prompt box |

## Core features walkthrough

**Context-aware generation.** Instead of typing a prompt into an empty box, select a cluster of sticky notes, a rough diagram, or an uploaded PDF and ask Miro AI to turn it into something structured — a flowchart, a SWOT grid, a project timeline. Because it reads what's already on the canvas, output tends to reflect the team's actual input rather than a generic template.

**Sticky note clustering and summarization.** After a live brainstorm with dozens of scattered notes, Miro AI can group related ideas and produce a written summary of themes — a task that used to eat 20 minutes of a facilitator's post-workshop time.

**AI Sidekicks.** Configurable agents scoped to a specific job — say, triaging feedback notes or drafting a first-pass user journey map — that carry board context forward rather than starting fresh each time.

**Flows and Playbooks.** The most ambitious piece: multi-step automated sequences that pull data from connected tools (250+ integrations, including Slack, Jira, and Granola), process it, and lay results out visually on the board. Playbooks are pre-built starting templates for use cases like research synthesis or technical architecture planning.

**MCP server access.** Business and Enterprise plans get meaningfully higher daily call limits for Miro's MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, which lets external AI tools like Claude or Cursor read from and write to a board directly.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo users and very small teams** — the Free plan's AI trial lets you kick the tires, but the 3-board cap and "limited trial" Flows mean you'll hit walls fast beyond occasional diagrams.
- **Small-to-mid product and design teams** — Starter gets unlimited boards and a modest AI credit allowance; fine for occasional assistance rather than daily reliance.
- **Teams running structured workshops or cross-functional planning** — Business is the tier Miro built AI Flows for: full Flow access, higher MCP limits, and enough credits to automate repeatable processes like sprint retros.
- **Large organizations with compliance needs** — Enterprise adds data residency and centralized admin controls alongside the highest credit allowance.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| AI reads full board context, not just an isolated prompt | AI credits are metered per plan — heavy Flow usage can run out fast |
| Flows/Playbooks give structure to multi-step AI automation, not just one-off generation | Full AI Flows access is gated behind the Business plan |
| Deep integration with 250+ existing tools (Slack, Jira, etc.) | Underlying AI model(s) aren't publicly disclosed |
| MCP server lets external AI tools (Claude, Cursor) connect to boards | Free plan's 3-board cap limits real-world testing more than the AI trial does |
| Security/compliance options (ISO 42001, data residency) for Enterprise | You're paying for the whole Miro platform, not AI alone — not a fit if you only want an AI diagramming tool |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Beyond the 250+ tool connections already covered above, the MCP server is the more technical integration point worth calling out separately: it exposes Miro boards to external AI agents (Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and others that support MCP) with daily call limits scaling by plan — 100/day on Free up to 10,000/day on Enterprise. For teams already using AI coding assistants or research agents, this can be more valuable than the in-app Sidekicks, since it lets those tools read and write directly to planning boards without a copy-paste workflow.

## Where it's a strong fit

Miro AI works best for teams already running planning, brainstorming, or workshop facilitation inside Miro who want AI to remove tedious cleanup work — turning scattered notes into a coherent summary, or a rough sketch into a presentable diagram — and for teams standardizing repeatable processes into reusable Flows.

## Where to think twice

Skip Miro AI, or at least don't budget for it as your primary reason to buy Miro, if:

- **You need a fully free AI tool** — the Free trial is limited, and the 3-editable-board cap will likely force an upgrade before the AI trial does.
- **You want AI Flows as your main use case** — that isn't fully unlocked until Business ($20/member/month billed yearly), so budget-constrained teams won't get the platform's most distinctive AI feature.
- **You need transparency about the underlying model** — Miro doesn't publish which LLM(s) power its AI features, which matters for organizations that restrict model providers.
- **Your team doesn't already use a visual whiteboard for planning** — a dedicated AI writing or summarizing tool will likely be cheaper than adopting a whole whiteboard platform for its AI layer.
- **You need heavy, unmetered AI usage** — every plan, including Enterprise, is credit-based, and constant AI generation risks running into credit exhaustion mid-cycle.

## Bottom line

Miro AI is a well-integrated feature, not an AI product you'd buy on its own — and that's the right way to evaluate it. If your team already lives on Miro's canvas for planning and workshops, the AI layer removes real friction: less manual sticky-note wrangling, faster first-draft diagrams, and Flows that automate parts of a recurring process. If you don't already use Miro, there's little reason to adopt the whole platform just to reach AI Sidekicks. The credit system is the main thing to watch: budget for Business if AI Flows are actually part of your daily workflow, since Starter's "limited trial" access won't cut it for sustained use.

## FAQ

**Is Miro AI free?**
There's a limited AI trial on Miro's Free plan, but it comes with a capped credit allowance and the Free plan itself is limited to 3 editable boards. For sustained AI use, you'll need a paid plan starting at Starter ($8/member/month billed yearly).

**How many AI credits do I get per month?**
Starter includes 25 credits per member per month, Business includes 50, and Enterprise offers a custom pool (2,500+ shared across the organization). Free includes a limited trial allotment that Miro doesn't specify in exact numbers on its pricing page.

**What happens when I run out of AI credits?**
Miro's pricing page doesn't detail the exact fallback behavior — confirm with Miro's sales or support team before relying on AI-heavy workflows.

**What AI model does Miro AI use?**
Miro doesn't publicly disclose which large language model(s) power its AI features. If model provenance matters for your organization's compliance requirements, ask Miro directly before subscribing.

**Does Miro AI work with tools like Slack, Jira, or GitHub?**
Yes — Miro states its AI Flows and Sidekicks connect to more than 250 tools, with Slack, Jira, and Granola specifically named. Separately, Miro's MCP server lets external AI agents read and write to boards directly.

**Is Miro AI good for beginners?**
The core generative features (turning notes into diagrams, summarizing a board) are approachable for anyone comfortable with Miro's canvas. Building custom Flows is more involved and closer to light workflow automation than a simple chat prompt.

**Is Miro AI available on the Business plan, or do I need Enterprise?**
Full AI Flows access and higher MCP call limits are included starting on Business ($20/member/month billed yearly) — Enterprise is only needed for custom security/compliance controls or org-wide custom credit pools.

title: AssemblyAI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: AssemblyAI review covering Universal-3.5 Pro pricing, LeMUR, streaming transcription, add-ons, and who this speech-to-text API is really built for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is AssemblyAI a good speech-to-text API?

AssemblyAI is a solid pick if you're building a product on top of speech-to-text rather than using transcription as an end-user tool — it's a developer-facing API, not a consumer app. It offers accuracy across English and dozens of other languages, pay-as-you-go pricing starting around $0.15/hour of audio, and add-ons for speaker labels, sentiment, and PII redaction, but it requires code to use.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Best for** | Developers and teams building transcription, voice agents, or audio analytics into a product |
| **Starting price** | $0.15/hour (Universal-2, pre-recorded) or $0.21/hour (Universal-3.5 Pro) |
| **Free tier** | $50 in free API credits on signup, no credit card required |
| **Standout feature** | LeMUR — an LLM layer built on top of transcripts for summarization, Q&A, and action-item extraction |
| **Interface** | REST API, Python/JS/Go/Ruby/etc. SDKs, no-code UI for testing only |

AssemblyAI has no matching store entry on this site, so pricing and feature details below come from its official pricing and product pages.

## What AssemblyAI actually is

AssemblyAI is a speech AI company that sells transcription and "audio intelligence" as an API — you send it an audio or video file (or live stream), and it returns text, timestamps, speaker labels, and, if you ask for them, higher-level outputs like sentiment scores, chapter summaries, or PII-redacted transcripts. It isn't a transcription app with a dashboard you type into by hand; it's infrastructure other companies build products on — call-center analytics tools, meeting-notes apps, podcast platforms, and voice agents all use APIs like this one under the hood.

The company runs its own speech models. Its lineup centers on two families: **Universal-3.5 Pro**, positioned as the highest-accuracy option for messy real-world audio (accents, background noise, crosstalk), and **Universal-2**, a lower-cost model with broader language coverage. Both handle pre-recorded transcription; a separate **Universal-Streaming** family handles real-time audio. AssemblyAI calls Universal-3.5 Pro its most accurate pre-recorded model but doesn't publish a specific word-error-rate percentage publicly — if benchmark accuracy is a hard requirement, request the company's own comparison data or run your own test set first.

Beyond raw transcription, AssemblyAI's bigger differentiator is **LeMUR** (Leveraging Large Language Models to Understand Recognized Speech) — a layer that runs LLM prompts against a transcript without you feeding the whole thing into a general-purpose chat model yourself. Ask it to summarize a call, pull action items, or answer a question about what was said, and LeMUR handles the context window and prompt plumbing for you.

## Pricing

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability below were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — confirm current rates on [AssemblyAI's pricing page](https://www.assemblyai.com/pricing) before budgeting.

| Service | Price | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-recorded — Universal-2 | $0.15/hour | Broadest language support |
| Pre-recorded — Universal-3.5 Pro | $0.21/hour | Highest accuracy per AssemblyAI, best for difficult audio |
| Streaming — Universal-Streaming | $0.15/hour | English and multilingual real-time transcription |
| Streaming — Universal-3.5 Pro Realtime | $0.45/hour | Premium real-time accuracy tier |
| Voice Agent API | $4.50/hour ($0.075/min) | All-in-one: speech recognition + LLM processing + text-to-speech |
| Free tier | $50 in credits | No credit card required to sign up |

On top of the base rate, AssemblyAI charges for optional add-ons per hour of audio, stacking additively: speaker ID (+$0.02/hr), sentiment (+$0.02/hr), profanity filtering (+$0.01/hr), translation (+$0.06/hr), entity detection (+$0.08/hr), PII redaction (+$0.08/hr), streaming diarization (+$0.12/hr), and medical vocabulary or content moderation (+$0.15/hr each). Keyterms prompting is free on some models, +$0.04–$0.05/hr on others.

Separately, an **LLM Gateway** bills LeMUR calls by tokens — GPT-5 access runs roughly $1.25/$10.00 per million input/output tokens, Claude Sonnet 4.6 closer to $3.00/$15.00 — on top of base transcription cost. There's no flat monthly subscription for individual users; everything is consumption-based, a real adjustment if you're used to fixed SaaS pricing.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

- **Dual model tiers.** Pick Universal-2 for cheaper, broad-language jobs, or Universal-3.5 Pro when audio quality is poor and getting names/technical terms right matters.
- **LeMUR for post-transcript reasoning.** Most transcription APIs stop at text-out. LeMUR summarizes a call, extracts commitments made on it, or answers a question about the conversation without you managing the context window yourself.
- **Granular add-on pricing instead of bundled tiers.** You only pay for diarization, sentiment, redaction, or translation if you use them — but a fully-featured transcript costs meaningfully more than the headline $0.15–$0.21/hour rate.
- **Purpose-built Voice Agent API.** Rather than wiring together STT, an LLM, and TTS separately, AssemblyAI bundles all three into one endpoint at a flat rate.
- **Session-based streaming billing.** Real-time transcription bills for connection time, not spoken-audio duration — a detail that trips up teams that keep sockets open between utterances.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo developers/indie builders** prototyping a transcription feature will likely stay inside the $50 free-credit tier for testing, with no minimum spend before shipping an MVP.
- **Product teams building on top of transcription** — meeting-notes tools, podcast platforms, call analytics, captioning — are the core audience; the add-on model maps well onto features you'd expose to end users without building the NLP layer yourself.
- **Voice-agent builders** get a shortcut in the dedicated Voice Agent API, avoiding separate STT/LLM/TTS vendor integrations.
- **Enterprises with compliance-heavy audio** (healthcare, financial, legal) can use medical vocabulary mode and PII redaction, though anyone with hard HIPAA/SOC 2 requirements should verify current certifications directly with AssemblyAI's sales team.
- **Non-developers wanting a drag-and-drop app** are not the target audience — this is API-first, with a playground UI for testing but no consumer product for people who don't want to write code.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Pay-as-you-go pricing, no forced subscription | No flat plan — metered pricing can be unpredictable at scale |
| LeMUR adds LLM summarization/Q&A without a separate integration | Add-ons stack, so a full-featured transcript costs more than the base rate |
| Two model tiers balance cost against accuracy per job | Requires developer resources — not usable by non-technical users directly |
| Dedicated Voice Agent API simplifies voice assistants | Streaming bills on connection time, not just spoken audio |
| $50 free credit, no card required, for testing | No published word-error-rate benchmark on the pricing page |

## Integrations and ecosystem

AssemblyAI ships official SDKs for Python, JavaScript/Node, Go, Ruby, and other backend languages, plus a REST API that works with any HTTP client. There's no no-code Zapier-style connector — the integration surface is squarely API/SDK-based. Its LLM Gateway proxies models like GPT-5 and Claude, so teams using LeMUR don't need a separate OpenAI or Anthropic account, though that convenience comes at the gateway's own token pricing rather than the provider's direct rate.

## Where it's a strong fit

If you're shipping a product that needs transcription as a feature — not as the whole product — AssemblyAI's combination of competitive base pricing, optional add-ons, and LeMUR for downstream reasoning covers a lot of ground without stitching together three separate vendors. Teams building call analytics, meeting summarization, or captioning tools get a fairly complete toolkit from one API, and voice-agent builders avoid separately managing STT, LLM, and TTS latency and billing.

## Where to think twice

Skip AssemblyAI if you need a **fully free, no-cost tool** for occasional personal transcription — there's no free consumer plan beyond the initial trial credit, and once that's spent, every hour of audio costs money.

Think twice if your team **can't write or maintain API integration code** — this isn't a drag-and-drop app, and there's no polished dashboard for daily manual use the way a consumer transcription tool offers.

Be cautious if you need **hard compliance guarantees** (HIPAA, SOC 2, data residency) baked in — verify certifications and data-handling terms directly with AssemblyAI's sales or legal team, especially for healthcare or financial audio.

And if usage is unpredictable or very high-volume, model out the **fully-loaded cost** (base rate plus every add-on you'll use) — the advertised $0.15/hour rate understates what a feature-rich transcript with diarization, sentiment, and redaction really costs.

## Bottom line

AssemblyAI is a capable, developer-first speech-to-text API with genuinely useful extras — LeMUR for LLM-powered transcript reasoning, a dedicated Voice Agent API, and granular add-ons for diarization, sentiment, and redaction — priced transparently on a pay-as-you-go basis. It's not for people who want a transcript with no coding involved, and à la carte add-on pricing means a full-featured transcript costs more than the headline rate suggests. For teams building a product where transcription and audio intelligence are core functionality, it's a strong, well-documented option worth trialing against the $50 free credit.

## FAQ

**Is AssemblyAI free to use?**
New accounts get $50 in free API credits with no credit card required, enough to test most workflows. There's no permanent free tier for production use — after the credit is spent, transcription bills per hour of audio processed.

**How much does AssemblyAI cost per hour of audio?**
Pre-recorded transcription starts at $0.15/hour (Universal-2) or $0.21/hour (Universal-3.5 Pro). Streaming starts at $0.15/hour, with a $0.45/hour premium tier. Add-ons like speaker diarization or PII redaction are billed separately, per hour, and stack.

**Does AssemblyAI require coding to use?**
Yes, for production use. It's a REST API with SDKs for Python, JavaScript, Go, Ruby, and other languages. There's a playground UI for testing transcripts, but no polished consumer app for non-developers.

**What is LeMUR?**
LeMUR is AssemblyAI's LLM layer built to run on top of transcripts — summarizing calls, extracting action items, or answering questions about what was said — without you manually managing a long transcript's context window in a separate LLM.

**Does AssemblyAI support real-time transcription?**
Yes, via its Universal-Streaming models, billed per hour of connection time (not just spoken audio) starting at $0.15/hour, with a $0.45/hour premium tier.

**Is AssemblyAI accurate?**
It describes Universal-3.5 Pro as its highest-accuracy pre-recorded model for noisy or accented audio, but doesn't publish a specific word-error-rate figure publicly. If a guaranteed benchmark matters, request AssemblyAI's own comparison data or test it against your own audio sample first.

**What are the alternatives to AssemblyAI?**
Other speech-to-text APIs include Deepgram, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Amazon Transcribe, and OpenAI's Whisper-based API — each with different pricing, language coverage, and add-ons. Compare per-hour pricing and the specific add-ons you need before choosing.

**Does AssemblyAI handle sensitive or regulated audio?**
It offers a medical vocabulary mode and PII text redaction as paid add-ons, but teams with hard compliance requirements like HIPAA or SOC 2 should confirm current certifications directly with AssemblyAI's sales team rather than assume coverage from the pricing page alone.

For more AI and software tools worth comparing on price and features, see our roundup of [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Supabase Review 2026: Pricing, AI Features and Verdict
excerpt: Supabase pairs Postgres, auth, storage, and native pgvector support for AI app backends. Here's how it's priced and who it actually suits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Supabase Review: Is It Good for AI App Backends?

Supabase is a strong pick for AI apps that need a Postgres database, authentication, file storage, and vector embeddings in one platform instead of stitched-together services. It's not AI-first — it's a backend-as-a-service that supports pgvector natively, making it a practical choice for RAG apps, semantic search, and AI chat tools.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (Pro plan starts at $25/month) |
| **Free tier** | 500 MB database, 1 GB storage, unlimited API requests, 50,000 MAUs |
| **Best for** | Developers building AI apps who want Postgres + auth + storage + vectors in one place |
| **Standout feature** | Native pgvector support — embeddings live in the same database as your app data |

## What Supabase Actually Is

Supabase describes itself as "the Postgres development platform" — an open-source alternative to Firebase built around a dedicated Postgres instance rather than a proprietary NoSQL store. It's maintained by Supabase Inc. and is open source, with the core stack self-hostable via Docker if you'd rather run it yourself than use their hosted plans.

It isn't a chatbot, a copilot, or a model provider — there's no Supabase-branded LLM. What it offers instead is the plumbing an AI application needs behind the scenes: a Postgres database with pgvector enabled, row-level-security-backed authentication, S3-compatible file storage, serverless edge functions for running inference calls or webhooks, and realtime subscriptions for pushing updates to a UI as an AI job completes. For a team building a document-Q&A tool or an AI support widget, that combination covers most of the non-model infrastructure in one dashboard and one bill.

This matters for AI development specifically because most RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) apps need to store embeddings, query them by similarity, and join that against regular relational data — user accounts, documents, permissions, chat history. Running a separate dedicated vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) alongside a separate Postgres instance means syncing two systems and paying two bills. Supabase's own pitch is that "the best vector database is the database you already have" — put embeddings in a `vector` column next to your schema and query them with regular SQL.

## Pricing

Supabase runs a tiered subscription model, plus self-hosting for free if you're willing to manage your own infrastructure.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | 500 MB database, 1 GB file storage, unlimited API requests, 50,000 monthly active users, community support; projects pause after a week of inactivity, max 2 active projects |
| Pro | $25/month | 8 GB database disk (then metered), 100 GB storage (then metered), 100,000 MAUs (then metered), email support, 7-day backups, 250 GB egress included |
| Team | $599/month | Everything in Pro, plus SOC 2 and ISO 27001 compliance reporting, SSO access, priority support, 14-day backups |
| Enterprise | Custom | Dedicated support manager, 24/7 premium support, uptime SLAs, AWS PrivateLink, custom compliance/security reviews |

The Free and Pro tiers are usage-based past their included allowances rather than hard-capped — Supabase bills extra database storage, file storage, and bandwidth ("egress") by the GB once you exceed what's bundled. That's a different shape than most AI SaaS tools, which cap you on "credits" or "messages"; cost scales with actual infrastructure usage, which can be cheaper for a low-traffic app and pricier for a high-traffic one if you're not watching the metered add-ons.

Pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm current numbers on [Supabase's pricing page](https://supabase.com/pricing) before budgeting, especially the metered add-on rates.

## Core Features Walkthrough

**Postgres database with pgvector for embeddings.** Every Supabase project is a real, dedicated Postgres database — not a proprietary abstraction over one. Enabling the `pgvector` extension turns any table into a place you can store embedding vectors alongside your normal columns, then query them with cosine-distance or similarity operators in plain SQL. Embeddings, document metadata, user tables, and chat logs can all live in one schema with foreign keys between them, instead of syncing IDs across a separate vector store.

**Auth built for app-level access control.** Supabase Auth handles email/password, magic links, phone/OTP, and social logins from 20-plus providers, tied directly into Postgres row-level security (RLS). For a per-user document assistant, RLS lets you enforce "a user can only query embeddings tied to their own documents" at the database layer, not just in application code.

**Storage for the files behind your AI pipeline.** RAG apps ingest PDFs, transcripts, images, and other source documents before they ever get embedded. Supabase Storage is S3-compatible object storage with CDN distribution, so raw files sit in the same project as everything else, under the same auth rules.

**Edge Functions and Realtime.** Edge Functions are serverless Deno (with Node.js compatibility) functions for calling an LLM API, generating an embedding, or running a webhook when new data lands — a convenient place to glue your database to whatever model you're calling. Realtime pushes database changes over WebSockets, a natural fit for showing a user their document finished embedding without polling.

**AI provider integrations.** Supabase documents integrations with OpenAI, Hugging Face, LangChain, Amazon Bedrock, and LlamaIndex, plus a Python client for managing embeddings — none are Supabase's own models, but the common RAG-building toolchain has documented, first-party paths into a Supabase project.

## Who It's Actually For

**Solo developers and indie hackers building an MVP.** The free tier's 500 MB database and unlimited API requests are enough to prototype a small RAG app, AI chatbot, or embeddings-backed search feature at no cost. The tradeoff: free-tier projects pause after a week of inactivity.

**Small teams and startups shipping a real AI product.** The $25/month Pro plan is where most production AI apps will sit — enough database headroom, storage, and MAUs for early traction, with metered overages rather than a hard wall. For a team already choosing Postgres as their database of record, adding vector search removes a whole separate vendor from the stack.

**Compliance-conscious and enterprise teams.** The Team plan's SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reporting and SSO access target companies that need to pass a security review before piloting a tool internally, while Enterprise adds PrivateLink support, a dedicated support manager, and uptime SLAs for companies running AI features at a scale where a support ticket queue isn't good enough.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| pgvector keeps embeddings in the same database as your app data — no separate vector-store sync | Not a dedicated vector database — very large-scale, high-QPS search may favor a purpose-built tool like Pinecone or Qdrant |
| Generous, genuinely usable free tier for prototyping | Metered overage pricing can get harder to predict at scale than flat-rate competitors |
| Open source and self-hostable — no hard vendor lock-in | No Supabase-native AI models; you bring and pay for your own LLM/embedding provider |
| Auth, Storage, Realtime and Edge Functions cover most of an AI app's non-model backend in one dashboard | Free-tier projects pause after a week of inactivity |
| SOC 2/ISO 27001 compliance available on the Team plan | Team plan's jump to $599/month is steep, with little in between for a growing team |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Supabase connects to the AI toolchain most developers already use: OpenAI, Hugging Face, LangChain, Amazon Bedrock, and LlamaIndex all have documented integration paths for pulling data from or pushing embeddings into a project. Beyond that, it offers a CLI for local development and migrations, a REST/GraphQL API auto-generated from your Postgres schema, client libraries for JavaScript, Python, Flutter, Swift, and Kotlin, and webhooks for triggering external services off database events.

## Where It's a Strong Fit

Supabase makes the most sense when you're building an AI app that needs real relational data alongside its vector search — a SaaS product with user accounts and permissions, a document assistant where access control matters, or an internal tool joining embeddings against existing business data. If your team already knows SQL and Postgres, the learning curve for adding vector search is small: it's an extension and a column type, not a new query language. It's also sensible for teams that want to avoid vendor lock-in, since the underlying database is standard Postgres and the whole stack can be self-hosted.

## Where to Think Twice

Supabase is a poor fit if you need a dedicated, high-throughput vector database at genuinely large scale — millions of vectors with heavy concurrent query load are a workload where purpose-built vector databases have an edge in raw performance and indexing options. It's also not right if you want an all-in-one AI platform that includes model hosting — you'll still bring and pay for your own LLM and embedding provider. Teams that need flat-rate costs may find Pro's metered overages harder to forecast than a fixed-price competitor. And if you need enterprise compliance sign-off (SOC 2, ISO 27001) but can't justify the jump to the $599/month Team plan, budget for that gap before committing.

## The Bottom Line

Supabase isn't trying to be an AI company, and that's arguably its strength for AI app backends — it's a mature, open-source Postgres platform that happens to support the exact feature (pgvector) that RAG and semantic-search apps need, without forcing you to adopt a separate vector database vendor. For a developer or small team building an AI product who wants auth, storage, realtime, and vector search under one Postgres schema, it's a genuinely efficient default. If your workload is vector search at massive scale, or you want a vendor that also hosts the model, compare it against dedicated vector databases or full AI-platform offerings first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Supabase free to use?**
Yes. The free tier includes a 500 MB database, 1 GB of file storage, unlimited API requests, and up to 50,000 monthly active users, with no time limit — though inactive free projects pause after a week and need manual restarting.

**Does Supabase support vector embeddings for AI apps?**
Yes, through the `pgvector` Postgres extension. You store embedding vectors in a regular table alongside other application data and query them for similarity search using standard SQL, which is the core reason developers pick Supabase for RAG and semantic-search projects.

**Is Supabase actually open source?**
Yes. Its core tools are open source and available for self-hosting via Docker, in addition to the hosted (paid) plans, central to its positioning as an open alternative to Firebase.

**Does Supabase host or provide its own AI models?**
No. It provides the database, auth, storage, and functions layer around an AI application, but you bring your own model or embedding provider — it documents integrations with OpenAI, Hugging Face, LangChain, Amazon Bedrock, and LlamaIndex rather than shipping its own LLM.

**Is Supabase good for beginners?**
If you already know SQL and basic Postgres concepts, yes — the dashboard, auto-generated APIs, and docs are approachable. If you've never worked with a relational database before, there's a real learning curve versus simpler NoSQL-style backends.

**What are the main alternatives to Supabase for an AI app backend?**
Firebase is the closest comparison for the "backend-as-a-service" category, though it lacks native vector search. For a dedicated vector database instead of a bundled Postgres extension, Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant are common alternatives, typically paired with a separate database for relational data.

title: Portkey AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Portkey AI review covering pricing, the AI gateway, observability, caching, and the 2026 Palo Alto Networks acquisition — is it worth it?
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Portkey AI Worth Using for LLM Infrastructure?

Portkey AI is an AI gateway and LLMOps platform giving development teams one API to call any large language model, plus observability, caching, guardrails, and cost controls layered on top. It's a solid pick for teams running production LLM apps across multiple providers, though its free tier targets prototyping, not scale. Note: Portkey was acquired by Palo Alto Networks in 2026 and is being folded into the Prisma AIRS AI Gateway line, which matters for anyone evaluating it long term.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (Developer plan); paid plans from $49/month |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — 10,000 recorded logs/month, 3-day log retention |
| **Best for** | Engineering teams running multiple LLM providers in production |
| **Standout feature** | Unified gateway API with automatic fallbacks, caching, and per-request observability |

## What Portkey Actually Is

Portkey started as a San Francisco-based AI infrastructure startup building an "AI gateway" — a single API layer that sits between an application and the dozens of LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, open-weight models hosted on Groq or Together) a team might call in production. Instead of writing separate integration code for every provider, a developer points requests at Portkey's endpoint, which handles routing, retries, fallbacks, caching, and logging behind the scenes.

The company's own materials describe support for well over a thousand model and provider combinations (marketing copy cites figures ranging from "250+ providers" to "1,600+ LLMs" depending on the page, so treat the exact number as a moving target). Most mainstream commercial and open-source models are reachable through one OpenAI-compatible API format, which is the main reason teams adopt it — code written to call GPT stays nearly identical to code that calls Claude or Gemini.

In 2026, Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey, reportedly roughly doubling its prior valuation, and is integrating the gateway into its Prisma AIRS security platform under the name Prisma AIRS AI Gateway. As of this writing the standalone Portkey product, docs, and pricing pages are still live, but teams building on it today should expect branding, support channels, and possibly pricing to shift as integration continues.

## Pricing

Portkey runs a standard SaaS tiering model layered on top of a genuinely free, self-hostable open-source core.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Open Source (self-hosted) | Free | Universal API, retries/timeouts, routing, basic guardrails, fallbacks, load balancing, community support, unlimited requests |
| Developer | Free | 10,000 logs/month, 3-day log retention, 30-day metrics retention, logs/traces/feedback, 3 prompt templates, simple caching |
| Production | $49/month | 100,000 logs/month ($9 per extra 100K), 30-day log retention, alerts, LLM & partner guardrails, unlimited prompt templates, RBAC, service-account API keys, simple & semantic caching |
| Enterprise | Custom pricing | 10 million+ logs/month, custom retention/guardrail hooks, SSO, granular budgets, private cloud/VPC, SOC 2 Type 2, GDPR, HIPAA compliance |

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly for AI infrastructure tools — confirm current numbers on [Portkey's pricing page](https://portkey.ai/pricing) before committing.

The self-hosted open-source option is worth calling out: unlike most gateway products, Portkey doesn't force you into its hosted plan for a real feature set. Teams with strict data-residency requirements can run the gateway themselves, though they lose the managed dashboard and take on operational overhead in exchange.

## Core Features Walkthrough

**Unified AI Gateway.** The core product: one API endpoint, one authentication scheme, one request/response format, routed to whichever underlying model or provider you configure. Automatic fallbacks mean that if your primary provider has an outage or hits a rate limit, Portkey retries against a secondary model without your application code needing to handle that logic. For teams burned by a single-provider outage taking down their product, this feature justifies adoption on its own.

**Observability and tracing.** Every request routed through the gateway is logged automatically — latency, token counts, cost, and (on paid plans) full traces across multi-step agent workflows. That's useful for debugging why a chain of LLM calls produced a bad output or ran slowly, otherwise a black box once you're chaining multiple model calls.

**Caching (simple and semantic).** Simple caching returns a stored response for an identical request; semantic caching serves a cached response for a request that's semantically similar but not byte-identical, cutting costs for applications with repetitive query patterns (support bots, FAQ tools, internal search). Portkey's own customer references cite meaningful savings here, though results depend on how repetitive your traffic is — test against your own workload rather than assuming a fixed percentage.

**Guardrails.** PII redaction, content filtering, and policy enforcement can be applied at the gateway level before a request reaches the model or a response reaches your user. This is where the Palo Alto Networks logic becomes obvious — a network-level control point for AI traffic is exactly the kind of asset a security company would want, and this area will likely see more investment (and more enterprise-only gating) going forward.

**Prompt management.** Centralized prompt templates with versioning and a playground, separate from your application code. The free Developer plan caps you at 3 templates; Production removes that cap.

## Who It's Actually For

**Solo developers and small prototypes** get real value from the free Developer plan — 10,000 logs a month is enough to build and test a proof of concept, and the unified API saves the annoyance of juggling multiple SDKs.

**Small-to-mid engineering teams shipping a production LLM feature** are the clear target for the $49/month Production plan — log volume, semantic caching, and alerting make sense once you have real user traffic.

**Enterprises running agentic workflows at scale** need the Enterprise tier for compliance (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR), SSO, and private/VPC deployment — also the tier most likely to see continued investment given the acquisition's strategic rationale.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free self-hosted open-source option with unlimited requests | Free hosted tier's 3-day log retention is thin for real debugging |
| Broad model/provider coverage through one API | Model-count claims vary across the vendor's own marketing pages |
| Semantic caching can meaningfully cut LLM costs on repetitive workloads | Advanced guardrails and RBAC gated behind paid Production tier |
| Genuine production features at a reasonable $49/month | Palo Alto Networks integration adds pricing/branding uncertainty |
| Enterprise-grade compliance (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR) for regulated teams | Overage pricing ($9/100K logs) can add up fast at high volume |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Portkey exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so most existing tooling built for OpenAI's SDK format can point at Portkey's endpoint with minimal changes. The company documents SDKs for Node.js and Python, plus REST API access for other languages. It also supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP), positioning it as a gateway for tool-calling and agent-to-agent traffic, not just chat completions — a meaningful differentiator as more teams build multi-agent systems.

Enterprise plans add SSO and private cloud/VPC deployment. Beyond that, don't assume deep native integrations with tools like Zapier or Slack — Portkey is infrastructure that sits between your app and model providers, not a no-code automation platform, so integration work mostly means pointing existing LLM SDK calls at Portkey's endpoint.

## Where It's a Strong Fit

- Teams already calling multiple LLM providers who are tired of maintaining separate integration code for each.
- Production apps that need automatic failover so a provider outage doesn't become a customer-facing outage.
- Teams with repetitive query patterns where semantic caching can produce real cost savings.
- Organizations building MCP-based agent systems that need a control point for tool-calling traffic.
- Regulated industries that need SOC 2/HIPAA/GDPR-compliant AI infrastructure and can pay for Enterprise.

## Where to Think Twice

- **If you need a fully free tool beyond prototyping** — the free Developer plan's 3-day log retention and 10K log cap feel restrictive once you have real users, and self-hosting means running the infrastructure yourself.
- **If you only ever call a single LLM provider** — the core value proposition (unified API, automatic fallback) matters much less if you're not multi-provider.
- **If you need long-term product stability guarantees** — the acquisition is still working through integration into Prisma AIRS; factor that transition risk into any multi-year commitment.
- **If your workload is one-off, non-repetitive queries** — semantic caching's cost benefit shrinks to near zero.
- **If you need guaranteed low overage costs at very high volume** — model the $9/100K overage rate against your actual traffic first.

## Bottom Line

Portkey AI does what it says: it turns messy multi-provider LLM integration into a single API call with observability, caching, and guardrails built in, backed by a genuinely usable free tier and a real open-source self-hosted option, not just a marketing-page freemium trap. The $49/month Production plan is reasonably priced for what it unlocks, and the feature set reflects real production needs rather than a generic checklist. The one factor that should give any evaluator pause is timing: Portkey is mid-acquisition into Palo Alto Networks' Prisma AIRS platform, and how that shakes out for independent users isn't fully settled yet. Teams that need a multi-provider gateway today and can re-evaluate in a year if the product's identity shifts will find it a strong choice; teams that need multi-year platform certainty right now should watch the transition play out before committing at the Enterprise tier.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Portkey AI free to use?**
Yes. Portkey offers a free, self-hosted open-source version with unlimited requests, and a free hosted Developer plan with 10,000 recorded logs per month and 3-day log retention, suitable for prototyping.

**How much does Portkey cost for production use?**
The Production plan starts at $49/month for 100,000 recorded logs, with overage priced at $9 per additional 100,000 logs. Enterprise pricing is custom and scales to 10 million+ logs per month with compliance and private-deployment options.

**Is Portkey AI still called Portkey, or is it Prisma AIRS now?**
Both, during the transition. Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey in 2026 and is integrating it into its Prisma AIRS AI Gateway product. The standalone Portkey site, docs, and pricing are still active as of this writing, but expect branding and pricing to shift as integration continues.

**How many AI models does Portkey support?**
Portkey's own marketing pages cite different figures — ranging from around 250 providers up to 1,600+ models — so treat the exact number as directional and check current docs for the provider you need.

**Does Portkey handle data privacy and security?**
Portkey offers guardrails including PII redaction on paid plans, and its Enterprise tier includes SOC 2 Type 2, GDPR, and HIPAA compliance plus private cloud/VPC deployment. Confirm current certifications directly with Portkey for your compliance needs.

**What are the alternatives to Portkey?**
Other AI gateway/LLMOps platforms include LiteLLM (open source, developer-focused), Helicone, and cloud-native options like Azure AI Gateway or Amazon Bedrock's built-in routing. The right choice depends on provider count and whether you want self-hosted or fully managed.

**Is Portkey beginner-friendly for developers new to LLM infrastructure?**
The gateway is straightforward to integrate, with setup advertised in a few lines of code using an OpenAI-compatible format. The steeper learning curve is understanding what you need (caching strategy, guardrail policy, fallback logic) once running in production.

**Can I self-host Portkey instead of using the hosted version?**
Yes. Portkey publishes an open-source gateway that can be self-hosted for free with unlimited requests, an option for teams with data-residency requirements.
