A freelancer spinning up a client's first draft, a founder testing a landing page before committing to a developer, or a small business that wants SEO and analytics tooling included rather than bolted on afterward will all find the free-to-cheap entry point and the code-export option genuinely useful. The template breadth (1,000+ across 18+ industries, per the vendor) also means most common business types have a reasonable starting point rather than a single generic template stretched across every use case.

## Where to think twice

If your priority is best-in-class visual design fidelity — pixel-perfect animations, a highly refined design system, or agency-grade presentation — a design-first AI builder like Framer AI is likely to get you there with less manual cleanup. Skip CodeDesign.ai if you need a fully transparent, itemized pricing page before you're willing to start a trial; the vendor's own pricing page is noticeably less detailed than most competitors', so verify current tier pricing directly rather than assume the numbers here are current. It's also not the right choice if you specifically need a bundled CRM and invoicing system tied to the site builder — that's Durable's territory. And because independent review volume on platforms like Trustpilot is currently thin for this vendor, don't expect much external social proof beyond the vendor's own claims.

## Bottom line

CodeDesign.ai is a reasonable choice specifically because it doesn't ask you to trust it forever — the code-export option is a real differentiator in a category where most AI builders keep your site locked inside their own editor. If you want a fast AI-generated starting point with a genuine exit path to owned code, and you're comfortable confirming exact pricing directly on the vendor's site before paying, it's worth a trial run on the free plan. If your priority is design polish over code ownership, or you need CRM and invoicing bundled in, one of the other AI builders covered here is likely the better match.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is CodeDesign.ai free to use?**
Yes, there's a free plan that includes up to three projects hosted on a CodeDesign subdomain. Custom domains and code export require a paid plan.

**Can I export the code from a site I build with CodeDesign.ai?**
Yes — the platform states you can export your project to React or HTML code, which is its main differentiator from most AI website builders that keep sites locked inside their own editor.

**How much does CodeDesign.ai cost?**
The vendor doesn't publish a detailed, itemized price list for every paid tier on its main pricing page beyond noting a 20% annual-billing discount and a free domain with annual plans. Confirm current pricing directly on [CodeDesign.ai's pricing page](https://codedesign.ai/pricing) before subscribing.

**Does CodeDesign.ai use ChatGPT or another AI model?**
The vendor states it integrates with OpenAI's technology and operates under OpenAI's zero data retention policy, meaning prompts aren't used to train OpenAI's models.

**Is CodeDesign.ai good for beginners with no coding experience?**
Yes — the AI-chat editing mode is designed for plain-language instructions, and the drag-and-drop visual editor doesn't require code knowledge. Coding becomes relevant only if you choose to export the project.

**What are the best alternatives to CodeDesign.ai?**
If you want more design polish, look at Framer AI. If you want 3D, prompt-to-site generation from a Figma file, Dora AI is closer to that use case. If you want a built-in CRM, bookings and invoicing alongside the generated site, Durable is worth comparing.

**Does CodeDesign.ai offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes, the vendor states paid plans include a 7-day money-back guarantee and can be canceled at any time.

**Does CodeDesign.ai integrate with WordPress?**
Yes, the platform documents a WordPress integration for teams that want to connect their AI-generated content workflow to an existing WordPress setup.

For more AI website builder options, see our reviews of [Durable](/blog/durable-ai-review), [Framer AI](/blog/framer-ai-review) and [Dora AI](/blog/dora-ai-review), or browse [AI & software deals](/category/software) for more tool coverage.

title: Diagram AI Review 2026: What It Was, Now Part of Figma
excerpt: Diagram was an AI design plugin startup best known for Magician. Figma acquired it in 2024 — here's what happened and where the tools live now.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Diagram still a standalone AI design tool in 2026?

No. Diagram was an AI design startup — best known for its "Magician" plugin that generated icons, copy, and layout suggestions inside Figma — that Figma acquired in February 2024. It was never sold as a separate paid product afterward; its team and technology were folded into Figma's own AI features, and the original plugins were phased out as native Figma AI tools took over.

**At a glance**

| | Diagram |
|---|---|
| Status | Discontinued as a standalone product; acquired by Figma (Feb 2024) |
| Former starting price | Free plugin tier, with paid Magician credits for heavier use |
| Best for (historically) | Figma users wanting AI-generated icons, copy, and mockups inside the canvas |
| Standout feature | Magician — prompt-to-icon and prompt-to-mockup generation inside Figma |
| What replaced it | Figma's own native AI tools (Figma AI, First Draft, Figma Weave) |

If you searched for "Diagram AI review" hoping to sign up for it today, there's nothing left to sign up for — this review covers what Diagram was, why Figma wanted it, and where to actually find that functionality now.

## What Diagram actually was

Diagram was a small AI-focused startup built around a simple bet: most designers were already living inside Figma, so instead of building a separate AI design app, Diagram built a family of plugins that plugged directly into Figma's existing canvas. The best known of these was **Magician**, which let designers type a prompt and get back things like custom icon sets, AI-generated images, filler copy, and simple mockup layouts without leaving Figma.

Alongside Magician, Diagram shipped a handful of smaller, more experimental AI plugins — tools aimed at things like automatically renaming and organizing layers, suggesting design variations, and speeding up repetitive parts of the design process that don't require much creative judgment. None of these were marketed as a single unified "Diagram app" the way, say, Notion or Canva is a destination product — Diagram was a plugin company, and Figma's marketplace was effectively its only distribution channel.

That plugin-first approach is exactly what made Diagram attractive to Figma. Figma didn't need to convince users to adopt a new app or migrate their files anywhere — Diagram's plugins already lived inside Figma's own ecosystem, generating real usage data and design-specific training signal that a general-purpose AI lab wouldn't have easy access to.

## The Figma acquisition, and why it happened

Figma announced it had acquired Diagram in February 2024, a deal reported to be worth around $50 million, though neither company published exact terms. The founders — designer and prolific product-tinkerer Jordan Singer among them — and the rest of the Diagram team joined Figma directly, rather than continuing to operate Diagram as an independent brand or subsidiary.

The strategic logic was straightforward. Figma had already been experimenting publicly with its own AI features (things like auto-generated FigJam content and early AI search), but building genuinely useful, design-native AI from scratch is slow and expensive. Diagram had already spent roughly two years building and iterating on AI tools specifically for designers, inside the exact product Figma wanted to enhance. Acquiring that team and codebase let Figma accelerate its own AI roadmap rather than compete with a plugin that, ironically, ran on top of Figma's own platform.

This is a familiar pattern in software — closer to an "acqui-hire with a working product" than a hostile takeover, similar in shape to how several small AI tooling startups get absorbed into larger platforms once their idea proves out but their standalone growth ceiling looks limited next to the acquirer's distribution.

## What happened after the deal

In the months following the acquisition, Diagram's standalone plugins didn't get shut down overnight, but they also weren't actively developed as separate products going forward. Figma's public messaging at the time focused on using the team's expertise to build AI capability directly into the core Figma product, rather than maintaining Diagram as a side offering.

Over the following product cycles, Figma shipped its own native AI features under the Figma AI banner — including tools for generating first-draft designs from a prompt, rewriting and editing UI copy, searching and organizing large files, and later, more advanced generative capabilities under names like Figma Weave (added via a separate 2025 acquisition of AI startup Weavy). Functionally, a lot of what Magician originally did — turn a text prompt into icons, images, or a rough layout — is now something Figma offers itself, built into the core product rather than bolted on as a plugin.

Pricing and feature availability for Figma's current AI tools were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly, since Figma has iterated on its AI feature set and pricing tiers multiple times since the Diagram acquisition — always confirm current details on Figma's own pricing page before assuming a specific feature is included in your plan.

As of this writing, Diagram no longer operates as an independent website, app, or plugin brand that you can sign up for. If you're trying to find the functionality Diagram used to provide, the place to look is Figma itself, not a separate "Diagram" product.

## Who Diagram was actually for, back when it existed

For the roughly two years Diagram operated as an independent plugin suite, it was most useful for:

- **Solo designers and small teams** already working in Figma who wanted quick AI-generated icon sets or placeholder imagery without switching to a separate image-generation tool.
- **Product designers under time pressure** who needed rough mockup copy or layout starting points rather than a blank canvas.
- **Figma power users** comfortable installing and managing third-party plugins, since Diagram's tools lived entirely inside Figma's plugin ecosystem rather than as a destination app.

It was a poor fit for anyone who wanted a standalone design tool independent of Figma, or who needed guaranteed long-term support for a specific plugin version — as the acquisition ultimately demonstrated, a venture-backed plugin startup's roadmap can change completely once a platform decides to build the same capability natively.

## Where the functionality lives now

| Then (Diagram) | Now (Figma) |
|---|---|
| Magician plugin — prompt-to-icon, prompt-to-image | Figma AI's native image and asset generation |
| AI copywriting assistance inside plugins | Figma AI's text/content generation tools |
| Prompt-to-mockup layout suggestions | Figma AI's "First Draft" feature |
| Third-party plugin, separate install | Built directly into the core Figma product |

If you're evaluating Figma's current AI capabilities rather than trying to track down the original Diagram plugins, that's really the more useful comparison to make — how good is Figma AI today, not whether a 2024-era plugin startup is still around. We don't currently have a dedicated Figma review on this site, but it's the product worth researching directly if AI-assisted design inside Figma is what you're after — check the [AI & software deals](/category/software) hub for current design-tool coverage as we add it.

## Pros and cons, viewed in hindsight

| Pros (as Diagram) | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely useful, design-specific AI inside the tool designers already used | Never operated as an independent, durable product — always dependent on Figma's plugin platform |
| Fast iteration as a small, focused team | Absorbed into Figma within about two years of raising meaningful funding |
| Proved out real demand for AI-assisted design workflows | No transparency on exact acquisition terms or what specific plugin code survived intact |
| Talent and IP didn't disappear — it shaped Figma's own AI roadmap | Anyone who built a workflow around the standalone Diagram plugins had to migrate |

## Where this leaves you if you searched for "Diagram AI"

**If you want AI-generated icons, mockups, or copy inside your design files today**, the practical answer is to use Figma's own built-in AI tools rather than looking for the original Diagram plugins, which are no longer being actively maintained as a separate product.

**If you're researching this as a case study in AI-startup acquisitions**, Diagram is a reasonably clean example of a plugin-first company getting absorbed by the platform it depended on — worth knowing about if you're evaluating whether to build a product on top of someone else's platform versus as an independent app.

**If you need a currently-supported, actively developed AI design tool**, skip searching for Diagram entirely and evaluate Figma AI (or alternatives like Framer AI, Uizard, or Canva's AI tools) on their current feature sets and pricing instead — chasing down a discontinued plugin's old documentation won't get you a working product.

## Bottom line

Diagram was a genuinely well-regarded early example of AI plugins built specifically for designers, and its Magician plugin was popular enough inside the Figma community that Figma decided buying the team was more efficient than out-building them. But as of 2026, Diagram is not something you can sign up for, pay for, or install as a standalone tool — it's part of Figma's internal AI story now, not a live product. If the goal is AI-assisted design work today, evaluate Figma's current AI features (or a genuinely active competitor) on their own merits rather than searching for a startup that stopped operating independently more than two years ago.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Diagram still available to download or install?**
No. Diagram operated as a set of Figma plugins (most notably Magician) that were phased out as a separate offering after Figma's February 2024 acquisition. There isn't a current standalone app or plugin listing to install under the Diagram name.

**What was Diagram's Magician plugin?**
Magician was a Figma plugin that let designers generate icons, images, filler copy, and rough layout suggestions from a text prompt, directly inside the Figma canvas, without switching to a separate AI tool.

**Why did Figma acquire Diagram?**
Figma wanted to accelerate its own native AI roadmap. Diagram had already built AI tools specifically for designers, working inside Figma's own plugin ecosystem, which made the team and technology a faster path to shipping AI features than building everything from scratch internally.

**How much did Figma pay for Diagram?**
The deal was reported at around $50 million by industry press at the time, though neither company officially confirmed exact financial terms.

**Is there a free alternative to what Diagram used to offer?**
Figma's own AI features (available to users on eligible plans) now cover much of the same ground Magician did — generating images, copy, and first-draft layouts inside Figma. Availability and pricing for these features have changed multiple times since 2024, so check Figma's current plans directly rather than assuming free access.

**Did Diagram's founders stay involved in AI design tools?**
Yes — the Diagram team, including co-founder Jordan Singer, joined Figma as part of the acquisition and continued working on AI-related product development there rather than at an independent company.

**Is this the same "Diagram" as diagramming software like Lucidchart or draw.io?**
No. This Diagram was an AI-plugin startup for product design inside Figma, unrelated to flowchart/diagramming tools like Lucidchart, draw.io, or Miro, which are separate, still-active products with a different purpose.

**Should I still search for Diagram-specific tutorials or documentation?**
Generally no — since the product isn't independently maintained, any tutorials you find are likely outdated. For current AI-assisted design workflows, Figma's own help center and product pages are the more reliable, up-to-date source.

title: AISEO Review 2026: AI Writer and Visibility Tracker
excerpt: AISEO combines AI writing, SEO auditing, and AI-visibility tracking across ChatGPT and Gemini — see pricing, features, and who it's actually for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## AISEO Review 2026: AI Writer Meets AI Visibility Tracking

AISEO (aiseo.ai) is a good fit if you want one subscription that covers AI-assisted content writing, technical SEO auditing, and tracking whether your brand gets mentioned by ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude. It's less compelling if you just need a focused long-form writing tool, since its pricing and interface are split across several distinct products.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Around $24/month for writing tools; AI Visibility/Brand Monitor plans start near $39–49/month |
| **Free tier/trial** | $1 one-day trial on paid plans (no permanent free tier) |
| **Best for** | Marketing teams and agencies that want writing + SEO auditing + AI-search visibility tracking in one vendor |
| **Standout feature** | Brand Monitor / AI Visibility scanning across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude |

## What AISEO actually is

AISEO started as an AI writing assistant aimed at SEO content — blog posts, product descriptions, and marketing copy generated from a keyword or topic prompt. Over the past couple of years the product has expanded well beyond writing. The current lineup, based on the company's own site, includes:

- **AI Writer / Article Generator** — long-form content generation with keyword targeting
- **SEO Agent** — an automated site crawler that checks technical SEO signals and prioritizes fixes by ranking impact
- **Brand Monitor / AI Visibility** — tracks where a brand gets cited inside AI answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude, benchmarked against competitors
- **Reddit Agent** — surfaces Reddit threads relevant to a brand or its competitors, since those threads increasingly rank on Google
- **A cluster of smaller utilities** — AI Humanizer, Paraphraser, AI Detector, Plagiarism Checker, Schema Markup Generator, Keyword Rank Checker, and an AI image generator/detector

In other words, AISEO isn't a single tool anymore — it's a suite, and which part of it matters to you depends heavily on whether you're evaluating it as a writer, an SEO auditor, or a "generative engine optimization" (GEO) tracker. The company doesn't publicly disclose which underlying language model(s) power the writer or the humanizer, so that detail should be treated as unconfirmed rather than assumed to be GPT- or Claude-based.

No store entry exists for AISEO in this site's coupon catalog, so pricing and feature details below come directly from the vendor's own pricing and marketing pages.

## Pricing

AISEO's pricing is confusing in a way worth flagging upfront: the writing tools and the AI Visibility/SEO Agent tools are sold as separate plans rather than one unified subscription, and the numbers shown on different parts of the site don't always match cleanly.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Writer plans | From ~$24/month | AI-generated articles, paraphrasing, and related content tools |
| AI Visibility — Entry | ~$39/month ($470/year annually) | 1 AI visibility scan/month, 1 Reddit credit/month, scans across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, competitor rankings, sentiment analysis |
| AI Visibility — Pro | ~$119/month ($1,430/year annually) | 3 scans/month, 3 Reddit credits/month, everything in Entry |
| SEO Agent credits (add-on) | ~$284/month for 6M credits | Bulk site audits, ranked fixes, credits roll over and scale with usage |

Nearly every plan opens with a **$1, one-day trial** rather than a genuinely free forever tier, which is worth knowing before you hand over a card — the trial converts automatically to the paid rate unless cancelled.

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) per the vendor's own pricing page, but AI tool pricing changes often and different pages on AISEO's site quote slightly different numbers for the same tier — confirm current figures on [aiseo.ai/pricing](https://aiseo.ai) before subscribing.

## Core features walkthrough

**AI Visibility / Brand Monitor.** This is the part of AISEO that differentiates it most from a plain AI writer. Instead of only tracking Google rankings, it queries major AI assistants to see whether — and how — a brand gets cited or recommended, then compares that visibility against named competitors. As more searches get answered directly inside chat interfaces rather than a list of blue links, this kind of monitoring addresses a real, growing gap that classic rank-tracking tools don't cover.

**SEO Agent.** AISEO describes this as a crawler that checks dozens of on-page and technical SEO signals daily and prioritizes fixes by how much they're estimated to be hurting rankings. It's positioned as a "fix it for me" layer on top of a standard technical audit, rather than a full technical SEO platform replacement — teams running deep crawl audits on large sites will likely still want a dedicated crawler alongside it.

**Reddit Agent.** A more unusual addition: it watches Reddit for threads mentioning a brand or its competitors, on the logic that Reddit threads now rank prominently in Google results and get cited by AI answer engines. This is a genuinely useful angle for consumer brands where Reddit sentiment shapes both organic search and AI-generated recommendations, but it's a narrow tool — it won't replace a proper social listening platform.

**AI Writer and Article Generator.** The original core product: keyword-to-article generation with on-page SEO targeting (headings, keyword density, meta suggestions). It's competent for producing a first draft quickly, but like most AI writers it needs a human editing pass for voice, factual accuracy, and to avoid the generic tone that AI detectors and readers alike can spot.

**AI Humanizer and Detector.** Paired utilities — one rewrites AI-generated text to read more naturally, the other flags text likely to be AI-written. Worth noting: AI detection tools across the industry (not just AISEO's) have known false-positive and false-negative rates, so results should be treated as a signal, not a verdict.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo bloggers/creators on a tight budget** — the entry writer plan is affordable, but a dedicated writer tool without the SEO-agent/visibility add-ons will likely feel more focused and cost less overall.
- **In-house marketing teams at growing brands** — the combination of technical SEO auditing and AI-visibility tracking is genuinely useful here, since it puts both "can Google find us" and "does ChatGPT recommend us" checks under one roof.
- **Agencies managing multiple client brands** — the Pro AI Visibility tier's competitor benchmarking and Reddit Agent are aimed squarely at this use case, though the per-scan credit limits (3 scans/month on Pro) mean agencies with many clients will likely need multiple accounts or the add-on credit packs.
- **Enterprise teams needing deep technical crawls** — the SEO Agent is a lighter-weight, prioritized-fix tool rather than a full enterprise crawler; teams with large, complex sites should expect to pair it with (or stick with) a dedicated technical SEO platform.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Combines content writing, technical SEO, and AI-visibility tracking in one vendor | Pricing is split across multiple separate plans that aren't always consistent across the site |
| Brand Monitor addresses a real, current gap (AI answer-engine citations) that most legacy SEO tools don't cover | No meaningful permanent free tier — trials are $1 for one day and auto-convert |
| Reddit Agent is a distinctive angle competitors mostly don't offer | AI visibility scan allowances are low even on the Pro plan (3/month) |
| Useful for producing quick first-draft content at scale | Underlying AI model(s) for writing/humanizing aren't publicly disclosed |
| Annual billing saves roughly 20% versus monthly | AI-generated text and AI-detection results both carry accuracy caveats industry-wide |

## Integrations and ecosystem

AISEO's site does not prominently advertise a public API, Zapier connector, or native CMS plugins (e.g. WordPress). If API access or a specific integration is a requirement, confirm directly with AISEO support before subscribing rather than assuming parity with dedicated SEO platforms like Surfer or Ahrefs, which do offer documented APIs and browser/CMS integrations.

## Where it's a strong fit

AISEO makes the most sense for teams that specifically want to monitor brand visibility inside AI answer engines alongside more traditional SEO and content work, without stitching together three or four separate vendors. The Reddit Agent and AI Visibility scanning in particular are addressing a search-behavior shift — more users asking ChatGPT or Perplexity directly instead of scrolling Google results — that's still underserved by most established SEO tool suites.

## Where to think twice

Skip AISEO, or at least the AI Visibility side of it, if you need a fully free tool — there's no lasting free tier, only a $1 trial. Skip it if your team needs a strict, unified per-seat price: the writer, SEO Agent, and AI Visibility products are billed separately, which complicates budgeting for larger teams. Teams that need deep enterprise-grade site crawls (hundreds of thousands of URLs), documented API access, or verified SOC 2/enterprise compliance should confirm those specifics directly with AISEO's sales team before committing, since none of that is clearly documented on the public marketing pages. And if your primary need is AI-generated writing quality alone, a dedicated writing tool may give a more polished, purpose-built experience than a suite where writing is one feature among many.

## Bottom line

AISEO has evolved from a straightforward AI writing tool into a broader SEO-plus-AI-visibility suite, and that shift is its biggest strength and its biggest source of friction. The Brand Monitor and Reddit Agent features tackle a real and growing need — tracking whether AI assistants recommend your brand — that most legacy SEO software still hasn't caught up to. But the fragmented pricing across writer, SEO Agent, and AI Visibility plans, combined with low scan allowances and a lack of public API/integration detail, means it's worth mapping your actual use case (content generation vs. technical audits vs. AI-citation tracking) to the specific AISEO plan that covers it, rather than assuming one subscription does everything at one flat price.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is AISEO free?**
No. AISEO doesn't offer a lasting free plan — most tiers start with a $1, one-day trial that automatically converts to the paid monthly or annual rate unless you cancel first.

**What's the difference between AISEO's writer plans and its AI Visibility plans?**
They're sold separately. The writer plans (from roughly $24/month) cover AI-generated content, paraphrasing, and related writing tools. The AI Visibility plans (from roughly $39/month) cover Brand Monitor scanning across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude, plus Reddit Agent credits. Check the current pricing page carefully, since it's easy to sign up for the wrong tier.

**Does AISEO disclose which AI model powers its writer?**
Not publicly, as of this review. If the specific underlying model matters for your workflow (for compliance, accuracy expectations, or vendor lock-in reasons), confirm directly with AISEO support rather than assuming it's built on any particular model.

**How accurate is the AI Detector / Humanizer pairing?**
AISEO doesn't publish independent accuracy figures for either tool, and AI-detection tools generally (across vendors, not just AISEO) carry known false-positive and false-negative risk. Treat results as a directional signal rather than a definitive verdict, especially for anything with real consequences like academic or publishing decisions.

**Is AISEO good for SEO beginners?**
The AI Writer and SEO Agent are approachable for beginners since they automate a lot of the technical guesswork. The AI Visibility/Brand Monitor concept (tracking citations inside AI answers) is newer and less intuitive than classic keyword rank tracking, so expect a short learning curve there even if the interface itself is simple.

**What are the main alternatives to AISEO?**
For AI writing specifically, tools like Jasper or Copy.ai are more narrowly focused writing assistants. For technical SEO auditing, dedicated platforms like Ahrefs or Semrush offer deeper crawls and documented APIs. For AI-answer-engine visibility tracking, this newer category (sometimes called GEO or AEO tooling) is where AISEO's Brand Monitor competes with a handful of emerging, purpose-built trackers — see our [Answer Engine Optimization guide](/blog/answer-engine-optimization-guide) for more on evaluating this category.

**Can agencies manage multiple client brands on one AISEO account?**
The Pro AI Visibility plan supports multiple competitor comparisons, but its monthly scan allowance (3 scans/month per the vendor's own pricing page) is limited relative to what an agency managing several client brands would likely need — budget for add-on credits or multiple accounts if that's your situation.

For more AI and SaaS tool coverage and current deals, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Sudowrite Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Sudowrite is an AI writing tool built for novelists. Here's how its Story Bible, Muse model, and credit-based pricing hold up for fiction writers.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Sudowrite worth it for fiction writers?

Sudowrite is an AI writing tool built specifically for novelists rather than marketers or bloggers, and it's a genuinely useful one if you're drafting long fiction and want help with brainstorming, pacing, or breaking through a stuck scene. It starts at $10/month, runs on a proprietary model called Muse, and is best suited to writers who already have a story and want a collaborator, not a tool that writes a book for you from scratch.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $10/month (Hobby & Student plan) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Free trial, no credit card required |
| **Best for** | Novelists and screenwriters drafting long-form fiction |
| **Standout feature** | Story Bible + Muse 1.5, a model trained specifically for fiction |

Sudowrite was built by writers Amit Gupta and James Yu, and it's pitched squarely at people writing novels, screenplays, and long-form fiction — not the generic "write me a blog post" tools that dominate the AI writing category. That focus shows up in almost every design decision, from how it structures a manuscript to the vocabulary it uses in its interface (chapters, character arcs, beats, rather than "content" and "campaigns").

## What Sudowrite actually is

Sudowrite is a browser-based writing app that pairs a text editor with a set of AI tools purpose-built for fiction. Instead of one generic chat box, it splits its capabilities into named tools: Write (autocomplete that continues your prose in your voice), Describe (sensory detail generation), Expand (slows down rushed scenes), Rewrite (targeted revision suggestions), Brainstorm/Canvas (idea generation for plot and character), and Feedback (a simulated beta-reader pass that flags pacing, tension, and clarity issues).

The company says its core model, Muse 1.5, was trained specifically to understand narrative structure, character voice, and tone rather than being a general-purpose chatbot repurposed for fiction. Sudowrite doesn't publish full technical detail on Muse's architecture, so treat "trained for fiction" as the vendor's own framing rather than an independently verified claim.

The centerpiece of the product is the **Story Bible**, a structured workspace that walks you from a one-line premise through synopsis, characters, outline, and chapter-by-chapter drafting, with each stage feeding context into the next so later generations stay consistent with earlier decisions. There's also **Canvas**, a visual brainstorming board for exploring plot branches and character arcs, and **Visualize**, which generates character portraits from your written descriptions.

## Pricing

Sudowrite runs on a credit-based subscription model — you pick a monthly credit allowance, and generations (not every action, but the AI-generation ones) draw down against it. As of this post's publish date, the plans are:

| Plan | Price | Credits/month | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hobby & Student | $10/month | 225,000 | Entry tier for recreational writers and students |
| Professional | $22/month | 1,000,000 | Most popular tier; adds a work-feedback feature |
| Max | $44/month | 2,000,000 | For prolific authors; unused credits roll over for 12 months |

Annual billing knocks a meaningful chunk off the monthly price — Sudowrite advertises up to 50% off with a yearly commitment, though the exact discounted rate should be confirmed at checkout since promotional pricing shifts. All three tiers include a free trial that doesn't require a credit card, and Sudowrite says your written work stays accessible even if you let a subscription lapse.

Pricing, credit allowances, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — AI writing tools adjust credit limits and tiers often, so double-check the current numbers on Sudowrite's own pricing page before subscribing.

One thing worth understanding before you commit to a plan: credits aren't a flat "X generations per month" number. Longer generations (a full chapter draft vs. one paragraph of description) cost more credits, so it's worth starting on Hobby, watching how fast you burn credits in your first week, and upgrading only if you're actually hitting the ceiling.

## Features that actually differentiate it

**Story Bible.** This is the feature that separates Sudowrite from a generic AI chat wrapper. It holds your premise, character sheets, worldbuilding notes, and outline in one place, and every downstream generation pulls from that context automatically. In practice this means the AI is less likely to forget that a character is left-handed or that your protagonist already revealed a secret in chapter 3 — a common failure mode when you paste raw prompts into a general chatbot with no persistent memory of your manuscript.

**Chapter-length generation with your own voice.** Sudowrite lets you feed it a sample of your own writing so its output leans toward your style rather than a generic "AI voice." This won't make it indistinguishable from your actual prose, but it noticeably reduces the editing needed to make generated text fit the rest of your manuscript.

**Canvas for structural brainstorming.** Before you're ready to write scenes, Canvas gives you a visual space to lay out plot branches, character motivations, and "what if" alternatives — closer to a corkboard than a chat window. Writers who plan loosely (pantsers) may skip this entirely; outliners will find it more useful.

**Feedback and beta-reader simulation.** On the Professional and Max tiers, Sudowrite can analyze a draft and return specific notes on pacing, clarity, and tension, positioned as a stand-in for an early beta reader. It's not a substitute for a human editor, but as a first pass before sending a manuscript to actual readers, it can catch obvious structural issues.

**Visualize.** Generates character art from your written descriptions — a nice-to-have for a reference image or mood board, though secondary compared to the text tools.

## Who it's actually for

**Solo novelists drafting a first book** get the most obvious value from the $10 or $22 tier — the Story Bible alone is worth the price if you've ever lost track of a subplot or contradicted an earlier chapter three drafts in.

**Screenwriters and serialized fiction writers** producing high volume are the target audience for the Max tier, mainly because of the larger credit allowance and 12-month rollover, which matters if your output is bursty rather than steady.

**Writing groups or co-writing teams** aren't really what Sudowrite is built for — it's a single-user tool with no built-in collaboration or shared-workspace features.

**Non-fiction writers, marketers, and bloggers** are better served by general-purpose AI writing tools; Sudowrite's feature set (Story Bible, character arcs, fiction-tuned output) is wasted on landing pages and blog posts.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Purpose-built for long-form fiction, not generic content | Credit-based pricing is harder to predict than flat "unlimited" plans |
| Story Bible keeps character/plot details consistent across a manuscript | No real team/collaboration features |
| Muse model reportedly tuned for narrative voice, not generic chat output | Output still needs a human editing pass — it's a drafting aid, not a finished-manuscript machine |
| Free trial with no credit card required | Heavier generations (full chapters) can burn through credits quickly on lower tiers |
| Written work stays accessible after a subscription lapses, per Sudowrite | No offline or on-prem option — fully cloud-based |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Sudowrite is a standalone web app, not a plugin for Scrivener, Word, or Google Docs — you draft inside its own editor and export or copy text out when you're ready to move it elsewhere. The company markets a plugin/prompt library (Sudowrite states it supports over 1,000 customizable plugins) for extending specific generation tools, but this is an in-app extensibility layer, not third-party API access like Zapier or Slack integrations. There's no publicly documented public API for developers to build on top of it.

## Where it's a strong fit

If you're mid-draft on a novel and keep hitting the same wall — a scene that won't come together, a description that reads flat, an outline that's gone stale — Sudowrite's targeted tools (Describe, Expand, Rewrite) are built for exactly that kind of stuck moment rather than generating an entire manuscript unsupervised. Writers who plan meticulously with outlines and character sheets will get the most out of the Story Bible, since it rewards structured input with more consistent output.

It's also a reasonable fit for writers producing genre fiction at volume — serialized web fiction, romance, or fantasy where readers expect frequent releases — since the credit-based Max tier is built around sustained, high-output use.

## Where to think twice

If you need a fully free tool with no spending cap, Sudowrite isn't it — every meaningful generation draws down a credit allowance, and there's no permanently free tier, only a limited trial. If your workflow depends on writing inside Scrivener, Word, or Google Docs with native plugin support, you'll be copying text back and forth rather than working in place. Teams that need shared workspaces or multi-user editing won't find that here — it's built for a single author's manuscript, not collaborative writing. And if you're writing for a market or publisher with strict policies on AI tool use in submissions, check those guidelines first — Sudowrite doesn't currently publish clear guidance on how its output should be disclosed to publishers or contests.

Writers should also go in expecting an editing pass: generated scenes and chapters read more like a solid rough draft than a publication-ready one, and leaning on Sudowrite to skip revision entirely tends to produce prose that still reads AI-generated.

## The bottom line

Sudowrite is one of the few AI writing tools built around how novelists actually work — outlining, character consistency, scene-level pacing — rather than repurposing a general chatbot for fiction. The $10 entry tier is low-risk enough to test on a real work-in-progress, and the Story Bible is the standout reason to pick it over a general-purpose AI assistant. It won't write a finished novel for you, and the credit system means heavy users need to watch their usage, but for writers who want a focused collaborator rather than a blank chat window, it's a solid pick worth trialing.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Sudowrite free?**
Sudowrite offers a free trial with no credit card required, but there's no permanently free tier — after the trial, you need a paid plan starting at $10/month to keep generating.

**What AI model does Sudowrite use?**
Sudowrite runs on a proprietary model it calls Muse (currently Muse 1.5), which the company says was trained specifically for fiction writing rather than being a general-purpose chatbot repurposed for creative text.

**How do Sudowrite credits work?**
Each plan includes a monthly credit allowance, and AI generations draw down against it — longer outputs (a full chapter) cost more credits than short ones (a line of dialogue). Unused credits roll over for 12 months on the Max plan; check the current terms for lower tiers before assuming the same applies.

**Does Sudowrite write entire novels by itself?**
No. It's designed as a drafting and brainstorming aid — tools like Story Bible, Write, and Expand help you generate and revise scenes and chapters, but the output typically needs human editing and direction throughout, not a one-click "generate my novel" workflow.

**Can I use my own writing style with Sudowrite?**
Yes. You can feed it samples of your own prose so its generations lean toward your voice rather than a generic AI style, though matching your exact style consistently across a long manuscript still requires editing.

**Does Sudowrite integrate with Scrivener or Google Docs?**
Not natively. Sudowrite is a standalone browser-based editor; there's no built-in plugin for Scrivener, Word, or Google Docs, so you'll copy or export text if you want to work in those tools.

**Is Sudowrite good for beginners?**
The interface is approachable and the free trial makes it low-risk to test, but writers with a clearer sense of their story (basic outline, character ideas) will get noticeably more out of the Story Bible than someone starting from a completely blank page.

**What's a free alternative to Sudowrite?**
Open-source options like StoryCraftr exist for writers who want AI assistance without a subscription, though they typically require more setup and lack Sudowrite's polished Story Bible workflow and fiction-tuned model — see our [StoryCraftr review](/blog/storycraftr-review) for a closer look at that trade-off.

Looking for other AI writing tools to compare against? Browse our latest [AI & software deals](/category/software) for more options and current offers.

title: Mindreader Review 2026: Lead Intelligence, Pricing, Verdict
excerpt: Mindreader promises AI-driven lead scoring for sales teams, but its self-serve SaaS app is closed. Here is what is actually available in 2026.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Mindreader Worth It in 2026?

Mindreader (themindreader.ai) is a lead-intelligence platform from Personality Central that scores leads and suggests conversion angles for sales teams. It's worth considering if your team needs pre-call intelligence and can work with a pilot-based sales process — but its self-serve SaaS app has been retired, so there's no plan you can just sign up for today.

That last point matters more than anything else in this review, so it's worth stating upfront rather than burying it: as of this writing, Mindreader no longer accepts logins, sign-ups, or subscriptions for what used to be a standard SaaS product. The company says on its own site that "the logged-in Mindreader application has been discontinued" and that it is "no longer accepting logins, sign-ups, or subscriptions for the former SaaS product." What remains is a public website, a blog, and a pilot-engagement model built around booking a call.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Not published — custom/pilot pricing via sales call |
| **Free tier / trial** | None — self-serve signups are closed |
| **Best for** | B2B sales teams (finance, insurance, real estate, enterprise) wanting pre-call lead intelligence |
| **Standout feature** | Personality-based lead scoring and "conversion angle" messaging suggestions |
| **Current access model** | "Lead Intelligence Pilot" booking, not open subscription |

## What Mindreader actually is

Mindreader is built by Personality Central, a company whose core business is personality-based sales training — the kind of program that has reportedly trained sales staff at organizations like Citibank, DBS, AIA, and Medtronic, according to Mindreader's own site. The product takes that psychology-and-sales background and turns it into a software layer: you feed it a list of raw leads, and it enriches each record with a fit score, a set of "buying signal" flags, and a suggested conversion angle — essentially, what a rep should lead with when they make first contact.

The pitch is specific and, credit where it's due, not the usual "AI writes your emails" positioning most sales tools default to. Mindreader's homepage frames the problem directly: "You are not losing pipeline because of generic copy. It is because your team lacks lead intelligence." Instead of generating outreach copy, it's trying to tell a rep who to call first and what personality-driven angle is likely to land — closer to a scoring and enrichment layer that sits upstream of whatever CRM or sequencing tool a team already uses.

It's not built on a named foundation model that's publicly disclosed anywhere on the site or in its docs — Mindreader doesn't state whether it runs on GPT, Claude, Gemini, or a proprietary model, so that detail should be confirmed directly with the company if it matters to your evaluation.

## Pricing: no published tiers, pilot-only access

This is the section where most reviews would drop in a pricing table pulled straight from the vendor's pricing page. Mindreader doesn't have one to pull from anymore. Its `/pricing` URL, at the time of writing, redirects into the same retirement notice as the rest of the site rather than listing plans, and the only calls to action on the homepage are "Book a Lead Intelligence Pilot" and "Talk to Tony" — a Calendly-style discovery call.

That means there is no self-serve monthly or annual plan to compare against competitors. Instead, Mindreader operates on what looks like a sales-led pilot model: a team books a call, presumably discusses lead volume and use case, and gets a scoped engagement rather than a credit-card checkout. For a solo user or small team hoping to try a tool for $20–$50/month, that's a genuine access barrier, not a minor inconvenience.

Pricing, free-tier availability, and feature details for AI sales tools change quickly, and this is doubly true for Mindreader given its transition away from self-serve SaaS — treat everything in this review as accurate as of September 2026 and confirm current access directly on [themindreader.ai](https://themindreader.ai) before assuming anything below still applies.

| Plan | What you'd need to do | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Former self-serve SaaS | Not available | Logins and subscriptions are closed |
| Lead Intelligence Pilot | Book a call via the site | Custom scope; pricing not disclosed publicly |
| Public resources (blog, comparisons) | Free, no signup | Not the product itself — informational only |

## Core features (as described by the vendor)

Since the logged-in app is closed, this section reflects what Mindreader publicly describes as its capability set rather than a hands-on walkthrough — treat these as vendor-stated features to verify during a pilot call, not confirmed specs.

- **Lead scoring** — a fit evaluation meant to help reps prioritize which leads in a list are worth calling first, rather than working a list top-to-bottom.
- **Buying signal detection** — flags intended to surface purchase-intent indicators within a lead record, though Mindreader doesn't publicly detail what data sources feed this.
- **Conversion angles** — personality-informed messaging suggestions for how a rep should frame an opener, drawing on Personality Central's underlying sales-psychology methodology.
- **Next-best-action recommendations** — guidance on what a rep should do after the first touch, rather than a one-time score.
- **Workflow integration** — Mindreader states the intelligence is meant to be delivered "directly into existing sales tools," though it doesn't name specific CRMs or sequencers on its public pages.

## Who it's actually for

- **Enterprise and mid-market sales orgs already running trained processes** — teams in finance, insurance, real estate, or enterprise B2B who have existing lead volume and are comfortable scoping a paid pilot rather than clicking "start free trial," are the clearest fit given Mindreader's positioning and client list.
- **Sales leaders evaluating lead-intelligence vendors broadly** — Mindreader is worth a look alongside tools like Clay, Apollo, Crystal, or Humantic AI (all of which Mindreader itself publishes comparison pages against), but expect a sales conversation, not a self-serve trial, before you can compare hands-on.
- **Solo reps, freelancers, or bootstrapped startups wanting a cheap self-serve tool** — this is not that. With no published pricing and no open signup, Mindreader isn't accessible to someone who wants to try a tool this afternoon on a personal card.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Specific, differentiated angle (personality-based lead scoring) rather than generic AI copywriting | Self-serve SaaS app is fully retired — no logins or subscriptions |
| Built on an established sales-training methodology with named enterprise clients | No public pricing, so cost can't be compared upfront |
| Positions itself against real competitors (Clay, Apollo, Crystal, Humantic AI) with published comparisons | No free tier or trial to test the product hands-on |
| Clear target use case (pre-call lead intelligence for sales teams) | Underlying AI model and data sources for "buying signals" aren't disclosed |
| Active pilot-booking and support channel still available | Requires a sales call before you can even see the interface |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Mindreader states that its intelligence is designed to feed "directly into existing sales tools," but the public site doesn't name specific integrations — no confirmed Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach, or Zapier connector is documented on the pages reviewed here. There's also no public API reference available for developers to inspect. Anyone evaluating this for a specific tech stack should ask about exact integration points during the pilot call rather than assuming compatibility.

## Where it's a strong fit

Mindreader is a reasonable fit if you're a sales organization already sold on the idea that generic outreach copy isn't your bottleneck, and you want a vendor with sales-psychology pedigree rather than a generic AI SDR wrapper. Teams with real lead volume in finance, insurance, real estate, or enterprise sales — the specific verticals Mindreader names as its focus — get the clearest match to its stated use case. If you're comfortable with a scoped pilot instead of a self-serve subscription, this is a workable path.

## Where to think twice

Skip Mindreader for now if you need a fully self-serve tool you can sign up for and cancel on your own schedule — that option doesn't currently exist. Skip it if you need transparent, published pricing to get budget approval before a sales conversation; Mindreader won't give you a number without a call. Skip it if your team is small enough that a formal pilot process is overkill — a $29/month tool with an open trial will get you testing faster. And skip it, at least for now, if you need a documented public API or named CRM integrations to plan an implementation, since none of that is published. Given the "former SaaS product" language on Mindreader's own site, there's also a reasonable chance the company is mid-transition to a new offering — worth asking directly what's actually available before committing time to a pilot conversation.

## The bottom line

Mindreader has a genuinely differentiated idea — personality-informed lead scoring instead of another AI email generator — backed by a sales-training company with real enterprise clients. But as of today, it isn't really a self-serve SaaS tool anymore; it's a pilot-based sales engagement wrapped around a public marketing site. That's not a dealbreaker for an enterprise sales team that books a call and negotiates scope and pricing directly, but it does mean this isn't a tool you can trial on your own time or compare price-to-price against competitors. If you fit the enterprise-sales profile Mindreader targets, book the call and ask pointed questions about data sources, integrations, and pricing before committing. If you need something you can start using today, look elsewhere.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Mindreader still available?**
The public website and its resources are still live, but the logged-in SaaS application — the actual scoring product — is closed to new logins, sign-ups, and subscriptions. Access now goes through booking a "Lead Intelligence Pilot" call.

**How much does Mindreader cost?**
Pricing isn't published. The only path to pricing information is booking a discovery call through the site, which suggests custom or pilot-based pricing rather than fixed tiers.

**Is there a free trial or free plan?**
No. There's no open free tier, and self-serve signups of any kind are currently closed.

**Who makes Mindreader?**
Personality Central, a company built around personality-based sales training, developed Mindreader as a software extension of that methodology.

**What does Mindreader actually do?**
It's positioned as a lead-intelligence layer: it scores leads for fit, flags buying signals, and suggests personality-informed conversion angles and next-best actions, meant to feed into whatever sales tools a team already uses.

**What AI model powers Mindreader?**
That isn't publicly disclosed on Mindreader's site. If the underlying model matters to your evaluation, ask directly during a pilot call.

**What are the alternatives to Mindreader?**
Mindreader's own site publishes comparisons against Clay, Apollo, Crystal, and Humantic AI — all worth evaluating if you want a tool with an actual self-serve trial or transparent pricing today.

**Is Mindreader good for solo users or freelancers?**
Not really. Its target clients are named as finance, insurance, real estate, and enterprise sales teams, its access model runs through a sales pilot rather than self-serve signup, and there's no published low-cost tier — all of which point toward team and enterprise use rather than individual, budget-conscious use.

title: Crayo AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Crayo turns scripts and Reddit threads into faceless TikTok/Reels videos with AI voiceovers. Here's what its credit-based pricing actually gets you.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Crayo worth it for faceless video creation in 2026?

Crayo is an AI video tool built around one job: turning a script, a Reddit thread, or a long recording into a ready-to-post faceless short for TikTok, Reels, or Shorts. It's worth it if you're producing Reddit-story, fake-text, or clipped-streamer content at volume and want a workflow-credit system built for exactly those formats; it's less compelling if you mainly need long-to-short repurposing of talking-head podcasts, where the credit math works differently.

### At a glance

| | Crayo |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $13/month (Hobby plan) |
| Free tier/trial | None found — Crayo does not advertise a free plan or trial; it does list some standalone free tools separate from the main app |
| Best for | Faceless-content creators doing Reddit stories, fake-text videos, split-screen and streamer clips at scale |
| Standout feature | Workflow-credit system built specifically around faceless video formats (Reddit stories, fake texts, split-screen, streamer clips), not generic clipping |

## What Crayo actually is

Crayo bills itself as an AI-powered video creation and clipping platform aimed at short-form creators, per its own marketing copy claiming "over 3.2 million users worldwide." It was built by co-founder Musa Mustafa, who describes running creator channels that crossed a million subscribers before starting the product — the pitch is that Crayo automates the repetitive parts of faceless-content production he was doing by hand.

Functionally, Crayo covers two overlapping jobs. The first is faceless video generation: type or paste a script (or a Reddit thread URL), pick a format — Reddit story, fake text conversation, split-screen, or AI voiceover narration — and Crayo assembles the video with captions, background footage or gameplay, and a synthesized voice. The second is clipping: upload or link a longer video (a stream, podcast, or YouTube upload) and Crayo's auto-editor pulls out shorter segments, reframes them vertically, and adds subtitles.

Crayo doesn't publish which underlying AI models power its voice synthesis, image generation, or auto-clip detection — like most consumer video tools in this space, it markets the pipeline as proprietary "auto-editing" technology rather than naming a specific foundation model or voice provider. If that matters for compliance or attribution needs, ask Crayo's support team directly rather than relying on the marketing site.

## Pricing

Crayo runs three paid tiers — Hobby, Clipper, and Pro — priced by a combination of monthly "workflow credits," export minutes, voiceover minutes, AI image generations, and cloud storage, rather than a flat per-video cap. A workflow credit is spent on one AI-auto-edited video (Reddit story, fake-text video, split-screen, or streamer clip); a separate "export minutes" allowance governs total rendered video length.

| Plan | Price | Workflow credits/mo | Export minutes | Voiceover minutes | AI images | Storage | Social accounts tracked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hobby | $13/month | 50 | 40 min | 30 min | 100 | 25GB | 1 |
| Clipper (most popular) | $27/month | 150 | 2 hrs | 120 min | 300 | 100GB | 3 |
| Pro | $55/month | 250 | 4 hrs | 180 min | 500 | 500GB | 10 |

Crayo's listed pricing did not show a clearly separate free trial or free plan at the time of research; the site references some standalone free tools outside the paid workflow, but the core auto-editing product requires a paid subscription from the start. Crayo also states plainly that it does not offer refunds — you can cancel anytime, but your plan stays active (and billed) through the end of the current cycle rather than being prorated back.

Pricing, credit allowances, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (2026-09-19) and can change — confirm current numbers on Crayo's own pricing page before subscribing.

## Core features that actually matter

**Format-specific faceless templates.** Rather than one generic "text to video" box, Crayo separates Reddit story videos, fake-text conversation videos, split-screen content, and streamer/gameplay clips into distinct workflows — less setup fiddling than a general-purpose tool that makes you rebuild the look every time.

**AI voiceovers with a dedicated minutes budget.** Voiceover generation is metered separately from workflow credits (30–180 minutes/month depending on tier), a second usage cap layered on top of the video-credit cap that matters if you're narrating scripts rather than relying on captions alone.

**Auto-clipping from long-form source.** Crayo can pull shorter clips out of longer uploads or linked videos, similar in concept to tools like SendShort, though its own positioning leans harder into faceless-format generation than podcast/webinar repurposing.

**Built-in image generation, face swap, and background removal.** These sit inside the same credit system (AI images budgeted separately, 100–500/month) and let you build thumbnail art or swap elements in generated visuals without leaving the app.

**Multi-account social tracking.** Each tier caps connected social accounts you can track (1 on Hobby, up to 10 on Pro) — relevant for multi-channel creators or agencies, since this is a hard tier gate rather than an add-on.

## Who it's actually for

**Solo faceless-content creators** producing one Reddit-story or fake-text channel a few times a week will likely fit on Hobby's 50 monthly workflow credits and single tracked account, assuming videos stay short enough for the 40-minute export budget.

**Small teams or creators running multiple channels** — say, a Reddit-story account plus a streamer-clips account — will need Clipper's three tracked accounts and larger credit pool; it's also the tier Crayo pushes as its default recommendation.

**Agencies or high-volume operators** managing client accounts or publishing daily across formats will want Pro for the 10 tracked accounts, 500GB storage, and largest voiceover/image allowances, though at $55/month it's a meaningfully bigger commitment than Hobby.

**Podcast or webinar repurposers** whose main need is turning one long recording into many shorts may find Crayo's per-format, credit-metered structure a less natural fit than a tool built around long-to-short extraction — worth comparing against a dedicated clipping tool like [SendShort](/blog/sendshort-review) before committing.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Purpose-built templates for Reddit stories, fake texts, split-screen, and streamer clips | No published free trial or free plan to test before paying |
| Multiple usage dimensions (credits, export minutes, voiceover, images) can stretch further than a flat per-video cap | That same multi-dimensional system makes usage harder to predict |
| Full monetization rights granted on generated videos, per Crayo's own terms | Explicit no-refund policy — cancellation only stops future billing |
| Also covers auto-clipping from long-form source, not just script-to-video | Underlying AI models for voice, image, and clip-detection aren't disclosed |
| Multi-account social tracking scales with plan tier for teams/agencies | Lower tiers cap at 1–3 tracked accounts, restrictive for multi-channel operators |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Crayo integrates with YouTube and TikTok for content pulling and/or account tracking, and includes a social media video downloader as part of its toolset. It's a self-contained web app rather than a plugin or extension — there's no publicly documented API, Zapier integration, or Slack/Discord connector on its marketing pages. If Crayo output needs to flow automatically into a broader publishing or scheduling stack, expect a manual export/hand-off rather than built-in automation.

## Where Crayo is a strong fit

If content already lives in one of Crayo's core formats — Reddit story narration, fake-text conversations, split-screen gameplay-plus-content, or streamer highlight clips — Crayo's templates save the repetitive setup work of building that look from scratch in a general editor. The tiered credit system scales reasonably from a single hobbyist channel up through an agency managing ten tracked accounts, and the full-rights/monetization stance removes ambiguity about running ads against what you publish. It's also a reasonable pick for bundling AI voiceover, basic image generation, and face-swap/background-removal into one subscription instead of stitching together separate point tools.

## Where to think twice

Skip Crayo if you specifically need a free tier to test the product first — there's no documented free plan or trial, so you're committing to at least $13/month before knowing how well the output matches your channel's style. The no-refund policy compounds this: a bad first month costs the full cycle.

Think twice too if your workflow is primarily long-form-to-short repurposing rather than templated faceless formats — the credit system is optimized around Crayo's specific video types, and a tool built primarily for podcast/webinar clip extraction may fit more cleanly. Teams needing enterprise compliance documentation, a public API, or Zapier/Slack automation won't find that here. And since Crayo doesn't name its underlying AI models, anyone needing to vet specific providers for legal or platform-policy reasons should ask Crayo directly.

## Bottom line

Crayo earns its place if you're already producing (or want to start producing) Reddit-story, fake-text, split-screen, or streamer-clip content and want a subscription bundling voiceover, auto-clipping, and basic image generation into one credit pool built around those exact formats. It's a narrower, more opinionated tool than a general AI video editor, and that's the point — but the lack of a free trial and strict no-refund policy mean taking Crayo's word on output quality before verifying it against your own footage. If that trade-off doesn't sit well, test a free-tier alternative first and treat Crayo as the upgrade once the format fits.

## FAQ

**Is Crayo free to use?**
No published free plan or trial was found at the time of writing; the cheapest option is Hobby at $13/month. Confirm on [Crayo's official site](https://www.crayo.ai) in case this has changed.

**What does the Hobby plan include?**
Hobby ($13/month) includes 50 monthly workflow credits, 40 minutes of export capacity, 30 voiceover minutes, 100 AI image generations, 25GB storage, and one tracked social account.

**Can I get a refund if Crayo doesn't work for my channel?**
No. Crayo states it does not offer refunds. You can cancel anytime, but your plan stays active — and billed — through the end of the current cycle rather than being prorated.

**What counts as a "workflow credit"?**
One video auto-edited by Crayo's AI across supported formats — Reddit stories, fake-text conversations, split-screen content, and streamer clips. Export minutes are a separate allowance governing total rendered video length.

**Does Crayo disclose which AI models it uses?**
No. It markets voice synthesis, image generation, and clip-detection as proprietary auto-editing technology without naming underlying model providers, fairly common among consumer AI video tools.

**How is Crayo different from SendShort or similar clipping tools?**
Crayo leans harder into templated faceless-video formats with a multi-dimensional credit system (credits, export minutes, voiceover minutes, images metered separately). [SendShort](/blog/sendshort-review) centers more on long-to-short repurposing from podcasts or webinars with a simpler clip cap — compare both if your content is mostly long-form talking-head material.

**Who owns the rights to videos made with Crayo?**
Crayo states users fully own the rights to videos created on the platform and grants full monetization rights.

**Is Crayo beginner-friendly?**
The format-specific templates lower the setup curve versus a blank-canvas editor, though newcomers should budget time to learn how credits, export minutes, and voiceover minutes interact before committing to a paid tier.

title: Typewise Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Typewise resolves support tickets end-to-end with resolution-based pricing. Here's what it costs, who it fits, and where the model breaks down.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Typewise Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict

Typewise is an AI customer support platform that resolves tickets end-to-end across email, chat, WhatsApp, and voice rather than just routing them. It suits small teams and mid-market support operations wanting per-resolution pricing tied to real outcomes, but the cost model needs modeling before committing, especially at higher ticket volumes.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $99/month (Starter plan) |
| **Free tier / trial** | 14-day trial with 100 resolution credits |
| **Best for** | Small-to-mid support teams wanting outcome-based AI resolution |
| **Standout feature** | Nova AI Operator — build support agents in plain language, no code |

## What Typewise Actually Is

Typewise started out as a Swiss-built predictive-text keyboard focused on privacy (no cloud typing data, on-device prediction), and that DNA still shows up in how the company talks about data handling. The product that matters today, and the one this review focuses on, is Typewise's AI customer service platform — a system built to close support tickets on its own, not just suggest replies for a human agent to send.

The company draws a clear line in its own marketing: "Typewise is a resolution engine, not a chatbot." A lot of AI support tools stop at deflection — they answer easy questions and hand everything else to a human. Typewise's pitch is that its AI actually completes the request: looking up an order, checking it against policy, issuing a refund, and closing the ticket, only pulling in a human when the AI genuinely can't finish the job. Whether that holds up ticket-for-ticket in your workflow is something you'd need to test with your own data — vendor case studies aren't the same as your queue.

Setup is built around a tool called **Nova AI Operator**, a conversational configuration layer that lets a support lead describe policies and workflows in plain language rather than writing rules or code. Typewise says this gets a working agent live in around 15 minutes, which is plausible for a narrow use case (order status, simple refunds) but optimistic for multi-step policy logic — budget more time if your support flows are complex.

## Pricing

Typewise uses a hybrid pricing model: a flat monthly subscription per tier plus a per-resolution fee that drops as volume increases. A "resolution" is the billing unit — a fully AI-closed ticket counts as one, a partial hand-off to a human counts as half, and anything the AI never touches isn't charged.

| Plan | Price | Users | AI Operator budget | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $99/mo ($999/yr) | 1 | $20/month included | Email + chat only; pay-as-you-go at $2/resolution beyond budget |
| Growth | $599/mo ($5,999/yr) | 5 | $100/month included | All digital channels; volume packages down to $1/resolution |
| Business | $2,000/mo (annual billing) | Multiple workspaces | Custom | Dedicated success consultant, custom integrations |
| Enterprise | Custom quote (annual billing) | Unlimited workspaces | $1,500/month included | SSO, custom DPA, consultant + engineer support |

Additional seats run $89/month on any plan. New signups get a 14-day trial with 100 resolution credits, and Typewise has run a launch promotion offering 1,000 resolutions plus three months free — worth checking if it's still live, since launch promos rarely stay in place indefinitely.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability above were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly for AI tools — confirm current figures on Typewise's pricing page before budgeting against them.

The resolution-based model is the thing to model carefully. At $2 per resolution on Starter, a team closing 500 AI-resolved tickets a month faces $1,000 in overage on top of the $99 base — more than Growth's flat $599 fee, before Growth's own per-resolution costs kick in. If ticket volume is unpredictable or spiky, a flat seat-price SaaS tool can end up cheaper and more predictable than success-based billing, even if Typewise's per-ticket economics look better on paper at steady volume.

## Core Features Walkthrough

**Nova AI Operator.** The centerpiece of Typewise's setup experience — you describe your policies, tone, and escalation rules conversationally, and Nova translates that into a working support agent, lowering the bar for non-technical teams compared to tools that require building decision trees by hand.

**End-to-end resolution, not deflection.** Typewise's agents take action — looking up an order, checking it against a return policy, processing a refund — rather than just generating a helpful-sounding reply. This requires deeper integration work than a simple FAQ chatbot, but it's also the feature that determines whether the "resolution" pricing model actually saves money versus a flat-fee competitor.

**Multi-channel unified inbox.** Email, live chat, WhatsApp, social messaging, and voice are handled from one inbox with context carried across channels, so a conversation starting in chat and continuing over email doesn't lose history.

**Human-in-the-loop controls.** Every AI action is logged, and teams can set approval rules or pause automated responses for specific ticket types (refunds above a threshold, VIP customers, legal-sensitive language) — useful for teams nervous about handing irreversible actions to an unsupervised agent.

**Self-improvement loop.** Typewise says the platform monitors resolution quality over time, proposes fixes to underperforming flows, and tests updates before rolling them out, reducing manual prompt-tuning. As with any vendor claim about self-improving AI, treat the underlying accuracy numbers as something to validate in your own account rather than take at face value.

**3,500+ integrations.** Typewise connects to existing help desks, CRMs, and e-commerce platforms, which matters because the resolution engine needs to actually reach your order data, refund tools, and policy documents to do anything beyond generic replies.

## Who Typewise Is Actually For

- **Solo founders / very small teams:** Starter ($99/month, 1 user, email + chat) suits teams with manageable, predictable ticket volume where the $2/resolution overage won't spiral.
- **Growing support teams (5+ agents):** Growth opens all channels and a larger AI Operator budget, with per-resolution cost dropping to $1 at volume — a fit for teams outgrowing a simple helpdesk plugin.
- **Established teams wanting hands-on help:** Business tier customers get a dedicated success consultant and custom integration work, suited to teams without in-house support-ops engineering.
- **Large enterprises with compliance requirements:** Enterprise adds SSO, a custom DPA, and dedicated engineering support for teams with procurement or security review in the buying process.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely resolves tickets end-to-end, not just deflects | Resolution-based pricing can get expensive at high or spiky volume |
| Nova AI Operator lowers the setup bar for non-technical teams | 15-minute setup claim likely applies only to simple flows |
| Human-in-the-loop controls for sensitive actions | No published self-serve free plan — trial only |
| 3,500+ integrations across help desks and CRMs | Business/Enterprise pricing requires talking to sales, hard to compare upfront |
| Multi-channel with context preserved across handoffs | "70–95% autonomous resolution" figures are vendor case studies, not independently audited |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Typewise doesn't publish a detailed public API reference on its marketing pages alongside its 3,500+ listed integrations, so if your workflow depends on a specific custom connection, confirm feasibility directly with sales before signing an annual contract.

## Where Typewise Is a Strong Fit

Typewise makes the most sense for support teams with clear, codifiable policies (return windows, refund thresholds, standard troubleshooting steps) that want an AI layer that acts on those policies rather than just suggesting answers. Teams switching from a pure chatbot-deflection tool, frustrated that customers still wait for a human on every non-trivial request, are the clearest audience.

It's also reasonable for teams wanting governance built in from day one — logging and approval rules on refunds and other sensitive actions let support leads trust automation without fully removing oversight.

## Where to Think Twice

If you need a fully free tool to get started, Typewise isn't it — there's a 14-day trial with a fixed resolution credit allotment, not an ongoing free plan.

If your support volume is unpredictable or seasonal, model the per-resolution overage costs before committing — a flat-fee competitor can end up cheaper during a volume spike.

If you need transparent, self-serve enterprise pricing, Business and Enterprise both require direct contact — there's no published per-seat rate to compare upfront.

If your support policies are highly nuanced or change frequently, the resolution-engine model works best on well-defined, repeatable request types — it's a harder fit for edge-case-heavy queues.

## The Bottom Line

Typewise's core idea — bill for outcomes, not seats or messages — is a genuinely different pitch from most AI support tools, and Nova AI Operator makes that model accessible without an engineering team. For teams with well-defined policies and steady ticket volume, the economics can work out favorably, and human-in-the-loop controls address a real concern about handing refunds to an unsupervised system. The catch: resolution-based pricing shifts risk onto you if volume spikes, and the top two tiers require a sales call rather than self-serve signup. Run the numbers against your actual volume, and pressure-test the "70–95% autonomous resolution" claims during the trial.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Typewise free?**
No. Typewise offers a 14-day trial with 100 resolution credits, but there's no ongoing free tier. Paid plans start at $99/month.

**How does Typewise's pricing actually work?**
Each plan has a flat monthly subscription plus an included AI Operator budget for resolutions. Beyond that budget, resolutions are billed per ticket — $2 each on Starter, dropping to $1 with volume on Growth. A full AI resolution counts as one unit; a partial hand-off to a human counts as half.

**What counts as a "resolution" for billing purposes?**
A support request the AI closes end-to-end without further human action. A partially AI-handled ticket that a human finishes counts as half. Tickets the AI never touches aren't billed.

**Is Typewise a chatbot or something different?**
Typewise describes itself as a "resolution engine, not a chatbot" — the emphasis is on the AI completing actions (refunds, order lookups, policy checks) rather than just generating replies for a human to act on.

**Does Typewise handle voice support, not just chat?**
Yes — email, chat, WhatsApp, social channels, and voice from a unified inbox with shared context, per the company.

**How does Typewise handle data privacy and compliance?**
Typewise states it's ISO 27001 and GDPR-compliant, and Enterprise adds a custom Data Processing Agreement and SSO. Confirm current certification status directly with Typewise if this is a deciding factor.

**How long does setup actually take?**
Typewise advertises roughly 15-minute setup via Nova AI Operator. That's plausible for simple use cases like order-status lookups; complex, multi-step policies will take longer to configure and test.

**What are the alternatives to Typewise?**
