title: Krea Review 2026: Real-Time AI Image and Video Tool
excerpt: Krea review covering real-time AI image generation, video and 3D models, LoRA training, pricing tiers, and who this creative AI suite fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Krea good for AI image and video generation?

Krea is a browser-based creative AI suite built around real-time image generation, plus editing, upscaling, video, 3D, and LoRA training on top of third-party and in-house models. It's strong for fast visual iteration and covers a wide model roster, but the free tier is credit-limited and the pricing structure takes getting used to.

| At a glance | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (daily credits); paid plans from $21/month (Pro, billed annually) |
| Free tier | Yes — daily credits, real-time generation, Krea's own Krea 2 model, no credit card required |
| Best for | Designers, marketers, and indie creators who want fast image iteration and access to many models in one place |
| Standout feature | Real-time canvas that generates images as you type or draw, updating live |

### What Krea actually is

Krea is made by Krea AI, a San Francisco-based startup, and its core pitch is a single workspace that wraps a large number of image and video generation models rather than building one model and stopping there. The product includes its own in-house model (branded "Krea 2") alongside third-party models it licenses access to, including image generators and video models from providers like Google (Veo), OpenAI (Sora), and Kling, according to Krea's own plan descriptions. It doesn't train or claim ownership of most of these underlying models — it's primarily an interface and credit-metering layer that gives one account access to many of them, plus its own real-time and upscaling tools built on top.

The defining feature, and the one that gives Krea its name recognition, is real-time generation: a canvas where an image updates live as you type a prompt or sketch a rough shape, instead of making you wait for a full render each time. That's a different interaction model from a typical "type a prompt, wait, get an image" tool, and it's most useful for rapid visual exploration — mood boards, concept sketches, style testing — rather than a single final polished output.

### Pricing

Krea uses a credit-based subscription model with self-serve tiers plus a custom Enterprise plan. Pricing below reflects plans and features Krea currently lists on its pricing page; Pro/Max/Business figures show the discounted annual-billing rate first, standard monthly rate in parentheses.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Daily credits, real-time generation, Krea 2 access, no credit card required; no full model roster |
| Pro | $21/mo annual ($35/mo monthly) | All image/video models (Veo3, Sora, Kling), all 3D/lipsync models, LoRA training up to 50 images, upscaling to 22K, Nodes, App Builder |
| Max | $63/mo annual ($105/mo monthly) | Everything in Pro, plus LoRA training up to 2,000 images, unlimited concurrency, relaxed limits, premium upscaling |
| Business | $160/mo annual ($200/mo monthly) | Flat team pricing for up to 50 seats, Business Terms of Service (data protection, no-training clauses), private Node App sharing |
| Enterprise | Custom | Dedicated support, admin controls, custom seat count, custom roles/permissions |

Krea's FAQ notes purchased credits are added instantly and expire after 90 days, and that Business/Enterprise plans allow unused compute credits to roll over between billing periods (Pro and Max do not). Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — confirm current numbers on Krea's own pricing page before subscribing, since AI tool pricing moves fast.

### Core features that actually differentiate it

**Real-time canvas.** Krea's signature capability: images regenerate live as you adjust a prompt, sketch strokes, or move sliders, instead of forcing a full re-render cycle for every tweak. It's built for iteration speed, not one-shot precision.

**Multi-model access from one account.** Rather than locking you into a single house model, paid Krea plans unlock the company's own Krea 2 model plus a roster of third-party image, video, 3D, and lipsync models — useful if you don't want to juggle separate subscriptions to a still-image generator, a video generator, and an upscaler.

**LoRA training built in.** Pro plans support training custom LoRA models from up to 50 of your own images to generate consistent characters, styles, or objects; Max raises that ceiling to roughly 2,000 images with what Krea describes as effectively unlimited training runs. This targets brand- and character-consistency use cases rather than one-off image generation.

**Krea Nodes and App Builder.** Paid tiers include a visual, node-based workflow editor for chaining models, prompts, and processing steps together, plus an "App Builder" that turns a saved workflow into a reusable, shareable mini-app — closer to what tools like ComfyUI offer, wrapped in a friendlier interface, and useful for teams standardizing a repeatable generation pipeline.

**High-resolution upscaling.** Paid plans include access to premium upscalers (Krea names Topaz among its partners) supporting outputs up to 22K resolution on Pro and above, which matters for print or large-format output where native AI-generated resolution isn't enough alone.

### Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and hobbyists** — the free tier is enough to try the real-time canvas and Krea 2 without a credit card, though daily credit limits cap serious output.
- **Freelance designers and marketers** — Pro's model breadth (image, video, 3D, lipsync) and 22K upscaling make it a reasonable single subscription to replace several narrower tools, provided the credit allotment matches actual output volume.
- **Power users doing character/brand-consistent work** — Max's larger LoRA training ceiling and unlimited concurrency suit anyone training custom models repeatedly or running many generations in parallel.
- **Small creative or marketing teams** — Business bundles up to 50 seats under one flat price with business-grade terms of service, a different value proposition than per-seat pricing.
- **Agencies and larger orgs with compliance needs** — Enterprise adds admin controls, custom roles, and dedicated support, but pricing is quote-based, not self-serve.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Real-time generation speeds up visual iteration | Credit-based system means heavy users can burn through allotments fast |
| Wide model roster (image, video, 3D, lipsync) under one account | Access to third-party models like Sora and Veo3 depends on Krea's licensing deals, which can change |
| LoRA training and Nodes/App Builder support repeatable, brand-consistent workflows | Nodes/App Builder has a learning curve for node-based-workflow newcomers |
| Free tier requires no credit card | Free tier credits are daily-capped, not enough for serious production volume |
| Business plan's flat 50-seat pricing differs from typical per-seat SaaS pricing | No published on-prem or self-hosted option for strict data-residency needs |

### Integrations and ecosystem

Krea is primarily a hosted web app rather than an API-first platform aimed at developers — its integration story centers on the breadth of models available inside the product itself rather than external plugin ecosystems like Zapier or Slack. The Nodes/App Builder feature is Krea's internal automation layer, letting you chain generation steps and models together and turn the result into a shareable app within the workspace. Anyone needing programmatic API access should confirm current availability directly with Krea.

### Where it's a strong fit

Krea earns its keep for visual concepting work where iteration speed matters more than a single perfect output on the first try — mood boards, style exploration, rapid client mockups, and marketing visuals where you need many variations quickly. Real-time generation combined with access to several video and image models under one subscription also makes it a reasonable consolidation move for a freelancer or small studio currently paying for multiple separate AI tools.

### Where to think twice

Skip Krea, or at least the paid tiers, if you need a genuinely free and unlimited tool — the free plan's daily credit cap gets restrictive fast beyond casual testing. Teams with strict compliance requirements (SOC 2, HIPAA, or similar formal certifications) should verify Krea's current compliance posture directly, since its listed plans emphasize business terms and data-protection clauses rather than named third-party certifications. If your workflow depends on offline or on-premises generation, Krea's fully hosted, browser-based model won't fit — a self-hosted option running an open model like [FLUX.1 [dev]](/blog/flux-1-dev-review) locally is a better match. And if your priority is one narrow capability, like cinematic video generation specifically, a dedicated tool like [Runway](/blog/runway-review) may go deeper in that one lane than Krea's broader, multi-model approach.

### Bottom line

Krea is a capable, fast-moving hub for AI image and video generation, and its real-time canvas is a genuinely useful interaction model rather than a marketing gimmick. The pricing is credit-metered rather than flatly unlimited, so it rewards users who'll actually use the model breadth, and it's less compelling if you only need one narrow capability a cheaper, single-purpose tool already covers well. For designers, marketers, and small creative teams wanting one subscription covering image, video, upscaling, and LoRA training, it's worth trialing on the free tier before committing to Pro or Max.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Krea free to use?**
Yes. Krea offers a free tier with daily credits and no credit card required, including real-time generation and its Krea 2 model. Paid plans (Pro, Max, Business, Enterprise) unlock the full model roster, higher-resolution upscaling, and larger LoRA training limits.

**How much does Krea Pro cost?**
Pro starts at $21/month billed annually, or $35/month billed monthly, based on Krea's published pricing at the time of writing. Confirm current pricing on Krea's official pricing page, as AI subscription pricing changes frequently.

**What models does Krea give access to?**
Paid plans include Krea's own Krea 2 model plus third-party image, video, 3D, and lipsync models it licenses access to — plan pages reference video models including Veo3, Sora, and Kling. Availability can change as licensing deals evolve, so check the current plan comparison page.

**Do unused Krea credits roll over?**
Per Krea's own FAQ, Business and Enterprise plans allow unused compute credits to roll over with customizable windows; Pro and Max do not carry over unused credits, and purchased credits expire 90 days after purchase.

**Is Krea good for beginners?**
The real-time canvas is approachable since it doesn't require prompt-engineering expertise for quick visual feedback. Nodes and App Builder are more advanced, aimed at users comfortable with workflow-style, node-based tools.

**What's the difference between Krea Pro and Max?**
Both include the full model roster, but Max raises the LoRA training image cap from 50 to roughly 2,000, removes generation concurrency limits, and adds premium upscaling for higher-volume production use.

**Does Krea have an API for developers?**
Krea's public plans center on its hosted web app rather than developer API access; confirm current API availability directly with Krea, since that isn't clearly covered by the subscription tiers described here.

**What are good alternatives to Krea?**
For dedicated video generation, [Runway](/blog/runway-review) is a strong single-purpose alternative. For running an open-weight image model yourself, [FLUX.1 [dev]](/blog/flux-1-dev-review) and [FLUX.1 [schnell]](/blog/flux-1-schnell-review) are worth comparing. See also [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Amazon Bedrock Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Amazon Bedrock review covering per-token pricing, multi-model access, Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, and who this AWS AI platform fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Amazon Bedrock worth using in 2026?

Amazon Bedrock is worth using if your team is already on AWS and wants a managed way to call multiple foundation models — Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Amazon's Titan/Nova, and others — through one API with built-in security, agents, and data-grounding tools. It's overkill for a single chatbot; it's built for teams shipping production AI applications.

| At a glance | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Pay-as-you-go per token; no flat subscription (see pricing breakdown below) |
| Free tier | No dedicated Bedrock free tier — you pay for every token from the first request, though AWS occasionally runs promotional credits |
| Best for | Engineering teams building production AI apps/agents on AWS who need multi-model choice, governance, and enterprise compliance |
| Standout feature | One API for dozens of foundation models plus managed Knowledge Bases, Agents, and Guardrails without running your own inference infrastructure |

Amazon Bedrock is AWS's managed platform for building generative AI applications and agents. It isn't a single model — it's a serverless layer giving developers API access to foundation models from Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, Cohere, AI21 Labs, Stability AI, DeepSeek, OpenAI, and Amazon's own Titan and Nova families, through one consistent API and billing relationship. AWS calls it "the platform for building generative AI applications and agents at production scale," positioning it against a DIY approach where a team would otherwise provision GPUs, manage model weights, and negotiate separate vendor contracts per model.

Because Bedrock is infrastructure rather than a branded app, there's no single "Bedrock model" — the intelligence behind any request is whichever foundation model you pick, called through Bedrock's runtime. That's the core trade-off worth understanding first: Bedrock is a distribution and management layer, not a model in its own right.

## Pricing: usage-based, not a tiered plan

Bedrock doesn't have "Starter/Pro/Enterprise" plans like most SaaS AI tools. You pay AWS for what you actually use, billed through your existing AWS account, as a function of which model you call, how many tokens go in and out, and which optional features (Knowledge Bases, Guardrails, model customization) you turn on. There are three main billing modes:

- **On-Demand** — pay per token, per request, no commitment. What most teams start on. Pricing is per model, quoted per 1 million input tokens and per 1 million output tokens separately (output tokens cost more, since generation is more compute-intensive).
- **Provisioned Throughput** — commit to a fixed hourly capacity for a model over a 1-month or 6-month term, for predictable throughput and lower effective per-token cost at high, steady volume. Aimed at production workloads, not experimentation.
- **Batch Inference** — for select models, roughly a 50% discount versus on-demand pricing for non-time-sensitive, asynchronous jobs (e.g. bulk document processing overnight).

To give a sense of the spread: Claude 3.5 Sonnet is listed around $6 per 1 million input tokens and $30 per 1 million output tokens on Bedrock's pricing page, Llama models run roughly $0.75–$1.95 per 1 million input tokens by size, Titan text models are priced far lower (a fraction of a cent per 1,000 tokens), and Mistral's models span roughly $0.04–$2.00 per 1 million tokens by size. Figures move as AWS re-prices models, and vary by region.

Several features bill separately from raw inference: **Knowledge Bases** (storage per GB/month plus a per-1,000-query fee), **Guardrails** (per 1,000 text units, by filter type), **image generation** (per image, not per token), and **model customization/fine-tuning** (separate training-compute and storage charges).

There's no dedicated Bedrock free tier the way OpenAI or Google AI Studio offer free monthly credits — you're billed from your first token, though AWS periodically runs promotional credits for specific programs. Pricing, free-tier availability, and feature packaging here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AWS revises model pricing and adds/removes models often, so confirm current rates on the [official Bedrock pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/) before budgeting a production workload.

## Core features that actually matter

**Multi-model access through one API.** Instead of separate SDKs and billing relationships for Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and others, you call one Bedrock API and swap the `modelId` parameter to switch providers — a real time-saver for teams that A/B test models or want to avoid single-vendor lock-in.

**Knowledge Bases (RAG).** Bedrock manages the retrieval-augmented-generation pipeline for you — ingesting documents, chunking and embedding them, storing vectors, and retrieving context at query time — instead of you wiring a vector database by hand. It supports S3 and other data sources, and keeps your data isolated from the underlying model's training.

**Agents and AgentCore.** Bedrock Agents let you build multi-step, tool-using AI agents that call your own APIs and Lambda functions and complete tasks rather than just answer single prompts. AWS's newer AgentCore framework extends this toward "any framework" agent deployment with, as AWS describes it, production-grade session isolation and security.

**Guardrails.** A configurable safety layer applicable to any model on Bedrock — filtering harmful content, blocking topics, redacting PII, and checking for ungrounded claims against your source data. AWS states Guardrails can block a high majority of harmful content and flag ungrounded responses with high accuracy; these are AWS's own published figures, not independently verified benchmarks, so test against your own content policy first.

**Model customization and cost tooling.** Bedrock supports fine-tuning select models on your own data, plus cost levers like prompt caching and model distillation, which AWS says can cut inference costs substantially for suitable workloads.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo developers / indie builders** — usable, but the AWS setup and per-model pricing complexity is more overhead than a hosted API key from a model vendor. For one model on a side project, that vendor's own API is usually simpler.
- **Startups and small teams already on AWS** — a strong fit: multi-model flexibility and usage-based billing inside infrastructure you likely already use.
- **Enterprises with compliance requirements** — Bedrock's security posture (encryption at rest/in transit, eligibility under SOC, ISO, GDPR-relevant controls, FedRAMP High, and HIPAA) plus AWS's stated policy that customer data isn't used to train the underlying models makes it realistic for regulated industries.
- **Teams building AI agents at scale** — Agents and AgentCore target this directly, with tool-calling and production session management built in.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| One API for models from Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Amazon, and others | No flat/free plan — every token is billed, harder to forecast for unpredictable workloads |
| Usage-based pricing scales down to near-zero for low-traffic apps | Per-model pricing varies widely and changes often, adding cost-monitoring overhead |
| Deep AWS ecosystem integration (IAM, Lambda, S3, CloudWatch, VPC) | Steeper setup than calling a vendor's API directly — account, IAM roles, region/model availability |
| Built-in Knowledge Bases, Agents, and Guardrails reduce custom engineering | Some newer models land on their own vendor's API before Bedrock |
| Enterprise compliance certifications (SOC, ISO, HIPAA-eligible, FedRAMP High) | Provisioned Throughput requires confident volume forecasting to pay off |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Bedrock sits inside the AWS ecosystem rather than existing as a standalone product, so its strongest integrations are AWS-native: IAM for access control, Lambda for agent tool execution, S3 as a Knowledge Base source, CloudWatch for monitoring, and VPC endpoints for private network access. AWS publishes SDKs (Python/Boto3, JavaScript, Java) and an API compatible with orchestration frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex. There's no Zapier-style no-code integration — Bedrock is built for developers working through code and infrastructure-as-code (CloudFormation/Terraform), not no-code automations.

## Where it's a strong fit

Bedrock earns its complexity when a team runs multiple models in production, wants usage-based cost that scales with real traffic instead of a flat subscription, and needs the compliance paperwork (SOC 2, HIPAA eligibility, FedRAMP High) regulated industries require before sending data to an AI API at all. It's also strong for agentic workflows calling internal tools and APIs safely, since Agents and Guardrails handle plumbing that would otherwise be hand-built.

## Where to think twice

Skip Bedrock if you need a fully free tool to experiment with — there's no free tier, and even light testing accrues real token costs from the start. Skip it too if your team has no existing AWS footprint; the setup overhead is real, and a direct API key from a single model vendor gets you to a working prototype faster. Teams needing on-premises or offline deployment should look elsewhere, since Bedrock is cloud-only. And if cost predictability matters more than model flexibility, a flat-rate hosted AI product may be simpler to budget for.

## Bottom line

Amazon Bedrock isn't trying to be the best individual model — it's trying to be the best way to access and operate many models safely inside AWS. For teams already building on AWS who need multi-model flexibility, managed RAG and agent tooling, and enterprise compliance, it's a genuinely strong piece of infrastructure that removes a lot of undifferentiated engineering work. For solo builders or low-traffic experiments, the setup overhead and pay-per-token billing make it more than most projects need on day one.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Amazon Bedrock free to use?**
No. There's no dedicated free tier — you're billed per token (or per image, per API call for Knowledge Bases) from your first request, though AWS occasionally runs promotional credits for specific programs. Confirm current promotions on the official AWS site.

**How is Amazon Bedrock priced?**
Primarily on-demand, per-token pricing that varies by model (Claude models, for example, are priced per 1 million input and output tokens separately). AWS also offers Provisioned Throughput for committed hourly capacity and Batch Inference at roughly a 50% discount for select models on non-time-sensitive jobs.

**Which AI models are available on Bedrock?**
Models from Anthropic (Claude), Meta (Llama), Mistral AI, Cohere, AI21 Labs, Stability AI, DeepSeek, Amazon's own Titan and Nova, and OpenAI models for certain managed-agent capabilities. The lineup changes as AWS adds and retires models, so check the model catalog for what's current.

**Does Bedrock train on my data?**
AWS states customer data sent through Bedrock isn't used to train the underlying foundation models and stays encrypted in transit and at rest. Confirm current terms in AWS's official documentation before sending sensitive data.

**Is Amazon Bedrock beginner-friendly?**
Not particularly. It assumes familiarity with AWS accounts, IAM permissions, and API-based development, so developers new to AWS face a steeper ramp.

**What's the difference between Bedrock and using OpenAI's or Anthropic's API directly?**
A vendor's own API is simpler to start with and may get you that vendor's newest models sooner. Bedrock trades some immediacy for multi-model flexibility inside one AWS billing/security relationship, plus managed extras like Knowledge Bases, Agents, and Guardrails.

**What are the main alternatives to Amazon Bedrock?**
Google's Vertex AI and Microsoft Azure AI Foundry offer similar multi-model, managed-platform approaches. Teams wanting a single model without cloud-platform overhead often go directly to that vendor's own API instead.

**Does Bedrock support fine-tuning custom models?**
Yes, for select models, with separate charges for training compute and for storing the resulting custom model.

For more usage-based cloud and developer AI tools, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: CelestialPDF Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: CelestialPDF review 2026: pricing, free-tier limits, multi-document comparison, mindmap generation, and honest pros and cons.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## CelestialPDF Review 2026: Is This ChatPDF Alternative Worth It?

CelestialPDF is a browser-based AI document assistant from Misora AI that lets you upload PDFs, Word, and Excel files and ask questions about their contents instead of reading them line by line. It's a reasonable ChatPDF alternative if you regularly compare multiple documents or want mindmap-style summaries, and its free plan is unusually generous for daily light use.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free; Pro plan €8.99/month (discounted with an annual plan) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — 10 PDFs/month, 250 pages per file, 16MB upload limit, unlimited questions |
| **Best for** | Students, researchers, and small teams who need to chat with and compare multiple documents |
| **Standout feature** | Multi-document comparison plus automatic mindmap and graph generation from a single file |

The "chat with your PDF" category is crowded — ChatPDF, PDF.ai, and Adobe's own AI Assistant all do some version of this. CelestialPDF's pitch is that it goes further than single-document Q&A: it lets you cross-reference several files at once and turns a document's structure into a visual mindmap, which is a genuinely different use case from most competitors that stop at chat.

## What CelestialPDF actually is

CelestialPDF is built by Misora AI and runs entirely in the browser — there's no desktop app or browser extension to install. You create an account, upload a document (or several), and then interact with it through a chat interface, asking things like "summarize the third section" or "what are the payment terms in this contract." The tool describes itself on its marketing site as "the best ChatPDF alternative," which is a fair positioning statement rather than an objective claim — it's competing directly against that category leader, not replacing document editing tools like Acrobat.

On the model side, CelestialPDF says its Pro plan gives users "unlimited chat with GPT-4 Turbo and Claude" — meaning it's built on top of third-party foundation models from OpenAI and Anthropic rather than a proprietary model Misora AI trained itself. That's a common architecture for document-chat startups: the value-add is the document-parsing pipeline and interface, not the underlying language model.

Because pricing, plan limits, and included models are something these smaller AI startups update often, the figures in this review reflect what was published on CelestialPDF's official pricing page as of September 2026 — confirm the current numbers on the official site before subscribing, since free-tier caps and feature lists in this category tend to shift with little notice.

## Pricing

| Plan | Price | Monthly limits | What's included |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | €0/month | 10 PDFs/month, 250 pages per PDF, 16MB file size limit | Unlimited questions, web search, high-quality AI responses, PDF support, priority support |
| Pro | €8.99/month (discounted on annual billing, per the site's offer) | 120 PDFs/month, unlimited pages per document, 50MB file size limit | Everything in Free, plus unlimited chat with GPT-4 Turbo and Claude, support for DOCX and XLSX in addition to PDF, priority support |

Two things stand out in that table. First, the free plan's page-per-document cap (250 pages) is actually higher than the file-count-limited free tiers many competitors offer, which makes it usable for genuinely long documents even before upgrading. Second, Pro doesn't unlock "unlimited" uploads outright — it raises the monthly cap to 120 files and removes the per-document page ceiling, which is a meaningful distinction if you're processing large batches of contracts or reports rather than one file at a time.

There's no publicly listed enterprise or team tier with seat management or SSO on the pricing page — if you need that, email Misora AI (notification@celestialpdf.com) to ask whether a custom plan exists, rather than assuming Pro scales to a full team.

## Core features walkthrough

**Multi-document comparison.** This is the feature that most separates CelestialPDF from single-file chat tools like the base version of ChatPDF. You can upload two or more documents — say, three vendor proposals or two versions of a contract — and ask the assistant to identify differences, overlaps, or which one better matches a set of criteria. For anyone doing due diligence, competitive research, or comparing quotes, this saves the manual work of flipping between tabs.

**Mindmap and graph generation.** Instead of only returning text answers, CelestialPDF can turn a document's structure into a visual mindmap or graph. This is useful for getting a birds-eye view of a long report or academic paper before deciding which sections are worth reading closely — it functions more like a document outline tool than a typical chatbot response.

**Multi-format support.** The Pro plan extends beyond PDF to DOCX and XLSX files, which matters if your workflow mixes contracts (PDF), reports (DOCX), and spreadsheets (XLSX) rather than living entirely in one file format. The free plan is PDF-only.

**Choice of underlying model.** Because Pro gives access to both GPT-4 Turbo and Claude, you can switch models depending on the task — useful if you've noticed one model handles a particular kind of document (dense legal language versus conversational reports) better than the other in your own testing.

**Web search integration.** Both plans include a web search function alongside document chat, letting the assistant pull in outside context rather than answering strictly from the uploaded file. This is a smaller differentiator but useful when a document references external standards, laws, or data you'd otherwise have to look up separately.

## Who it's actually for

- **Students and individual researchers** working through a handful of papers or reports per month will likely never need to leave the free plan — 10 documents and 250 pages each covers most coursework or thesis research.
- **Freelancers and consultants** who regularly compare proposals, contracts, or client documents get the most value from Pro's multi-document comparison and higher file cap.
- **Small teams reviewing high volumes of documents** (paralegals sorting contracts, analysts working through vendor reports) will find the 120-document monthly cap on Pro comfortable, though there's no visible team-seat pricing, so each person likely needs their own subscription.
- **Larger organizations needing compliance features** (SSO, audit logs, data residency guarantees) should look elsewhere or contact Misora AI directly, since none of that is advertised on the public pricing page.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Generous free tier (10 PDFs/month, 250 pages each) | No published enterprise/team plan or seat-based pricing |
| Multi-document comparison beyond single-file chat | DOCX/XLSX support is Pro-only, not available free |
| Mindmap and graph generation adds a visual layer other chat-only tools skip | Smaller company (Misora AI) with less track record than category leaders |
| Access to both GPT-4 Turbo and Claude on one plan | No desktop app or offline mode — browser-only |
| Reasonable Pro price (€8.99/month) relative to competitors | Support channel is email-only, no live chat visible on the site |

## Integrations and ecosystem

CelestialPDF is a standalone web application — there's no listed API, Zapier connector, Slack integration, or browser extension as of this review. Payments are processed through Stripe. If your workflow depends on piping document-chat output into another tool automatically (a CRM, a project board, or an automation platform), CelestialPDF doesn't currently support that; you'd be copying answers out manually.

## Where it's a strong fit

CelestialPDF works well if you need to compare several documents side by side rather than just chat with one at a time, and if a visual mindmap of a document's structure would actually save you time over reading it cover to cover. The free tier's page allowance is generous enough that you can genuinely evaluate the product on real, long documents before deciding whether Pro's higher caps and extra file formats are worth €8.99 a month.

## Where to think twice

If you need API access, workflow automation, or integrations with tools like Slack or Zapier, CelestialPDF doesn't offer any of that today — a more developer-oriented document AI platform would be a better fit. Teams that need SSO, admin roles, or compliance certifications for regulated industries (legal, healthcare, finance) won't find those features advertised here and should ask Misora AI directly or look at more established, enterprise-focused competitors. And if you specifically need a completely free tool with no caps at all, CelestialPDF's free plan — while generous — still limits you to 10 documents a month, which heavy users will hit quickly.

## Bottom line

CelestialPDF earns its "ChatPDF alternative" framing rather than just borrowing the tagline — the multi-document comparison and mindmap generation are real differentiators, not just add-ons on top of an identical single-file chat experience. It's not the tool to pick if you need enterprise compliance features or deep automation integrations, but for students, researchers, and small teams that need to read, compare, and visualize documents faster, the free tier is worth trying before deciding if Pro's €8.99/month is worth paying.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is CelestialPDF free to use?**
Yes. The free plan allows up to 10 PDFs per month, 250 pages per document, and a 16MB file size limit, with unlimited questions per document. No credit card is required to start on the free tier based on the plan structure published on the pricing page.

**What's included in the Pro plan?**
Pro costs €8.99/month and raises the monthly cap to 120 documents, removes the per-document page limit, increases the file size cap to 50MB, and adds support for DOCX and XLSX files in addition to PDF, along with unlimited chat using GPT-4 Turbo and Claude.

**Which AI models does CelestialPDF use?**
According to the company, Pro plan users get access to both GPT-4 Turbo and Claude for document chat. CelestialPDF doesn't appear to train its own foundation model — it's built on top of these third-party models.

**Can CelestialPDF compare multiple documents at once?**
Yes, this is one of its core differentiators — you can upload more than one file and ask the assistant to compare, contrast, or cross-reference their contents, which is useful for reviewing multiple contracts, proposals, or reports together.

**Does CelestialPDF have an API or integrations?**
Not as of this review. There's no publicly listed API, Zapier connector, or third-party app integrations — it's a standalone web app you use directly in the browser.

**Is CelestialPDF good for beginners?**
Yes. The interface is a straightforward three-step flow — sign up, upload a document, ask questions — with no technical setup required, making it accessible for anyone regardless of technical background.

**How does CelestialPDF handle uploaded document data?**
The company doesn't publish detailed data-retention specifics on its main marketing pages beyond standard account and payment handling through Stripe. If you're uploading sensitive documents, review CelestialPDF's privacy policy on its official site first, since data-handling practices should be confirmed there rather than assumed.

**How does CelestialPDF compare to ChatPDF?**
Both let you chat with a PDF, but CelestialPDF adds multi-document comparison, mindmap generation, and support for DOCX/XLSX files on its paid plan, while ChatPDF is more narrowly focused on single-document Q&A. Read our [ChatPDF review](/blog/chatpdf-review) for a closer look at that alternative if you only need to work with one document at a time.

title: v0.dev Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: An in-depth look at Vercel's v0 AI UI/code generator — pricing tiers, features, integrations, pros and cons, and who it's actually for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is v0.dev worth using in 2026?

v0 (now branded v0.app) is Vercel's AI agent for turning prompts into working React and Next.js interfaces, complete with backend wiring and one-click deployment. It's genuinely fast for prototyping and shadcn/ui-based front ends, but the credit-based pricing adds up quickly for daily use, and it's not a fit for teams outside the React/Next.js/Tailwind stack.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (7 messages/day, $5 in monthly credits) |
| **Paid plans from** | $30/month (Plus, per user) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — capped at 7 messages/day, no credit card required |
| **Best for** | Prototyping React/Next.js UIs and shipping to Vercel fast |
| **Standout feature** | Generates working code (UI + backend), not just static mockups |

v0 started as a UI-generation demo and has since grown into a full-stack AI development agent — it writes backend logic, debugs its own output, browses the web for context, and deploys straight to Vercel or opens a GitHub pull request. It also quietly changed domains from v0.dev to v0.app, so don't be surprised if old bookmarks still point at the .dev URL.

## What v0 actually is

Vercel built v0 as a companion to its hosting platform: type a description of a screen, dashboard, or feature, and v0 returns a live, editable React component styled with Tailwind CSS and built on shadcn/ui's component primitives. Unlike a lot of "AI website builder" tools that spit out a static image or a locked-down drag-and-drop canvas, v0's output is real, exportable code — you can copy it into an existing Next.js repo, push it to GitHub, or deploy it directly.

Vercel doesn't publish a single proprietary model name for v0; instead it routes prompts through a set of model options (Mini, Pro, Max, and Max Fast, each billed at different per-million-token rates), letting Vercel swap or blend underlying models as it improves the product. Worth knowing going in — "which AI is actually writing this code" doesn't have one fixed answer the way it does with a single-model tool.

The core workflow: describe what you want in plain language, watch v0 stream a live preview as it works, then iterate with follow-up prompts or by editing the generated code directly. It supports a Visual Design Mode for style tweaks without writing prompts for every pixel change, and it can connect to your own APIs and databases rather than working purely off mock data.

## Pricing

Note: pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability below were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AI coding tools iterate on pricing tiers often, so confirm current numbers on v0's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Price | Credits included | Notable limits/features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/month | $5/month in credits | 7 messages/day; Visual Design Mode, GitHub sync, deploy to Vercel |
| Plus | $30/month per user | $30/month + $2 daily login bonus | Access to all models, team collaboration, shared chats, centralized billing |
| Business | $100/user/month | $30/month + $2 daily login bonus | Training opt-out by default, priority support, data privacy protections |
| Enterprise | Custom | Same base as Business | Data never used for training, SAML SSO, role-based access control, guaranteed support SLAs |

A few things worth flagging here. Generation is metered by credits mapped to token usage across model tiers (Mini through Max Fast), so a multi-file app with several rounds of iteration can burn through the Free plan's $5 allowance within a single serious session. The Plus plan's listed price ($30/month) is also explicitly marked down from a $90/user/month reference price on v0's own pricing page — read that "was/now" framing skeptically rather than as a permanent floor. And credits are per-user even on team plans, so a five-person team on Plus isn't sharing one $30 pool; costs scale roughly linearly with seats.

## Core features that actually matter

**Code generation, not mockups.** The biggest differentiator versus tools like Uizard or older no-code builders is that v0's output is real React/Next.js/Tailwind/shadcn code you own and can move anywhere — including out of Vercel entirely, since the underlying stack is all open-source tooling.

**Backend and data wiring.** v0 isn't limited to front-end screens. It can scaffold API routes, connect to databases, and build data-driven flows, which pushes it closer to a full prototyping agent than a component generator.

**Visual Design Mode.** For style-level tweaks — spacing, color, copy — you can edit directly on the live preview instead of writing a new prompt for every small change, which cuts down on the back-and-forth that plagues chat-only AI builders.

**Self-debugging agent behavior.** Vercel describes v0 as diagnosing and fixing its own errors autonomously, plus browsing the web and inspecting sites for context when a prompt references an external reference or design pattern.

**One-click deploy and GitHub sync.** Ship straight to Vercel's hosting, or push changes as a GitHub pull request so the output slots into a normal code review workflow rather than living only inside v0's own editor.

## Who it's actually for

**Solo builders and indie hackers** prototyping a SaaS landing page, dashboard, or MVP will likely get the most value per dollar — the Free tier is enough to test whether v0's output fits your taste, and Plus at $30/month is cheap relative to hiring a contractor for the same throwaway prototypes.

**Product managers and designers** who want to hand engineers something more concrete than a Figma mockup can use v0 to produce a working, styled prototype that's closer to production code than a static comp — useful for stakeholder demos and faster handoff.

**Small product teams already on Next.js/Tailwind/shadcn** get the cleanest fit, since v0's output drops into that stack with minimal rework. Teams on Vue, Svelte, Angular, or a custom design system will spend more time adapting generated code than they save.

**Agencies and enterprises with compliance requirements** should look at Business or Enterprise specifically for the training opt-out and data-privacy guarantees — the Free and Plus tiers don't include those protections, which matters if you're prototyping anything under an NDA.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Generates real, exportable code (not locked-in mockups) | Free tier's 7-messages/day cap is tight for real project work |
| Deep fit with Next.js/Tailwind/shadcn — near-zero rework for that stack | Credit-based pricing makes cost less predictable than a flat subscription |
| One-click deploy to Vercel and GitHub PR integration | Weak fit outside the React/Next.js ecosystem |
| Visual Design Mode reduces prompt-only iteration | Per-user credits on team plans mean costs scale with headcount |
| Self-debugging agent reduces manual error-fixing | No single disclosed "core model" — output quality can shift as Vercel changes model routing |

## Integrations and ecosystem

v0's most meaningful integration is with Vercel's own deployment pipeline — generated projects can ship straight to production hosting in one click, which is the whole point of building this inside the Vercel ecosystem rather than as a standalone tool. GitHub sync lets generated changes land as pull requests, so teams that already gate merges through PR review can keep that workflow intact instead of copy-pasting code out of a chat window.

Beyond that, v0 exposes a model/platform API for programmatic access, letting teams call its generation capabilities from their own tooling instead of only through the web UI — useful for building v0 into an internal design-to-code pipeline. It doesn't ship native Zapier or Slack integrations the way general-purpose AI assistants do; its integration story is about the code and deployment layer, not workflow automation.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Rapid prototyping of dashboards, landing pages, and internal tools on a React/Next.js stack
- Turning a rough idea or wireframe into a clickable, styled prototype for stakeholder review
- Teams already using shadcn/ui who want AI-generated components that match their existing design system
- Solo developers and small teams who want to go from prompt to deployed URL in one sitting

## Where to think twice

- If you need a fully free tool for ongoing daily use, the 7-messages/day cap and thin $5 credit allowance on Free will feel restrictive fast — budget for at least the Plus plan
- If your team's stack isn't React/Next.js/Tailwind, expect meaningful rework rather than drop-in code
- If your team needs SOC 2-grade compliance or contractual data-training guarantees, only Business/Enterprise cover that — don't build anything sensitive on the Free or Plus tiers
- If unpredictable, usage-based billing is a dealbreaker for budgeting, the credit model is harder to forecast than a flat per-seat SaaS price
- If you need to work fully offline or fully air-gapped, v0 is a cloud-only, browser-based tool with no local/on-prem option

## Bottom line

v0 is one of the more genuinely useful AI coding tools for anyone building on Next.js and Tailwind — it produces real code fast, deploys cleanly to Vercel, and its Visual Design Mode and self-debugging behavior cut down on the usual prompt-iteration grind. The catch is cost predictability: credit-based billing plus per-user pricing means a small team can burn through more than $30/month once real project work starts. If you're already on the Vercel/Next.js stack, it's easy to justify trying on the free tier first; if you're not, weigh the rework before paying for a seat.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is v0.dev free to use?**
Yes, there's a free tier that includes $5 in monthly credits and up to 7 messages per day, plus access to Visual Design Mode, GitHub sync, and deployment to Vercel. It's enough to test the tool but tight for ongoing project work.

**What happened to the v0.dev domain?**
Vercel has moved the product to v0.app; the .dev domain now redirects there. Bookmarks and older articles referencing v0.dev should still land on the current product.

**What tech stack does v0 generate code in?**
React components styled with Tailwind CSS and built on shadcn/ui, typically scaffolded for Next.js. It can also wire up backend logic and connect to external APIs and databases rather than only producing static UI.

**Can I use v0-generated code outside of Vercel?**
Yes — since the output is standard React/Next.js/Tailwind code, you can copy or push it into any repository and host it wherever you like, though the one-click deploy convenience is specific to Vercel's own hosting.

**How does v0's pricing actually work?**
Plans include a monthly credit allowance (plus a small daily login bonus on paid plans) that gets consumed based on model usage — pricier model tiers like Max and Max Fast burn credits faster than the cheaper Mini tier. You can buy additional credits on paid plans if you run out.

**Is v0 good for beginners with no coding experience?**
It lowers the barrier meaningfully since you can describe a UI in plain language and get a working result, but you'll get much more out of it if you can read and lightly edit the generated React/Tailwind code — it's built as a developer tool first, not a fully no-code platform.

**Does v0 keep my data private?**
Data-privacy protections and training opt-out are explicitly called out as Business/Enterprise-tier features according to v0's pricing page; confirm current data-handling terms for the Free and Plus tiers directly with Vercel before using it on sensitive projects.

**What are the alternatives to v0?**
Depending on what you need, alternatives include Vercel's own open-source [Vercel AI SDK](/blog/vercel-ai-sdk-overview) for building custom AI features into an app you control, general-purpose AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot or Cursor, and other AI UI generators such as Bolt.new or Lovable — each trades off differently on how much code you own versus how much the platform manages for you.

For more AI and developer-tool coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Shakker AI Review 2026: Features, Pricing and Shutdown
excerpt: Shakker AI closes September 30, 2026. Here's what the AI image platform did, what it cost, and where to migrate before the deadline.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Shakker AI still worth signing up for in 2026?

No — Shakker AI is shutting down. A banner on the site confirms the platform closes on September 30, 2026 at 00:00 UTC, and users are told to save their content and request refunds before then. This review covers what the tool did, what it cost, and where to go instead if you were mid-evaluation.

**At a glance**

| | Shakker AI |
|---|---|
| Status | Shutting down — closes September 30, 2026 at 00:00 UTC |
| Time left to act (as of this post's date) | About 11 days |
| Historical pricing model | Membership/credit-based plans (exact tiers no longer verifiable — see note below) |
| Best for (historically) | Illustration, concept art, product/photography mockups, anime and game-art generation |
| Standout feature | Online ComfyUI and A1111 WebUI access plus online model training, without local GPU setup |

Shakker positioned itself as a "streaming" AI image generator built for creators who wanted more control than a single-prompt tool but didn't want to manage their own Stable Diffusion install. It bundled a hosted image generator with browser-based versions of two workflow tools veteran Stable Diffusion users already know — A1111 WebUI and ComfyUI — plus the ability to train your own custom models on the platform itself. That combination is why it built a following among hobbyists and small studios rather than casual one-off image makers. It's also why the shutdown matters more than it would for a simpler tool: users with trained models, saved workflows and generated libraries on the platform have real migration work to do before the cutoff, not just a subscription to cancel.

## What Shakker AI actually did

**Shakker Generator.** This was the platform's primary image-generation surface — a streaming interface where users typed prompts (or built on reference images) and watched generations resolve in near-real time rather than waiting on a single batch render. It supported multiple creative domains out of the box, including illustration and concept art, photography and product design, logo and icon creation, architecture visualization, and game/anime art.

**Online A1111 WebUI.** Automatic1111's WebUI is one of the most widely used open-source front ends for Stable Diffusion, normally run locally on your own GPU. Shakker hosted it in-browser, giving users the full control surface — samplers, CFG scale, LoRA stacking, inpainting, ControlNet-style conditioning — without installing anything or owning capable hardware.

**Online ComfyUI.** Same idea, applied to ComfyUI, the node-based workflow builder that's become the preferred tool for anyone chaining multiple models or building repeatable generation pipelines. Running it in the browser removed the setup friction that keeps a lot of people from trying ComfyUI at all.

**Online model training.** Shakker let users train and publish their own custom models (commonly LoRAs and checkpoints in the Stable Diffusion ecosystem) directly on the platform, then reuse or share them inside the Shakker Generator. This is the feature that most separated it from single-purpose image generators like Midjourney or Adobe Firefly — it was aimed at people who wanted a specific character, style or product line to generate consistently, not just decent one-off images.

**Face swap and style transfer.** Shakker also included AI face-swapping and style-transfer utilities, useful for quick character consistency work or restyling existing art without a full retrain.

If you've read our [Leonardo AI review](/blog/leonardo-ai-review), [Krea review](/blog/krea-review) or [Dzine AI review](/blog/dzine-ai-review), the shape will feel familiar — all sit in the "more control than Midjourney, less setup than a local Stable Diffusion rig" category. Shakker's differentiator was hosting the actual open-source tooling (A1111, ComfyUI) rather than a simplified proprietary interface on top of it.

## Pricing — and why it doesn't matter anymore

Shakker ran on a membership/credit system, gated behind a "Membership" purchase page, with free daily generation credits for casual use and paid tiers unlocking higher generation volume, priority speed, and advanced tools like model training. We could not pull exact current tier prices or credit allotments from the live site — pricing pages that normally carried that detail were returning errors, consistent with a platform winding down rather than actively selling subscriptions.

Practically, this makes the pricing question moot: with the service closing September 30, 2026, buying a new membership now would mean paying for access you'd lose within days to weeks. If you're currently on a paid plan, the priority is requesting a refund through Shakker's official channels before the closure date, not evaluating whether the plan was competitively priced. Confirm any pricing or feature detail directly on shakker.ai before the deadline — this review reflects what could be verified as of the September 2026 publish date, and shutting-down platforms often pull pricing pages before final closure.

## Who it was actually for

**Hobbyist illustrators and concept artists** got the most out of Shakker's domain-specific generation presets and the ability to fine-tune a personal style through model training, without needing a GPU capable of running Stable Diffusion locally.

**Small game and anime studios** used the platform's model training and character-consistency tools to keep recurring characters visually consistent across many generations — a harder problem than single-image quality, and one general-purpose tools like Midjourney don't solve well out of the box.

**ComfyUI and A1111 power users without local hardware** were arguably the best-fit audience — Shakker gave them the actual open-source tools they already knew how to use, hosted, rather than a simplified proprietary substitute.

**Casual one-off image generators** — someone who just wants a nice image for a blog post or social post — were probably better served by simpler tools like Adobe Firefly or Google's Nano Banana anyway, and are the group with the least migration work to do now.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Hosted A1111 and ComfyUI removed local GPU/setup requirements | Platform is shutting down September 30, 2026 — no new value in signing up |
| Online model training for custom characters/styles | Exact current pricing/credit tiers could not be verified from the live site |
| Covered multiple creative domains (illustration, product, architecture, anime, logos) in one platform | Migrating trained models and generation history elsewhere takes real effort, not a simple export |
| Familiar tooling for existing Stable Diffusion users | Face-swap and style-transfer tools raise the usual likeness/consent considerations common to this category |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Shakker's ecosystem hooks were mostly internal — its hosted A1111 and ComfyUI environments are compatible with the broader Stable Diffusion model and LoRA ecosystem, so models trained or used elsewhere could generally be brought in, and vice versa (subject to each model's license). We found no evidence of a public API or Zapier/Slack app tier on the current site; anyone who needs programmatic image-generation access going forward should look at [Replicate](/blog/replicate-review) or the [FLUX.1 API](/blog/flux-1-pro-review).

## Where it was a strong fit

Shakker made sense for creators who wanted ComfyUI- or A1111-level control without owning a capable GPU, and for anyone training a recurring character or brand style who needed that model reusable across many generations rather than starting fresh each session. Teams doing concept art, game asset iteration, or anime-style character work got real value from bundling generation, editing, and training in one place instead of juggling separate local tools.

## Where to think twice (and what to do now)

Don't sign up now. With the service closing September 30, 2026, there's no scenario where starting fresh on Shakker makes sense — new users should look directly at alternatives instead.

If you're an existing user, act on three things before the deadline: export any generation history and trained models you want to keep, confirm whether your LoRAs/checkpoints can be downloaded in a standard format usable elsewhere in the Stable Diffusion ecosystem, and submit a refund request for unused membership time through official support well before the cutoff — support queues on shutting-down platforms tend to back up in the final days.

If you need ongoing hosted ComfyUI access, [RunComfy](/blog/runcomfy-review) is a direct functional substitute we've reviewed separately. For general AI image generation without the workflow-builder layer, [Leonardo AI](/blog/leonardo-ai-review), [Krea](/blog/krea-review), [Midjourney](/blog/midjourney-review) and [Adobe Firefly](/blog/adobe-firefly-review) are all active, actively maintained options worth comparing against your specific use case.

## The bottom line

Shakker AI was a genuinely capable platform for creators who wanted real Stable Diffusion-grade control — hosted ComfyUI, hosted A1111, and on-platform model training — without managing their own GPU rig. That made it a reasonable pick throughout 2025 and early 2026 for illustrators, small studios and power users who knew what those tools did. None of that changes the current situation: the service closes September 30, 2026, and the only sensible actions left are exporting your work, requesting a refund if you're on a paid plan, and picking a replacement tool from the active alternatives above. Don't sign up for a new membership at this point — there isn't enough runway left to get value from it.

## FAQ

**Is Shakker AI shutting down?**
Yes. The official site displays a banner stating Shakker.ai closes on September 30, 2026 at 00:00 UTC, and instructs users to save their content and request refunds before that date.

**Can I still sign up for Shakker AI?**
Technically the site may still allow it, but there's no practical reason to — a new membership would only be usable for days to weeks before the platform closes.

**How do I get a refund for an unused Shakker membership?**
Shakker's shutdown notice directs users to request refunds through its official support channel, well before September 30, 2026, since refund processing on shutting-down platforms can slow near the deadline.

**Will I be able to download my trained models and generated images?**
The shutdown banner tells users to save content before closure, implying an export path exists, but we couldn't verify the exact format or process from the public site. Confirm directly with Shakker support and start early.

**What was Shakker AI's pricing before the shutdown?**
It ran on a membership/credit system with a free tier for casual generation and paid tiers unlocking higher volume and features like model training. We could not verify current exact tier prices from the live site at the time of writing, and with the shutdown in progress this detail is largely moot for new users.

**What's the closest alternative to Shakker AI?**
For hosted ComfyUI specifically, [RunComfy](/blog/runcomfy-review) is the most direct substitute. For general AI image generation, [Leonardo AI](/blog/leonardo-ai-review), [Krea](/blog/krea-review), [Midjourney](/blog/midjourney-review) and [Adobe Firefly](/blog/adobe-firefly-review) are all active options depending on whether you need illustration, photorealism, or design-asset generation.

**Is it safe to use Shakker's face-swap tool?**
As with any face-swap or likeness-manipulation tool, only use it on images you have the rights and consent to alter, and check the platform's usage policy (while it's still available) for restrictions on identifiable real people.

**Why did Shakker AI shut down?**
The public shutdown notice does not state a reason. We could not independently verify the cause (funding, acquisition, or a business decision), so we're not speculating on it here — treat any third-party claim about the reason as unconfirmed unless Shakker itself states it.

Looking for tools that are still actively adding features rather than winding down? Browse our [AI & software deals](/category/software) for current, actively maintained platforms across image generation, writing, coding and more.

title: Rewind.ai Review: What It Was, and Why It Shut Down
excerpt: Rewind.ai recorded your screen and calls for searchable recall. It rebranded to Limitless, was acquired by Meta, and shut down in 2025.
author: Editorial Team
