title: Branded AI Review 2026: Naming Tool Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: Branded (branded.ai) helps founders generate startup names, check domain availability, and create logos in one AI-powered tool. Here is what it does well.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Branded (branded.ai) worth using for naming a startup?

Branded is a free-to-try AI tool built by Alana Goyal of the venture firm basecase that generates startup names, checks whether the matching domain is available, and produces a basic logo and one-pager. It's genuinely useful for the first hour of naming a company, but it's not a full branding or trademark-search platform, and it stops well short of what a design agency or a tool like Looka would give you.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Made by** | Alana Goyal / basecase |
| **Starting price** | No public pricing listed — sign-in required to use |
| **Free tier/trial** | Appears free to access with a Google/email sign-in; no published paid tier |
| **Best for** | Early-stage founders brainstorming a startup name and checking domain availability fast |
| **Standout feature** | One-click name generation paired with instant domain-availability lookup |

## What Branded actually is

Branded lives at branded.ai and describes itself, in its own meta tags, as a tool offering "AI-generated names for your next project" that lets you "name your startup, secure the domain, and brand it — all in one place." It's built by Alana Goyal, a partner at the early-stage venture firm basecase. Branded isn't a basecase portfolio product in the traditional sense — it reads more like a tool basecase built for its founder network and then opened up publicly, which explains why the homepage leans on testimonials from people at Vercel, Figma, Stripe, Cloudflare, Supabase, Alpharun, Braintrust, and Instacart rather than a typical SaaS pricing page.

There's no public documentation naming which language model powers the tool, and Branded doesn't publish a model card or an API. That's worth flagging: unlike Jasper or Copy.ai, which are explicit about being built on GPT- and Claude-class models, Branded treats the underlying AI as an implementation detail you won't find documented anywhere on the site as of this review.

The product itself is organized around three connected steps rather than three separate tools:

1. **Startup Names** — you describe your company or idea and the tool generates a list of candidate names in one pass.
2. **Domain Availability** — an AI-assisted lookup checks which of those names (or names you type in yourself) have available matching domains.
3. **Branded Content** — once you've settled on a name, the tool can generate a simple logo and a one-pager to go with it.

## Pricing

As of this review's publish date, Branded does not display a pricing page, plan comparison, or checkout flow anywhere on its public site. The homepage and sign-in screen are the only pages that load without an account, and neither mentions a subscription, credit system, or free-tier cap. That's unusual in 2026 — most naming and branding tools (Looka, Namelix, BrandCrowd) publish tiered pricing because logo and brand-kit downloads are their monetization point.

The most likely explanation, based on how the product is positioned and who's quoted using it, is that Branded is currently free behind a login wall, possibly as a goodwill tool tied to basecase's founder community rather than a standalone commercial product. That's an inference, not a confirmed fact — Branded hasn't published a statement on monetization, so **confirm current pricing and account requirements directly on branded.ai before relying on it for a real launch**, since a product without a pricing page can add paid tiers or usage caps without much notice.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described in this review were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly for a young, VC-adjacent tool like this one — always double-check the live site before you commit real work to it.

| Plan | Price | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Only tier observed | Not published | Sign-in (Google/email), name generation, domain-availability lookup, basic logo + one-pager generation |

## Features walkthrough

**AI name generation.** You give Branded a short description of your startup or idea, and it returns a batch of candidate names in a single generation pass — the site's own copy calls this going "from idea to iconic name in one click." This is the core of the product and, based on the founder testimonials on its homepage (including Vercel's Guillermo Rauch, who called it "shockingly good"), the part that's earned it word-of-mouth traction inside startup circles.

**Domain availability lookup.** Rather than making you copy each generated name into a separate registrar search, Branded checks domain availability as part of the naming flow. This is what differentiates it most from a plain "AI name generator" prompt run in any chatbot — it closes the loop between "I like this name" and "can I actually buy the .com." Checking availability inside Branded doesn't register the domain, though. Once you've found a name with a free domain, you still need to buy it through an actual registrar — see the [Namecheap coupon page](/coupons/namecheap) if that's where you plan to register it.

**Branded content generation.** Beyond naming, the tool can produce a simple logo and a one-pager once you've locked in a name. This is positioned as a starting point rather than finished brand collateral — it won't replace a designer for a company that needs a full identity system (color palette, typography rules, brand guidelines document), but it's enough to put a placeholder mark on a pitch deck or a landing page while you validate the idea.

**Single-flow workflow.** The naming → domain-check → basic-brand sequence happens without switching tools, which is the main practical value proposition over doing the same three tasks with a general chatbot, a separate registrar search, and a separate logo maker.

**Social proof from real operators.** Branded's homepage names specific people at specific companies (Vercel, Figma, Stripe, Cloudflare, Alpharun, Supabase, Braintrust, Instacart) who've used it, rather than generic "loved by thousands" copy — a stronger signal than most AI-tool marketing pages, though it's still vendor-selected and not an independent review.

## Who Branded is actually for

- **Solo founders in the idea stage** get the most value — a fast way to brainstorm names and see which have an open domain, without opening five browser tabs.
- **Small founding teams pressure-testing a pivot** can run a batch of alternative names past the domain check before committing to a rebrand.
- **Design agencies or teams needing a finished, trademark-cleared brand identity** are not the target user — Branded doesn't do trademark screening, and its output is a starting sketch, not deliverable-grade design work.
- **Enterprise or agency teams needing procurement-grade vendor terms** (SLAs, DPAs, SOC 2) won't find any of that published, since there's no enterprise tier yet.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Combines naming, domain-availability checking, and basic branding in one flow | No public pricing page — unclear what happens once/if it becomes paid |
| Fast — generates a batch of names in one pass | No trademark or legal-conflict screening, so a name being "available" doesn't mean it's safe to use |
| Real, named testimonials from operators at recognizable companies | No documented AI model, so you can't evaluate what's generating the output |
| Requires no separate registrar tab-switching to check domains | Domain availability lookup doesn't let you actually register the domain inside the tool |
| Low friction to try — sign in and generate | No API, integrations, or team/collaboration features documented |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Branded does not publish an API, a Zapier connection, or Slack/Notion-style integrations. It's a standalone, browser-based tool you sign into directly — nothing to wire into an existing workflow beyond opening the site when you need a name. If your process depends on pulling generated names into a project-management tool automatically, you'll be copying and pasting rather than automating that step.

## Where it's a strong fit

Branded is a strong fit for the common moment when a founder has an idea and needs a name, a domain check, and a rough logo fast, without paying for or learning a heavier branding suite. The single-flow design saves time compared with doing each step separately, and real operators at companies like Vercel and Figma vouching for it publicly is a stronger signal than most AI tools get at this stage.

## Where to think twice

Skip Branded, or don't rely on it alone, if you need a trademark-cleared name — it checks domain availability, not USPTO or international trademark conflicts, and a domain being open doesn't mean the name is legally safe to use. Skip it if you need finished, deliverable-grade brand design — the logo and one-pager output is a sketch to iterate from, not a brand kit. Skip it if you need team collaboration, API access, or enterprise compliance documentation (SOC 2, DPAs), because none of that is published. And verify pricing before depending on it for a real launch if you need a tool with a stable, published pricing plan — Branded's no-pricing-page status makes it harder to plan around than a tool with a clear free tier and paid ceiling.

## Bottom line

Branded is a genuinely handy, narrowly-scoped tool for picking a startup name and checking whether you can actually get the domain for it — faster than stitching together a chatbot, a registrar search, and a logo generator yourself. It isn't a full branding platform, doesn't screen for trademark conflicts, and its lack of a public pricing page makes it hard to plan around beyond a quick brainstorm. Use it to generate and shortlist names, then take the winner to a registrar to lock down the domain and to a trademark search before you print it on a business card.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Branded (branded.ai) free?**
There's no published pricing page as of this review, and the tool appears to be free to use once you sign in with Google or email. That could change without notice, so confirm current terms on branded.ai before relying on it for ongoing work.

**Who built Branded?**
Branded was built by Alana Goyal, a partner at the early-stage venture firm basecase. It isn't tied to a large existing SaaS company — it reads as a founder-community tool that's since been made publicly accessible.

**What AI model does Branded use?**
Branded doesn't publish which language model powers its name generation. There's no model card, API documentation, or technical write-up on the public site describing the underlying system as of this review.

**Does Branded register domains for me?**
No. It checks domain availability as part of the naming flow, but you still need to register any domain you choose through an actual registrar.

**Does Branded check for trademark conflicts?**
No. Domain availability and trademark availability are different things — a name can have a free .com and still infringe on an existing trademark. Run a proper trademark search (or consult a lawyer) before committing to a name Branded generates.

**Is the logo Branded generates good enough to launch with?**
It's a reasonable placeholder for a pitch deck or an early landing page, but it's not positioned as a finished, deliverable-grade brand identity. Most founders who get real traction end up commissioning custom design work later.

**What are the alternatives to Branded?**
Namelix and NameSnack are common comparisons for AI naming. Looka and BrandCrowd go further for a paid logo/brand-kit suite. For domain registration itself, see the [Namecheap coupon page](/coupons/namecheap).

**Is Branded beginner-friendly?**
Yes — there's no learning curve. You sign in, describe your idea, and get a list of names with domain-availability status attached. The simplicity is arguably the whole point.

For more AI and software deals and reviews, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Phind AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Phind pairs live web search with code-focused AI chat for developers. Here's its pricing, standout features, and who should use it in 2026.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Phind still around, and is it worth using in 2026?

Yes — Phind is still an active, independently operated product as of this review, despite recurring rumors online that it shut down. It's an AI answer engine built specifically for developers: it searches the live web and your own docs, then answers coding questions with citations and runnable code rather than a generic chat reply. It's a solid pick if you want sourced, code-first answers instead of a plain chatbot, but it's a narrower tool than Cursor or Copilot if you want an editor built around AI pair-programming.

**At a glance**

| | Phind |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free tier available |
| Free tier / trial | Yes — limited number of searches per day on a smaller model |
| Best for | Developers who want sourced, cited answers to technical questions, not just generated code |
| Standout feature | Web-search-grounded answers with inline citations to docs, GitHub issues, and forums |

You'll see the shutdown rumor on a few low-effort aggregator sites and in scattered forum threads — it doesn't hold up. As of this writing, phind.com is live, serving traffic, and shipping new features (including agentic "run" capabilities layered on its original search-and-answer format). What has genuinely happened is narrower: Phind has leaned harder into developer-specific and enterprise use rather than a broad consumer search pitch, which is why it can feel like it's "gone quiet" if you only knew its earlier, more consumer-facing version.

## What Phind actually is

Phind was built by a small, YC-backed team (led by founder Michael Royzen) with one specific pitch: developers ask technical questions in a search box, Phind crawls the live web and relevant documentation in real time, and returns a synthesized answer with code blocks and clickable citations back to the sources it pulled from — official docs, Stack Overflow-style Q&A, GitHub issues and READMEs, and blog posts. That's different from asking ChatGPT or Claude a coding question cold, where the model draws only on training data and doesn't necessarily tell you where an answer came from.

Under the hood, Phind has historically run a mix of its own fine-tuned code models for fast, cheaper responses, alongside access to frontier third-party models on paid tiers for harder questions. Phind doesn't publish one static "the model" it runs — it routes between models by plan and query complexity, and that mix has changed since launch, so treat any specific model name cited elsewhere as a snapshot, not a permanent fact.

The product ships across a few surfaces: the web search/chat interface at phind.com, a VS Code extension bringing the same search-and-cite behavior into your editor, and (on higher tiers) API and enterprise access for teams that want Phind pointed at private/internal documentation and codebases rather than only the public web.

## Pricing

Phind's core positioning has always been a usable free tier plus a paid unlock for higher usage caps and stronger models. Historically, that has looked like:

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | A capped number of searches per day, served by Phind's faster/smaller model |
| Pro (Phind Pro) | Paid, monthly subscription | Higher/unlimited search volume, access to more capable models for complex questions, priority response speed |
| Enterprise / Teams | Custom pricing | Private codebase and internal-docs indexing, team seats, admin controls — sold via direct sales contact rather than self-serve checkout |

Pricing, free-tier limits, and model availability for Phind were last verifiable as of this post's date and can shift quickly, as is typical for AI tools — confirm current numbers on Phind's own pricing page before you commit, especially on the Enterprise tier, where terms are negotiated per account.

## Features that actually differentiate it

**Search-grounded answers with citations.** Phind's core differentiator: instead of a black-box answer, you get inline links back to the specific doc page, GitHub thread, or blog post the answer drew from — useful for verifying a claim about a library version, an API behavior, or a recent framework change rather than trusting the model's memory blindly.

**Real-time web awareness.** Built around live search rather than a static knowledge cutoff, Phind can surface answers about libraries and APIs that shipped after a general chatbot's training cutoff — a real advantage for fast-moving ecosystems and breaking changes announced last week.

**Code-first answer formatting.** Answers are structured around runnable code blocks with explanation around them rather than prose with code as an afterthought — a small but real usability difference if you're pasting straight into an editor.

**VS Code extension.** Lets you ask the same search-and-cite questions without leaving your editor, pulling in surrounding file context for a more relevant answer than a cold search-box query.

**Private/internal source indexing (paid tiers).** On paid and enterprise plans, Phind can index a team's internal documentation, wikis, and (in some configurations) private repositories, so answers cite your own internal sources rather than only the public web — a genuinely different use case from coding assistants that don't do retrieval-augmented search this way by default.

## Who Phind is actually for

- **Solo developers debugging unfamiliar errors or APIs** — the free tier is enough if you're occasionally stuck on an error message, library quirk, or "why doesn't this work" question and want a sourced answer rather than a guess.
- **Developers in fast-moving or niche ecosystems** — Phind's live-search grounding is more likely to be current than a chatbot relying purely on training data for a library version that shipped recently.
- **Small teams that want shared, cited answers** — Pro-tier usage limits suit someone asking technical questions daily, not occasionally.
- **Engineering orgs with internal knowledge bases** — enterprise private-source indexing is aimed at teams that want "search our internal docs like this," a different buying decision from a per-seat coding assistant.
- **Not a great fit if you want an AI-native code editor** — for inline autocomplete and multi-file refactoring, [Cursor AI](/blog/cursor-ai-review) or [GitHub Copilot](/blog/github-copilot-review) are built around that directly; Phind is closer to a specialized search engine than an editor replacement.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Cited, sourced answers instead of an unverifiable black box | Not an editor-native coding assistant — thinner IDE integration than Cursor or Copilot |
| Real-time web search catches recent library/API changes | Free tier daily search cap can feel restrictive for heavy daily use |
| VS Code extension for in-editor context | Enterprise pricing isn't published — requires a sales conversation |
| Enterprise private-source indexing for internal docs/codebases | Smaller brand recognition than ChatGPT/Claude/Copilot means less third-party tooling built around it |
| Genuinely useful for niche/fast-moving framework questions | Model routing and lineup has changed over time, so past reviews' model claims may be stale |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Phind's ecosystem is narrower and more purpose-built than a general chatbot's: the VS Code extension, an API for teams building Phind's search-and-cite behavior into internal tools, and enterprise connectors for indexing private documentation on paid plans. It isn't a broad automation platform with Zapier-style triggers or a plugin marketplace — if that matters, a general-purpose assistant like [ChatGPT](/blog/chatgpt-review) or an automation tool like [Zapier](/blog/zapier-review) fits that need better, and you can still run Phind alongside it purely for coding research.

## Where it's a strong fit

Phind earns its keep when you're stuck on something technical and need to know not just an answer but where it comes from — debugging an obscure error, checking whether an API changed recently, or comparing two libraries' current documentation. If you already default to opening ten browser tabs alongside a chatbot to cross-check its coding answer against real docs, Phind collapses that workflow into one query.

## Where to think twice

If you want one AI tool that both answers questions and writes/edits code across your whole project inline, Phind alone won't cover that — pair it with an editor-native tool like Cursor or Copilot. If you need a fully free, unlimited-use tool for heavy daily research, the free tier's search cap will bite; budget for Pro if that's your pattern. If your team needs formal compliance documentation (SOC 2 reports, data-processing agreements) before adopting any AI tool, get that in writing directly from Phind's sales team — it's not verifiable from the public site alone. Teams needing strictly offline or on-prem AI tooling should also look elsewhere, since Phind's value proposition depends on live web search.

## The bottom line

Phind is a genuinely useful, still-active tool for one specific job: getting a sourced, code-first answer to a technical question faster than manually searching and cross-referencing docs yourself. It isn't trying to be a full coding-assistant editor or a general-purpose chatbot — that focus is its strength for the questions it's built for, and its limitation everywhere else. If your workflow is "I'm stuck on something specific and need a trustworthy, cited answer," it earns a spot in your toolbar; if you want one tool that also writes and refactors code inline, keep an editor-native assistant alongside it.

## FAQ

**Is Phind free to use?**
Yes, Phind has historically offered a free tier with a capped number of daily searches on a faster, smaller model. Paid Pro access removes or raises that cap and unlocks stronger models for harder questions. Confirm current limits on Phind's own pricing page, since AI tool free tiers change often.

**Did Phind shut down?**
No — as of this review, phind.com is live and operating. The shutdown claim circulating on some low-effort sites doesn't match the live site or recent third-party coverage. What's changed is that Phind has shifted emphasis toward developer- and enterprise-specific use rather than a broad consumer pitch.

**How is Phind different from ChatGPT or Claude for coding questions?**
The core difference is grounding: Phind searches the live web and cites its sources inline, while a general chatbot answers primarily from its training data unless you explicitly enable a browsing feature. For questions about very recent library or API changes, Phind's live-search approach is more likely to be current.

**Is Phind better than GitHub Copilot or Cursor?**
They solve different problems. Copilot and Cursor are built around inline code generation and editing inside your editor. Phind is built around answering technical questions with sourced, cited responses. Many developers use a coding assistant for day-to-day writing and something like Phind for research-style debugging questions — see our [GitHub Copilot review](/blog/github-copilot-review) and [Cursor AI review](/blog/cursor-ai-review) for the editor-native side of that comparison.

**Does Phind have a VS Code extension?**
Yes, Phind offers a VS Code extension that brings its search-and-cite answers into the editor with surrounding file context, rather than requiring you to switch to a browser tab.

**Can Phind index our company's private codebase or internal docs?**
On enterprise/team plans, yes — Phind supports indexing private documentation and, in some configurations, internal codebases, so answers cite your own internal sources instead of only public web content. Pricing and exact setup for this tier aren't published and require contacting Phind's sales team directly.

**Is Phind a good alternative to Perplexity for developers?**
Both are search-grounded AI answer engines with citations, but Perplexity is general-purpose across any topic, while Phind is purpose-built for coding and technical questions specifically. If your queries are mostly non-technical, [Perplexity AI](/blog/perplexity-ai-review) is the broader tool; if they're almost entirely code and API questions, Phind's narrower focus tends to produce more directly usable answers.

**Is Phind beginner-friendly?**
Yes — the interface is a simple search box, and you don't need to understand prompt engineering to get a useful answer; asking a plain-language technical question works. The learning curve is closer to "using a smarter search engine" than "learning a new tool."

For more AI and developer-tool coverage, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Fotor Review 2026: Pricing, AI Features and Verdict
excerpt: Fotor combines free photo editing, AI enhancement, and design templates. Here's the real pricing, features, and where it falls short.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Fotor worth using for photo editing?

Fotor is a browser- and app-based photo editor that's genuinely useful for quick, no-install edits — background removal, batch touch-ups, AI enhancement, and collage templates all work well on the free tier. It's not a Photoshop replacement for pixel-level control, and its paid tiers plus recurring-billing complaints are worth reading first.

Fotor also has a dedicated AI Anime Generator; if that's specifically what brought you here, see our [full Fotor AI Anime Generator review](/blog/fotor-ai-anime-generator-review) for that tool's pricing, styles, and limitations. This article covers Fotor as a whole — the broader platform it's actually built around.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (Fotor Basic); paid plans from roughly $8.99/month |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — Fotor Basic is free forever, with limited credits and watermarked/lower-res exports on some features |
| Best for | Quick photo edits, background removal, batch processing, casual design/collage work |
| Standout feature | One-click AI background removal and photo enhancement without installing desktop software |

## What Fotor actually is

Fotor is made by Everimaging, which has been building online photo-editing tools since around 2012. It started as a simpler collage and touch-up app and has grown into a broader suite: a full photo editor, a Canva-style design tool with templates, and AI features layered on top — background removal, object removal, AI enhancement/upscaling, photo restoration, AI headshot generation, and text-to-image generation. Fotor states it serves hundreds of millions of users worldwide, though that figure comes from the company's own marketing and isn't independently verifiable.

Unlike single-purpose AI apps, Fotor isn't built around one model or trick. It's closer to an all-in-one editing workspace: crop and color-correct a photo, run it through an AI enhancer, remove the background, drop it into a collage template, and export — all in one browser tab. The AI tools sit alongside, not instead of, the manual editing that made Fotor's reputation.

## Fotor pricing

Fotor runs a freemium model with a free "Basic" tier and paid tiers that unlock higher resolution exports, more AI credits, batch tools, and cloud storage. Based on Fotor's own plan structure and pricing corroborated across third-party software directories, the tiers break down roughly like this:

| Plan | Approx. price | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Fotor Basic | Free | Core editing/design tools, limited AI credits, 1 concurrent AI generation, watermarked/lower-res exports on some features, 500MB storage |
| Fotor Pro | ~$8.99/mo (cheaper annually) | 100+ editing tools, 20+ retouch features, 100,000+ templates, more AI credits, 10 concurrent generations, watermark-free exports, 2GB storage |
| Fotor Pro+ | ~$19.99/mo (cheaper annually) | Everything in Pro, plus batch background removal/replacement, commercial stock photos, custom fonts, brand kits, AI slide generation, more storage |
| Fotor Max | Custom pricing (not publicly listed) | Highest AI credit allowance, 50 concurrent generations, largest storage tier, aimed at teams and heavy users |

Fotor doesn't display exact Pro+/Max pricing consistently across regions and promotions, and the figures above are cross-checked against third-party software directories rather than pulled from a single source — confirm current pricing on Fotor's own pricing page before subscribing. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability noted here were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change without notice.

One thing worth flagging: Fotor has a pattern of billing-related complaints on review sites like Trustpilot — users reporting being auto-renewed into annual plans with little warning, and describing difficulty getting refunds under the company's no-refund policy for digital purchases. That doesn't mean the editing tools are bad, but it's a real reason to read the cancellation terms and set a reminder before your first term renews.

## Core features that actually matter

**AI background removal and replacement.** One of Fotor's most-used tools, and it's fast — upload a photo, and it isolates the subject in a few seconds, with an option to swap in a new background, color, or gradient. Free-tier users get this, though batch background removal is a Pro+ feature.

**AI photo enhancer and upscaler.** Fotor's enhancer sharpens blurry or low-resolution images and upscales photos for larger prints. Like most AI upscalers, it works best on moderately degraded images — it can't reliably recover detail that was never captured in the original, and heavily compressed source images will still show artifacts after enhancement.

**Batch editing.** For anyone processing a folder of product photos, event shots, or headshots, batch editing applies the same crop, filter, resize, or background treatment across many files at once. It's a genuinely time-saving feature, but gated behind paid plans for anything beyond basic use.

**Design templates and collage tools.** Fotor's template library (100,000+ assets on paid plans, per Fotor) covers social graphics, posters, flyers, and collages — closer to Canva's territory than a pure photo editor. Useful if you want one tool for both photo touch-ups and simple marketing graphics.

**AI headshot and avatar generation, plus the anime generator.** Fotor also offers AI headshot generation and the separate AI Anime Generator feature, both running on a credit system layered on top of subscription tiers. We cover the anime generator's styles, credit costs, and limitations in the [dedicated Fotor AI Anime Generator review](/blog/fotor-ai-anime-generator-review) rather than duplicating that detail here.

## Who Fotor is actually for

- **Casual users and social posters** — the free Basic tier covers most one-off editing needs without ever requiring a card on file.
- **Small businesses and solo creators doing bulk work** — Pro or Pro+ makes sense if you're regularly batch-editing product photos, headshots, or event galleries and want to skip Photoshop's learning curve and cost.
- **People who want one tool for photos and simple design** — combined edited photos and Canva-style graphics (flyers, social posts, presentations) can replace two subscriptions.
- **Teams needing brand consistency** — Pro+'s multiple brand kits and commercial-license stock photos target small marketing teams, though collaboration features are lighter than dedicated team design tools.

Fotor is a weaker fit for professional photographers or designers who need layer-level control, advanced masking, RAW support, or plugin ecosystems — that's Photoshop or Affinity Photo territory, not Fotor's.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier covers useful editing without watermarks on core tools | Billing complaints around auto-renewal and refunds are common |
| No install required — browser-based, plus desktop/mobile apps | AI credit systems can feel restrictive even on paid plans |
| Combines editing, AI tools, and design templates in one app | Not a substitute for professional software (no RAW, limited layers) |
| Batch editing saves real time for bulk photo work | Advanced features locked behind Pro+/Max; Max pricing isn't published |
| Frequent new AI tools added (enhancer, anime generator, headshots) | AI output quality is inconsistent across image types |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Fotor is primarily a standalone web and mobile app rather than a platform built for deep third-party integration. It offers desktop apps for Windows and Mac and mobile apps for iOS and Android, syncing projects via Fotor's own cloud storage (capacity varies by plan). There's no public API and no native Zapier or Slack integrations — if workflow automation matters, tools like Remove.bg (API-first) or Canva (API on higher tiers) are better fits. Fotor exports standard formats (JPG, PNG, PDF), so getting work out isn't a problem — it's specifically automation that's limited.

## Where it's a strong fit

Fotor earns its keep for fast, no-fuss photo cleanup: removing a background for a listing photo, batch-resizing a folder of images, sharpening a slightly blurry shot, or building a quick social graphic from a template. If your editing needs are mostly "make this look better, quickly, without learning software," the free tier often does the job, and Pro is reasonably priced if you outgrow it.

## Where to think twice

Skip Fotor, or go in cautious, if:

- **You need pixel-level control** — no layers-based masking, limited RAW support, and no plugins mean serious retouching still belongs in Photoshop or Affinity Photo.
- **You're wary of subscription billing** — given the volume of Trustpilot complaints about auto-renewal and refund friction, read the cancellation policy closely rather than assuming "cancel anytime" is frictionless.
- **You need guaranteed AI accuracy for client work** — AI background removal and enhancement can misfire on complex edges (hair, fur, glass) or unusual lighting, so budget time to clean up results manually.
- **You need API access or workflow automation** — Fotor doesn't offer a public API, so a developer-first tool will serve automated pipelines better.
- **You need enterprise compliance guarantees** — Fotor doesn't publicly advertise SOC 2 or similar certifications; regulated industries should confirm compliance directly with Fotor first.

## Bottom line

Fotor is a solid, low-friction photo editor for everyday use — background removal, batch edits, AI enhancement, and templated design all work well enough on the free tier to be genuinely useful, and Pro is fairly priced if you need more. It's not aimed at professionals who need fine-grained manual control, and the billing complaints around auto-renewal are common enough not to ignore. For casual users, small businesses, and content creators who want one browser tab for photos and simple design without a steep learning curve, it's a reasonable pick — just read the subscription terms first.

## FAQ

**Is Fotor free?**
Yes — Fotor Basic is free forever and includes core editing, background removal, and some AI tools, with limited credits and watermarks or resolution caps on select premium features. Paid plans remove most limits.

**How much does Fotor Pro cost?**
Roughly $8.99/month (often less billed annually), per third-party pricing listings, since Fotor's own site doesn't always display fixed figures publicly. Confirm current pricing on Fotor's pricing page before subscribing.

**Does Fotor have a free trial for paid plans?**
Yes on some plans, but user reviews report being charged automatically once the trial ends, so track the trial end date if you sign up.

**Is Fotor good for professional photo editing?**
It's good for fast, everyday edits — background removal, enhancement, batch processing — but lacks the layer-based control, RAW support, and plugin ecosystem professionals expect from Photoshop or Affinity Photo.

**Does Fotor have an API?**
No public developer API currently. If you need to automate background removal or enhancement inside your own workflow, a developer-first tool is a better fit.

**How does Fotor's billing work, and can I cancel anytime?**
Paid plans auto-renew by default. Multiple user reviews describe unexpected renewal charges and refund friction, so cancel manually before your renewal date rather than assuming a trial lapses on its own.

**What's the difference between Fotor's general AI tools and its Anime Generator?**
The AI Anime Generator is one specific feature inside the broader platform, focused on turning prompts or photos into anime-style art. See our [dedicated Fotor AI Anime Generator review](/blog/fotor-ai-anime-generator-review) for its styles, credit costs, and limitations.

**What are good alternatives to Fotor?**
Canva for combined photo-editing-plus-design work, Remove.bg for sharper single-purpose background removal, and Adobe Photoshop (or the lighter Adobe Express) for professional-grade editing control.

For more AI and software coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Copyleaks Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Copyleaks bundles AI detection, plagiarism checking, code and image scanning with LMS integrations. Here's the pricing and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Copyleaks worth it?

Copyleaks is worth it if you need AI-detection and plagiarism checking bundled into one enterprise-grade platform with deep LMS integrations (Canvas, Blackboard, Moodle, Brightspace) and an API for building detection into your own workflow. It's less compelling for a solo writer who just wants a quick, cheap one-off scan.

Copyleaks has been building web-scale plagiarism-detection infrastructure since 2015, well before "AI content detector" was a category, and later layered AI-generated-text detection on top of that same scanning engine. That history shows in what it's good at: it isn't just guessing whether a paragraph "sounds like ChatGPT" — it also crawls indexed web pages and academic sources to catch copied text, and extends detection to source code and AI-manipulated images. That combination separates it from detector-only tools like GPTZero or Winston AI, both already covered on this site (see our [GPTZero review](/blog/gptzero-review) and [Winston AI review](/blog/winston-ai-review)), which focus narrowly on text-origin detection without the same plagiarism-database breadth or LMS footprint.

### At a glance

| | Copyleaks |
|---|---|
| Starting price | From roughly $7.99–$8.99 per user/month for single-purpose plans (AI Detector or Plagiarism Checker), around $13.99/user/month combined |
| Free tier/trial | Limited free scans plus a free trial on paid plans |
| Best for | Schools, publishers, agencies and enterprises needing bundled AI + plagiarism detection with LMS/API integration |
| Standout feature | Combined AI-text, plagiarism, source-code, and AI-image detection on one scanning engine, with native LMS plugins |

## What Copyleaks actually is

Copyleaks is a cloud-based content-authenticity platform built by Copyleaks LTD, an Israel-founded company that started as a plagiarism-detection API before expanding into AI-generated-content detection as large language models went mainstream. It isn't a single-purpose tool — it's a family of detectors running on shared infrastructure:

- An **AI Content Detector** that flags text likely written by models like GPT-4/GPT-5-class systems, Gemini, Claude, and other LLMs.
- A **Plagiarism Checker** that cross-references submitted text against a web-scale index plus academic and licensed-publisher content.
- **Codeleaks**, a source-code plagiarism and AI-code-detection product aimed at computer science departments and dev teams.
- An **AI Image Detector** for identifying AI-generated or manipulated images — a feature most text-only detectors simply don't offer.

Copyleaks doesn't publish the exact model architecture behind its detector (most vendors treat that as proprietary), but describes its approach as NLP classifiers trained to spot patterns typical of machine-generated text, combined with its plagiarism-matching engine for source attribution. Copyleaks states its AI detector achieves accuracy above 99% in its own testing; that's a vendor claim, not an independently replicated result, and independent testers have reported mixed results in practice — treat it as a starting point, not a guarantee, the same caveat that applies to every detector on the market.

## Pricing

Copyleaks sells access a few different ways: individual/small-team subscriptions billed per user, education-specific plans priced per student or institution, and enterprise/API plans priced on scan volume. Publicly listed self-serve pricing (tracked by third-party marketplaces, since Copyleaks' own pricing page requires navigating a plan selector) breaks down roughly like this:

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| AI Content Detector | ~$7.99 per user/month | AI-text detection only, with a monthly page/word allowance |
| Plagiarism Checker | ~$8.99 per user/month | Web and academic plagiarism scanning only |
| AI + Plagiarism Detection | ~$13.99 per user/month | Combined detection, the most common self-serve pick |
| Education plans | Custom, per-student/per-institution pricing | LMS integration (Canvas, Blackboard, Brightspace, Moodle), bulk scanning, admin dashboards |
| Enterprise / API | Custom, volume-based | API access, white-label options, SSO, dedicated support |

A free trial and a limited free-scan option are available for testing the detector before you commit. **Note:** pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can shift quickly in this category — confirm current numbers on Copyleaks' pricing page before buying.

Compared to GPTZero's and Winston AI's page-based credit systems, Copyleaks' per-user seat pricing can get expensive fast for a department with many reviewers, since adding users beyond a small starting allotment increases cost per seat rather than pooling credits — worth mapping against your actual team size before an annual plan.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**1. Multi-detector bundling on one dashboard.** Instead of buying separate tools for plagiarism and AI detection, Copyleaks scans the same document for both in a single pass and returns one combined report — a real time saver over stitching together two vendors.

**2. Source-code plagiarism via Codeleaks.** Very few detectors in this space handle code at all. Codeleaks compares submitted code against public repositories and other student submissions, making Copyleaks one of the few realistic options for a CS department catching both AI-generated and copy-pasted programming assignments — something GPTZero and Winston AI don't attempt.

**3. AI-generated image detection.** As AI image generators have gotten harder to spot by eye, Copyleaks added a detector for manipulated or AI-generated images, useful for publishers, insurance-claim reviewers, and moderators needing more than text coverage.

**4. Broad multilingual support.** Copyleaks' detectors work across a wide range of languages (vendor materials cite over 100), which matters for international schools and global publishers where English-only detectors fall short.

**5. Native LMS and API integration.** Rather than requiring instructors to copy-paste text into a web app, Copyleaks plugs directly into Canvas, Blackboard, Brightspace, and Moodle, and exposes a REST API for teams building detection into their own submission pipeline.

## Who it's actually for

- **K-12 and higher-ed institutions** already running Canvas, Blackboard, Brightspace, or Moodle get the most from Copyleaks, since the LMS plugin puts results directly in the grading workflow.
- **Computer science departments** get a genuine edge from Codeleaks, which none of the general-purpose text detectors offer.
- **Publishers and content agencies** vetting freelance submissions benefit from the combined AI + plagiarism report in one pass, especially at scale via the API.
- **Solo bloggers or individual writers** checking their own drafts occasionally are probably overpaying — a cheaper single-purpose detector (or Copyleaks' free scans) covers that need without a seat commitment.
- **Enterprises in regulated industries** (insurance, legal, financial services) use the API/enterprise tier for document-authenticity checks at volume.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Combines AI, plagiarism, code, and image checks in one platform | Per-seat pricing gets expensive for larger review teams |
| Deep, native LMS integrations most rivals don't match | Pricing page is hard to parse without contacting sales for enterprise tiers |
| Codeleaks covers a niche (code plagiarism) almost no rival addresses | Vendor accuracy claims (99%+) aren't independently verified |
| API access for custom workflows | Model documentation isn't public, hard to audit how flags are generated |
| Broad multilingual coverage (100+ languages per vendor materials) | Free tier is limited; real evaluation usually needs a paid trial |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Copyleaks' API is the backbone of its enterprise story — built to be embedded into LMSs, CMSs, and internal review tools rather than used only as a standalone web app. Confirmed integrations include the major LMS platforms (Canvas, Blackboard, Brightspace, Moodle), a Microsoft Word add-in for checking documents without leaving the editor, and browser-extension options for quick web-based checks. For teams that need something more custom — say, auto-flagging AI-generated content in a CMS pipeline before publish — the REST API is the more relevant integration point than the consumer dashboard.

## Where it's a strong fit

Copyleaks earns its keep in institutional settings: a university needing both plagiarism and AI detection inside its LMS, a coding bootcamp catching copied assignments, or a content marketplace vetting freelance submissions at scale through the API. In these cases, the combined detector and integration depth save real operational overhead versus running two or three separate tools.

## Where to think twice

If you're an individual writer or student checking a handful of documents a month, the per-seat subscription model is probably more than you need — a free scan tool or a cheaper single-purpose detector goes further per dollar. Skip Copyleaks if you need a fully free, unlimited tool with no login; it isn't one. Also think twice if your workflow depends on knowing precisely why a document was flagged — like every AI detector on the market, Copyleaks' classifier decisions aren't fully transparent, and false positives on heavily edited human writing or non-native English text are a documented risk across this whole category, not unique to Copyleaks but also not something it has solved. And if strict on-prem/offline processing is a hard requirement, a cloud-based SaaS API won't satisfy that without a custom enterprise arrangement.

## Bottom line

Copyleaks makes the most sense as an institutional platform rather than a casual detector: if you're a school, publisher, or enterprise needing AI detection, plagiarism checking, and optionally code or image analysis wired into an LMS or internal workflow via API, it's one of the few vendors covering that much ground under one login. For a quick, occasional gut-check on whether a paragraph looks AI-written, its per-seat pricing is more commitment than the job calls for, and a lighter tool will do fine.

## FAQ

**Is Copyleaks accurate?**
Copyleaks claims above 99% accuracy in its own testing, but that's a vendor figure, not an independently replicated one. Expect occasional false positives, especially on heavily edited or non-native-English text, and treat any single scan as one data point rather than proof.

**Does Copyleaks have a free plan?**
Yes, a limited free-scan option exists alongside free trials of the paid plans, but the volume is small enough that most institutions move to a paid plan for real evaluation.

**How is Copyleaks different from Turnitin?**
Turnitin is the dominant plagiarism-checking incumbent in higher ed and has its own AI detector add-on. Copyleaks competes as a lower-cost, API-friendlier alternative with broader LMS support and adds source-code and image detection Turnitin doesn't bundle the same way.

**Can Copyleaks detect AI-generated code?**
Yes, through Codeleaks, built specifically for source-code plagiarism and AI-code detection — a niche most general detectors don't touch.

**Does Copyleaks store the documents I upload?**
Retention periods and data-handling terms vary by plan, particularly for education customers under FERPA-related agreements — confirm specifics for your plan directly with Copyleaks before uploading sensitive documents.

**How does Copyleaks compare to GPTZero or Winston AI?**
GPTZero and Winston AI (reviewed separately on this site) focus narrowly on AI-text detection with simpler credit-based pricing. Copyleaks trades some simplicity for broader coverage — plagiarism, code, and image detection alongside AI-text detection, plus deeper LMS integration.

**Is Copyleaks beginner-friendly?**
The scan-and-review workflow is straightforward, but plan selection (individual vs. education vs. enterprise/API) takes more research than a single-purpose competitor, and LMS/API setup is really built for an administrator, not an individual end user.

**What languages does Copyleaks support?**
More than 100 languages per vendor materials, making it a stronger fit than English-only detectors for international schools and global content teams — though accuracy in lower-resource languages should be verified against your own samples.

For more coverage of AI writing and detection tools, browse our [AI & software deals](/category/software) category, or see our existing reviews of [GPTZero](/blog/gptzero-review) and [Winston AI](/blog/winston-ai-review) for how the narrower, detector-only competitors compare.

title: Pixelcut Review 2026: AI Product Photo Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: Pixelcut bundles background removal, AI product scenes, batch editing and video into one app. Real pricing, features and verdict.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Pixelcut worth it for product photography and photo editing?

Pixelcut is worth it if you need fast, brand-consistent product shots, background removal, and light video editing from a phone or browser without hiring a photographer — its free tier and $10/month Pro plan cover most solo sellers, while the credit system can get tight for teams pushing high volumes of AI-generated scenes.

Unlike Remove.bg (a pure background-removal API) or Pebblely (styled product backgrounds only), Pixelcut bundles background removal, AI-generated product scenes, batch editing, upscaling, and basic video tools into one app that works on mobile and desktop. That breadth is the whole pitch — and also where the trade-offs show up.

### At a glance

| | Details |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (limited); Pro from $8/month billed annually |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — limited background removal, limited upscale, watermark-free exports |
| Best for | E-commerce sellers, social sellers, small brand teams needing fast product visuals |
| Standout feature | Batch product photo editing (up to 1,000–2,000 exports/month on paid plans) |

## What Pixelcut actually is

Pixelcut is an AI photo and video editing app built primarily for e-commerce sellers, dropshippers, and social media creators who need product and marketing imagery quickly. It ships as both a mobile app (iOS and Android) and a web app, which sets it apart from most competitors in this space that are web-only. The company says it has been used by more than 70 million people, and that its background-removal and image tools have been adopted internally by teams at large brands.

Pixelcut says its background removal is "proprietary," which likely means a fine-tuned segmentation model rather than a from-scratch foundation model — a common and reasonable approach for this category, but worth knowing before assuming every feature is built entirely in-house. For newer generative features, it plugs into third-party models: Nano Banana Pro for image generation and Sora 2 for video, plus a partnership with Topaz for some upscaling.

That mixed approach — some proprietary tooling, some licensed model access wrapped in a simpler interface — is the more interesting story than "another background remover." Where Remove.bg does one job well via API, and Pebblely focuses narrowly on styled product backdrops, Pixelcut tries to be the single app a small e-commerce operation uses from raw product photo to finished listing image, ad creative, or short product video.

## Pricing

Pixelcut runs three tiers: a free plan, a Pro plan, and a Business plan. Paid plans are billed either monthly or annually, with the annual option knocking about 20% off the effective monthly price.

| Plan | Price | Credits/Exports | Key inclusions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Limited | Limited background removal, limited upscale, watermark-free exports |
| Pro | $10/mo (monthly) or $8/mo (annual) | 600 AI credits/month, 1,000 batch exports/month | All AI models, unlimited background removal, unlimited upscale, 3-person team, commercial license |
| Business | $30/mo (monthly) or $24/mo (annual) | 3,600 AI credits/month, 2,000 batch exports/month | All AI models, unlimited background removal, unlimited upscale, 10-person team, commercial license |

"Unlimited background removal and upscale" on paid plans is a genuinely strong offer compared to per-image pricing tools like Remove.bg, where every export costs a credit. But the AI-generation side — product scenes, AI personas, and video through Nano Banana Pro or Sora 2 — draws from the monthly credit pool, not the "unlimited" bucket. A seller leaning heavily on AI-generated backgrounds and video will burn through 600 Pro-tier credits faster than the "unlimited" language on the pricing page might suggest.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm current numbers on [Pixelcut's official pricing page](https://www.pixelcut.ai/pricing) before subscribing, since AI tool pricing and credit allowances shift often.

## Core features walkthrough

**Background removal (image and video).** This is Pixelcut's original feature and still its most reliable one. It handles the usual product-photo cases — flat lay items, apparel on models, jewelry, electronics — cleanly, and unlike Remove.bg it also extends background removal to video clips, which is unusual for a tool in this price range.

**AI product photography.** Instead of hand-picking a handful of styled backdrops (Pebblely's approach), Pixelcut generates product scenes from text prompts or references and aims for what it calls "character consistency" across a batch — useful if you're shooting the same product line across dozens of listings and want visual continuity rather than one-off generated backgrounds that don't match each other.

**Batch editing.** This is the feature that most separates Pixelcut from single-image tools. Paid plans allow applying the same edit — background swap, resize, watermark removal, resolution upscale — across up to 1,000 (Pro) or 2,000 (Business) exports per month. For a seller managing a catalog of hundreds of SKUs, this is the difference between an afternoon of manual editing and a five-minute batch job.

**Upscaling up to 16x.** Useful for pulling a usable print or large-format ad image out of a low-resolution supplier photo, though as with any AI upscaler, extreme upscales on already-blurry source images can introduce artifacts rather than genuine detail — treat 16x as a ceiling, not a guarantee of print-ready quality on every input.

**AI actors/personas and Creative Agent.** A newer addition lets brands generate a consistent AI persona to use across marketing content instead of hiring a model for every shoot, and a natural-language "Creative Agent" mode chains together edits from a single prompt. These lean on the underlying third-party models (Nano Banana Pro, Sora 2) and are the features most likely to consume credits quickly.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo sellers and dropshippers** on Etsy, Shopify, or Amazon who need clean, consistent product photos without a studio — the free plan or entry-level Pro tier covers occasional use, and unlimited background removal alone often justifies the $8–10/month.
- **Small e-commerce teams** managing a growing catalog — the Pro plan's batch export allowance and 3-seat team access fit a small operations team cleaning up supplier photos at scale.
- **Agencies and larger brand teams** producing high-volume AI-generated creative and short video content will want Business, and should budget for the fact that heavy AI-generation and video use eats into the monthly credit pool faster than casual background-removal use does.
- **Anyone who mainly needs one clean cutout per week** may find the free tier or even a one-off tool like Remove.bg's pay-as-you-go API cheaper than a recurring Pixelcut subscription.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Combines background removal, AI scene generation, upscaling, and light video editing in one app | AI-generation and video features draw from a shared, capped credit pool even on paid plans |
| Mobile app and web app both fully usable, unlike most desktop-only competitors | "Proprietary" background removal claims aren't independently benchmarked against rivals |
| Batch editing scales to hundreds of product photos at once | Heavier AI workflows (personas, Sora 2 video) can burn credits fast on the Pro tier |
| Unlimited background removal and upscaling on paid plans | No fully free unlimited tier — free plan is capped |
| Commercial license included from the Pro tier up | Team seats are capped even on Business (10 users) — not built for large enterprise rosters |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Pixelcut offers an API for developers who want to build background removal, upscaling, or product-photo generation directly into their own storefront or app rather than using the consumer-facing editor. Beyond the API, it doesn't advertise a broad native integration marketplace (no direct Shopify app, Zapier connector, or Slack integration listed on its site as of this writing) — workflows that need automated syncing with a specific e-commerce platform will likely rely on the API or manual export/import rather than a plug-and-play integration. That's a gap worth checking against your stack before committing, especially compared to tools that do offer native storefront plugins.

## Where it's a strong fit

Pixelcut earns its keep for sellers who photograph products themselves (even on a phone) and need those photos cleaned up, backgrounded, resized, and batch-exported quickly for multiple listings or ad platforms. The combination of unlimited background removal, generous batch limits, and a mobile-first workflow makes it genuinely useful for someone shooting product photos on-site and editing them the same day, without opening a laptop.

It's also a reasonable pick for small teams that want one subscription covering photo cleanup, occasional AI-generated backdrops, and simple video trims, rather than stitching together three separate single-purpose tools.

## Where to think twice

If you need a fully free, unlimited tool for occasional single-image background removal, a one-off use of a free background remover will likely serve you better than a subscription. If your workflow depends heavily on AI-generated video or persona content, budget carefully — those features consume the shared credit pool, and it's easy to underestimate how fast 600 monthly credits go once video generation is involved. If your team needs enterprise-grade seat counts, SOC 2 documentation, or dedicated account management, Pixelcut's team plans top out at 10 seats and don't publish enterprise compliance certifications, so larger organizations should confirm requirements directly with Pixelcut's sales team before assuming fit. And if you need offline or on-premises processing for sensitive product imagery, Pixelcut is cloud-only, like virtually every tool in this category.

## Bottom line

Pixelcut is a solid, reasonably priced all-in-one option for sellers who want background removal, AI product scenes, and batch editing without juggling separate subscriptions for each. It doesn't do any single one of those jobs with the surgical focus of a specialist tool — Remove.bg's background cutouts and Pebblely's styled backdrops are each narrower and, in their own lane, no less capable — but the breadth and the mobile-first workflow make Pixelcut a sensible default for a small e-commerce operation that wants one tool rather than three.

## FAQ

**Is Pixelcut free to use?**
Yes, there's a free plan with limited background removal and limited upscaling, and exports are watermark-free. Heavier use, batch editing, and AI-generated scenes require a Pro or Business subscription.

**How much does Pixelcut Pro cost?**
Pro is $10/month billed monthly, or effectively $8/month when billed annually (a 20% discount). It includes 600 AI credits per month and 1,000 batch exports.

**What's the difference between Pixelcut and Remove.bg?**
Remove.bg is a narrower, API-first background-removal tool priced per image or via subscription. Pixelcut bundles background removal with AI product photo generation, batch editing, upscaling, and video tools in one app, with unlimited background removal included on paid plans.

**What's the difference between Pixelcut and Pebblely?**
Pebblely focuses specifically on generating styled AI backgrounds for product photos starting around $9/month. Pixelcut covers that same use case plus background removal, batch processing across hundreds of images, upscaling, and basic video editing, at a comparable starting price.

**Does Pixelcut have a commercial use license?**
Yes — a commercial license is included starting with the Pro plan, which matters if you're using edited images for paid listings or ad campaigns.

**Can I use Pixelcut on mobile?**
Yes, Pixelcut has native iOS and Android apps in addition to its web app, which is less common among AI photo-editing tools that tend to be desktop/web-only.

**Does Pixelcut offer an API?**
Yes, Pixelcut provides an API for developers who want to integrate background removal, upscaling, or image generation into their own products rather than using the app directly.

**Is Pixelcut good for beginners?**
Yes — the interface is built around simple prompts and one-tap actions (remove background, upscale, generate scene) rather than a full editing suite, so it doesn't require design experience to get usable results quickly.
