title: GitMind Review 2026: AI Mind Mapping, Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: GitMind turns prompts, PDFs, audio and video into AI-generated mind maps and flowcharts. Here's the pricing, features and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is GitMind worth using for AI mind mapping?

GitMind is a solid pick if you want to turn messy notes, PDFs, articles, or a single prompt into a structured mind map or flowchart in seconds, and its free plan is generous enough to test that workflow properly. It's less convincing as a full team whiteboard replacement — for that, dedicated tools with deeper real-time collaboration go further.

### At a glance

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | $9/month, or $4.08/month billed annually |
| Free tier | Yes — up to 10 mind maps/whiteboards, 30 images per mind map |
| Best for | Solo users and small teams turning text, PDFs or prompts into mind maps and flowcharts fast |
| Standout feature | One-prompt and file-to-mind-map AI generation across text, PDF, audio, video and website inputs |

## What GitMind actually is

GitMind is a web, desktop and mobile mind-mapping and diagramming app; its own site doesn't name a parent company, describing its mission simply as helping users "build their second brains" through mind mapping. It started as a straightforward online mind-map editor and has since layered AI generation on top: instead of building a tree of nodes by hand, you can hand GitMind a prompt, a block of text, a PDF, a YouTube link, an audio file, or a webpage, and it will attempt to structure that content into a mind map, flowchart, or other diagram automatically.

The company doesn't publish which underlying language model powers the AI generation — treat "AI mind map" here as a proprietary pipeline built on a commercial LLM rather than a named, verifiable model. GitMind says it serves over 10 million users across 160+ countries, a figure that comes from the company's own marketing and isn't independently auditable.

Where GitMind differentiates itself from a plain mind-mapping app like classic FreeMind or XMind is input flexibility: most competitors start from a blank canvas or a text prompt, while GitMind explicitly supports turning PDFs, recorded audio, video transcripts and web pages into a visual structure, aimed at students, researchers and content creators who spend more time digesting existing material than starting from scratch.

## GitMind pricing

GitMind runs a fairly standard freemium model: a genuinely usable free tier, a subscription that unlocks unlimited use, and a rarer one-time multi-year option.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free (Basic) | $0 | Up to 10 mind maps/whiteboards, 30 images per mind map, 10 image uploads per whiteboard, 1 workspace ("planet") with up to 5 members, basic export, access on web/desktop/mobile |
| Monthly | $9/month | Unlimited mind maps and whiteboards, up to 500 images per mind map, 30 images per whiteboard, up to 5 workspaces with 30 members each, watermark-free exports, HD export, priority support |
| Annual | $4.08/month, billed annually | Same feature set as the monthly plan, at a lower effective monthly rate |
| 3-year plan | One-time payment (limited-time offer, has appeared around $79) | Same benefits as the annual/monthly plans for a fixed multi-year term instead of a recurring subscription |

GitMind also sells metered AI credits separately for specific generation features, and offers custom pricing for education and volume/team purchases. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — confirm current numbers on GitMind's own pricing page before subscribing, since multi-year promotional offers in particular tend to be time-limited.

There's no GitMind store entry on TheSmartFares yet, so there's no coupon page to link here — check [AI & software deals](/category/software) for other verified software discounts in the meantime.

## Core features that actually matter

**AI mind map generation from a single prompt.** Type a topic or question and GitMind drafts a branching mind map you can then rearrange, expand or prune. It's genuinely faster than building a map node-by-node when you're starting from a blank page, though the first draft is usually a starting skeleton rather than a finished document — expect to edit branch labels and reorganize depth after generation.

**File-to-mind-map and PDF summarization.** Upload a PDF, article, or block of text and GitMind extracts a structure from it — useful for turning a dense research paper or report into something skimmable before a meeting, or for students converting lecture notes into a study map.

**Video and audio-to-text conversion.** GitMind can pull a transcript from a YouTube link or an uploaded audio/video file and then summarize or map that content. This is one of the more distinctive features versus a plain mind-mapping tool — most competitors don't touch media transcription at all.

**AI flowchart and diagram generation.** Beyond mind maps, GitMind extends the same prompt/file-based generation to flowcharts, UML diagrams, ER diagrams and simple infographics, which matters if your actual need is a process diagram rather than a radial mind map.

**Built-in AI chatbot for document Q&A.** After uploading a document, you can ask GitMind questions about it directly rather than only getting a static summary — closer to a lightweight ChatPDF-style experience layered on top of the mapping tool.

## Who GitMind is actually for

- **Students and researchers** digesting long PDFs, lecture recordings or articles get the most direct value from the file-to-map and transcript features, and the free tier's 10-map limit is enough to test the workflow before subscribing.
- **Content creators and course builders** outlining video scripts or course modules can use the video/audio transcription feature to turn a rough recording into a structured outline quickly.
- **Small teams** collaborating on brainstorms or documentation can use the paid plan's multi-workspace and member limits, though collaboration depth is basic compared to a dedicated team whiteboard.
- **Solo project planners** who want a fast way to turn messy notes into a visual plan, without paying for a heavier all-in-one whiteboard suite, are well served by the $9/month or discounted annual tier.
- **Enterprise teams needing deep real-time collaboration or compliance certifications** should look elsewhere — GitMind doesn't publicly advertise SOC 2 or enterprise-grade admin controls.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Free tier is usable enough to actually test the workflow, not just a locked demo | AI-generated first drafts often need real editing before they're presentation-ready |
| Unusually broad input support (PDF, audio, video, web pages, prompts) | Underlying AI model isn't disclosed, so output quality is hard to benchmark against named-model competitors |
| Annual pricing is inexpensive relative to broader "AI workspace" suites | Real-time collaboration and permissions are lighter than dedicated whiteboard tools like Miro |
| Cross-platform: web, desktop, mobile, and a Chrome extension | Some AI features are metered separately via credits on top of the subscription |
| One-time multi-year plan avoids recurring billing for users who don't want a subscription | Multi-year promotional pricing has appeared as a limited-time offer, not a standing plan |

## Integrations and ecosystem

GitMind's ecosystem is built around its own apps rather than a large third-party integration marketplace: native apps for Windows and Mac, mobile apps for iOS and Android, and a Chrome extension for capturing web pages directly into a map. There's no publicly documented open API, and no listed native Zapier, Slack, or Notion integrations at the time of writing — confirm current integration support directly on GitMind's site if deep workflow automation is a requirement.

## Where it's a strong fit

GitMind earns its keep when the starting point is existing content rather than a blank canvas — a PDF you need to skim faster, a lecture recording you'd rather review as an outline, or a rough set of notes you want turned into something you can present. The free tier's 10-map cap is enough to genuinely trial that before paying, and the $4.08/month annual rate undercuts most competing "AI workspace" subscriptions if the mapping and summarizing features end up being your main use case.

## Where to think twice

If your actual need is heavy real-time team collaboration — multiple people editing the same board with granular comments, voting, and integrations into a broader project-management stack — a dedicated whiteboard platform will serve you better; see our [Miro AI review](/blog/miro-ai-review) for a heavier-duty comparison point. Skip GitMind if you need a fully free, unlimited tool long-term, since the 10-map cap on the free plan binds quickly for anyone mapping more than the occasional project. Enterprise buyers who need SOC 2 or similar compliance documentation, granular role-based permissions, or an audited API should also look elsewhere, since GitMind doesn't publish that kind of trust documentation. And because the underlying AI model isn't named, teams that need to vet model provenance for procurement reasons won't get enough disclosure from GitMind's own materials.

## Bottom line

GitMind does one thing convincingly: it takes content you already have — a PDF, a transcript, a rough set of notes, or just a topic prompt — and turns it into a visual map faster than building one by hand. The free tier is generous enough to judge that fit before paying, and the annual plan is cheap enough that upgrading isn't a big commitment. It's not trying to be a full enterprise whiteboard platform, and it shouldn't be judged as one — for straightforward personal or small-team mind mapping and diagram generation from existing content, it's a reasonable, low-cost tool worth trialing on the free plan first.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is GitMind free to use?**
Yes, GitMind has a free "Basic" plan that includes up to 10 mind maps or whiteboards, up to 30 images per mind map, and access across web, desktop and mobile. It's usable for genuinely testing the tool, though the map limit will bind quickly for anyone with ongoing projects.

**How much does GitMind cost after the free tier?**
The subscription is $9/month billed monthly, or roughly $4.08/month when billed annually. GitMind has also run a limited-time multi-year one-time-payment offer; confirm current availability and pricing directly on GitMind's pricing page since promotional plans change.

**What AI model does GitMind use?**
GitMind doesn't publicly disclose which underlying language model powers its AI mind map, flowchart, and summarization features. Treat the "AI-generated" claims as a proprietary pipeline rather than a named, independently benchmarked model.

**Does GitMind handle my data securely?**
GitMind's site references standard data-handling practices, but it doesn't publish SOC 2, ISO 27001, or similar third-party compliance certifications. If your organization requires formal compliance documentation for uploaded documents or PDFs, verify GitMind's current data-handling and retention policy directly with their team before uploading sensitive material.

**Is GitMind good for beginners?**
Yes — the prompt-to-mind-map and file-to-mind-map flows are simpler to start with than a blank-canvas mind-mapping tool, since GitMind gives you a first draft to edit rather than requiring you to build the structure node by node from scratch.

**What are the best GitMind alternatives?**
For heavier real-time team collaboration, our [Miro AI review](/blog/miro-ai-review) covers a more collaboration-focused alternative. For simpler PDF-specific summarization and Q&A without the mind-mapping layer, dedicated PDF chat tools are worth comparing as well.

**Can GitMind summarize YouTube videos?**
Yes, GitMind can pull a transcript from a YouTube link and generate a summary or mind map from it, which is a distinctive feature versus most plain mind-mapping competitors that don't touch video content at all.

**Does GitMind work offline or on-premise?**
GitMind is a cloud-based service delivered through web, desktop and mobile apps; there's no publicly advertised on-premise or fully offline deployment option, so teams that specifically require offline or self-hosted use should look at other tools.

For more verified software offers, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: OpenCopilot Review 2026: Is This Open-Source Copilot Dead?
excerpt: OpenCopilot's open-source AI copilot framework is archived and unmaintained. Here's what it did, its license, and what to use instead.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is OpenCopilot still worth using in 2026?

No — OpenCopilot is not actively maintained. The open-source repository was archived by its creators (OpenChat AI) on March 26, 2025, and its README now reads simply "No longer maintained." It's still usable as-is (MIT licensed, Docker-based, self-hostable), but with no security patches, no bug fixes, and no roadmap, it's a project to study or fork, not one to build production infrastructure on today.

### At a glance

| | Details |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free — MIT-licensed, self-hosted, no vendor pricing tiers |
| Free tier/trial | N/A — you self-host on your own infrastructure and pay only for your LLM API usage |
| Best for | Developers who want to study or fork an open-source "API-calling copilot" architecture |
| Standout feature | Turns a Swagger/OpenAPI 3.0 spec directly into an AI copilot that can call your product's own endpoints |
| Current status | Archived / no longer maintained (as of March 26, 2025) |

## What OpenCopilot actually was

OpenCopilot was an open-source framework, built by a team operating as OpenChat AI, for adding a custom AI copilot to your own SaaS product. Unlike a typical FAQ chatbot, its core idea was action-calling: you gave it your product's API definition (Swagger/OpenAPI 3.0), it validated that schema, and then an LLM decided whether a user's natural-language request ("cancel my last order," "create a new support case about X") mapped to one of your real API endpoints — filling in the request payload automatically and executing the call.

The project lived at `github.com/openchatai/OpenCopilot` (now redirected to `opencx-labs/copilot` after an organizational rename), was MIT licensed, and had picked up meaningful open-source traction before it stopped: roughly 5,100 GitHub stars, 396 forks, and over 3,000 commits across its life, starting in August 2023 and ending with its archive commit in March 2025.

It shipped as a self-hosted Docker stack with three main pieces:

- **llm-server** — the backend service that handled the LLM calls, API-schema validation, and action execution.
- **dashboard** — a web console (reachable at `http://localhost:8888` after setup) for configuring your copilot, uploading your OpenAPI spec, and defining fallback "flows" for complex multi-step requests.
- **copilot-widget** — an embeddable chat bubble, described in the docs as installable "in less than 10 lines of code" inside a web or desktop app.

Setup ran through a `make install` (or `make install-arm` for Apple Silicon) command that spun up the Docker containers, after which you dropped an OpenAI API key into an `.env` file. There was also a companion TypeScript SDK (`openchatai/typescript-sdk`) for developers who wanted to talk to the copilot programmatically rather than through the widget alone.

## Core capabilities (per the project's own documentation)

Based on OpenCopilot's own README before the archive, this is what it was built to do:

- **Bulk API import via OpenAPI 3.0** — you point it at a Swagger spec instead of hand-wiring individual actions, which made onboarding an existing REST API faster than most no-code chatbot builders.
- **Automatic field population** — the project's docs describe it inferring payload fields from context, e.g. filling in a "title" field from a user's phrasing rather than asking a follow-up question for every field.
- **Response transformation** — API responses were converted back into natural-language replies rather than raw JSON dumped into the chat window.
- **"Flows" for complex requests** — for multi-step or ambiguous actions the LLM couldn't reliably infer on its own, developers could define an explicit flow to guide the copilot.
- **Self-hosted by default** — there was no hosted SaaS tier baked into the open-source repo itself; the README pointed users toward a separate managed "cloud" version at `cloud.opencopilot.so` for teams that didn't want to run the Docker stack themselves, but that link no longer resolves to an active product page.

The project's own documentation was also candid about a real limitation: it explicitly said it "is not suitable for handling large APIs" without writing custom JSON transformers — a caveat worth repeating here rather than glossing over, since it's the kind of thing a vendor pitch would usually omit.

## Where the project — and the company — went

This is the part most surface-level "is X good" write-ups skip: OpenCopilot didn't just go quiet, its maintainers moved on to a different, commercial product. The GitHub organization behind it now operates as OpenCX Labs, and the company's current product is **Open** (marketed at `open.cx`), an enterprise customer-support automation platform built around a proprietary engine the company calls "Agent 5." Open is a paid product with a pay-per-resolution pricing model (the company states $0.90 per automated resolution, with no per-seat fees) rather than an open-source framework, and it targets multi-channel support automation (voice, chat, email, messaging, social) with SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications and EU data residency — a very different audience than a self-hosted developer framework.

In other words: if you're evaluating OpenCopilot today because you found it while researching AI copilot tools, the practical options are (1) self-host the archived MIT-licensed code as-is, accepting there will be no more fixes, (2) look at the same team's current commercial product if you actually need supported, enterprise-grade customer-support automation, or (3) pick an actively maintained alternative built for a similar job.

Because pricing, feature availability and project status all move fast in this space, everything above reflects what was verifiable via the GitHub repository, its commit history, and OpenCX Labs' current site as of this post's date — recheck the source repo directly before relying on it for a new project.

## How it compares to other self-hosted / builder-style AI chatbot tools

If the appeal of OpenCopilot was "self-hosted and open," a few tools on this site cover similar territory and are still maintained:

- **[Hexabot Review](/blog/hexabot-review)** covers a self-hosted, open-source AI chatbot builder that's still active — closer to a traditional multi-channel chatbot platform than an API-action copilot, but the same self-hosting appeal.
- **[Chatbase Review](/blog/chatbase-review)** and **[CustomGPT.ai Review](/blog/customgpt-ai-review)** cover hosted, no-code copilot builders for teams that don't want to run their own infrastructure — the opposite trade-off from OpenCopilot's Docker-and-API-key approach.
- **[Wonderchat Review](/blog/wonderchat-review)** is a simpler hosted FAQ-style chatbot, a useful baseline for what "answer questions from docs, no API-calling" looks like by comparison.

None of these are drop-in replacements for OpenCopilot's specific architecture — turning a Swagger spec into an LLM-driven action executor is a narrower, more developer-centric job than most hosted chatbot builders solve for. If that's specifically what you need, expect to fork the archived code, build a similar layer on top of an LLM's native function-calling/tool-use APIs, or evaluate current commercial AI agent platforms that explicitly support API/tool actions.

## Who this is (and isn't) for

**Worth a look if:**

- You're a developer who wants to study a real, moderately popular open-source implementation of LLM function-calling wired to OpenAPI specs.
- You need a one-off, internal, non-production proof of concept and are comfortable with unsupported code.
- You want to fork the codebase and maintain your own patched version in-house.

**Think twice if:**

- You need active support, security patches, or a vendor roadmap — none of that exists here anymore.
- You need a production customer-facing copilot without in-house engineering resources to maintain a forked, unsupported stack.
- You were hoping for the "cloud" hosted version referenced in the old docs — that link path no longer leads to an active signup product tied to the open-source project.
- You need compliance certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001) or enterprise SLAs — those now sit with OpenCX Labs' commercial "Open" product, not the open-source repo.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free, MIT-licensed, fully self-hosted — no vendor lock-in | Archived and no longer maintained as of March 2025 |
| Genuinely useful architecture: OpenAPI spec → LLM-driven action execution | No security patches or bug fixes going forward |
| Real open-source traction (5.1k+ stars, 396 forks, 3,000+ commits) to learn from | Project's own docs admit it struggles with large/complex APIs without custom transformers |
| Docker-based setup with a documented install path | The "cloud" managed version referenced in its docs is no longer an active product tied to this project |
| Includes a TypeScript SDK and embeddable widget | No commercial support channel — the team's current product (Open) targets a different, enterprise use case |

## Integrations and ecosystem

OpenCopilot's integration surface was narrow by design: it connected to whatever REST API you described via an OpenAPI 3.0 spec, used OpenAI's API as its LLM backend (per setup instructions requiring an `OPENAI_API_KEY`), and exposed a TypeScript SDK plus an embeddable chat widget. It didn't advertise native Zapier, Slack, or CRM connectors — those would need to be built as API endpoints your own backend exposes, which the copilot could then call. That's a different integration model from most hosted chatbot builders, which ship pre-built connectors instead of asking you to expose your own API surface.

## Bottom line

OpenCopilot was a genuinely interesting piece of open-source infrastructure — one of the earlier public attempts at wiring an LLM directly to a product's own OpenAPI-defined actions rather than just answering questions from a knowledge base. But it's now a historical artifact rather than a live option: archived, unmaintained, and effectively superseded by its own creators' pivot to a commercial enterprise product under a different brand. If you found this page because you're choosing an AI copilot framework today, treat OpenCopilot as a reference architecture to learn from, not a dependency to build on — and look at actively maintained self-hosted alternatives, or a hosted builder, depending on how much infrastructure you want to own.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is OpenCopilot still maintained?**
No. The GitHub repository was archived on March 26, 2025, with the README updated to state "No longer maintained." No further commits, patches, or releases are expected.

**Is OpenCopilot free to use?**
Yes, the codebase itself is MIT licensed and free to self-host. You'd still pay for whatever LLM API (e.g., OpenAI) it calls, plus your own hosting/infrastructure costs.

**What license is OpenCopilot released under?**
MIT, one of the most permissive open-source licenses — you can fork, modify, and use it commercially without needing to open-source your own changes.

**What happened to the "cloud" hosted version mentioned in OpenCopilot's docs?**
The archived documentation referenced a managed cloud version at `cloud.opencopilot.so`. That URL no longer resolves to an active signup product connected to the open-source project; the team behind OpenCopilot now operates a different commercial product, Open (at open.cx), aimed at enterprise customer support automation rather than the original developer-focused copilot framework.

**Is OpenCopilot a good alternative to Chatbase or CustomGPT.ai?**
Not directly — those are actively maintained, hosted, no-code chatbot builders, while OpenCopilot was a self-hosted, developer-oriented framework for calling your product's own APIs rather than answering questions from documents. For a maintained, self-hosted alternative with a similar spirit, see our [Hexabot Review](/blog/hexabot-review).

**Can I still download and run OpenCopilot?**
Yes — the code remains publicly available and MIT licensed, and its Docker-based setup instructions (`make install` / `make install-arm`) still describe a working local install as of the last commit. Archived means no more updates, not that the code was deleted.

**Does OpenCopilot support any LLM besides OpenAI's models?**
Its setup instructions specifically call for an `OPENAI_API_KEY`, indicating OpenAI was the primary supported provider. Since the project is unmaintained, verify current compatibility yourself in the archived source before assuming support for other providers.

**Is there a supported, commercial equivalent from the same team?**
Yes — OpenChat AI's parent organization now operates as OpenCX Labs and sells Open (open.cx), an enterprise customer-support automation platform with pay-per-resolution pricing and SOC 2/ISO 27001 certification. It is a different product built for a different audience than the original open-source copilot framework, not a hosted continuation of OpenCopilot itself.

For more currently maintained options in this space, browse our [AI & software deals](/category/software) coverage.

title: FileGPT Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: FileGPT review 2026: pricing tiers, token limits, multi-format document chat features, and honest pros and cons for researchers and teams.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is FileGPT worth it for chatting with documents?

FileGPT is a competent pick if you regularly need to query PDFs, Word docs, audio, video, or even handwritten scans in one place, but its token-based pricing and lack of a real free tier make it a harder sell than cheaper single-purpose tools like ChatPDF for someone who just wants to ask a PDF a few questions.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $100/year (Basic plan) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Free trial only, no permanent free plan |
| **Best for** | Multi-format research (PDF + audio/video + handwritten docs) |
| **Standout feature** | Cross-source querying across multiple uploaded files at once |

FileGPT bills itself as a large-language-model app for "chatting" with files rather than reading them line by line. Where it tries to stand apart from the crowded document-chat category is format breadth: instead of just PDFs, it also ingests Word files, plain text, audio and video recordings, YouTube links, webpages, and even handwritten documents run through text extraction first. The pitch is that you can drop a mixed pile of source material — a lecture recording, a scanned handwritten note, a research PDF — into one collection and ask questions across all of it at once.

## What FileGPT actually is

FileGPT is built as an LLM-powered application layered on top of document parsing and retrieval, though the vendor doesn't publicly name which underlying model (GPT-4, GPT-4o, or otherwise) it uses for a given plan — worth confirming with support if that matters for your use case. The workflow is straightforward: upload one or more files (or point it at a webpage or YouTube video), wait for it to parse and index the content, then ask questions in a chat interface and get answers grounded in that material.

The company behind FileGPT doesn't publish detailed "about us" information beyond contact channels (email, social accounts, a Discord community), so if you need vendor transparency for a compliance review, flag that gap before committing budget.

## FileGPT pricing (as of this review)

FileGPT structures its plans around monthly "token" allowances rather than a flat number of questions or documents, a different mental model than tools that cap you at X PDFs per month. Pricing below reflects yearly billing on FileGPT's pricing page, advertised as two months free versus paying monthly.

| Plan | Price (yearly) | Files/collections | Max file size | Monthly tokens | Notable extras |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | $100/year | 10 | 100 MB | 6,000 | Documents, webpages, YouTube; Discord support |
| Pro | $180/year | 20 | 200 MB | 12,000 | Adds audio/video/image, unstructured PDFs, handwriting |
| Growth | $480/year | — | — | 36,000 | Adds website embedding |
| Elite | $980/year | — | — | 75,000 | Basic usage analytics |
| Enterprise | $3,980/year | — | — | 300,000 | Priority processing, white-label (no FileGPT branding) |

FileGPT's site references monthly billing as an option too ("yearly plans have 2 months free"), but doesn't display monthly per-plan rates directly — confirm current monthly pricing on the official [pricing page](https://filegpt.app/pricing) before subscribing if you'd rather not commit annually.

There's no permanent free plan; FileGPT offers a free trial to test parsing quality and answer accuracy on your own documents before paying, but doesn't publish exact trial limits (upload count or token allowance). Pricing, trial terms, and feature availability here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly in the AI-tools space — double-check the live pricing page before buying.

## Core features that differentiate FileGPT

**Multi-format ingestion.** Most document-chat tools in this space are PDF-only. FileGPT's ability to also ingest Word documents, plain text, audio, video, YouTube links, and webpages in the same collection is the single biggest reason to pick it over a narrower competitor — if your research pile is genuinely mixed-format, consolidating into one tool saves real time.

**Handwritten document support.** FileGPT specifically calls out handwriting recognition as a Pro-tier-and-up feature, running scanned handwritten notes through text extraction before making them queryable. This is a niche but genuinely differentiated capability among document-chat tools, most of which assume typed, digital-native text.

**Cross-source querying.** Rather than restricting you to one file per chat session, FileGPT lets you ask questions that pull answers from multiple uploaded sources in a single collection — useful for literature reviews, due-diligence document sets, or comparing several reports at once.

**Token-metered usage.** Instead of a simple "10 PDFs per month" cap, usage is tracked in tokens that scale with document length and number of questions asked. This rewards light, targeted usage but means a handful of very long documents or chatty back-and-forth sessions can burn through a plan's allowance faster than expected.

**Website embedding (Growth tier and up).** Higher plans let you embed a FileGPT-powered chat widget on your site, turning uploaded documentation into a customer-facing Q&A assistant — closer to a support chatbot than a personal research tool.

## Who FileGPT is actually for

- **Students and independent researchers** working mainly with typed PDFs and webpages fit comfortably on the Basic plan, provided monthly usage stays modest — 6,000 tokens isn't much for extended back-and-forth chats on dense material.
- **Analysts, consultants, or content researchers** juggling mixed media (recorded interviews, scanned notes, long reports) are the clearest fit for the Pro tier, since that's where audio/video and handwriting support unlock.
- **Small teams building an internal or customer-facing knowledge assistant** are better served by Growth or Elite, where website embedding and usage analytics become available — though it's worth comparing against dedicated chatbot-builder tools at that price point.
- **Larger organizations needing white-labeling, priority processing, and compliance assurances** land in Enterprise territory, but should get direct answers from FileGPT on data handling and SLAs before signing an annual contract.
- **Anyone who just wants to ask a single PDF a few questions for free** is better served by a lighter, PDF-specific tool with a genuine free tier — FileGPT's format breadth is wasted if you never touch audio, video, or handwriting.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Supports far more file types than typical PDF-chat tools (audio, video, YouTube, handwriting) | No permanent free plan — trial only |
| Cross-source querying across a whole collection, not just one file at a time | Token-based limits are harder to predict than a flat document cap |
| Website embedding option for teams wanting a public-facing document assistant | Underlying AI model isn't clearly disclosed on the marketing site |
| Tiered plans scale from solo researcher up to enterprise white-label use | Company/team background is thin on the public site — limited transparency |
| Handwritten-document text extraction is a genuinely uncommon feature | Entry-tier file-size and token limits (100 MB, 6,000 tokens) are tight for heavy users |

## Integrations and ecosystem

FileGPT's public marketing pages don't advertise a developer API, browser extension, or native Zapier/Slack integrations at the time of this review — its main extensibility feature is the website-embed widget available from the Growth plan upward, letting businesses expose a document-trained chat assistant on their own site. If API access or workflow-automation integrations matter for your use case, confirm directly with FileGPT's support (email or Discord) before subscribing, since roadmap features can ship without being reflected in older marketing copy.

## Where FileGPT is a strong fit

If your work involves genuinely mixed-format source material — scanned handwritten notes, recorded interviews, and PDF reports you'd otherwise process with three separate tools — FileGPT's single-collection, cross-source chat is a real time-saver. It's also reasonable for a small business turning a folder of product documentation into an embeddable support widget without building a custom RAG pipeline from scratch.

## Where to think twice

FileGPT is not the right choice if you need a fully free tool for occasional PDF questions — there's no free tier, only a trial, so casual users end up paying for capacity they rarely use. It's also not ideal if your organization needs clear, published details on data handling, model provenance, or compliance certifications, since FileGPT's public site is thin on that documentation compared to larger, established AI platforms. And if predictable, flat-rate billing matters to your budgeting, the token-metered model needs more attention than a simple per-document cap — heavy chat sessions on long files can eat through an allowance faster than expected.

## Bottom line

FileGPT earns its place among document-chat tools by supporting more file types than most competitors, particularly audio, video, and handwritten text — a genuine differentiator from PDF-only tools like ChatPDF. But the absence of a permanent free plan, thin public information about the company and model, and a token-metering system that takes getting used to mean it suits people who know they need its specific format breadth, not casual users wanting a quick, free way to query a single PDF.

## FAQ

**Is FileGPT free?**
No. FileGPT offers a free trial to test the product, but there is no permanent free plan — using it beyond the trial requires a paid subscription starting at $100/year on the Basic tier.

**What file types does FileGPT support?**
PDFs, Word documents, plain text files, audio and video recordings, YouTube video links, webpages, and handwritten documents (via text extraction), with broader multimedia and handwriting support unlocked starting on the Pro plan.

**How is usage measured on FileGPT?**
Through a monthly token allowance rather than a flat document count — longer files and more extensive chat sessions consume more tokens, so heavy users should watch their allowance rather than assuming a fixed number of "questions."

**Does FileGPT have an API?**
FileGPT's public marketing pages don't advertise a developer API as of this review; its main integration option is an embeddable website chat widget available on Growth-tier plans and above. Confirm current API availability directly with FileGPT if that's a requirement.

**Is FileGPT good for beginners?**
The core workflow — upload a file, ask questions — is simple enough for non-technical users. The pricing structure (tokens, tiered file-size caps) takes more attention than tools with flat monthly document limits.

**How does FileGPT compare to ChatPDF?**
ChatPDF is a narrower, PDF-focused tool, while FileGPT covers far more formats (audio, video, YouTube, handwriting) and supports querying across multiple sources at once. If you only work with PDFs, a dedicated PDF tool may be simpler and cheaper; if your material is mixed-format, FileGPT's breadth is the more relevant advantage. See our [ChatPDF review](/blog/chatpdf-review) for a closer look.

**What happens if I exceed my monthly token limit?**
FileGPT indicates upgrading is required to increase usage once a plan's limit is reached; exact overage handling should be confirmed with support before relying on it for high-volume work.

**Does FileGPT support team or enterprise use?**
Yes — Elite and Enterprise tiers add usage analytics, priority processing, and white-labeling, aimed at businesses embedding document chat into their own products rather than individual researchers.

Looking for other document-chat options? Compare FileGPT against our [ChatPDF review](/blog/chatpdf-review) and [CelestialPDF review](/blog/celestialpdf-review), or browse more [AI & software deals](/category/software) for current offers on productivity tools.

title: MindsDB Review 2026: Open-Source AI Data Query Engine
excerpt: MindsDB federates SQL queries across 200+ databases for AI agents. Here's the pricing reality, features and who should self-host it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is MindsDB worth using?

MindsDB is worth it if you need a single SQL-based layer to federate live queries across 200+ databases and unstructured sources, then ground AI agents or semantic search in that data without building a custom ETL pipeline. It's a poor fit if you want a polished, managed SaaS product with clear self-serve cloud pricing, since MindsDB's own hosted cloud offering has effectively been folded into a separate, broader product.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (open source, self-hosted) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Full engine is free under Elastic License 2.0; no separate paid MindsDB Cloud tier currently advertised |
| **Best for** | Data/platform engineers building AI agents or semantic search over existing databases |
| **Standout feature** | Federated SQL queries across 200+ live data sources without ETL |

## What MindsDB actually is

MindsDB started out marketed as an "AI layer for databases" — a way to train and run machine-learning models directly from SQL, without moving data into a separate ML pipeline. The current version, now described by its own maintainers as a "query engine for AI analytics," has narrowed that pitch: it's a federated query layer that lets you connect to more than 200 data sources — Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Snowflake, Salesforce, Slack, flat files, and more — through one SQL dialect, then layer semantic search and AI agents on top of that unified view.

The project is open source (Elastic License 2.0) and actively maintained: as of writing, the PyPI package sits at version 26.1.0, with the GitHub repo shipping frequent releases. It runs self-hosted via Docker or pip, with an HTTP API, a MySQL-compatible wire protocol, and MCP (Model Context Protocol) support for wiring it into agent frameworks.

One thing worth flagging up front: MindsDB Inc. has shifted its primary commercial focus toward a separate product called MindsHub — an agent workspace for automating knowledge work, with its own pricing page and cloud console. As of this writing, mindsdb.com and docs.mindsdb.com both redirect to MindsHub's site and docs, and MindsDB Cloud's old hosted signup no longer resolves. The open-source "Query Engine" itself is still maintained and documented (via GitHub Pages and the GitHub repo), but a straightforward self-serve "MindsDB Cloud" tier doesn't appear to exist in its old form anymore. Confirm current cloud/enterprise availability directly with MindsDB before assuming a hosted plan is available.

## Pricing: open source core, unclear hosted tier

There's no conventional SaaS pricing table to report here, and that's itself useful information. Here's what's actually verifiable:

| Option | Cost | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Self-hosted (Docker / pip) | Free | Full query engine, connectors, knowledge bases, agents, SQL/HTTP/MySQL-protocol/MCP APIs — source-available under Elastic License 2.0 |
| Enterprise support | Contact sales | Historically offered for self-hosted deployments; confirm current terms directly, since this isn't on a public pricing page as of writing |
| Hosted "MindsDB Cloud" | Not currently confirmed | Legacy signup URL no longer resolves; commercial focus has visibly moved to the separate MindsHub product, which has its own distinct free-then-usage-based pricing |

Pricing, free-tier availability, and product structure were accurate as of this post's date (September 2026) — infrastructure and open-source projects like this can restructure commercial offerings with little notice, so verify directly on GitHub and the official docs before committing engineering time.

With no metered SaaS pricing to compare, the real cost consideration is **operational**: you're running database connectors, an inference layer, and potentially a vector store yourself, plus whatever you pay third-party LLM providers for embeddings and completions.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**Federated SQL across 200+ sources.** This is the foundation everything else sits on. You write one SQL dialect and query Postgres, MongoDB, Salesforce, Slack, or a CSV file as if they were tables in the same database — including joins across completely different systems (MindsDB's own docs show a join between MongoDB support tickets and Salesforce opportunity records as a canonical example). For teams that would otherwise build a custom ETL job just to correlate two systems for one report, this collapses a lot of plumbing.

**Knowledge Bases for hybrid search.** MindsDB lets you define a `KNOWLEDGE_BASE` object backed by an embedding model and a vector store, then populate it from `content_columns` (the unstructured text) plus `metadata_columns` (structured filters like customer segment or revenue). You can then run one SQL query combining semantic similarity search with precise metadata filtering — e.g., "find support tickets about data security, but only for customers above $1M ARR with a renewal pending." That hybrid retrieval pattern is genuinely useful and harder to replicate cleanly with a bare vector database.

**SQL-native AI agents.** You define an agent with `CREATE AGENT`, point it at a model provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, and others via configuration), and give it access to specific knowledge bases and tables. The agent then answers natural-language questions by querying live data rather than working off a stale export. This is the "conversational analytics" use case MindsDB pitches most heavily.

**Jobs and triggers for automation.** Beyond one-off queries, MindsDB supports scheduled jobs (SQL that runs on a cadence) so you can keep knowledge bases refreshed or run recurring analytics without an external orchestration tool.

**MCP and API access.** Because MindsDB exposes an HTTP API, a MySQL-compatible protocol, and MCP support, it slots into existing tooling — connect it to Cursor, Claude, or another MCP-aware client and let that client query your live data through MindsDB rather than through a bespoke integration.

## Who it's actually for

- **Data/platform engineers at companies with data spread across many systems** are the clearest fit — if your team already juggles Postgres, a CRM, a support tool, and flat files, MindsDB's federation layer removes real glue code.
- **AI/ML engineers building RAG or agent systems** who want structured and unstructured data unified behind one query interface, instead of stitching together a vector database, a SQL client, and custom retrieval code.
- **Solo developers or small teams** can run MindsDB locally via Docker for a prototype — it's free — but should expect real setup time and connector/agent tuning, not a five-minute wizard.
- **Enterprises wanting a fully managed, vendor-supported cloud product** are served least clearly today, given the apparent shift toward MindsHub. Get written confirmation of current terms before assuming a hosted, sales-assisted tier still exists as before.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free and open source (Elastic License 2.0), self-hostable via Docker or pip | No clear, current self-serve hosted "MindsDB Cloud" pricing page as of writing |
| Federated SQL across 200+ live data sources, no ETL required | Requires SQL fluency and comfort running/maintaining infrastructure yourself |
| Hybrid semantic + structured search via Knowledge Bases in a single query | Company's commercial focus has visibly shifted toward the separate MindsHub product |
| Native SQL syntax for agents, jobs, and triggers | Documentation is split across GitHub, PyPI, and GitHub Pages |
| MCP support for Cursor, Claude, and other agent tooling | Model/embedding costs from third-party LLM providers are separate |

## Integrations and ecosystem

MindsDB's integration story is its own selling point: 200+ connectors covering relational databases (Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Snowflake), NoSQL stores (MongoDB), SaaS platforms (Salesforce, Shopify), collaboration tools (Slack, Google Drive), and flat files. Agents can call OpenAI, Anthropic, and other model providers via an API key and model name in the `CREATE AGENT` statement, so MindsDB doesn't lock you into one vendor.

It also exposes a MySQL-compatible wire protocol (so existing SQL clients and BI tools can often connect without modification), a REST/HTTP API, and MCP support for agent frameworks like Cursor and Claude. There's no native Zapier integration documented, consistent with its positioning as developer/infrastructure tooling rather than a no-code automation platform.

## Where MindsDB is a strong fit

MindsDB fits best when you have data scattered across multiple databases and SaaS tools and want to query it as one logical layer without a heavy ETL project, or when you're building a RAG/agentic application that needs structured and unstructured retrieval unified behind SQL rather than a separate vector database client. It also suits teams that want to avoid model vendor lock-in, since agents can be pointed at different LLM providers per use case, and that are already comfortable running open-source infrastructure themselves.

## Where to think twice

- **If you want a fully managed SaaS with self-serve pricing you can compare in five minutes** — that product doesn't clearly exist for MindsDB right now; reach out directly and get current terms in writing.
- **If your team doesn't want to run and maintain infrastructure** — MindsDB assumes you're comfortable operating the engine yourself; it isn't a point-and-click dashboard tool.
- **If you need a simple, single-database tool** and don't actually have a multi-source federation problem, a plain vector database or your existing BI tool may serve you better.
- **If you need guaranteed enterprise compliance certifications (SOC 2, HIPAA, etc.) from a hosted vendor today** — verify current certification and hosting status directly, since the public pricing/product page structure has changed.
- **If you're not comfortable writing and debugging SQL** — nearly everything in MindsDB, from data connections to agent definitions to knowledge base queries, goes through its SQL dialect.

## Bottom line

MindsDB remains genuinely useful open-source infrastructure for querying fragmented data through one SQL interface and grounding AI agents in it without a bespoke integration layer. It's harder to recommend on the commercial side: the company's pricing and cloud offering appear to have shifted toward a separate, broader product (MindsHub), leaving the open-source engine well-documented on GitHub but without an obvious, current self-serve hosted tier. If you're an engineer fine with self-hosting and reading SQL docs, MindsDB is free and capable. If you wanted a turnkey managed product with transparent monthly pricing, budget time to email their team and get current specifics before planning around it.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is MindsDB free?**
The core query engine is free and open source under the Elastic License 2.0, self-hostable via Docker or pip. You'll still pay separately for any third-party LLM/embedding API usage and whatever infrastructure you run it on.

**Is MindsDB still actively maintained?**
Yes. As of this writing the project is at version 26.1.0 on PyPI, with an active GitHub repository and ongoing releases covering knowledge bases, agents, and new connectors.

**What happened to MindsDB Cloud?**
mindsdb.com and docs.mindsdb.com currently redirect to a separate product called MindsHub, and the old MindsDB Cloud signup URL no longer resolves. This suggests the commercial hosted offering shifted toward MindsHub, a broader AI agent workspace with its own distinct pricing. The open-source engine remains available and documented separately — confirm directly with the company for current commercial options.

**Does MindsDB require coding knowledge?**
It requires SQL fluency at minimum — data connections, knowledge bases, agents, and jobs are all defined through MindsDB's SQL dialect. It's built for developers, not no-code business users.

**What databases and tools does MindsDB connect to?**
MindsDB documents connectors for 200+ sources, including Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, Snowflake, Salesforce, Shopify, Slack, Google Drive, and flat files, queried through one SQL dialect.

**How does MindsDB handle data privacy, since it's self-hosted?**
Because you deploy the engine yourself, your data stays on your own infrastructure by default. Data leaves your environment only when agents call external LLM/embedding providers for inference — review those providers' own data-handling terms separately.

**What are the alternatives to MindsDB?**
Depending on your need: dedicated vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) paired with your own orchestration code, managed RAG platforms, or SQL-federation tools like Trino or Dremio for federation without a built-in AI-agent layer.

**Is MindsDB good for beginners?**
Not particularly. It assumes comfort with SQL, database administration, and (for self-hosting) Docker or Python environment management. Teams without a data engineer will find setup a real time investment.

For more AI and software tool coverage, see our [AI & software deals](/category/software) hub.

title: Glean Review 2026: Enterprise AI Search Pricing & Verdict
excerpt: Glean unifies enterprise search across 275+ apps with permission-aware AI. Here's how it works, what it costs, and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Glean worth it for enterprise search?

Glean is worth it for mid-size to large companies drowning in scattered internal knowledge across Slack, Google Drive, Confluence, Jira, and dozens of other apps — its permission-aware search and AI agents genuinely cut down time spent hunting for answers. It's overkill and cost-prohibitive for small teams or anyone wanting a free, self-serve tool.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Custom/quote-based (no published tiers) |
| **Free tier/trial** | No self-serve free tier; demo-based sales process |
| **Best for** | Mid-size to large companies (hundreds to tens of thousands of employees) |
| **Standout feature** | Permission-aware search across 275+ connected apps, plus a no-code agent builder |

## What Glean actually is

Glean is an enterprise AI platform built around a simple but hard-to-execute idea: most companies have knowledge spread across dozens of disconnected tools, and nobody can actually find anything. Founded by ex-Google search engineers, Glean started as an internal-search product and has since expanded into a broader "work AI" platform layering a chat assistant and agent-building tools on top of its search core.

Rather than building its own foundation model, Glean says it supports more than 40 different large language models, letting an organization pick which model handles which task — a lighter, cheaper model for simple lookups and a stronger reasoning model for more complex synthesis. That model-agnostic approach is a practical selling point: it doesn't lock a company into a single vendor's model roadmap.

At its core, Glean indexes content from the apps a company already uses — Slack, Google Drive, Microsoft 365, Confluence, Jira, GitHub, Salesforce, Zendesk, and Glean states it connects to 275+ work applications in total. It respects each source system's existing permissions, so a search result never surfaces a document a given employee wouldn't already access in the original app. On top of that index sits a chat-style assistant that answers questions in natural language, cites sources, and increasingly takes actions through agents rather than just returning links.

## Pricing

Glean does not publish self-serve pricing tiers. Instead, it runs an enterprise sales motion: you request a demo, a sales rep scopes your deployment (seats, connectors, data volume), and you get a custom quote. There's no published free tier and no self-serve monthly plan you can sign up for with a credit card.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Custom / Enterprise | Quote-based, contact sales | Full connector library, AI assistant, agent builder, admin/permissions controls, SSO |
| Add-ons | Quote-based | Additional connectors, usage tiers, and dedicated support may be priced separately |

Because there's no public price list, any per-seat figure you see outside Glean's own sales process should be treated as an estimate, not a confirmed rate — confirm current terms directly with Glean's team.

Pricing, free-tier availability, and feature details were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — enterprise AI platforms adjust packaging often, so confirm current terms before budgeting.

## Core features walkthrough

**Unified enterprise search.** This is Glean's original product and still its foundation. It crawls and indexes content across connected apps and returns results ranked by relevance and freshness, not just keyword match — closer to a modern web search engine than a typical internal wiki search bar.

**Permission-aware access control.** Every search result and AI-generated answer is filtered through the same access permissions that exist in the source system. If someone doesn't have access to a document in Google Drive, Glean won't surface it in search or use it to answer a question, even indirectly. This is arguably Glean's most important differentiator versus a general-purpose chatbot bolted onto a document dump, since a permissions mistake in an internal knowledge tool is a real compliance risk, not just an inconvenience.

**AI assistant with source citations.** Glean's chat assistant answers questions in natural language and links back to the documents, messages, or tickets it used to generate the answer — a reader can verify a claim rather than taking the model's word for it.

**No-code agent builder.** Beyond search and Q&A, Glean lets teams build agents that automate multi-step internal workflows — triaging a support ticket, summarizing a meeting thread, or drafting a first-pass response based on internal policy. Glean states some larger customers run thousands of these agents in production, signaling the layer is meant for real operational use, not just a demo feature.

**Broad, deep connector library.** With 275+ stated connectors spanning collaboration tools, code repositories, CRMs, ticketing systems, and cloud storage, Glean's usefulness scales with how much of a company's knowledge actually lives in supported systems.

## Who it's actually for

**Large enterprises (thousands of employees).** Companies with tens of thousands of employees are the clearest fit. At that scale, the cost of employees repeatedly re-discovering information that already exists somewhere in the company is genuinely large, and Glean is aimed at recovering that lost time.

**Mid-size, fast-growing companies with fragmented tooling.** A company that's grown quickly and now has knowledge split across five or six different SaaS tools, with no single source of truth, is a strong candidate even without enterprise-scale headcount.

**IT, knowledge management, and platform teams.** Because Glean requires connector setup, permissions configuration, and often coordination with security/compliance teams, it's best owned by an IT or knowledge-management function rather than adopted self-serve by an individual team.

**Not a fit: solo users, small teams, or anyone wanting a free tool.** If you're a freelancer or a five-person startup, Glean's quote-based, connector-heavy model isn't built for you — a lighter tool or a bundled assistant already inside your existing software stack gets you further for less friction and cost.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Permission-aware search respects existing access controls at the source | No published pricing — every deal requires a sales conversation |
| Broad connector library (275+ stated integrations) | No self-serve free tier or trial to test before committing |
| Model-agnostic — supports 40+ LLMs rather than locking into one | Deployment and connector setup require IT involvement, not a quick self-serve start |
| No-code agent builder for automating internal workflows | Overkill and cost-prohibitive for small teams or individuals |
| Strong compliance certification list (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, HIPAA, GDPR) | Answer quality depends on how clean the underlying connected data already is |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Glean's core value proposition is largely its integration breadth. It states connectors for Slack, Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Google Workspace, Confluence, Jira, GitHub, Salesforce, Zendesk, and more, adding up to 275+ supported data sources. It also supports SSO for identity verification before granting AI access to a user's data, tying into its permissions model rather than being a bolt-on login feature.

On the AI side, Glean is built to be model-agnostic, supporting 40+ different LLMs so an organization can route a task to whichever model fits the reasoning level and cost profile needed. Its integration story is aimed at IT-managed connectors and admin-configured data sources rather than individual no-code automation like a consumer-facing Zapier setup.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Large or mid-size organizations where employees regularly lose time re-finding information that already exists somewhere internally
- Companies with knowledge spread across many disconnected SaaS tools and no single reliable source of truth
- Organizations with real compliance needs (healthcare, finance, regulated industries) where Glean's certifications — SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, HIPAA, GDPR, TX-RAMP Level 2 — matter to a security review
- Teams wanting to build internal automation agents without a dedicated engineering team writing custom integrations

## Where to think twice

- If you need a free or cheap self-serve tool — Glean has no public pricing and no free tier, so budgeting requires a sales cycle first
- If your organization is small enough that a lighter, single-purpose assistant (or a feature already bundled into a tool you use, like Slack AI or Microsoft Copilot) covers your actual need
- If you don't have IT or admin resources to manage connector setup, permissions mapping, and ongoing maintenance
- If your internal documentation is already in poor shape — Glean surfaces and organizes existing knowledge, it doesn't create good documentation where none exists
- If you need to try before buying — there's no way to use Glean without a demo request

## The bottom line

Glean solves a real and expensive problem: knowledge trapped across disconnected apps that nobody can efficiently search or synthesize. Its permission-aware architecture is a genuinely important design choice for buyers who can't risk an AI tool leaking access to sensitive documents, and its connector breadth and model-agnostic approach keep it flexible rather than locked to one vendor's roadmap. The tradeoff: Glean is built entirely for the enterprise sales motion — no published pricing, no free trial, deployment that assumes IT involvement — a poor match for anyone outside its target profile of mid-size-to-large organizations with real budget and real data sprawl. If that's you, it's worth a demo. If not, look toward lighter, self-serve assistants instead.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Glean free to use?**
No. Glean doesn't offer a public free tier or self-serve trial. Pricing is quote-based and requires going through Glean's sales team, who scope a deployment based on seat count, connectors, and data volume.

**How much does Glean cost?**
Glean doesn't publish pricing publicly. You'll need to request a demo and get a custom quote. Any per-seat figure seen outside Glean's own sales process should be treated as an estimate, not a confirmed rate.

**What AI models does Glean use?**
Glean says it supports more than 40 different large language models rather than relying on a single proprietary model, letting organizations choose the model that fits each task's reasoning needs and cost profile.

**Does Glean respect existing document permissions?**
Yes — Glean's stated design enforces the same access permissions that exist in the original source system (Google Drive, SharePoint, Confluence, etc.) on every search result and AI-generated answer, so it won't surface content a given user doesn't already have access to.

**Is Glean secure and compliant enough for regulated industries?**
Glean lists SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, HIPAA, GDPR, and TX-RAMP Level 2 among its certifications, covering many common enterprise compliance requirements. Organizations with specific regulatory needs should confirm current certification status directly with Glean during procurement.

**What are the alternatives to Glean?**
Alternatives range from built-in assistants already bundled into tools you use — like Microsoft Copilot or Slack AI — to other dedicated enterprise search and knowledge-management platforms. The right alternative depends on your company size, budget, and how many separate tools your knowledge is spread across.

**Is Glean beginner-friendly?**
The end-user chat and search experience is straightforward — it works like a search bar or chat window. Setup and administration is not self-serve friendly, since connecting data sources and configuring agents typically requires IT involvement.

title: VEED.IO Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: VEED.IO pairs a real browser-based timeline editor with AI subtitles, avatars, and dubbing. Here's pricing, features, and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is VEED.IO worth it?

VEED.IO is worth it if you want a browser-based video editor that bolts AI subtitles, avatars, dubbing, and a full "Gen-AI Studio" onto a genuinely usable timeline editor, without installing desktop software. It's a weaker fit if you need offline editing, heavy color grading, or a truly free, watermark-free export.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $12/month (Creator plan, billed yearly) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Free plan available; paid plans reportedly offer a trial (confirm current terms on site) |
| **Best for** | Solo creators, marketers, and social teams doing browser-based editing + AI subtitles/avatars |
| **Standout feature** | Gen-AI Studio (all-in-one AI video/avatar/voice generation) built into the same editor as the manual timeline |

VEED has been positioning itself for years as the video tool for people who don't want to learn a "real" NLE (non-linear editor) like Premiere or DaVinci Resolve. It started as a simple browser-based subtitle-and-trim tool and has steadily bolted on AI features — auto subtitles, background removal, AI avatars, voice cloning, dubbing, and a text-to-video "Gen-AI Studio" — without abandoning the manual timeline editor underneath.

This site already has full reviews of [Invideo AI](/blog/invideo-review), [CapCut AI](/blog/capcut-ai-review), [FlexClip](/blog/flexclip-review), and [HeyGen](/blog/heygen-review), so it's worth being upfront about where VEED differs. Invideo and FlexClip lean harder into template-driven, prompt-to-video generation for people who don't want to touch a timeline. CapCut AI targets short-form, mobile-first social content and is free for most of its toolset. HeyGen is narrowly focused on AI avatars. VEED sits in between: a full browser-based editor first, with AI layered in as tools you reach for mid-edit — closer to "Canva for video with AI extensions" than a pure text-to-video generator.

There's no VEED.IO entry in this site's store catalog yet, so this review is built from VEED's own site and pricing page plus third-party listings, rather than a store record.

## What VEED.IO actually is

VEED is a browser-based video editing platform — no desktop install required — that combines a manual drag-and-drop timeline with a growing suite of AI tools. According to its own marketing, it's used by teams at companies including Amazon, Google, Netflix, Meta, and the BBC, though those are almost certainly enterprise/team accounts, not evidence of a typical solo-creator experience.

VEED doesn't publicly disclose which specific AI models power each feature, so treat "AI quality" claims as its own framing rather than a verifiable spec. The documented feature set: auto subtitles and captions, AI avatars and lip-sync, a "Talking Photo" tool, AI voice generation and voice cloning, text-to-speech, AI dubbing and translation into 50+ languages (paid plans), background removal for video and images, an image upscaler, an AI image generator, a voice/noise cleaner, and "Gen-AI Studio" for generating short AI video clips from text prompts.

## VEED.IO pricing (as of September 2026)

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Basic editor access; exports are limited and typically watermarked — confirm current export/length limits on VEED's site before relying on the free tier for finished work |
| Creator | $12/month billed yearly ($147/year), or higher billed monthly | No watermark, unlimited auto subtitles, full stock audio/video library, 15+ AI tools, ~6,000 AI credits (VEED estimates ~1,500 AI-generated video clips) |
| Pro | $22/month billed yearly ($265/year) | + multiple brand kits, translation into 50+ languages, up to 144 hrs/year AI voice, ~30,000 credits |
| Studio | $39/month billed yearly ($465/year) | + custom templates, project analytics, up to 960 hrs/year AI voice, access to all AI models, ~180,000 credits |
| Enterprise | Custom pricing | Centralized team/data management, review mode, privacy controls, custom credit allocations, dedicated support |

VEED prices per seat and advertises savings of "up to 51%" for annual billing versus month-to-month — third-party listings (e.g., GetApp) show slightly higher monthly-billed figures (around $24/month for Pro), consistent with that discount structure. VEED's pricing FAQ mentions a trial for paid plans, cancel-anytime billing, and a way to buy extra AI credits, but doesn't publish exact numbers — confirm trial length and add-on pricing on [veed.io/pricing](https://www.veed.io/pricing) before committing.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — AI video tool pricing and credit allowances move fast, and VEED has already restructured its plans more than once in recent years.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**A real timeline editor, not just a prompt box.** Unlike prompt-to-video-only tools, VEED gives you a proper multi-track timeline with manual trim, split, layering, transitions, and text overlays — useful when "AI does part of the work, I finish it by hand" is your workflow.

**Gen-AI Studio.** VEED's unified hub for AI-generated content — text-to-video clips, avatars, voice, and image generation — lives inside the same account and credit pool rather than as separate bolt-on products. Credits are shared, so a heavy month of avatar generation can eat into your subtitle/translation budget too.

**Auto subtitles with real styling control.** Goes beyond auto-transcription — animated caption styles, karaoke-style word highlighting, and multi-language subtitle export, a genuine differentiator for short-form content where captions drive watch time.

**AI dubbing and translation.** Translating into 50+ languages with AI voice dubbing (Pro and above) is a feature most competitors don't offer or gate behind enterprise plans. Hour allowances scale steeply by tier (144 hrs/year on Pro vs. 960 on Studio).

**Background and voice cleanup.** Background removal (video and stills) and a voice/noise cleaner ship as plain utility tools rather than headline AI features — useful for mediocre home-studio footage.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and freelancers** doing social clips, shorts, or client edits will likely land on Creator — it removes the watermark and unlocks the full AI toolset at the lowest price.
- **Small marketing teams** producing multilingual or high-volume branded content will want Pro or Studio for translation hours, brand kits, and larger credit pools.
- **Agencies and larger teams** needing approval workflows and data controls should look at Enterprise — pricing isn't published, so budget for a sales call.
- **Hobbyists wanting a free, occasional editor** can use the free plan, but shouldn't count on it for finished, brandable work given the watermark and limits.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Full timeline editor plus AI tools in one browser tab, no install | Free plan is watermarked/limited — not viable for finished branded output |
| Auto subtitles with strong styling control | Credits are shared across all Gen-AI Studio tools, so heavy avatar/video use eats your subtitle/translation budget too |
| AI dubbing/translation into 50+ languages on paid tiers | Underlying AI models aren't publicly named, so quality claims are hard to verify |
| Per-seat annual pricing gives a real discount vs. monthly | Enterprise pricing is opaque — requires a sales call |
| Used by large, recognizable brands per VEED's case studies | No offline editing mode, being cloud/browser-based |

## Integrations and ecosystem

VEED exports directly to common social formats and resolutions, and its help docs reference team features like brand kits and shared workspaces on Pro/Studio/Enterprise. It doesn't market a large third-party integration marketplace (no prominent native Zapier app or public API on its main marketing pages as of this writing) — if API access or automation hooks matter, verify current availability with VEED's sales team.

## Where it's a strong fit

- You want one browser tab covering manual editing, subtitles, avatars, and translation instead of stitching together three separate tools.
- Your content is caption-heavy (social clips, tutorials) and you want strong built-in subtitle styling rather than a bare auto-transcript.
- You need to localize video into multiple languages with AI dubbing without hiring voice talent per language.
- You're a small team that wants shared brand kits and templates without buying a full enterprise video CMS.

## Where to think twice

- **If you need a fully free tool with no watermark**, VEED's free plan won't get you there — budget for at least Creator.
- **If your team needs compliance documentation (SOC 2, HIPAA, etc.)**, that isn't published on VEED's marketing pages — request it directly; Enterprise pricing is quote-only too.
- **If you need offline or on-prem editing**, a browser-based tool is a structural mismatch regardless of its AI features.
- **If your priority is pure prompt-to-video with minimal manual editing**, a generator-first tool like Invideo AI may get you to a finished draft faster.
- **If translation hour limits matter to your volume**, check the math against your actual output before assuming Pro's 144 hours/year is enough.

## Bottom line

VEED earns its place by not forcing a choice between "manual video editor" and "AI video generator" — it's a capable timeline editor with strong AI subtitle, dubbing, and avatar tools built in, rather than a generator with a thin editor bolted on. The free plan is really a trial-by-another-name given the watermark and export limits, so most people who stick with VEED end up on Creator or Pro. It's a strong pick for creators and small teams whose workflow mixes manual editing with AI-assisted steps; weaker if you want a fully free tool or a pure one-click generator with no editor to learn.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is VEED.IO actually free?**
There's a free plan, but expect watermarked and/or limited exports. For unwatermarked, full-length exports, you'll need at least Creator at $12/month billed yearly.

**What does VEED.IO cost per month?**
Published tiers are Creator ($12/mo billed yearly), Pro ($22/mo billed yearly), and Studio ($39/mo billed yearly), with higher rates if billed monthly, plus a custom-priced Enterprise tier. Confirm current figures on [veed.io/pricing](https://www.veed.io/pricing).

**Does VEED.IO offer a free trial for paid plans?**
VEED's pricing FAQ references a trial for paid plans, but doesn't publish exact trial length in the crawlable page text — check current terms at signup.

**How do VEED's AI credits work across plans?**
Credits are shared across VEED's Gen-AI Studio tools (video generation, avatars, voice, images), so usage in one feature draws down the same pool available to others. Plans range from roughly 6,000 credits (Creator) to 180,000 (Studio), with custom allocations on Enterprise.

**Is VEED.IO good for beginners?**
Yes — the drag-and-drop timeline and templated AI tools suit people without prior editing experience, though it has more of a learning curve than a pure one-click generator since it's a full editor, not just a prompt box.

**What languages does VEED's AI dubbing support?**
VEED advertises translation and dubbing into 50+ languages on Pro and Studio, with annual usage caps that scale by tier (roughly 144 hours/year on Pro versus 960 on Studio).

**How does VEED.IO handle my uploaded video data and privacy?**
VEED doesn't publish detailed data-retention or compliance specifics (e.g., SOC 2 status) on its main marketing pages — request documentation directly if compliance is a decision factor.

**What are the best alternatives to VEED.IO?**
For a generator-first, template-driven experience, see our [Invideo AI review](/blog/invideo-review) or [FlexClip review](/blog/flexclip-review). For AI avatars specifically, see our [HeyGen review](/blog/heygen-review); for short-form social editing, see our [CapCut AI review](/blog/capcut-ai-review).

For more AI software and video-tool coverage, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Unriddle Review 2026: Now Anara — Pricing & Features
excerpt: Unriddle rebranded to Anara. Here's what the AI research assistant costs, its multi-document chat and citation features, and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Unriddle Worth It in 2026?

Unriddle is worth checking, with one caveat: it has rebranded to **Anara**, and unriddle.ai now redirects to anara.com. It's worth it if you need to chat across thousands of source documents at once with citations tied to exact passages; overkill if you just want to highlight a handful of PDFs.

## At a glance

| | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | Free; paid plans from $10/month/seat (Plus), billed yearly |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — limited AI usage, uploads capped at 20MB or 120 pages |
| Best for | Researchers, biopharma/clinical teams, and academics working across large document libraries |
| Standout feature | Chat and search across up to 10,000 files in a single conversation, with citations pointing to the exact passage |

## What happened to Unriddle, and what is it now?

If you tried Unriddle a year or two ago, here's the update: the company rebranded to **Anara**, and the old unriddle.ai domain now 301-redirects to anara.com. The underlying idea hasn't changed — it's still an AI reading and research assistant built around your document library — but the branding, pricing structure and feature set now sit under the Anara name. Anyone still searching "Unriddle" in 2026 is really evaluating Anara, so that's the product this review covers.

Anara positions itself for research workflows: it "searches your library and the web, summarizes what it finds, and helps you write with every claim cited back to its source." It's aimed less at casual readers and more at people doing serious literature review — the site lists academia, biopharma, clinical practice, engineering R&D and policy as core use cases, and names organizations like Biogen, GSK, Mayo Clinic, MIT and Caltech among its users. Whether those are paying enterprise customers or just logo placements isn't independently verifiable, so treat that list as a vendor claim.

The company doesn't publish which models power Free and Plus, but its pricing page states Pro gives "access to best AI models" — its own wording — naming a mix of frontier models. Since that lineup is a fast-moving marketing claim rather than documented fact, treat it as what Anara says it offers today, and confirm on the official pricing page before buying.

## Pricing

Anara runs a five-tier structure: a free plan, two individual paid tiers (Plus and Pro), a heavier Max tier, and custom Enterprise pricing. Everything below is billed per seat, yearly, based on the current pricing page.

| Plan | Price (billed yearly) | Upload limit | Key inclusions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0/month | 20MB or 120 pages | Limited AI usage, Zotero and Mendeley connectors, no credit card required |
| Plus | $10/month/seat | 100MB or 600 pages | Extended AI usage, PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov connectors, up to 5 collaborators per folder |
| Pro | $20/month/seat | 300MB or 10,000 pages | 4x the AI usage of Plus, access to Anara's listed frontier models, OCR/image-text extraction, Google Drive/Notion/OneDrive connectors, 50 collaborators |
| Max | $100/month/seat | Unlimited | 5x the AI usage of Pro, Deep Search for complex multi-step research, a "Model Council" multi-model query feature, unlimited collaborators, priority access at peak load |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom | Tailored features, dedicated support — contact sales |
