Worth flagging: all four paid tiers list "billed yearly" pricing — monthly billing, if offered, likely costs more per month, so check the toggle before assuming $20/month is the upfront cost. "AI usage" limits on Free and Plus aren't quantified in exact query counts publicly, so a heavy user could hit the ceiling faster than expected. And the jump from Pro ($20) to Max ($100) is steep for 5x usage and a couple of extra features, so most individual researchers will land on Plus or Pro.

Pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability described here were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AI tool pricing and feature sets move fast, so confirm current numbers on Anara's own pricing page before subscribing.

## Core features walkthrough

**Multi-document chat at scale.** The headline feature is holding a single conversation across up to 10,000 uploaded files (on Pro), rather than being limited to one document or a small folder at a time. For systematic literature review or due-diligence across hundreds of PDFs, that's a genuinely different working mode than uploading one paper into a chatbot at a time.

**Citation-grounded answers.** Answers are supposed to link back to the specific passage they were drawn from, rather than a vague "based on your documents" summary. That matters most for research and clinical use where you need to trace a claim back to its source before citing it — it's the core promise separating a research assistant from a general chatbot with file upload bolted on.

**Writing assistant with citation suggestions.** Beyond reading and summarizing, Anara includes a writing mode that matches your draft against your uploaded library and suggests citations as you write. That's a meaningfully different feature than what Glasp or Liner offer — those tools are built more around capturing and surfacing highlights, not drafting a paper with citations attached in real time.

**Database and reference-manager connectors.** Free users get Zotero and Mendeley sync; paid tiers add PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Google Drive, Notion and OneDrive. If your library already lives in Zotero, Free may cover basic sync, but PubMed search integration requires at least Plus.

**OCR and image-text extraction (Pro and up).** For scanned PDFs, older papers, or documents with text embedded in figures, OCR support on Pro and Max matters — without it, a chunk of older or lower-quality-scan literature would be unreadable to the assistant.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo grad students/independent researchers** with a moderate reading list fit Free or Plus — the 600-page cap and Zotero/Mendeley sync cover a typical thesis-scale review.
- **Clinical and biopharma teams** doing systematic reviews across large trial/publication sets are the clearest fit for Pro or Max, given the PubMed/ClinicalTrials.gov connectors and 10,000-file ceiling.
- **Engineering R&D and policy teams** cross-referencing large internal document sets alongside external literature benefit from Pro's Drive/Notion/OneDrive connectors.
- **Enterprise research organizations** needing procurement-level support and custom seat counts should go straight to Enterprise.
- **Casual readers** wanting to highlight a few articles a week are better served by a free tool like Glasp.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Handles very large document sets (up to 10,000 files) in one conversation | Rebrand from Unriddle to Anara means old reviews/bookmarks may be stale |
| Citation-grounded answers built for research/clinical use | Exact AI usage limits on Free/Plus aren't quantified publicly |
| Writing assistant suggests citations from your own library | Big price jump from Pro to Max ($20 to $100) |
| Tiered connectors cover academic (PubMed, Zotero) and productivity (Drive, Notion) tools | Free tier upload cap (120 pages) is tight for full-length papers |
| Enterprise tier available for compliance needs | No published info on which models power Free/Plus tiers |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Anara's connectors are split by tier rather than a flat menu. Free gets Zotero and Mendeley, covering basic academic library sync. Plus adds PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov. Pro layers in Google Drive, Notion and OneDrive, which matters if source documents live in a shared team drive rather than a personal reference manager. There's no public mention of a dedicated API, Zapier, or Slack integration on current marketing pages, so teams wanting to pipe output into automation tools should confirm API availability with sales.

## Where it's a strong fit

Anara earns its keep on genuinely multi-document work: a systematic review across dozens or hundreds of papers, a due-diligence pass across a large filing set, or ongoing research returning to the same growing library over months. The citation-to-passage linking matters most — it turns an AI summary you'd otherwise double-check line by line into one where verifying a claim is a one-click trace back to source. Teams already using Zotero, PubMed, or clinical trial databases will find the connectors map closely to how they already work.

## Where to think twice

Skip Anara, or stay on the free tier, if you need a fully free tool for casual reading — the 120-page upload cap on Free feels restrictive fast, and Glasp's free tier suits lighter highlight-and-summarize use better. Think twice if your team needs a quantified usage allowance up front rather than a vaguely worded "limited AI usage" tier — you may hit the ceiling mid-project without warning. And if you need offline or on-premises deployment for data-sensitivity reasons (common in pharma and government research), raise that with Enterprise sales directly — nothing on the public pricing page confirms on-prem availability.

## Bottom line

Anara (formerly Unriddle) is a legitimately different tool from lighter highlight-and-summarize apps — built for people who need to reason across thousands of documents at once with traceable citations, not just save a few articles for later. If that's your workload, Plus or Pro is a reasonable cost for the connector and scale advantages over general-purpose AI chat. If you're a casual reader who just wants help with a handful of PDFs, the free tier feels adequate at first but tight over time, and a lighter tool built for that scale may serve you better and cheaper.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Unriddle still around, or has it shut down?**
It hasn't shut down — it rebranded. The unriddle.ai domain now redirects to anara.com, and the same core reading/research-assistant concept continues under the Anara name.

**Does Anara have a free plan?**
Yes. The free plan allows limited AI usage with uploads capped at 20MB or 120 pages, plus Zotero and Mendeley connectors, and doesn't require a credit card.

**What's the cheapest paid plan?**
Plus, at $10/month per seat billed yearly, which raises the upload cap to 100MB or 600 pages and adds PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov connectors.

**Which AI models does Anara use?**
The company doesn't publish full model details for every tier. Its Pro plan pricing page states it includes access to a set of frontier models it names on that page — treat this as the vendor's own current claim, since model lineups change frequently, and confirm on the official site before subscribing.

**How many documents can I upload at once?**
Upload limits scale by tier: 120 pages on Free, 600 on Plus, 10,000 on Pro, and unlimited on Max. Pro is also the tier that supports holding a single conversation across up to 10,000 files.

**Is Anara good for beginners?**
The core chat-with-your-documents workflow is straightforward, but getting full value from the connector setup (Zotero/Mendeley sync, PubMed search, Drive/Notion linking) takes some initial configuration.

**Does Anara handle data privacy for sensitive research?**
The site doesn't publish detailed compliance certifications (like SOC 2) on its pricing page. Teams with strict data-handling needs should confirm compliance and data-residency details with sales before uploading sensitive documents.

**What are the alternatives to Anara?**
For lighter, free highlight-and-summarize use across web pages, PDFs, YouTube and Kindle, see our [Glasp review](/blog/glasp-review). For cited AI search with an academic Scholar mode, see our [Liner review](/blog/liner-review). For free literature search with AI summaries and no paid tier, [Semantic Scholar](/blog/semantic-scholar-review) is worth trying first.

For more AI and research-tool coverage, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: What The Diff Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: What The Diff auto-writes GitHub/GitLab pull request descriptions from code diffs. Here's how the pricing, features and limits hold up in 2026.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## What The Diff Review 2026: Is This PR-Writing AI Worth It?

What The Diff is a solid pick if your team is tired of blank pull request descriptions — it reads the code diff and writes the summary automatically, on both GitHub and GitLab. The free plan covers about 10 PRs a month; the $19/month Pro plan covers roughly 40. It's narrow by design, not a full code-review replacement.

| At a glance | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free ($0/mo, 25,000 tokens) |
| Paid entry price | $19/month (Pro – 200k) |
| Free tier / trial | Yes — no credit card required |
| Best for | Teams that want auto-written PR descriptions and non-technical status updates |
| Standout feature | Reads the diff itself (no manual prompt) and posts plain-language summaries |

### What What The Diff actually is

What The Diff is a narrowly scoped AI tool built by Beyond Code (beyondco.de). It hooks into a GitHub or GitLab repository, watches for new and updated pull requests, and generates a written description of what changed — pulled directly from the diff rather than from a prompt you type in. The pitch is specific: instead of engineers writing (or skipping) PR descriptions, and instead of product managers pinging the team to ask "what did you ship this week," the tool auto-generates both.

It's not a general-purpose coding assistant like GitHub Copilot or Cursor, and it doesn't try to be. It doesn't autocomplete code as you type, and it isn't a chat interface you converse with about your codebase. It's closer to a single-purpose bot that sits in your CI/PR pipeline and does one job well: turn a diff into readable prose. The company doesn't publicly state which underlying language model powers the summaries, so that detail should be treated as unconfirmed rather than assumed.

### Pricing

What The Diff prices by token consumption rather than by seat count, which is a little unusual for a dev tool and worth understanding before you commit.

| Plan | Price | Tokens/month | Roughly | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 25,000 | ~10 PRs | Unlimited repos, inline refactor suggestions, rate-limited, no card required |
| Pro – 200k | $19/month | 200,000 | ~40 PRs | Unlimited repos, Slack/Webhook/Email notifications, priority email support |

Beyond Code says an average pull request consumes roughly 2,300 tokens, which is how it arrives at the "~10 PRs" and "~40 PRs" estimates above — actual usage will vary with how large and how frequent your diffs are. Unused tokens don't roll over to the next month, and if you burn through your allotment mid-cycle there's no automatic overage billing — you either upgrade or wait for the reset. The pricing page also references going "unlimited," but at the time of research only the two tiers above were listed with concrete numbers; anything past 200k tokens appears to require contacting the team directly rather than self-serve checkout.

Pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — always confirm current numbers on [whatthediff.ai](https://whatthediff.ai) before buying, since AI tool pricing moves quickly.

There's no dedicated coupon page for What The Diff on this site yet, so check the vendor's own pricing page directly for the latest numbers, or browse [AI & software deals](/category/software) for other tools with active offers.

### Core features that actually differentiate it

**Automatic PR descriptions.** This is the headline feature. Open (or update) a pull request and the bot fills in a description based on the actual code changes — what files moved, what logic changed, what the intent looks like from the diff. No prompt-writing required on the engineer's side.

**Plain-language summary notifications.** Beyond the PR description itself, What The Diff can push simplified, non-technical summaries to Slack, email, or a webhook — aimed at product managers, founders, or stakeholders who need to know what shipped without reading a diff. The vendor also mentions translation of these summaries, useful for distributed teams.

**Public changelogs with a JSON API.** Merged PR summaries can be rolled up into a public-facing changelog, with API access to pull that data into your own site or dashboard — handy if you want an auto-generated "what's new" page without maintaining it by hand.

**Weekly progress reports.** A rollup of what happened across the week's merged PRs, again aimed more at keeping non-engineering stakeholders in the loop than at engineers themselves.

**Inline AI refactor suggestions.** Alongside descriptions, the tool flags minor issues during review and can suggest small refactors — this is a secondary feature, not a substitute for a dedicated code-review AI, but it's included on both the Free and Pro tiers.

**Configurable behavior.** Settings include skipping the bot on CI-only commits, delaying summary generation for draft PRs, and adjusting token limits per repo — small touches, but they matter if you don't want the bot firing on every WIP commit.

### Who it's actually for

- **Solo developers and small teams** on the Free tier get a genuinely useful tool for close to zero cost — 25,000 tokens covers a meaningful chunk of a side project's PR volume, and there's no credit card required to try it.
- **Small-to-mid engineering teams** shipping regularly will likely need the Pro plan once PR volume climbs past roughly 10 a month. The $19/month price is low enough that it's an easy expense to justify against the time saved writing (or nagging people to write) PR descriptions.
- **Teams with non-technical stakeholders** — founders, PMs, support leads who want visibility into engineering progress without reading GitHub — get the most distinctive value here, via the Slack/email summary notifications and weekly reports.
- **Larger orgs needing more than 200k tokens/month**, or wanting a formal enterprise agreement, will need to contact Beyond Code directly since there's no self-serve tier above Pro listed on the pricing page.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier with no credit card, genuinely usable for small projects | Only two self-serve pricing tiers; nothing between $19/mo and a custom quote |
| Reads the diff directly — no prompt engineering needed | Token-based pricing means usage on large PRs can burn through a plan faster than expected |
| Supports both GitHub and GitLab | Underlying AI model isn't publicly disclosed |
| Stakeholder-facing summaries and weekly reports are a genuinely different angle than most PR tools | Unused tokens don't roll over month to month |
| Public changelog + JSON API is a nice bonus for release notes | Not a full code-review or code-completion tool — narrow scope by design |

### Integrations and ecosystem

What The Diff connects to GitHub and GitLab repositories as its core integration point. On top of that, the Pro plan adds outbound notification channels — Slack, generic webhooks, and email — so summaries can land wherever your team already looks for updates. The public changelog feature exposes a JSON API for pulling PR summary data into your own site or internal tooling. There's no mention of a native Bitbucket integration, a VS Code extension, or a standalone API for programmatic PR-description generation outside the GitHub/GitLab app flow — if any of those matter to your workflow, confirm availability directly with the vendor before signing up.

### Where it's a strong fit

- Teams where PR descriptions are consistently thin, empty, or skipped entirely, and where "just write better descriptions" hasn't worked as a policy.
- Organizations with non-engineering stakeholders who want a lightweight, ongoing view of what's shipping without sitting in on engineering meetings.
- Projects that want auto-generated, public-facing changelogs without hand-writing release notes every cycle.
- Anyone testing the water — the free tier is a low-risk way to see if the summaries are actually useful for your codebase before paying anything.

### Where to think twice

- If you need a fully free tool at any real PR volume — the free tier's 25,000-token/~10-PR ceiling is tight for an active team, and the next tier up is a hard jump to a paid plan with no smaller in-between option.
- If your team needs a full AI code-review tool that catches bugs, security issues, or style violations — What The Diff's refactor suggestions are a minor bolt-on, not a substitute for tools built specifically for that job.
- If you need enterprise compliance documentation (SOC 2, formal DPAs, on-prem or self-hosted deployment) — none of that is advertised on the public site, so if procurement requires it, get written confirmation from Beyond Code before committing budget.
- If unpredictable token-based billing is a dealbreaker for your finance team — a plan that's sized for "40 PRs" can run out faster in a month with a few unusually large diffs, since pricing scales with diff size, not just PR count.
- If your repos live on Bitbucket or another platform outside GitHub/GitLab — there's no indication of support for that today.

### Bottom line

What The Diff does one thing and does it without much friction: it turns a code diff into a readable PR description, and it turns a week of merged PRs into a summary a non-engineer can actually follow. That's a genuinely useful, fairly unglamorous problem to solve, and $19/month for ~40 PRs is cheap relative to the time most teams currently spend (or lose) on writing descriptions by hand. It's not trying to be a full AI code-review platform, and treating it as one will disappoint you — but as a focused PR-summary and stakeholder-update tool, it's worth the free trial to see if your team's PR habits actually improve.

### FAQ

**Is What The Diff free?**
Yes, there's a free tier with 25,000 tokens per month (roughly 10 pull requests), no credit card required. It includes unlimited repositories and inline refactor suggestions, though it's rate-limited compared to the paid plan.

**How much does the paid plan cost?**
The Pro plan is $19/month for 200,000 tokens (roughly 40 PRs), and adds Slack, webhook, and email notifications plus priority email support.

**What platforms does it support?**
GitHub and GitLab repositories. There's no publicly listed Bitbucket support at this time.

**Does What The Diff store my code?**
The vendor states it does not store code, nor does any third-party service it uses, and that user code is not used to train its AI model. For anything beyond that general statement, review the company's current privacy policy directly before connecting a private repository.

**What AI model does it use?**
Beyond Code hasn't publicly specified the underlying model on its marketing pages, so this should be treated as unconfirmed rather than assumed.

**Do unused tokens roll over?**
No. Both the free and paid plan's token allotments reset monthly and don't carry over unused balance.

**What happens if I run out of tokens mid-month?**
You can upgrade to a higher plan, or wait until the next billing cycle for your allotment to reset — there's no automatic overage charge mentioned on the pricing page.

**Is there a plan above 200k tokens?**
Not as a self-serve option at the time of writing. Teams needing more volume appear to need to contact the company directly rather than checkout online.

**Is What The Diff beginner-friendly?**
Yes — setup is a matter of connecting a GitHub or GitLab account and authorizing the app on the relevant repositories; there's no prompt-writing or configuration required to get a basic PR description generated.

For more AI tools that plug into a developer workflow, browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Cody AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Sourcegraph's Cody pairs AI chat with codebase-wide search, but its Free and Pro plans are gone — here's what remains and who it's for.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Cody AI still worth using in 2026?

Cody is Sourcegraph's AI coding assistant, built on the company's code-search engine so it can pull context from an entire codebase rather than just the open file. The catch: Sourcegraph sunset the self-serve Free and Pro plans on July 23, 2025, so Cody is now bundled only into Sourcegraph Enterprise — a sales-led, five-figure-minimum contract, not a $10/month IDE plugin.

### At a glance

| | Cody AI |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Not self-serve — part of Sourcegraph Enterprise, minimum annual contract around $16,000 |
| Free tier | None as of July 23, 2025 (Free/Pro/Enterprise Starter plans were sunset) |
| Best for | Enterprises already on Sourcegraph who need AI chat/autocomplete tied to large, multi-repo codebase search |
| Standout feature | Context pulled from Sourcegraph's code-search index across an org's entire codebase, not just open files |

### What Cody actually is

Sourcegraph built its name on enterprise code search — the ability to search and navigate across every repository a large organization owns, not just the one open in an editor. Cody is the AI layer on top of that index: a chat and autocomplete assistant that uses Sourcegraph's search API to retrieve relevant functions, symbols, and usage patterns from across an entire codebase before generating an answer or a completion.

That's the pitch that separates Cody from most AI coding assistants: instead of relying only on the handful of open tabs and files an editor can see, it can, in principle, reason about how a function is used three repositories away. Sourcegraph doesn't publish an exhaustive model list in its public docs, but its documentation names Anthropic's Claude models as the default backbone for chat and edits, with OpenAI models available as an alternate configuration, and a DeepSeek-Coder-V2 model (hosted via Fireworks.ai) used for autocomplete. Enterprise customers can also bring their own API keys or route to self-hosted models, which matters for regulated industries that can't send code to a third-party inference endpoint.

Cody ships as extensions for VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Visual Studio, and a web app, plus a CLI for scripted or agentic use.

### The pricing situation you need to know about first

This is the part that makes Cody different from every other assistant in this comparison set: **it no longer has a self-serve plan**. Sourcegraph's own FAQ states plainly that "starting July 23, 2025, Cody will no longer be available for Free, Pro and Enterprise Starter plans," and that the change "will not impact Cody Enterprise customers." Individual developers and small teams who want a Sourcegraph-branded AI assistant are being pointed instead toward Amp, Sourcegraph's newer, separately billed agentic coding product — Cody itself now lives exclusively inside Sourcegraph Enterprise.

Sourcegraph's public pricing page lists Enterprise at a minimum annual contract "starting at $16K," which includes a pool of credits for AI features that scales with team size, with volume credit buckets available as an add-on and no monthly credit expiry. There's no listed per-seat monthly price and no self-serve checkout — every Enterprise deal goes through a sales conversation.

| Plan | Price | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Free | Discontinued July 23, 2025 | No longer available for new or existing self-serve users |
| Pro | Discontinued July 23, 2025 | Existing users were offered $10–$40 in migration credits toward Amp |
| Enterprise Starter | Discontinued July 23, 2025 | Folded into full Enterprise |
| Enterprise | From $16,000/year minimum, custom quote | Cody chat/autocomplete/edit, full Sourcegraph code search, Deep Search, Batch Changes, Insights, Monitoring, MCP server/API/CLI access, single-tenant deployment, enterprise security controls, 24×5 support |

Pricing, plan availability, and feature sets were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly for AI coding tools — confirm current terms directly with Sourcegraph sales before budgeting around them.

### Core features that still differentiate it (inside Enterprise)

- **Codebase-wide context retrieval.** Cody's chat and completions are grounded in Sourcegraph's search index, so answers can cite where a function is defined and every place it's called, across repos — a meaningfully different approach from assistants that only see open files or a local embeddings cache.
- **Deep Search.** Sourcegraph markets an AI-powered search mode built for large, sprawling codebases, aimed at answering architecture and dependency questions that a single-repo assistant can't.
- **Batch Changes with agentic assistance.** Sourcegraph's Batch Changes tooling — for making the same code change across hundreds of repositories at once — now has an AI layer to help draft and apply large-scale refactors, which is a genuinely enterprise-scale use case most consumer coding assistants don't attempt.
- **Bring-your-own-model / self-hosted routing.** Enterprise customers can point Cody at their own model deployment or API keys rather than relying solely on Sourcegraph's hosted inference, which matters for companies with strict data-residency or model-approval requirements.
- **Multi-IDE support tied to one backend.** VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, and a web client all share the same context engine, so a team standardized on Cody isn't locked to a single editor.

### Who it's actually for

- **Large engineering orgs already paying for Sourcegraph.** If your company already licenses Sourcegraph Enterprise for code search across dozens or hundreds of repos, adding Cody is a natural extension — the context engine is already there.
- **Teams doing large-scale, cross-repo refactors.** The Batch Changes + AI combination is aimed squarely at "update this pattern across 300 repositories" work that individual-developer tools aren't built for.
- **Regulated or security-conscious enterprises.** Self-hosted model routing and single-tenant deployment options matter for finance, healthcare, and government engineering teams that can't send code to arbitrary third-party APIs.
- **Not a fit for solo developers, freelancers, or small startups.** With no free tier and a five-figure minimum contract, Cody is now priced entirely out of reach for individuals and small teams — those users are the exact audience Sourcegraph is steering toward Amp instead.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuine cross-repository context via Sourcegraph's search index | No self-serve plan — Free/Pro/Enterprise Starter were discontinued July 23, 2025 |
| Deep Search and Batch Changes address real enterprise-scale problems | Minimum contract starts around $16,000/year, sales-only |
| Supports Claude and OpenAI models, plus bring-your-own-model for compliance needs | No published per-seat price, making budgeting hard before a sales call |
| Multi-IDE support (VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, web) sharing one backend | Individual developers are explicitly redirected to a different product (Amp) |
| Single-tenant deployment and enterprise security controls available | Slower iteration cadence on the consumer-facing editor experience compared with Cursor or Copilot |

### Integrations and ecosystem

Cody's ecosystem is built around Sourcegraph's existing enterprise tooling rather than the plugin marketplaces consumer tools lean on. It offers a CLI and full API access for scripting and CI integration, an MCP server for connecting external tools and agents, and ties into Batch Changes, Insights, and Monitoring. There's no Zapier or Slack-app-style consumer integration layer publicized — the integration story here is "plug into your existing Sourcegraph Enterprise deployment," not "connect to your personal productivity stack."

### Where it's a strong fit

Cody makes the most sense for organizations that are already Sourcegraph Enterprise customers, or that need an AI assistant which understands relationships across a large, multi-repository codebase rather than a single project. The Deep Search and Batch Changes capabilities are legitimately hard to replicate with editor-native tools like Copilot or Cursor, which mostly reason about the files a developer has open or has recently touched.

### Where to think twice

Skip Cody if you're an individual developer, freelancer, or small team — there is no way to buy it without a sales conversation and a five-figure annual commitment, and Sourcegraph itself is pointing that segment of users toward Amp instead. Skip it if you need a transparent, published per-seat price to compare against Copilot's or Cursor's listed plans — Cody Enterprise pricing is quote-only. And skip it if you just want fast, low-friction autocomplete in a single repo; that's a job Copilot, Cursor, or Supermaven-style tools solve with a lighter footprint and a real free or low-cost tier.

### Bottom line

Cody's underlying idea — ground an AI assistant in real, indexed knowledge of an entire codebase rather than just open files — is still a technically credible approach, and Deep Search plus AI-assisted Batch Changes are genuinely enterprise-grade capabilities. But Sourcegraph restructured the product in mid-2025 so it's no longer accessible outside an Enterprise contract, removing it from consideration for most developers evaluating AI coding tools on their own budget. If you're already inside a Sourcegraph Enterprise deployment, Cody is worth activating. If not, Copilot, Cursor, or Tabnine will get you a usable AI coding assistant today without a sales call.

## FAQ

**Does Cody AI have a free plan?**
No. Sourcegraph discontinued the Free, Pro, and Enterprise Starter plans on July 23, 2025. Cody is now available only as part of a paid Sourcegraph Enterprise contract.

**How much does Cody cost?**
Sourcegraph doesn't publish a per-seat price. Enterprise plans start at a minimum annual contract of roughly $16,000, which includes a pool of AI-feature credits that scales with team size, and require contacting sales for a quote.

**What happened to Cody's individual Pro plan?**
It was sunset alongside the Free plan in July 2025. Existing Pro users were offered a small amount of migration credit toward Amp, Sourcegraph's newer AI coding product aimed at individual developers.

**What AI models does Cody use?**
Sourcegraph's documentation names Anthropic's Claude models as the default for chat and edits, with OpenAI models available as an alternative, and a DeepSeek-Coder-V2 model for autocomplete. Enterprise customers can also configure their own API keys or self-hosted models.

**Which IDEs does Cody support?**
VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Visual Studio, and a web app, all sharing the same Sourcegraph context engine, plus a CLI for scripted use.

**Is Cody good for solo developers or small teams?**
Not anymore. Without a self-serve plan, Cody isn't practically accessible to individuals or small teams; Sourcegraph directs that audience to Amp instead.

**How is Cody different from GitHub Copilot or Cursor?**
Cody's core differentiator is pulling context from Sourcegraph's code-search index across an organization's entire set of repositories, plus enterprise-scale tooling like AI-assisted Batch Changes and Deep Search. Copilot and Cursor are built around single-repo, open-editor context and have accessible self-serve pricing that Cody no longer offers.

**Can I use Cody if I have data-residency or compliance requirements?**
Enterprise plans support self-hosted/bring-your-own-model routing and single-tenant deployment, which can help meet data-residency needs — confirm specifics with sales, since exact compliance certifications aren't detailed publicly.

For broader AI coding options with accessible pricing, see our [GitHub Copilot review](/blog/github-copilot-review), [Cursor AI review](/blog/cursor-ai-review), and [Supermaven review](/blog/supermaven-review), or browse [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Tabnine Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Tabnine skips the free tier for enterprise-grade AI coding: on-prem/air-gapped deployment, zero code retention, and team pricing from $39/user.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Tabnine worth it in 2026?

Tabnine is an AI coding assistant built for teams that need code privacy and compliance more than they need the flashiest agent demo. It offers completions, in-IDE chat, and agentic workflows like Copilot or Cursor, but its real selling point is deployment flexibility — SaaS, VPC, or fully air-gapped — with zero data retention. It's priced and positioned for engineering orgs, not solo hobbyists.

## At a glance

| | Details |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $39/user/month (Code Assistant Platform, billed annually) |
| **Free tier** | None listed on the current pricing page — enterprise trials are arranged through sales |
| **Best for** | Regulated industries, enterprise engineering teams, air-gapped/on-prem environments |
| **Standout feature** | Flexible deployment (cloud, VPC, or fully air-gapped) with zero code retention |

## What Tabnine actually is

Tabnine has been around since well before "AI coding assistant" was a category — it started as a code-completion plugin and has since rebuilt itself into a full platform spanning completions, chat, and autonomous coding agents. In 2026 it operates as a product within Tricentis, the enterprise software-testing company that acquired Tabnine, though Tabnine continues to run as its own product line with its own pricing, docs, and IDE integrations.

Unlike tools built around a single house model, Tabnine lets teams choose or configure which large language model powers completions and chat, rather than locking everyone into one vendor's model — useful for enterprises with existing model-procurement agreements or compliance rules about which vendors can touch their code.

The platform installs into IDEs developers already use — VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and others — rather than asking teams to switch editors the way Cursor does. If your org has already standardized on VS Code or IntelliJ, Tabnine slots in as an extension instead of a replacement.

## Pricing

Tabnine currently lists two paid tiers on its pricing page, both billed per user per month on an annual subscription. As of this article's publish date, pricing and feature availability were accurate per Tabnine's public pricing page — AI tool pricing and plan structures change frequently, so confirm current figures on [Tabnine's official site](https://www.tabnine.com/pricing) before buying.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| **Code Assistant Platform** | $39/user/month (annual) | AI code completions (line and multi-line), in-IDE AI chat across the SDLC, support for major IDEs, Jira Cloud/Data Center integration, flexible deployment (SaaS, VPC, on-prem, air-gapped), zero code retention, SOC 2/ISO 27001/GDPR compliance, IP-protected suggestions, priority support |
| **Agentic Platform** | $59/user/month (annual) | Everything in Code Assistant, plus autonomous coding agents with optional human oversight, customizable "coaching guidelines" for org coding standards, a Tabnine CLI for terminal-based agentic workflows, an unlimited-codebase Context Engine, MCP tool integrations, Git/Jira/Confluence/API connectors, advanced governance and analytics, and an optional Headless Agents add-on for CI/CD pipelines |

Notably, Tabnine's public pricing page does not advertise a free-forever individual plan the way GitHub Copilot or Cursor do. If you're a solo developer wanting to try an AI autocomplete tool for free, [our GitHub Copilot review](/blog/github-copilot-review) and [Cursor review](/blog/cursor-ai-review) both cover tools with usable free tiers. Tabnine is priced for teams evaluating it through a sales conversation, not casual individual signup — anyone who wants a trial should contact Tabnine directly, since trial terms aren't published on the pricing page itself.

## Core features that differentiate it

**Deployment flexibility (SaaS, VPC, or fully air-gapped).** This is Tabnine's clearest differentiator against Copilot, Cursor, and Supermaven, all of which are cloud-hosted-only products. Tabnine can run entirely inside a customer's own infrastructure with no outbound calls to Tabnine's servers, which matters for defense contractors, financial institutions, and any org where code genuinely cannot leave a private network.

**Zero data retention and IP protection.** Tabnine states it does not retain submitted code for training and includes license-safe AI usage designed to reduce the risk of suggestions that echo copyrighted or improperly licensed training data. For legal and compliance teams, this is often the deciding factor over model quality alone.

**Enterprise Context Engine.** On the Agentic Platform, Tabnine maps an organization's codebase, architecture, and internal coding standards so suggestions are grounded in how a specific team writes code, not just generic patterns. Tabnine describes this as connecting to an unlimited number of codebases per org on that tier.

**Model choice.** Rather than shipping a single proprietary model, Tabnine lets organizations select or configure the underlying LLM, which gives procurement and security teams a say in which vendor's model actually touches their source code.

**Agentic CLI and CI/CD hooks.** The Agentic Platform includes a terminal-based CLI for agent-driven workflows and an optional Headless Agents add-on that can run agent tasks inside CI/CD pipelines rather than only interactively inside an IDE — a use case Copilot and Cursor don't emphasize as heavily in their own marketing.

## Who it's actually for

**Solo developers and hobbyists** are probably better served elsewhere. With no published free tier and a $39/month entry price aimed at teams, Tabnine is a hard sell for personal projects — Copilot's free tier or Cursor's Hobby plan get you further for $0.

**Small teams without compliance requirements** may find Tabnine pricier and more enterprise-flavored than needed. If your team just wants faster autocomplete and in-editor chat, Copilot Pro or Cursor Pro cost less per seat and skip the sales conversation.

**Regulated and security-conscious enterprises** are Tabnine's actual target market — healthcare, finance, government contractors, and any org with an air-gapped or VPC-only requirement will find few AI coding tools that even offer on-prem deployment, let alone as a headline feature.

**Engineering leaders who need governance and audit trails** get real value from the Agentic Platform's coaching guidelines and analytics, which let a platform team enforce coding standards across dozens or hundreds of developers.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| On-prem/VPC/air-gapped deployment options rare among AI coding tools | No published free tier for individuals |
| Zero code retention and strong compliance posture (SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR) | $39–$59/user/month is pricier than Copilot Pro or Cursor Pro |
| Model choice instead of lock-in to one vendor's LLM | Pricing requires annual commitment for the listed rates |
| Context Engine grounds suggestions in actual org codebase and standards | Less buzz/community content than Copilot or Cursor, so troubleshooting resources are thinner |
| CLI and CI/CD agent hooks extend beyond the IDE | Best features (agents, Context Engine) are gated to the pricier Agentic tier |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Tabnine integrates with the major IDEs developers already use, including VS Code and JetBrains products, so teams don't need to migrate editors — a contrast with Cursor, which is itself a forked editor. It connects to Jira (Cloud and Data Center), and the Agentic Platform adds Confluence, Git, and general API connections plus MCP (Model Context Protocol) support for wiring in custom tools. The Headless Agents add-on runs agent tasks as part of CI/CD rather than only inside an editor session.

Tabnine doesn't publish a consumer-style plugin marketplace, so its ecosystem story is aimed squarely at enterprise dev-tool stacks (Jira, Confluence, CI/CD) rather than broad no-code automation.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Organizations that legally or contractually cannot send source code to a third-party cloud and need on-prem or air-gapped deployment
- Teams already standardized on VS Code or JetBrains IDEs that want AI assistance without switching editors
- Engineering leaders who need audit trails, coding-standard enforcement, and governance controls across many developers
- Companies that want the option to swap the underlying LLM rather than being tied to one vendor's model

## Where to think twice

- If you need a fully free tool to experiment with, Tabnine isn't it — go with Copilot's free tier or Cursor's Hobby plan instead
- If your team is small, cost-sensitive, and has no compliance mandate, Copilot Pro or Cursor Pro deliver similar day-to-day value for less per seat
- If you want the most talked-about agentic coding experience with the biggest community and tutorial base, Cursor and Copilot currently have more mindshare
- If you can't get through Tabnine's sales process to a trial quickly, that friction may push time-boxed evaluations toward tools with instant self-serve signup

## Bottom line

Tabnine isn't trying to be the flashiest AI pair programmer — it's trying to be the one compliance and security teams will actually approve. If your org's blocker on AI coding tools has been "we can't send our code to someone else's cloud," Tabnine's on-prem and air-gapped options solve a problem Copilot, Cursor, and Supermaven don't address. For everyone else — solo developers, small teams, or anyone without a hard compliance requirement — the lack of a free tier and enterprise-first pricing make it a harder recommendation than the more consumer-friendly alternatives already covering this category.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Tabnine free?**
Tabnine's current public pricing page lists two paid plans starting at $39/user/month with no free-forever tier. Individuals or teams wanting to evaluate it should contact Tabnine's sales team directly, since trial terms aren't published.

**What's the difference between Tabnine's two plans?**
The $39/month Code Assistant Platform covers completions, IDE chat, and enterprise compliance/deployment options. The $59/month Agentic Platform adds autonomous coding agents, a CLI, unlimited codebase context via the Context Engine, MCP tool support, and governance/analytics controls.

**Does Tabnine store or train on my code?**
Tabnine states it operates with zero code retention, meaning submitted code isn't kept or used to train its models. Enterprises with stricter requirements should verify the exact data-handling terms in the contract, since marketing claims and contractual guarantees can differ in scope.

**Can Tabnine run without internet access?**
Yes — Tabnine supports air-gapped deployment alongside standard SaaS and VPC options, which is unusual among mainstream AI coding assistants.

**Which IDEs does Tabnine support?**
Tabnine integrates with major IDEs including VS Code and JetBrains products. Check Tabnine's docs for the current full list before assuming support for a less common editor.

**How does Tabnine compare to GitHub Copilot or Cursor?**
Copilot and Cursor are cloud-only, priced for individuals as well as teams, and both offer usable free tiers — see our [GitHub Copilot review](/blog/github-copilot-review) and [Cursor review](/blog/cursor-ai-review). Tabnine skips the free tier in favor of deployment flexibility and compliance features neither competitor currently matches.

**Is Tabnine good for beginners?**
It's usable inside a supported IDE, but its pricing and enterprise positioning mean individual learners will likely get more value from a free tool first. Tabnine makes more sense once you're evaluating it as a team or company decision.

**Who owns Tabnine now?**
Tabnine was acquired by Tricentis, an enterprise software-testing company, but continues to operate as its own product with its own pricing and roadmap.

Looking for more AI coding options? Browse [AI & software deals](/category/software) for current offers, or compare Tabnine against [GitHub Copilot](/blog/github-copilot-review), [Cursor](/blog/cursor-ai-review), and [Supermaven](/blog/supermaven-review) to see which fits your team's workflow and budget.

title: Speechify Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Speechify turns PDFs, ebooks, and web pages into natural AI speech. Here is what the free tier and $29/month Premium actually offer.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Speechify worth it in 2026?

Speechify is a text-to-speech app that reads PDFs, ebooks, web pages, and scanned documents aloud in natural-sounding AI voices. It's a strong pick if you read a lot and want to listen instead, especially for dyslexia, ADHD, or vision-related reading fatigue. The free plan is limited to 10 robotic voices and 1.5x speed, so most people who need natural voices end up on the $29/month Premium plan.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (limited voices); Premium from $29/month |
| **Free tier** | Yes — 10 basic voices, 1.5x max speed, core TTS only |
| **Best for** | Students, professionals, and readers with dyslexia or ADHD who consume long documents |
| **Standout feature** | 1,000+ natural AI voices across 60+ languages with OCR scan-and-listen |

## What Speechify actually is

Speechify is a voice productivity app built by Cliff Weitzman, who has dyslexia and started the company after building his own text-to-speech workaround in college. What began as a reading tool has grown into a broader platform: alongside text-to-speech, it now includes voice typing/dictation, AI summaries, an AI voice assistant, and AI-generated podcasts. The company says it has more than 200 employees and has picked up recognition including a 2025 Apple Design Award and a "Chrome Extension of the Year" nod — both notable, though these are Speechify's own claims worth treating as marketing points rather than independently audited facts.

The core product converts written text into spoken audio using AI voice models, not simple robotic text-to-speech. It works across a browser extension (Chrome and Edge), native Mac and Windows apps, iOS and Android apps, and a web app, so the same library of documents and settings can follow you between devices. There's also a developer-facing Speechify API for building TTS into other apps, and a separate product called Speechify Studio aimed at voiceover and dubbing production — both priced and sold separately from the consumer app this review focuses on.

## Speechify pricing

Speechify's plan structure is simpler than most AI tools — there's no confusing middle tier, just a hard line between the free version and Premium.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 10 robotic-sounding voices, up to 1.5x playback speed, basic text-to-speech only |
| Premium | $29/month (billed monthly); Speechify advertises roughly 60% savings on annual billing | 1,000+ natural AI voices, 60+ languages, up to 5x playback speed, Scan & Listen (OCR), AI summaries and chat, voice typing, AI podcast creation, voice AI assistant, Google Drive/Dropbox/OneDrive integrations |

Speechify's pricing page doesn't spell out the exact annual dollar figure alongside the "60% savings" badge, so if you're planning to pay yearly, confirm the exact checkout total before committing — it should land somewhere in the low-teens per month, but treat that as an estimate rather than a quoted price. There's no published free trial for Premium; you either stay on the free tier or subscribe directly. Speechify also lists a separate "Speechify for Education" option in its footer navigation but doesn't publish student pricing on the main page, so check directly with Speechify if you're eligible.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability above were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — AI tool pricing moves quickly, so double-check current numbers on Speechify's own pricing page before subscribing.

## Core features that actually matter

**Natural AI voices at real reading speed.** The free tier's 10 voices are genuinely robotic-sounding and cap out at 1.5x speed — fine for testing the app, not for daily use. Premium's 1,000+ voices hold intonation reasonably well at faster speeds, and Speechify lets you push playback up to 5x. Most competing readers start losing clarity above 2-3x; going faster without the audio turning to mush is the biggest reason people upgrade from a free screen reader.

**Scan & Listen (OCR).** Point your phone camera at a printed page, textbook, or handout and Speechify will OCR the text and read it back. This is one of the features that separates it from a plain "read my PDF aloud" tool — it works on physical paper, not just digital files.

**Multi-format library support.** Speechify reads PDFs, Word docs, ePub ebooks, web articles (via the browser extension), Google Docs, and email. Documents sync across the mobile, desktop, and web apps, so you can start a chapter on your phone during a commute and pick it back up on your laptop.

**AI summaries and voice assistant.** Premium adds a layer on top of raw text-to-speech: you can ask Speechify's AI assistant to summarize a document, answer questions about what you just listened to, or generate a quiz from the content. This is closer to a study companion than a pure reader.

**Voice typing and AI podcasts.** Voice typing lets you dictate instead of type, which Speechify says can be roughly five times faster than typing for most people — a vendor claim worth testing yourself rather than taking at face value, since typing speed varies by person. AI Podcasts turns a document or topic into a podcast-style audio conversation, for people who'd rather listen to a discussion than a flat read-aloud.

## Who Speechify is actually for

- **Students and researchers** reading dense textbooks, journal articles, or long PDFs will get the most out of Scan & Listen and the AI summary/quiz features — this is close to a built-in study buddy.
- **People with dyslexia, ADHD, or low vision** are Speechify's original and most natural audience; the app was built from that use case first, and the OCR and speed controls address real friction points other readers don't solve as directly.
- **Busy professionals** who want to "read" long emails, reports, or web articles during a commute or workout will find the browser extension and mobile sync genuinely useful for reclaiming otherwise dead time.
- **Casual readers who only occasionally need TTS** may be better served sticking with a phone's built-in accessibility reader (iOS VoiceOver, Android TalkBack) or a free browser extension, since $29/month is a real ongoing cost for infrequent use.
- **Teams needing bulk voiceover or dubbing production** should look at Speechify Studio specifically, not the consumer app reviewed here — it's sold and priced separately.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Natural-sounding voices remain clear even at 3-5x speed | Free plan is genuinely limited — 10 robotic voices, 1.5x cap |
| OCR "Scan & Listen" works on physical printed pages, not just digital files | No published free trial for Premium; it's free tier or full subscription |
| Cross-device sync across mobile, desktop, browser extension, and web | $29/month is pricier than several TTS-only alternatives once you compare feature-for-feature |
| AI summaries, quizzes, and voice assistant go beyond plain read-aloud | Exact annual price isn't shown up front on the pricing page — you need to check at checkout |
| Broad platform support: iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, Chrome, Edge | Voice typing speed claims are Speechify's own marketing figures, not independently verified |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Premium includes direct integrations with Google Drive, Dropbox, and Microsoft OneDrive, so documents stored there can be opened and read without manually uploading files first. The Chrome and Edge browser extensions turn any web page or article into audio with one click — arguably the most-used entry point for daily readers. Developers can also use a separate Speechify API for embedding voice models into other apps; it's billed and documented independently from the consumer subscription, so check Speechify's developer pages for current pricing rather than assuming it matches the $29/month plan.

## Where it's a strong fit

Speechify earns its subscription price for anyone who reads long-form text daily and finds their eyes or attention give out before the page does. High playback speed without robotic-sounding audio, OCR for physical documents, and cross-device sync cover most of the friction points that make people abandon free text-to-speech tools. For students cramming through assigned reading or professionals working through long reports, the AI summary and quiz layer adds value beyond just "hearing the words."

## Where to think twice

If you need a fully free tool and only occasionally listen to text, Speechify's Premium price is hard to justify — built-in options like iOS VoiceOver, Android TalkBack, or free browser extensions cover light, occasional use at no cost. Teams that need enterprise compliance documentation, SOC 2 reports, or formal data-processing agreements should confirm those details directly with Speechify's sales team before rolling it out organization-wide, since that isn't published on the consumer pricing page. And if your priority is voice cloning or dubbing production rather than reading your own documents aloud, a tool built specifically for that — such as [ElevenLabs](/blog/elevenlabs-review) — is a closer match.

## Bottom line

Speechify does one thing very well: it turns dense reading into listening without sacrificing speed or clarity, backed by genuinely useful extras like OCR scanning and AI summaries. The free tier is a fair way to test whether TTS fits your workflow, but anyone who decides it does will likely need Premium's natural voices to make it stick long-term. At $29/month, it's not the cheapest reader around, but for students, professionals, and anyone managing dyslexia or reading fatigue, it's one of the more complete options available.

## FAQ

**Is Speechify free?**
There's a free plan, but it's limited to 10 robotic-sounding voices and a maximum 1.5x playback speed. The natural AI voices, faster speeds, OCR scanning, and AI features are gated behind the $29/month Premium plan.

**How much does Speechify Premium cost?**
Premium is listed at $29/month for monthly billing. Speechify advertises around 60% savings for annual billing, though the exact annual total isn't shown directly on the pricing page — confirm it at checkout.

**Does Speechify offer a free trial?**
Speechify's pricing page doesn't list a published free trial for Premium; you either use the free tier or subscribe to Premium directly. Trial availability can change, so check the current pricing page before assuming one is or isn't offered.

**Can Speechify read physical books and printed pages?**
Yes. The Scan & Listen feature uses OCR to scan printed text via your phone's camera and convert it to speech, which is separate from uploading digital files like PDFs or ebooks.

**Is Speechify good for students with dyslexia or ADHD?**
Speechify was originally built by its founder as a personal tool for dyslexia, and features like adjustable speed, OCR scanning, and AI summaries aim squarely at reducing reading friction. Many students and educators use it for this reason, though it's worth trying the free tier first to see if the voices and interface work for you.

**What's the difference between Speechify and ElevenLabs?**
Speechify is built primarily for reading your own documents and web pages aloud, with OCR and study features layered on top. [ElevenLabs](/blog/elevenlabs-review) is built more for voice generation, cloning, and content creation — dubbing, voiceovers, and character voices for video or audio projects. They overlap on "AI voices" but solve different core problems.

**Does Speechify handle multiple languages?**
Yes, Premium includes access to 60+ languages across its voice library, according to Speechify's own product pages.

**Is Speechify available on all my devices?**
Yes — Speechify has iOS and Android apps, native Mac and Windows desktop apps, Chrome and Edge browser extensions, and a web app, with documents and settings syncing across them.

Looking for more AI reading and accessibility tools? See our [ElevenLabs review](/blog/elevenlabs-review) for AI voice generation and cloning, or browse [AI & software deals](/category/software) for current discounts on productivity tools.

title: Stepsize AI Review 2026: What It Was, Now Part of ClickUp
excerpt: Stepsize AI made automated engineering reports from Jira/Linear data. It was acquired by ClickUp in 2025 — here is what it did and what replaced it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Stepsize AI still worth signing up for in 2026?

No — not as a standalone product. Stepsize AI, which turned Jira and Linear activity into automated engineering reports, was acquired by ClickUp and its website now displays an acquisition notice instead of a working signup flow. This review covers what Stepsize actually did, why engineering leaders liked it, and what to use instead now that it no longer operates independently.

## At a glance

| | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price (historical) | Free tier; Team plan from roughly $19–23/user/month |
| Free tier/trial | Yes — a free tier plus a no-credit-card first AI-generated report |
| Best for (historically) | Engineering managers and VPs of Engineering who needed recurring status reports without manually compiling them |
| Standout feature | Auto-generated weekly reports from Jira/Linear data, with plain-language commentary explaining the numbers |
| Current status | Acquired by ClickUp — no longer sold or onboarded as an independent product |

If you landed here searching for "Stepsize AI review" hoping to sign up, stop: the company's own homepage now reads "Exciting news! Stepsize has been acquired by ClickUp," with a link pushing visitors toward ClickUp instead of a Stepsize signup form. What follows is an honest account of what Stepsize built, who it was for, and where that functionality lives now.

## What Stepsize AI actually was

Stepsize positioned itself as an "AI engineering intelligence" tool — software that sat on top of a team's existing issue tracker (Jira or Linear) and turned raw ticket activity into narrative reports a non-technical stakeholder could actually read. The pitch was straightforward: engineering managers spend real hours every week manually assembling status updates for leadership, and most of that work is just translating burndown charts and ticket counts into sentences. Stepsize tried to automate that translation layer.

Rather than asking teams to adopt a new workflow, Stepsize connected directly to tools engineers already used — Jira, Linear, and Slack — and generated dashboards and written reports without requiring manual setup. The company described this as "zero setup": connect your tracker, and a report generates itself using the epics, issues, and status changes already in your data.

It's worth being upfront here: Stepsize's own marketing described these reports as "zero setup" and AI-generated from real ticket data — those are vendor claims, not something independently benchmarked, and there's no way to verify report accuracy for a product no longer accepting new signups.

## Core features, as the product described them

Based on Stepsize's own site and product pages before the acquisition notice replaced them, these were the capabilities it built its pitch around:

- **Automated weekly reports.** Stepsize generated recurring, scheduled reports summarizing engineering progress without anyone manually compiling data — pulled straight from Jira or Linear activity.
- **Metrics with automatic commentary.** Rather than just showing a chart, Stepsize's dashboards paired data (cycle time, throughput, issue counts) with AI-written plain-language explanations of what the numbers meant.
- **Project-level insights from epic structure.** The tool used the way teams had already organized epics and issues in their tracker to identify themes in the work — surfacing what a sprint or quarter was actually about, not just how many tickets closed.
- **Risk detection and suggestions.** Stepsize flagged likely delivery risks (stalled tickets, scope creep signals, slipping due dates) and paired the flag with an actionable suggestion rather than a bare alert.
- **Multiple report formats for different audiences.** The product listed use cases spanning daily standups, team syncs, sprint reports, kanban reports, and executive summaries — the idea being one data source, several audience-appropriate outputs.

## Who it was actually for

Stepsize wasn't aimed at individual developers. Its value proposition only made sense at the team-and-above level, where someone (an EM, a director, a VP of Engineering) is regularly expected to explain engineering output to people who don't read Jira boards directly.

- **Engineering managers running weekly or sprint-level reporting** were the clearest fit — the "zero setup" pitch specifically targeted the recurring status-update chore on an EM's plate.
- **VPs of Engineering and CTOs** needing leadership-facing summaries without pulling an EM off real engineering work were the audience for the "executive summaries" use case and Enterprise's quarterly leadership reports.
- **Small startups on the free tier** got a taste of automated reporting with a 20-open-issue cap — workable for an early team, not past a handful of active workstreams.
- **Solo developers and freelancers** were never the target; there's no individual-contributor use case, since the whole product summarizes a team's collective output for someone else to read.

## Pricing — what it cost, and important caveats

Pricing details below reflect what Stepsize published before the acquisition notice replaced its marketing pages. Because the product is no longer independently sold, none of this can be verified against a live checkout flow, and figures should be treated as historical rather than current.

| Plan | Historical price | What it included |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0/month | Unlimited users, capped at 20 open issues, editor extensions |
| Team | ~$19/user/month billed annually (~$23/user/month billed monthly) | 5 users included, unlimited issues, PR and issue-tracker integrations |
| Business | Custom/negotiated pricing | Everything in Team, plus SSO (SAML), priority support, deeper Jira integration |
| Enterprise | Custom pricing | Everything in Business, plus admin tools, custom SSO, custom roles, quarterly leadership reports |

One note: the scraped Business-tier figure on Stepsize's cached pricing page was inconsistent and not a reliable per-user monthly number, so it's omitted here — treat the Free and Team rows above as the only ones worth citing, and confirm anything else with ClickUp directly. Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability described in this article reflect information available as of this post's publish date (2026-09-19) and, for a product no longer sold independently, should not be assumed current.

## Pros and cons (as it operated)

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Genuinely "zero setup" — connected straight to Jira/Linear without new workflow adoption | No longer available as a standalone product to sign up for |
| Covered multiple report formats (standup, sprint, executive) from one data source | AI-generated commentary is inherently only as good as ticket hygiene in the source tracker |
| Free tier existed for small teams to try before paying | Business/Enterprise pricing was opaque, requiring a sales conversation |
| Risk detection paired flags with suggested next steps, not just alerts | Data never used to train models is a hard claim to verify from the outside |
| Encrypted data at rest and in transit (AES-256, per the vendor) | Limited to Jira and Linear — no support for other trackers like Azure DevOps or Asana |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Stepsize's integration story was narrow by design: Jira and Linear as the primary issue-tracker connections, plus Slack for delivering reports where engineering teams already communicate. There was no broad app marketplace, Zapier connector, or public API documented — this was a point solution built to plug into two specific trackers, not a general-purpose automation platform. If your team ran a different tracker (Azure DevOps, Asana, monday.com), Stepsize's integration surface never covered you.

## Where it was a strong fit

Teams already living inside Jira or Linear, with an EM tired of manually writing the same weekly update, got real value from Stepsize's core loop: connect the tracker, get a written report, stop copy-pasting ticket counts into a Slack message by hand. The risk-detection layer — flagging stalled work with a suggested fix rather than a bare red dot — was a genuinely useful step beyond a plain burndown chart, assuming your tracker data was clean enough for the AI commentary to be trustworthy.

## Where to think twice (and what replaced it)

Since Stepsize AI is no longer sold as an independent product, the honest answer here is simple: everywhere, right now, because you can't actually buy it. If you're evaluating this category today:

- **If you need to sign up for a new tool today** — skip Stepsize entirely; there's no active checkout flow, and the company's own site redirects interest toward ClickUp.
- **If your team doesn't use Jira or Linear** — Stepsize's reporting depended entirely on those two trackers, so even historically it wouldn't have fit teams on other systems.
- **If you need guaranteed long-term support and a roadmap** — post-acquisition products routinely get folded into the acquirer's roadmap on the acquirer's timeline, not the original company's; assume Stepsize's feature set will change shape inside ClickUp rather than persist unmodified.
- **If you already use ClickUp** — look at ClickUp's own reporting and AI features directly, since that's where Stepsize's team and technology have landed.

## Bottom line

Stepsize AI solved a real, specific problem — automating the weekly ritual of turning Jira or Linear activity into a report a non-engineer could read — without asking teams to change how they tracked work. That's a sound idea, and it's presumably why ClickUp acquired the team and technology rather than letting a competitor build the same thing. But as a product you can evaluate and buy today, Stepsize AI doesn't exist independently anymore. If engineering-report automation is what you're after, your realistic options now are ClickUp's own reporting tools (where Stepsize's technology has gone) or a fresh look at competing engineering-intelligence platforms, not a Stepsize signup.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Stepsize AI still available to sign up for?**
No. Stepsize's website now displays an acquisition notice pointing visitors to ClickUp instead of a working signup or onboarding flow.

**Who acquired Stepsize AI?**
ClickUp. The acquisition is confirmed directly on Stepsize's own homepage, though a detailed public deal announcement with financial terms wasn't independently verifiable at the time of writing — confirm current details on ClickUp's own site if that matters for your evaluation.

**What did Stepsize AI actually do?**
It connected to a team's Jira or Linear issue tracker and generated automated reports — daily standups, sprint summaries, and executive-level updates — using AI-written commentary layered on top of real ticket activity, without requiring manual setup.

**Did Stepsize AI have a free tier?**
Historically, yes — a free plan capped at 20 open issues with unlimited users, plus a "first report free" trial offer that didn't require a credit card. Neither should be assumed to still exist now that the product isn't independently sold.

**What issue trackers did Stepsize AI support?**
Jira and Linear were the two primary integrations, along with Slack for delivering generated reports. There was no support documented for other trackers like Azure DevOps or Asana.

**Is my data safe if I was a former Stepsize customer?**
Stepsize's published security claims included AES-256 encryption at rest and in transit and a commitment that customer data was never used to train AI models. For current data-handling questions post-acquisition, that's a question for ClickUp directly rather than Stepsize's own (now largely dormant) policies.

**What should I use instead of Stepsize AI now?**
The most direct path is ClickUp's own reporting and AI features, since that's where Stepsize's team and technology were absorbed. Outside of ClickUp, teams looking for automated engineering reporting from Jira or Linear data should evaluate current engineering-intelligence platforms directly, since this space has moved quickly and this article shouldn't be read as an endorsement of any specific alternative.

**Is Stepsize AI beginner-friendly for a non-technical manager?**
That was the core pitch — turning raw ticket data into plain-language reports for people who don't read Jira boards directly — but since it's no longer available to trial, that claim can't be independently verified today.

For more AI and software tool coverage, see [AI & software deals](/category/software).

title: Boomy Review 2026: AI Music Generator Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: Boomy turns text-free prompts into original songs and distributes them to Spotify and Apple Music. Here is what it costs and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Boomy worth it for making AI music?

Boomy is a browser-based AI music generator that lets anyone with no musical training assemble original songs in minutes and push them to Spotify, Apple Music and 150+ other stores. It's a solid pick for quick background tracks, social clips and experimentation, but the free plan is limited and the output rarely sounds like a fully produced human record.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free plan available; paid tiers commonly listed around $9.99/month and up (confirm current pricing on site) |
| **Free tier/trial** | Yes — limited song creations, save-only (no download/distribution) |
| **Best for** | Non-musicians, content creators, hobbyists wanting quick original tracks |
| **Standout feature** | One-click distribution to Spotify, Apple Music, TikTok and 150+ stores |

Boomy has been around since 2019, which makes it one of the older names in AI music generation — it predates the current wave of prompt-based tools like Suno and Udio, and its interface still reflects that earlier, more template-driven approach rather than a single text-box prompt.

## What Boomy actually is

Boomy is a web app (no downloadable software, works in a browser) that generates the instrumental foundation of a song — chord progressions, drums, bass, melody — from a set of style and mood selections, then lets you tweak the arrangement, swap sections, and layer your own vocals or an AI voice on top. It isn't a single-prompt text-to-song generator in the way Suno or Udio have become known for; it leans more on guided style/genre pickers and a track editor, which makes it faster to get a usable instrumental but gives you less control over lyrical content than prompt-first tools.

The company doesn't publish which underlying model architecture powers its generation engine, and there's no public confirmation of a specific foundation model — so treat "the AI" here as a proprietary, in-house system rather than a named large model you'd recognize from other tools.

Once a track is generated, Boomy's core pitch is what happens next: it has its own distribution pipeline that pushes finished songs to Spotify, Apple Music, TikTok, YouTube Music and a long list of other stores and streaming services, positioning itself less as a novelty generator and more as an end-to-end "make a song, release a song" pipeline for people without a label or distributor.

## Pricing

Boomy runs a freemium model: a free plan lets you generate and save songs inside the app, while paid membership tiers unlock downloading your audio files, higher creation limits, and — critically — the ability to submit songs to Boomy's distribution network so they land on streaming platforms.

Boomy's pricing page is a JavaScript-rendered single-page app, which makes it hard to pull a clean, current price table from outside the app. Publicly referenced price points for Boomy's paid tiers cluster around $9.99/month for an entry-level tier and roughly $29.99/month for a higher-volume tier with more creation credits and a better royalty split; some listings also reference a higher tier near $89.99. Treat these as directional rather than exact — **confirm plan names, prices and inclusions directly on boomy.com/pricing before subscribing**, since AI tool pricing pages change often.

| Tier | Typical price range | What it generally unlocks |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | Generate and save songs in-browser; no downloads or streaming distribution |
| Entry paid tier | ~$9.99/mo (verify) | Song downloads, higher creation limits, distribution eligibility |
| Higher paid tier | ~$29.99/mo (verify) | More monthly credits, better revenue share on distributed tracks |
| Top-end / annual option | Reported up to ~$89.99 (verify) | Highest volume and/or annual billing discount |

Pricing, free-tier limits and feature availability were accurate to the best of available research as of this post's publish date and can change — always check Boomy's own pricing page for the current numbers before you commit.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**Guided style-based song generation.** Instead of a single free-text prompt, Boomy leans on genre, mood, and instrumentation pickers to build the instrumental base of a track. This is faster for getting to "something usable" quickly but gives less granular control over structure than a detailed text prompt would in a tool built around prompting.

**In-app track editing.** You can swap sections, regenerate individual parts, and adjust arrangement elements after the initial generation, rather than only being able to regenerate the whole song from scratch — useful if 80% of a generated track works and you just want to fix the chorus or the drum pattern.

**Vocal layering.** Boomy supports adding your own recorded vocals (or, depending on plan/feature availability, AI-generated vocals) over the generated instrumental, which is the difference between an instrumental beat and something that functions as a finished "song."

**Direct-to-streaming distribution.** The standout piece: paid Boomy plans include submission to a distribution network covering Spotify, Apple Music, TikTok, YouTube Music and 150-plus stores, without needing a separate distributor like DistroKid or TuneCore. This is the feature that most separates Boomy from pure "generate an audio file and download it" tools.

**Royalty/revenue participation.** Boomy has publicly talked about creators earning a share of streaming royalties on distributed tracks, though the exact split, payout thresholds and terms are the kind of detail that's genuinely worth reading in Boomy's own terms of service rather than taking at face value from any third-party summary — including this one.

## Who it's actually for

- **Hobbyists and non-musicians** who want a finished-sounding track for a video, podcast intro, or personal project without hiring anyone — the free plan is enough to test whether the output style fits what you need before paying.
- **Content creators and social video makers** who need a steady supply of royalty-safe-feeling background music and don't need deep compositional control — a paid tier's higher creation limits and downloads matter more here than the distribution feature.
- **Aspiring "artists" chasing streaming presence** who want a low-effort path to having tracks live on Spotify/Apple Music without going through a traditional distributor — this is arguably Boomy's most distinctive use case, though it's worth being honest that AI-generated catalog music competing for real listenership is a crowded, low-payout space.
- **Not a great fit** for musicians who want fine-grained compositional or lyrical control, for anyone who needs a specific named-model text-to-song workflow (Boomy isn't built that way), or for professional productions where a human-composed, mixed and mastered track is the deliverable.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| No musical skill or software needed to get a finished-sounding track | Free plan can't download or distribute — you're paying to actually use your songs anywhere |
| Built-in distribution to 150+ stores is genuinely differentiating | Pricing page is hard to verify from outside the app; tier names/prices aren't consistently published |
| In-app editor lets you fix parts of a generated track instead of starting over | Guided style pickers give less granular control than free-text prompt tools |
| Long track record (platform since 2019) versus newer, less-tested competitors | Underlying model/architecture isn't publicly disclosed |
| Supports layering your own vocals over AI instrumentals | Output can sound generic or repetitive, especially on longer or more complex requests |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Boomy's main "integration" is its own distribution pipeline rather than third-party API access — there's no widely documented public API for plugging Boomy generation into other apps, and no confirmed Zapier or Slack-style integrations. Its ecosystem value is the built-in path from "generated track" to "live on Spotify/Apple Music/TikTok" without stitching together a separate distributor.

## Where it's a strong fit

Boomy earns its keep when the goal is speed and a finished output, not deep creative control. If you need a usable instrumental for a YouTube video in the next ten minutes, want to test whether "having a song on Spotify" is something you actually want to pursue, or need a steady low-cost supply of background tracks for a content pipeline, Boomy's guided workflow gets you there faster than tools that expect a detailed compositional prompt.

## Where to think twice

Skip or think twice about Boomy if you need a fully free, no-strings way to download and use tracks — the free tier is a save-only sandbox, not a usable output source. Skip it if your workflow depends on precise lyrical or structural control via detailed text prompts, since Boomy's picker-based generation is a different paradigm.
