Skip it too if you need enterprise-grade licensing clarity or compliance documentation for commercial use at scale — Boomy is built for individual creators, not enterprise procurement, and you should read its actual terms of service before using generated tracks in any commercial context where licensing certainty matters. And if what you actually want is a specific, well-known foundation model's output, Boomy's non-disclosed generation engine won't satisfy that the way a tool built explicitly around a named model would.

## Bottom line

Boomy is a reasonable, low-friction entry point into AI music generation, especially for people who want a finished, streamable track without learning a DAW or a detailed prompting workflow. Its biggest real advantage is the built-in distribution pipeline, which few competing AI music tools bundle in the same way. The tradeoffs are real, though: the free tier is a demo more than a usable product, current pricing is genuinely hard to verify from outside the app so budget some time to check boomy.com directly before subscribing, and the picker-driven generation style gives up some control compared to prompt-first competitors. If your goal is "get something on Spotify quickly with minimal effort," it's worth trying the free tier first to see if the output style fits before paying for downloads or distribution.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Boomy free to use?**
Yes, Boomy has a free plan that lets you generate and save songs in the browser. Downloading the audio file and submitting a track for streaming distribution requires a paid membership tier.

**Can I actually put a Boomy song on Spotify?**
Yes — paid Boomy plans include submission to a distribution network that covers Spotify, Apple Music, TikTok, YouTube Music and 150-plus other stores, without needing a separate distributor.

**Do I own the songs I make with Boomy?**
Boomy has publicly described creators as being able to own and monetize songs made on the platform, but exact ownership terms and royalty splits are laid out in its own terms of service — read those directly before using a track commercially.

**What does Boomy cost?**
Boomy uses a freemium model with a free tier plus paid membership tiers; publicly referenced price points cluster around $9.99–$29.99 per month, with a higher tier reported near $89.99. Confirm exact current prices and inclusions on Boomy's own pricing page, since they can change.

**Is Boomy good for beginners with no music experience?**
Yes — that's its core audience. The guided style, mood and instrument pickers are built specifically so people with zero music theory or production background can get a finished-sounding track.

**How is Boomy different from Suno or Udio?**
Suno and Udio are largely prompt-first: you describe a song in text and get a full track, often with AI-generated vocals and lyrics, back. Boomy leans more on guided pickers and an in-app editor to build the instrumental, then layers vocals on top, and its distinguishing feature is its built-in streaming distribution pipeline rather than prompt sophistication.

**Can I use my own vocals with Boomy?**
Yes, Boomy supports layering your own recorded vocals over its AI-generated instrumentals, which is how most finished "songs" on the platform come together rather than relying purely on generated audio.

**Is there a way to try Boomy risk-free?**
The free plan itself is the risk-free way to evaluate the output style and workflow before paying — since it doesn't require a subscription to start generating, you can judge fit before committing to a paid tier for downloads or distribution.

Looking for more ways to save on the software and AI tools in your stack? Check out [AI & software deals](/category/software) for current offers across the category.

title: Bugasura Review 2026: AI Bug Tracking Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: Bugasura pairs bug tracking and test management with AI testing agents. Here's what its free plan includes and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Bugasura Worth Using for Bug Tracking and QA?

Bugasura is a solid pick if you want bug tracking, test management, and AI-assisted testing in one tool without paying per seat — its free plan covers unlimited users and bug reports. It suits QA and engineering teams wanting AI help surfacing duplicate bugs, mapping risk, and running automated test agents, rather than teams needing just a bare-bones issue tracker.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | Free (unlimited users, unlimited bug reports) |
| **Free tier / trial** | Free forever plan with the full core platform; no time limit or seat cap |
| **Best for** | QA teams, engineering leads, and companies wanting AI-assisted bug tracking and test management |
| **Standout feature** | Asura AI agents (Browser, API, Mobile, Duplicate Bug) plus an MCP server for Claude/Cursor integration |

Bugasura is made by Moolya, a quality-engineering company, and positions itself as a "customer-focused" QA platform built for AI-era software development — leaning on AI agents throughout the bug-tracking and test-management workflow rather than treating AI as a bolt-on chatbot.

## What Bugasura Actually Is

At its core, Bugasura is a bug tracker: you log issues, attach screenshots or screen recordings, assign them, and move them through a workflow. What separates it from a plain issue tracker like a basic Jira board is the layer of AI features sitting on top — an AI issue tracker that helps triage and categorize bugs, a set of "Asura" testing agents that run automated checks, and a reporting tool (Eagle Eye) aimed at engineering leaders who want a quality dashboard rather than a raw bug list.

The platform also folds in test management and requirements management, so teams juggling a separate test-case tool, bug tracker, and requirements spreadsheet could consolidate into one product. A Chrome extension and web widget handle in-context bug capture (screenshots, console logs, network data) directly from the browser, cutting down on "can you send me a screenshot and the steps to reproduce" back-and-forth.

Bugasura doesn't publicly name the specific underlying LLM(s) powering Testpert, the Asura agents, or the AI issue tracker — the vendor describes capabilities rather than the model stack, so confirm that directly with Bugasura if it matters for your evaluation.

## Bugasura Pricing

Bugasura's pricing is simple compared to most SaaS tools in this category: a full-featured free plan, then a custom enterprise tier for larger or regulated organizations.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0, no expiration | Unlimited users, unlimited bug reports, test management, AI issue tracker, requirements management, knowledge base, MCP server, Chrome reporter + web widget, 25+ integrations, 50 GB storage, SOC 2 Type II certification, unlimited Asura agent runs |
| **Custom (Enterprise & Scale)** | Contact sales for quoted pricing | Everything in Free, plus Testpert AI (advanced Q&A, risk mapping), Eagle Eye quality dashboards, on-premises deployment, SSO/SAML, dedicated infrastructure, private AI mode, and a dedicated success manager |

The notable thing here is that Bugasura doesn't gate core features or seat counts the way most competitors do — you get the full bug tracker, test management, AI issue tracker, and unlimited Asura agent runs without paying. The paid tier is really an enterprise/compliance upgrade: on-prem deployment, SSO, dedicated infrastructure, and the more advanced Testpert AI layer, rather than a "you've hit 3 users, now pay up" wall.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability above were accurate as of this article's publish date and can change — confirm current numbers on Bugasura's [pricing page](https://bugasura.io/pricing/) before committing, since AI tool pricing moves quickly.

## Core Features Walkthrough

**AI Issue Tracker.** Rather than a plain list of tickets, Bugasura's tracker uses AI to categorize incoming bug reports, flag likely duplicates, and route issues — useful for teams flooded with reports across multiple channels.

**Asura agents.** Bugasura's most distinctive feature set: specialized AI agents that run actual testing work rather than just organizing tickets. Browser Asura runs end-to-end web tests, API Asura validates contracts and edge cases, Mobile Asura handles mobile end-to-end testing, and Duplicate Bug Asura continuously scans incoming reports to catch repeats before they clutter the backlog. Having these unlocked on the free plan is a meaningful differentiator versus tools that keep automated testing agents behind a paywall.

**Test and requirements management.** Bugasura bundles test-case management and requirements tracking alongside bug tracking, helping QA teams trace a bug back to a specific requirement or test case rather than treating bugs as standalone tickets.

**MCP server for AI coding tools.** An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server connects to tools like Claude and Cursor, letting developers pull bug and quality context directly into their coding environment — a modern touch most legacy bug trackers don't offer yet.

**Eagle Eye and Testpert (paid tier).** Eagle Eye is a quality-visibility dashboard for engineering leaders, surfacing where quality risk is concentrated. Testpert is described by Bugasura as an AI that "thinks like experienced testers," asking clarifying questions and mapping risk across user journeys; both are reserved for the Custom/Enterprise plan.

## Who Bugasura Is Actually For

- **Solo developers or tiny teams** get a genuinely usable free bug tracker with AI triage help and unlimited users — no reason to pay unless you specifically need on-prem hosting or SSO.
- **QA teams and mid-size engineering orgs** benefit most from the Asura agents and combined test/requirements management, consolidating multiple QA tools into one platform.
- **Engineering leaders at larger companies** wanting quality-risk visibility (Eagle Eye) or SSO/on-prem deployment will likely need the Custom plan and a sales conversation.
- **Regulated industries** requiring data residency or private AI processing should plan on the enterprise tier from the start rather than trying to make the free plan work.

## Pros and Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Full feature set — AI issue tracking, unlimited Asura runs — free with no seat cap | Enterprise pricing isn't published; requires a sales call |
| Combines bug tracking, test management, and requirements tracking in one tool | Underlying AI model(s) not disclosed |
| MCP integration with Claude and Cursor is a useful, modern touch | Free plan storage capped at 50 GB |
| SOC 2 Type II certification available even on the free tier | Testpert and Eagle Eye locked to the paid Custom tier |
| 25+ integrations out of the box (GitHub, Jira, Asana, Slack, ClickUp) | No published trial for enterprise features |

## Integrations and Ecosystem

Bugasura lists more than 25 integrations, including GitHub, Jira, Asana, Slack, and ClickUp, covering most existing workflows without a wholesale process change. The Chrome Reporter and web widget let anyone — including non-technical stakeholders — file a bug with screenshots and technical context directly from the browser.

The MCP server is worth calling out again: it plugs into AI coding assistants like Claude and Cursor, so developers can query bug and quality context without leaving their editor — a category most established bug trackers (Jira, Linear, etc.) haven't caught up on, and arguably Bugasura's sharpest differentiator.

## Where Bugasura Is a Strong Fit

Bugasura fits well for QA-heavy teams already dealing with fragmented tooling — a bug tracker here, a test-case spreadsheet there, requirements buried in a doc — who want to consolidate without paying for three subscriptions. It's also strong for teams building with AI-assisted development workflows (Claude, Cursor, Copilot-style tools) wanting QA data queryable from inside the coding environment via MCP. Because the free plan doesn't cap users or core AI features, it also works for budget-conscious startups wanting automated Asura test agents rather than fully manual bug entry.

## Where to Think Twice

Bugasura is less compelling if you need enterprise pricing transparency upfront — the Custom plan requires a sales call, harder to budget for than tools with published per-seat pricing. If your team specifically needs Testpert or Eagle Eye, those sit behind that same opaque Custom tier, not a mid-priced plan.

Teams with heavy attachment storage needs (large video recordings of test runs, for instance) should watch the 50 GB free-tier cap closely. Because Bugasura doesn't publish which LLM(s) power Testpert and the Asura agents, teams with strict AI-vendor or data-processing requirements should raise that directly with sales before committing, particularly around private AI mode on the Custom plan.

If you're a solo developer who just wants the simplest possible bug list with zero AI involved, Bugasura's feature depth (test management, requirements tracking, multiple AI agents) may be more tool than you need.

## Bottom Line

Bugasura stands out mainly because it doesn't ration its AI features behind a paywall — the free plan includes unlimited users, unlimited bug reports, an AI issue tracker, and unlimited Asura testing agent runs, a genuinely generous starting point for QA tooling. The tradeoff is that its more advanced AI layer (Testpert, Eagle Eye) and enterprise compliance features live behind an unpriced Custom tier requiring a sales conversation. For QA teams and engineering orgs wanting to consolidate bug tracking, test management, and AI-assisted testing without an immediate spend, it's well worth a trial run; enterprises with strict compliance or budgeting needs should expect that pricing conversation before rolling it out broadly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Bugasura free to use?**
Yes. Bugasura offers a free-forever plan with unlimited users and bug reports, including its AI issue tracker, test management, requirements management, MCP server, and unlimited Asura agent runs — no published expiration date.

**How much does Bugasura's paid plan cost?**
The paid tier is called "Custom" and is priced individually per organization — contact sales for a quote. It targets enterprise and scale use cases like on-premises deployment, SSO/SAML, and dedicated infrastructure.

**Who makes Bugasura?**
Bugasura is built by Moolya, a quality-engineering company, according to Bugasura's own site.

**What AI features does Bugasura include?**
An AI issue tracker, specialized "Asura" testing agents (Browser, API, Mobile, and Duplicate Bug Asura), and — on the paid tier — Testpert (AI test generation and risk mapping) and Eagle Eye (a quality-visibility dashboard).

**Does Bugasura integrate with GitHub, Jira, or Slack?**
Yes. Bugasura lists 25+ integrations including GitHub, Jira, Asana, Slack, and ClickUp, plus a Chrome Reporter and web widget for in-browser bug capture.

**Is Bugasura good for non-technical stakeholders reporting bugs?**
The Chrome Reporter and web widget let anyone file a bug with screenshots and technical context without deep tool knowledge, making it approachable for non-engineers.

**What is the MCP server used for in Bugasura?**
It connects to AI coding tools like Claude and Cursor, letting developers pull bug and quality context directly into their coding environment instead of switching apps.

**Does Bugasura offer on-premises hosting?**
Yes, but only on the Custom/Enterprise plan — it isn't included in the free tier.

**What data privacy or compliance certifications does Bugasura have?**
Bugasura states it holds SOC 2 Type II certification, available even on its free plan. Enterprise customers needing additional compliance documentation, private AI mode, or data residency should raise specifics directly with Bugasura's sales team.

title: Playground AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Playground AI turns prompts into logos, social graphics, and AI-edited images. Here is how its free tier, pricing, and models hold up in 2026.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Playground AI Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict

Playground AI is a browser-based design and image-generation tool that's good for quick logos, social graphics, and AI-edited photos without a learning curve, but it's no longer a pure "type a prompt, get art" generator. The free plan is genuinely usable (10 images every 3 hours), and paid tiers add faster generation, more AI edits, and commercial-use clarity.

| At a glance | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | Free ($0/mo, 10 images every 3 hours) |
| Paid entry price | $15/month (Pro), $12/month billed annually |
| Free tier / trial | Yes — no credit card required |
| Best for | Solo creators and small businesses making logos, social posts, and quick photo edits |
| Standout feature | Combined access to GPT-4o image edit, Google's Nano Banana, and ByteDance's Seedream in one interface |

### What Playground AI actually is

Playground (playground.com) started out a few years ago as a straightforward AI image generator with a canvas-style editor, and it trained and released its own open-weight diffusion models — Playground v2 and v2.5 — competitive enough at the time to get benchmarked against Stable Diffusion XL and DALL-E 3 in independent comparisons.

The product has since shifted. As of this review, Playground's own homepage positions it as a "Free AI Design Tool" for logos, T-shirts, and social media graphics rather than a raw prompt-to-image generator, with templates sitting alongside generation and editing. Editing features now lean on named third-party models — Playground's pricing page lists **GPT-4o image edit, Google's Nano Banana (Gemini's image model), and ByteDance's Seedream** as the models powering its "edits" credits. If you remember Playground purely as an indie-model image generator, it's worth knowing the product has broadened into a general AI design surface.

Playground says it's used by more than 13 million creators — that's the company's own figure, not something independently auditable, so treat it as a scale claim rather than a verified statistic.

### Pricing

Playground runs three tiers: a genuinely free plan, a $15/month Pro plan (discounted to $12/month if you pay annually, at $144/year), and a $45/month Pro Plus plan (discounted to $36/month annually, at $433/year).

| Plan | Price | Images | Combined AI edits/month | Notable inclusions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/mo | 10 every 3 hours | 3 | Commercial use allowed, but with wait times at peak hours and a cooldown after 10 images |
| Pro | $15/mo ($12/mo billed annually) | 120 every 3 hours | 150 | Faster generation, all premium design templates, upscaling and background removal |
| Pro Plus | $45/mo ($36/mo billed annually) | Unlimited | 1,000 | Unlimited upscaling/background removal, early feature access, priority support, API access |

A few things worth flagging before you commit:

- The Free plan is not a locked-down trial — it's a permanently free tier, just rate-limited to 10 images per rolling 3-hour window, with wait times during busy periods.
- "Combined AI edits" is a shared pool across GPT-4o, Nano Banana, and Seedream edits — it's not 150 of each on Pro, it's 150 total.
- API access is not self-serve even on Pro Plus. Per Playground's own FAQ, the company is "prioritizing potential partners whose users will generate more than 1M images a month" and asks interested developers to apply through a form rather than just enabling a key.
- Only credit and debit cards are accepted; there's no listed support for PayPal or invoicing on the standard plans.

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — AI image tool pricing and model lineups move fast, so double-check the current numbers on Playground's own pricing page before subscribing.

### Core features that actually differentiate it

**Multi-model editing in one place.** Rather than picking a single house model, Playground routes "edit" requests across GPT-4o's image editor, Google's Nano Banana, and ByteDance's Seedream, all metered from the same monthly credit pool — genuinely convenient if you don't want separate subscriptions just to compare how each model handles the same edit.

**Commercial usage rights baked in from the free tier.** Per Playground's FAQ, you own the images you create and can use them commercially (YouTube thumbnails, Etsy products, Instagram posts, etc.) as long as you follow its terms — even on the free plan. That's a meaningfully different stance from tools that gate commercial use behind a paywall.

**Rolling rate limits, not a hard monthly cap.** The free plan's 10-images-per-3-hours limit resets on a rolling basis rather than a fixed daily or monthly quota, so bursty use (a batch of logo drafts one evening, nothing for days) isn't penalized the way a strict "10 per day" cap would penalize it.

**Design templates alongside raw generation.** The homepage's framing around logos, T-shirts, and social graphics suggests Playground has invested in template starting points rather than a blank prompt box — useful for a usable design fast, not artistic exploration.

**Upscaling and background removal as first-class features.** These land on Pro (capped) and Pro Plus (unlimited) — useful if your real goal is a print-ready or e-commerce-ready asset, not just an on-screen image.

### Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and side-hustlers making a handful of assets a month** — the free plan's 10-images-per-3-hours limit is workable off a deadline, with commercial use allowed from day one.
- **Small businesses and marketers needing quick, repeatable graphics** (social posts, product mockups, simple logos) — Pro's 120-images-per-3-hours and 150 combined edits/month covers a steady content cadence.
- **Agencies or high-volume shops generating dozens of assets a day** — Pro Plus's unlimited generation and 1,000 edits/month is the realistic floor; the API is still gated behind a manual application, so don't plan around self-serve automation.
- **Teams needing deep design control** (layers, vector export, brand kits) — Playground is a generation and light-editing tool, not a full design suite; pair it with a dedicated design tool for precise typography and vector work.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Usable free tier with real commercial rights, not just a demo | API access is invite/application-only, not self-serve even on the top plan |
| Access to multiple third-party editing models (GPT-4o, Nano Banana, Seedream) from one subscription | "Combined edits" pool means heavy users of any single model burn through the monthly allowance faster |
| Rolling rate limits are more forgiving than fixed daily caps | Free and Pro tiers both have generation limits, so it's not truly unlimited until Pro Plus |
| Upscaling and background removal included, not a separate paid add-on | Card-only payment, no listed invoicing/PayPal option |
| Annual billing knocks 20% off both paid tiers | Product positioning has shifted toward templated "design tool" branding, which may not suit users who specifically want an open-ended art generator |

### Integrations and ecosystem

Playground's ecosystem is comparatively narrow next to full design suites. There's no self-serve API — access is limited to applicants the company selects, with a stated preference for partners generating over a million images a month, ruling out most individual developers and small teams. There's no listed native Zapier, Slack, or Figma plugin on the pricing and FAQ pages reviewed here. If integrations into an existing workflow are a hard requirement, verify current plugin/API availability directly on Playground's site before subscribing, since this area tends to change without much announcement.

### Where it's a strong fit

- You want a no-cost way to generate commercially usable images without a workaround to unlock commercial rights.
- You want to try GPT-4o, Nano Banana, and Seedream edits without paying for three separate subscriptions.
- Your volume is bursty rather than constant — rolling rate limits suit occasional heavy use better than a hard daily ceiling.
- You want templated starting points (logos, social graphics, T-shirts) rather than a blank prompt every time.

### Where to think twice

- **If you need programmatic/API access now** — the application-only gate, aimed at partners doing 1M+ images/month, makes Playground a poor fit for developers wiring image generation into their own app on a normal timeline.
- **If you need a fully free tool with no rate limiting** — the rolling 3-hour cap and peak-hour wait times mean it's not suited to anyone needing fast, unthrottled output on demand.
- **If your team needs enterprise compliance documentation** (SOC 2, dedicated data-processing agreements, procurement contracts) — nothing in Playground's public pricing or FAQ pages references compliance certifications, so confirm directly with their team.
- **If you want deep manual design control** — vector editing, brand-kit management, and multi-page layout aren't what this tool is built for.
- **If you specifically want an "old-school" open-ended art generator** — the current homepage framing suggests a move toward practical design outputs over freeform artistic generation, which may not match expectations set by Playground's earlier reputation.

### Bottom line

Playground AI is a reasonable pick if what you actually want is fast, commercially usable images and edits without juggling separate subscriptions to the underlying models — its free tier is unusually generous, and Pro/Pro Plus scale sensibly for small teams. Where it falls short is anyone expecting self-serve API access or enterprise compliance documentation; both require going through Playground directly rather than just upgrading a plan. If your needs are templated, everyday design assets rather than deep creative control or developer integration, it's worth trying the free tier before paying.

### FAQ

**Is Playground AI actually free?**
Yes — the free plan has no credit card requirement and allows 10 images every 3 hours plus 3 combined AI edits (GPT-4o, Nano Banana, Seedream) per month, with commercial use rights included. It's rate-limited rather than time-limited, so it stays free indefinitely.

**How much does Playground AI cost per month?**
Pro is $15/month billed monthly, or $12/month ($144/year) if billed annually. Pro Plus is $45/month billed monthly, or $36/month ($433/year) billed annually.

**Can I use Playground AI images commercially?**
Yes, according to Playground's own FAQ, you own the images you generate and can use them commercially (product listings, social media, YouTube, etc.) as long as you follow the site's terms of service — this applies even on the free plan.

**Does Playground AI have an API?**
Not as a self-serve product. Access is granted by application, and Playground states it's currently prioritizing partners whose usage would exceed 1 million images a month, so smaller developers should expect a wait or a rejection rather than instant access.

**What AI models power Playground's image edits?**
Per Playground's pricing page, editing credits are shared across GPT-4o's image editor, Google's Nano Banana, and ByteDance's Seedream. The models behind straight text-to-image generation aren't broken out the same way on the pricing page, so confirm current model options directly in the app if that's a deciding factor.

**How does Playground AI compare to Midjourney or Google's Nano Banana directly?**
Playground incorporates Nano Banana as one of its editing models rather than competing purely head-to-head with it. See our [Google Nano Banana review](/blog/google-nano-banana-review) for that model alone, or our [Midjourney review](/blog/midjourney-review) for a prompt-driven generator with a different pricing model.

**Is Playground AI beginner-friendly?**
Yes — the interface leans on templates and straightforward prompt/edit workflows rather than exposing complex parameter controls, which makes it approachable for people without prior AI image generation experience.

**What payment methods does Playground AI accept?**
Only credit and debit cards, per its FAQ. There's no listed self-serve option for invoicing or PayPal; the company suggests contacting support directly for other arrangements.

title: Tome AI Review: What the App Was, and What Happened
excerpt: Tome pioneered AI-generated pitch decks with a narrative canvas format. Here's what it offered, and why tome.app now returns a 404.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Tome (tome.app) still around in 2026?

No — tome.app no longer resolves to a working product. Both its homepage and pricing page return a 404 error as of September 2026, and independent news coverage of the company has effectively gone quiet since its early buzz years. This review covers what Tome actually did as an AI presentation tool, why it mattered when it launched, and what to know if you land on its old links today.

**At a glance**

| | Tome |
|---|---|
| Launched | Beta March 2022; Tome 1.0 + iOS app October 2022 |
| Starting price | Historically had a free tier, with paid plans layered on top (last-known pricing, not currently verifiable) |
| Free tier | Yes, historically |
| Best for (historically) | Founders and marketers who wanted an AI-generated first draft of a pitch deck or narrative presentation |
| Standout feature | AI-generated "story starting points" plus live Figma/Airtable/Framer embeds |
| Current status | tome.app returns HTTP 404 on its homepage and pricing page; no working signup flow found |

If you're here because an old bookmark, a "best AI presentation tools" list, or a coworker's link pointed you to tome.app, that specific product doesn't appear to be reachable anymore. What follows is an honest account of what Tome was, what set it apart from slide software, and what to use instead now.

## What Tome actually was

Tome launched in beta in March 2022 and shipped its 1.0 version (plus an iOS app) that October, at the front edge of the wave of "AI-native" presentation tools that arrived alongside the broader generative-AI boom. It was built by a small team backed by venture investors, with the pitch that presentations shouldn't be built slide-by-slide in a grid-based editor the way PowerPoint or Google Slides had trained a generation of professionals to work. Instead, Tome framed itself as a "storytelling format" — a scrollable, narrative-driven canvas where each page could hold a mix of text, images, embedded prototypes, or live data, generated first by AI from a prompt or outline and then refined by hand.

That AI-first framing was Tome's real differentiator at launch. Where Google Slides and PowerPoint added AI features on top of an existing grid-based editor years later, Tome built the AI-generation step into its core workflow from day one: you'd type a topic or paste in rough notes, and Tome would produce a full first-draft deck — structure, copy, and imagery — that you'd then edit rather than build from a blank canvas.

Tome doesn't appear to have publicly documented exactly which underlying AI model(s) powered its generation features at any given point, which was fairly typical for AI startups in 2022–2023 before "powered by GPT-4" or similar became a standard marketing line. Its Product Hunt listing and public materials focused on the product experience rather than the model stack.

Pricing, plan tiers, and specific feature availability described below reflect what was publicly documented about Tome during its active years — treat this as a historical record rather than a live product page, since tome.app doesn't currently serve a working site to verify current terms against.

## Features that actually differentiated it

**AI-generated "story starting points."** Instead of a blank template, Tome would generate a structured first draft from a prompt — headings, body copy, and suggested imagery — that functioned as a starting point to edit rather than a finished product. This was the feature most reviewers and early users pointed to as genuinely useful, since it solved the "blank page" problem that eats the most time in deck-building.

**A narrative, scrollable canvas instead of a slide grid.** Tome pages weren't fixed 16:9 rectangles in the traditional sense — content could flow more like a long-form scrollable page, which suited narrative pitch decks and "about us" style presentations better than dense data-heavy slides.

**Live embeds from Figma, Airtable, and Framer.** Rather than pasting in a static screenshot of a prototype or spreadsheet, Tome let you embed live, interactive versions directly into a page — genuinely useful for product and design teams presenting work-in-progress.

**Mobile-optimized, link-shareable output.** Tome decks were built to be viewed and read well on a phone via a shareable link, not just projected on a screen or exported as a PDF — a deliberate bet that more presentations were being read asynchronously than presented live.

**Reasonably fast iteration loop.** Early reviewers consistently cited ease of use and speed to a presentable first draft as Tome's strength, at the cost of some layout flexibility compared to a traditional slide editor.

## Where Tome sat versus other AI presentation tools

If Tome's pitch sounds familiar, that's because the category it helped popularize is now crowded. [Gamma](/blog/gamma-review) picked up much of the same "prompt-to-deck" premise and is still an active, actively-priced product as of 2026, with a credits-based free tier and paid plans. [Plus AI](/blog/plus-ai-powerpoint-maker-review) took a different approach, building AI generation directly inside PowerPoint and Google Slides rather than a standalone canvas, which suits teams who don't want to leave tools they already know. [SlidesAI](/blog/slidesai-review) is narrower still, focused specifically on turning notes and documents into Google Slides decks.

Tome's scrollable, narrative-canvas format was arguably its most distinctive idea relative to all three — none of those tools abandoned the traditional slide grid the way Tome did. Whether that was a strength or a limitation depended on what you were building: a founder pitch deck suited Tome's format well; a data-heavy quarterly business review, less so.

## Who it was actually for (historically)

- **Startup founders building pitch decks**, where a narrative, less rigidly formatted presentation style suited fundraising and "tell a story" use cases well.
- **Marketing and brand teams** who wanted a polished, on-brand first draft fast, without needing a designer for every internal or external deck.
- **Product teams presenting work-in-progress**, thanks to live Figma and Framer embeds that kept prototypes interactive instead of static.
- **People building lightweight, shareable async presentations** meant to be read on a phone rather than projected in a room.
- **Users who needed rigid pixel-level layout control, dense data tables, or PDF export as a hard requirement** were consistently the group early reviews flagged as a worse fit — Tome's own Product Hunt reviews cited inflexible layouts and no PDF download among the recurring complaints even while it was active.

## Pros and cons (as the product stood while active)

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Genuinely fast AI-generated first drafts, not just a blank template | Layouts were less flexible than a traditional slide editor for precise design control |
| Narrative, scrollable format well-suited to pitch decks and async reading | No PDF export was a recurring complaint in user reviews |
| Live Figma, Airtable, and Framer embeds kept prototypes interactive | Customer support responsiveness was inconsistently reviewed |
| Free tier made it easy to try before committing to a paid plan | Mobile app and cross-platform support were more limited than desktop-first competitors like Google Slides |
| 4.8-star rating across 39 Product Hunt reviews reflected strong early user sentiment | The product and company are no longer verifiably reachable as of 2026 |

## Integrations and ecosystem (historically)

Tome's most-cited integrations were with **Figma** (embedding live design files and prototypes), **Airtable** (embedding live database views), and **Framer** (embedding interactive prototypes) — all aimed at product, design, and startup teams who needed their decks to show working software rather than static screenshots. There's no public record of a broad Zapier integration, a documented public API, or enterprise-grade SSO/compliance tooling comparable to what larger, still-active competitors offer today; Tome's integration story stayed centered on the design and product tooling stack rather than broad workflow automation.

## What happened to Tome

As of September 2026, both tome.app's homepage and its `/pricing` page return an HTTP 404 error on repeated checks — consistent with the site being taken offline or the domain no longer being actively maintained, rather than a temporary outage. There's no current signup flow, pricing page, or working product to evaluate.

Independent, verifiable reporting on exactly why or precisely when Tome went offline is thin. We were not able to find a clear on-the-record statement from the company itself (a shutdown notice, an acquisition announcement, or a pivot post) confirming the exact date or reason for the site going dark. If you need a definitive answer on Tome's corporate fate — shutdown, acquisition, or quiet wind-down — treat that as unconfirmed and worth checking directly with any former Tome team members' current public profiles, since we can't verify it from official sources.

One thing worth flagging for anyone searching for Tome now: a domain called **tomeapp.ai** — a different, unrelated site — has been promoted through paid press releases claiming to be an AI presentation tool "powered by Claude Opus 4.7." That domain is not the original tome.app covered in this review, has no verifiable connection to the original company, and its claims come from a paid press release rather than independent reporting. Be careful not to confuse the two if you're searching for the original product.

## Bottom line

Tome was a genuinely early and, by most contemporary accounts, well-executed entry into AI-generated presentations — its "story starting points" and narrative canvas format predated most of what's now standard in the category, and its 4.8-star Product Hunt rating reflected real user enthusiasm during its active years. But the product isn't reachable today: tome.app 404s on every page we checked, and there's no current pricing, signup, or support channel to point readers toward. If you need what Tome used to offer — fast AI-generated decks, live embeds, and a narrative format — [Gamma](/blog/gamma-review) is the closest active equivalent, with [Plus AI](/blog/plus-ai-powerpoint-maker-review) and [SlidesAI](/blog/slidesai-review) worth a look if you'd rather stay inside PowerPoint or Google Slides. For more options across the AI software space, see our [AI & software deals](/category/software) hub.

## FAQ

**Is Tome (tome.app) still available?**
No, not as far as we could verify. Both the tome.app homepage and its pricing page returned HTTP 404 errors as of September 2026, with no working signup or product to evaluate.

**Did Tome shut down, get acquired, or just go quiet?**
We couldn't find a clear, on-the-record confirmation of exactly what happened. The site returning 404 across multiple pages is consistent with a shutdown or discontinued domain, but we don't have a verified official statement pinning down the date or reason — treat any specific shutdown date you see elsewhere with caution unless it links back to an official company source.

**What was Tome's pricing when it was active?**
Tome offered a free tier historically, with paid plans layered on top, based on publicly available information from its active years. We can't verify current or final pricing figures since the site no longer serves a working pricing page.

title: CodiumAI (Qodo) Review 2026: Pricing, Features, Verdict
excerpt: CodiumAI is now Qodo, an AI code review platform. Here's what it costs, how the rebrand changed the product, and who should use it.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is CodiumAI (Qodo) worth it for code review and testing?

CodiumAI rebranded to Qodo in 2024 and has since shifted focus from an IDE test-generation plugin toward a full AI code review and governance platform. It's a solid pick for teams drowning in AI-generated pull requests, with a 14-day free trial and a $30/month starting tier, but solo developers who just want test generation may find its current scope heavier than needed.

### At a glance

| | Details |
|---|---|
| **Starting price** | $30/month (Pro Team, per workspace, up to 30 users) |
| **Free tier/trial** | 14-day free trial, no credit card required; free open-source program for qualifying projects |
| **Best for** | Engineering teams reviewing PRs written partly or fully by AI coding agents |
| **Standout feature** | Rules system that auto-discovers your team's coding standards from PR history and enforces them in every review |

Qodo is the AI code review company formerly known as CodiumAI. The tool you remember as a VS Code/JetBrains plugin for auto-generating unit tests still exists — it's now called Qodo Gen — but the product's marketing center of gravity has moved to Qodo Merge (formerly PR-Agent) and a broader "code review and governance" pitch aimed at engineering teams, not individual developers writing tests by hand.

## What CodiumAI (now Qodo) actually is

Qodo was founded as CodiumAI, built around the idea that AI-written code needs AI-assisted testing to be trustworthy. Its original product analyzed a function, inferred its intent, and generated unit tests to cover edge cases a developer might miss. That's still part of the offering, but Qodo's own site now describes the company primarily as an "AI code review and governance platform" — tracking the broader shift toward AI coding agents (Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) writing large volumes of code that still needs a quality gate.

The platform spans several surfaces built on a shared "Context Engine":

- **Qodo Gen** — the IDE extension (VS Code, JetBrains) for in-editor code review, test generation, and chat-based coding assistance.
- **Qodo Merge** — PR review automation for GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps, descended from the open-source PR-Agent project CodiumAI released.
- **Rules system** — scans PR history and existing code to infer team coding standards, then enforces them automatically.
- **Software Map** — a repository-relationship and risk-intelligence layer for governance and audit needs.

Unlike a general-purpose assistant such as GitHub Copilot or a full agentic IDE like [Cursor](/blog/cursor-ai-review), Qodo doesn't primarily position itself as a code *generator*. Its job is reviewing, testing, and gatekeeping code already written — increasingly by other AI tools — a category some vendors now call "AI code governance."

## Pricing

Pricing, free-tier limits, and feature availability were accurate as of this post's publish date and can change quickly in the AI coding-tools space — confirm current figures on [qodo.ai/pricing](https://www.qodo.ai/pricing/) before subscribing.

| Plan | Price | What's included |
|---|---|---|
| **Trial** | Free for 14 days | No credit card required; Qodo describes it as unlimited reviews and credits during the trial window, giving full access to core features |
| **Pro Team** | From $30/month, up to 30 users | Agentic PR code review, unlimited custom rules, Git + IDE integrations, pre-PR review skills, dashboard and analytics, standard support; billed monthly with no annual lock-in |
| **Enterprise** | Custom quote | Everything in Pro Team plus SSO/SAML, audit logs, a governance analytics dashboard, advanced self-learning, bring-your-own-LLM-key (BYOK) support, single-tenant SaaS or on-prem deployment, and a dedicated customer success manager |
| **Open source** | Free | Qualifying open-source projects get access through a dedicated program |

Two things worth flagging. Pro Team is priced in credit tiers rather than a flat seat price — rough usage bands run around 18, 36, or 144 reviews per month depending on the credit pack, and you can switch packs or add overage at the same per-credit rate with a spending cap you set. That's flexible, but your actual bill depends on review volume, not a fixed number. Separately, the free IDE extension (Qodo Gen) is free with optional premium features — a developer who only wants in-editor test generation may never need Pro Team at all.

## Core features that actually differentiate it

**Rules that write themselves from your PR history.** Instead of manually configuring a style guide, Qodo's Rules system scans past pull requests and existing code to infer what your team already enforces informally — naming conventions, error-handling patterns, architectural boundaries — then applies those rules automatically to new reviews. It's a genuinely different approach from a static `.eslintrc` file or fixed vendor checks.

**Full-repo, multi-repo context.** Qodo's review agents claim to pull context from the whole codebase rather than just the diff in front of them, meant to catch cross-file breaking changes a line-by-line review would miss. How well this holds up depends on repo size and how well-indexed the context engine is — worth testing on your own codebase before trusting it on a high-stakes merge.

**Agentic PR review, not just comments.** Beyond flagging issues, Qodo positions its review agents as capable of "1-click issue resolution" — proposing and applying fixes rather than only leaving a comment. Treat this as a productivity accelerant that still needs a human sign-off, not a replacement for one.

**Multi-surface consistency.** Qodo says the same Context Engine, rules, and review agents run whether you're in the IDE, reviewing a PR, or using the CLI, so a rule enforced in your editor should match what's flagged later at the PR stage — governance visibility (Software Map) adds risk intelligence and repository-relationship mapping on top, aimed squarely at engineering leaders rather than individual contributors.

## Who it's actually for

**Solo developers and small teams** who mainly want AI-assisted test generation and in-editor review can use Qodo Gen for free and may never need a paid plan — though it's worth weighing whether a bundled assistant like Copilot or Cursor already covers that need.

**Mid-size engineering teams (up to 30 people)** reviewing a steady volume of PRs, especially ones written by AI coding agents, are the target audience for Pro Team. The Rules system pays off once there's enough PR history to learn from.

**Regulated or enterprise organizations** needing SSO/SAML, audit logging, on-prem deployment, or BYOK will need the Enterprise tier — the sales process and price are custom.

**Open-source maintainers** can apply for free access, a meaningful cost-saver for community projects.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Rules system automatically infers team standards instead of manual config | Credit-based Pro Team pricing is harder to predict upfront |
| Works across IDE, PR, and CLI with a shared context engine | Docs now lean toward PR/team review; original test-generation use case is less prominent |
| 14-day free trial, no credit card, plus a genuinely free IDE tier | Multi-repo context claims are hard to verify without hands-on testing |
| SOC 2 Type II certification and zero data retention option | Enterprise pricing is quote-only, requiring a sales conversation |
| Broad IDE/Git support (VS Code, JetBrains, GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps) | Rebrand from CodiumAI has left some docs and naming inconsistent |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Qodo integrates with GitHub (cloud and Enterprise), GitLab (cloud and self-managed), Bitbucket (Cloud and Data Center), and Azure DevOps for PR-level review automation. On the editor side, it ships as extensions for VS Code and the JetBrains suite (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, CLion, RubyMine, PhpStorm) plus Visual Studio. A CLI-based "agentic toolbox" treats AI coding agents as managed, observable programs — useful if your team runs Copilot or Claude Code and wants a review layer downstream. Enterprise customers can bring their own LLM API keys (BYOK) instead of routing everything through Qodo's default models.

## Where it's a strong fit

Qodo makes the most sense for teams that have already adopted AI coding agents and are feeling the review bottleneck that creates — when code is generated faster than humans can review it line by line, a tool built to triage and enforce standards has a clear job. It also suits teams wanting review consistency without hand-writing a style guide, since Rules builds that from existing PR history. Organizations with compliance needs around AI-assisted development will find the Enterprise tier's SSO, audit logs, and on-prem options address concerns a lighter review bot wouldn't.

## Where to think twice

If you're a solo developer who just wants free, no-frills unit test generation, the free Qodo Gen extension may cover you — but if you wanted the deeper CodiumAI test-generation workflow from a couple of years ago, the product's center of gravity has moved toward PR review and governance. If your team needs a fully free tool beyond the trial and doesn't qualify for the open-source program, budget at least $30/month once the trial ends. And if you need independently benchmarked accuracy numbers before committing, you won't find them published by Qodo itself — close that gap with your own pilot, not vendor claims.

## The bottom line

Qodo (formerly CodiumAI) has repositioned itself sensibly for the moment: as AI agents generate more code, someone — or something — needs to review it at the same speed, and that's the problem Qodo Merge and its Rules system solve. The 14-day trial and a genuinely free IDE tier make it low-risk to test before paying anything, and credit-based Pro Team pricing at $30/month is accessible for small teams. The tradeoffs are a pricing model that takes some math to predict, and a product identity shifted enough that returning users should expect a different tool. For teams wrestling with AI-generated PR volume, it's worth the trial; for developers who just want free unit tests, the free tier alone may be enough.

## FAQ

**Is CodiumAI the same as Qodo?**
Yes. CodiumAI rebranded to Qodo in 2024, and its products — the IDE extension, PR review bot, and related tools — now carry the Qodo name (Qodo Gen, Qodo Merge). Some older documentation and search results still reference CodiumAI or the earlier PR-Agent project name.

**Is Qodo free to use?**
The IDE extension (Qodo Gen) for VS Code and JetBrains is free with optional premium features. The team-oriented PR review product offers a 14-day free trial with no credit card required, after which Pro Team pricing starts at $30/month. Qualifying open-source projects get free access through Qodo's dedicated program.

**What does Qodo actually review — code, tests, or both?**
Both, though its current focus is weighted toward pull request code review: detecting bugs, standards violations, and architecture-level issues across a diff. Test generation is still available through Qodo Gen, but it's no longer the primary marketing focus it was under the CodiumAI name.

**Does Qodo work with GitHub Copilot or Cursor?**
Qodo isn't a replacement for a coding assistant like [GitHub Copilot](/blog/github-copilot-review) or [Cursor](/blog/cursor-ai-review) — it sits downstream of whatever wrote the code and reviews it. Many teams run Qodo alongside a coding assistant rather than instead of one.

**How does Qodo handle code privacy and data retention?**
Qodo states it offers a zero data retention option and holds SOC 2 Type II certification for enterprise customers. The free IDE extension transmits code snippets to Qodo's servers for analysis, though users can adjust privacy settings. Enterprise customers can choose single-tenant SaaS or on-prem deployment and BYOK. Confirm current data-handling terms directly with Qodo before sending proprietary code through any tier.

**Is Qodo beginner-friendly?**
The free IDE extension is approachable — install it and it works inline in your editor. The Pro Team and Enterprise tiers take more setup to get value from.

**What are the main alternatives to Qodo?**
Alternatives include GitHub Copilot's code review features, Cursor's built-in review tooling, and other dedicated PR-review bots. The right choice depends on whether you need standalone review/governance or an all-in-one coding-plus-review assistant.
